stories.title: No immediate changes to military training after CFB Wainwright fire kills four soldiers: defence minister
stories.summary: Defence Minister David McGuinty said no changes have been made to military training procedures following a deadly fire at CFB Wainwright that killed four soldiers and sent 39 others to hospital during a training exercise on Saturday.
stories.author: Graham Richardson
stories.content:
Ottawa - Defence Minister David McGuinty said no changes have been made to military training procedures as of now, following a deadly fire at CFB Wainwright that killed four soldiers and sent 39 others to hospital during a training exercise on Saturday.

Ahead of a cabinet meeting on Parliament Hill on Tuesday, McGuinty was asked whether he had directed any changes to existing protocols. He told reporters that it was too soon to make adjustments before the facts are known.

“It’s very difficult to provide advice on the merits of how the protocols, which are in place, ought to be amended until we get the facts,” McGuinty said.

Pressed on why no interim measures have been introduced before formal inquiries are completed, McGuinty said decisions about training adjustments rest with Canadian Armed Forces officials.

“Listen, I’m going to leave it right now to the chief of defence, the commander of the army and the professionals who conduct these processes, to take the time they need to evaluate,” McGuinty said. “This happened 48 hours ago.”

Sgt. Morgan Wong and Privates Shaun Farrell, Aidan Goulding and Hayden Lykkemark were killed during the training exercise. The soldiers, who served with Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, were preparing to deploy to Latvia next year.

Military lawyer and former soldier Col. Michel Drapeau told CTV News Monday, the military should not investigate itself given the scale of the tragedy.

Drapeau called for a public coroner’s inquest instead.

“Let there be an open audience. People can attend. People can listen and people can testify,” said Drapeau. “The purpose of this is to prevent recurrence, to prevent (future) fatalities. We need to get to the bottom of it, not assign blame.”

McGuinty said the investigations that are underway will be independent and transparent.

“Look, we’re going to let the processes that have been engaged move forward. These are independent. We are independent from these. There are three (independent investigations). There is the RCMP working with the military police on a formal investigation. There is the fire marshal that will also examine the situation independently and of course, there is the board of inquiry,” McGuinty said.

Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan told CTV’s Power Play that she intends to make the military’s board of inquiry into the tragedy public.

“The board of inquiry is the mechanism that we have to have a broader range of visibility on what happened and the findings will be released publicly. That is my intention,” Carignan said.

stories.title: Trump jokingly says Canada can keep hockey and O Canada in his latest '51st state' offer
stories.summary: President Donald Trump said that while he liked Canada's national anthem, the country has been "screwing" the United States.
stories.author: National Post Staff
stories.content:
Canada

'Canada's been ripping us off for so many years. People got used to it. I didn't get used to it. We got it under control'

U.S. President Donald Trump yells during a campaign rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas, a suburb of Wichita, ON October 19, 2026.Photo by Kent Nishimura /AFP via Getty Images

U.S. President Donald Trump made an offer to Canada at a rally in Kansas on Monday, saying that he would let the country keep its national anthem and hockey if it became the 51st state.

The comments were made about half way through his speech in Park City, where he was supporting U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall in the midterm election. Trump mentioned how car plants were thriving in the United States, but were leaving Mexico and Canada.

“They’re leaving O Canada,” he said, in reference to the beginning of the country’s national anthem. “Canada’s been ripping us off for so many years. People got used to it. I didn’t get used to it. We got it under control.”

He questioned why Americans would even need Canadian-made cars, but added: “I do like their national anthem.”

“And I promise them if they become a 51st state…I said, ‘I will let you keep ice hockey and I will let you keep your O Canada national anthem,'” he said. “They can have it as a state anthem.”

He followed up his offer by adding that he was “only kidding” and “having a good time.”

“But they have been screwing us,” he said, adding that now Canada wants to make a deal. The U.S. does very little business with Canada, while the northern country does 95 per cent of business with Americans, he said. The U.S. loses $90 billion a year because of this, according to Trump.

“I would say that’s a little too much for the privilege of having people live through very cold weather,” he said.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has not specifically addressed Trump’s claim that Canada is the cause of a $90 billion deficit in the U.S. However, Canadian-founded research institute Centre for Future Work published an article earlier this month, debunking some of Trump’s “big lies about Canada.”

“The true deficit for 2025, based on official U.S. government data, was $27 billion. That consisted of a $55 billion deficit on merchandise, partly offset by a $28 billion U.S. surplus on services,” the post said.

“That’s just 3 per cent of the massive two-way $900 billion bilateral flow. America’s trade with Canada is far more balanced than with the rest of the world – adding to the mystery of why Canada is suddenly Public Enemy Number One.”

A child wearing a Donald Trump mask is seen during a campaign rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas, a suburb of Wichita, ON October 19, 2026.Photo by Kent Nishimura /AFP via Getty Images

Trump made reference to the border between the two countries, saying it was a straight line drawn by “some guy with a ruler” who said, “Let those people have that cold air.”

Later in the speech, Trump walked back threats he previously made against Canadian jet manufacturer Bombardier.

“I’m going to be helping a certain air company get themselves straightened away,” he said.

He said he viewed Bombardier as a Canadian company, but since they have a presence in Kansas “we’re not hurting them.” According to Reuters, Bombardier employs around 1,500 people in Wichita.

“We’ll take care of those people,” said Trump.

content_blocks.text: 'Canada's been ripping us off for so many years. People got used to it. I didn't get used to it. We got it under control'

U.S. President Donald Trump yells during a campaign rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas, a suburb of Wichita, ON October 19, 2026.Photo by Kent Nishimura /AFP via Getty Images
U.S. President Donald Trump made an offer to Canada at a rally in Kansas on Monday, saying that he would let the country keep its national anthem and hockey if it became the 51st state.

The comments were made about half way through his speech in Park City, where he was supporting U.S. Sen. Roger Marshall in the midterm election. Trump mentioned how car plants were thriving in the United States, but were leaving Mexico and Canada.

“They’re leaving O Canada,” he said, in reference to the beginning of the country’s national anthem. “Canada’s been ripping us off for so many years. People got used to it. I didn’t get used to it. We got it under control.”
He questioned why Americans would even need Canadian-made cars, but added: “I do like their national anthem.”

“And I promise them if they become a 51st state…I said, ‘I will let you keep ice hockey and I will let you keep your O Canada national anthem,'” he said. “They can have it as a state anthem.”
He followed up his offer by adding that he was “only kidding” and “having a good time.”

“But they have been screwing us,” he said, adding that now Canada wants to make a deal. The U.S. does very little business with Canada, while the northern country does 95 per cent of business with Americans, he said. The U.S. loses $90 billion a year because of this, according to Trump.
“I would say that’s a little too much for the privilege of having people live through very cold weather,” he said.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has not specifically addressed Trump’s claim that Canada is the cause of a $90 billion deficit in the U.S. However, Canadian-founded research institute Centre for Future Work published an article earlier this month, debunking some of Trump’s “big lies about Canada.”

“The true deficit for 2025, based on official U.S. government data, was $27 billion. That consisted of a $55 billion deficit on merchandise, partly offset by a $28 billion U.S. surplus on services,” the post said.

“That’s just 3 per cent of the massive two-way $900 billion bilateral flow. America’s trade with Canada is far more balanced than with the rest of the world – adding to the mystery of why Canada is suddenly Public Enemy Number One.”

A child wearing a Donald Trump mask is seen during a campaign rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas, a suburb of Wichita, ON October 19, 2026.Photo by Kent Nishimura /AFP via Getty Images
Trump made reference to the border between the two countries, saying it was a straight line drawn by “some guy with a ruler” who said, “Let those people have that cold air.”
Later in the speech, Trump walked back threats he previously made against Canadian jet manufacturer Bombardier.
“I’m going to be helping a certain air company get themselves straightened away,” he said.
He said he viewed Bombardier as a Canadian company, but since they have a presence in Kansas “we’re not hurting them.” According to Reuters, Bombardier employs around 1,500 people in Wichita.
“We’ll take care of those people,” said Trump.

stories.title: Trump walks back threat to ban Bombardier sales in U.S.
stories.summary: Montreal - U.S. President Donald Trump is backing down on a threat to ban Bombardier Inc. plane sales in the United States.
stories.author: Christopher Reynolds The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Trump said Monday night in Wichita, Kan., that he’s changed his view of the Quebec-based business jet maker as a purely Canadian company and does not want to follow through on “hurting” it, given its presence in the city, where the company employs 1,500 workers.

Wichita serves as the seat of its defence division, and is one of several states where Bombardier counts about 3,500 American employees in total.

Article continues below

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Kansas, where farmers have felt the cost of the Iran war in higher diesel prices, has turned into a political battleground as Republicans and Democrats fight for control of the typically red state ahead of next month’s midterm elections.

Last month, Trump suggested he would bar Bombardier’s business in the United States unless it moved its operations there, despite the harm experts said such a move would inflict on American workers.

Bombardier shares rose $9.10 or about three per cent to $320.57 by midday Tuesday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

stories.title: Canadian dollar hits four-week high as market cheers Alberta remain vote
stories.summary: Strategist: ‘The Alberta vote could not have ⁠gone better from a market perspective’
stories.author: Fergal Smith
stories.content:
The Canadian dollar strengthened to a four-week ​high against its U.S. counterpart ‌on Tuesday, boosted by a narrower gap between Canadian and U.S. interest rates and after Alberta voted by a large majority to remain part ⁠of ​Canada

The loonie was trading 0.5 per cent higher at 1.4045 per U.S. dollar, or 71.20 U.S. cents, after touching its strongest intraday level since September 22 at 1.4033. Among Group of ​10 currencies, only sterling posted a bigger ‌gain.

“The Canadian discount to the US has fallen sharply in the last few days which has helped fuel this correction in the Canadian dollar,” said Marc Chandler, chief market strategist at Bannockburn Capital Markets.

The ‌gap between ​Canada’s 2-year yield ‌and the U.S. equivalent has narrowed to 146 basis points ​from about 160 basis points earlier this ⁠month as investors raised bets on a Bank ⁠of Canada interest rate hike next week.

Swap market data indicates an ​80-per-cent chance the BoC raises its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.50 per cent on October 28. It follows hawkish comments by Governor Tiff Macklem on Saturday and evidence on Monday of rising long-term inflation expectations.

The ⁠remain side won 76 per cent of tallied votes in Alberta’s first-ever referendum on separation, handing Prime Minister Mark Carney a much-needed win as he attempts to unify the country amid a trade war with the U.S..

“The Alberta vote could not have ⁠gone better from a market perspective,” Chandler ​said. “This is the least disruptive alternative because it preserves the status ⁠quo.”

The price of oil, one of Canada’s major exports, pulled back from its ‌highest level since April as traders priced in Houthi attacks on Saudi ​infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf. U.S. crude oil futures were trading 0.9 per cent lower at US$102.75 a barrel.

Canadian government bond yields moved lower across ​the curve, with the 10-year down 6.8 basis points at 3.894 per cent.

stories.title: Health care, affordability and the economy are the priorities in N.B. throne speech
stories.summary: Fredericton - Health care and new export markets outside the U.S. are among the priorities in the New Brunswick government’s throne speech.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Lt.-Gov. Louise Imbeault read the speech on behalf of the government as the legislature opened in Fredericton today.

It says health care, affordability and growing the economy are priority areas for the coming year.

Article continues below

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

The speech says the opening of 30 new collaborative care clinics are ahead of schedule and will be completed by the end of 2027.

The province says it will name a mental health advocate and will launch a health and long-term care workforce strategy.

It’s also creating a diversification plan to find high-potential markets outside the U.S. and providing more money for new housing infrastructure.

“We are focused on delivering results, like improving access to health care close to home and making life more affordable,” Premier Susan Holt said in a statement.

stories.title: Fire burned for hours before CFB Wainwright tragedy: satellite data
stories.summary: Training continued at CFB Wainwright on Saturday even though a fire had been burning on the base since noon and forecasts warned of high winds and an approaching cold front.
stories.author: Ashleigh Stewart
stories.content:
The military let training continue at CFB Wainwright on Saturday even though a fire had been burning on the base since noon and forecasts had already warned of high winds, dry conditions and an approaching cold front.

Hours later, a grass fire overtook soldiers during a live-fire exercise at the base, about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, killing four members of the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) and injuring 39, 19 of them critically.

The military says a sudden shift in wind turned a fire it believed was contained into a deadly one.

“The fire was a kilometre away when the wind shifted. It is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds,” said Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division.

But satellite imagery reviewed by Global News and weather records reveal warning signs around four hours before the blaze expanded.

Forecasters had also flagged unusually powerful winds days earlier.

Satellite data from Nasa’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (Firms) detected 59 possible fire hotspots across an area roughly 1.6 kilometres wide at CFB Wainwright at approximately 12:20 p.m. Saturday. Global News could not independently confirm whether it was the same fire that turned fatal.

Mike Flannigan, a wildfire researcher at Thompson Rivers University, said the data definitively showed at least one fire burning on the base roughly four hours before the tragedy, although he could not rule out multiple fires.

To be detectable by satellite, he said, it likely started “at least half an hour before that, maybe even hours before that.”

The detections do not show the fire’s size, when it began, or whether the blaze that later turned deadly was the one detected.

The Office of the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal declined to answer questions from Global News about the event, as the investigation is ongoing and requires co-operation from multiple agencies.

As the afternoon wore on, strong-wind forecasts escalated into Environment Canada warnings, while warm, dry conditions and an approaching cold front created what wildfire experts call a potentially lethal combination.

“This was just a confluence of really extreme conditions that all played out at the exact moment when they had an active fire in the area,” says Jen Beverly, an associate professor of wildland fire at the University of Alberta.

Rutland said at a press conference Sunday that a fire burned on the base “for several hours,” but training continued “for a certain amount of time” because commanders believed the fire was contained.

“The weather for the majority of the day was well within standard procedures, well below 50 kilometres,” he added. “This was uncommon, rapid, and I certainly hadn’t seen anything like it. Certainly we train in all types of conditions because you don’t know where you’re going to operate.”

Three former senior military officers interviewed by Global News said training exercises often continue while a fire burns nearby, provided the base’s Range Control deems it safe. They also said strong winds alone wouldn’t necessarily be grounds to suspend training.

The Wainwright area is consistently windy, partly because of its exposed prairie landscape. Environment Canada records from nearby Lloydminster – the closest available long-term climate data – show prevailing westerly winds for most of the year, with stronger average winds outside the summer months.

But more than a dozen residents interviewed by Global News described the gusts as stronger than anything they’d ever experienced. The same winds tore across the province before they reached Wainwright, kicking up dust storms, damaging property and even pushing semi-trailer trucks off the highway.

“I was outside, and it almost blew me away. I had to seek shelter in the building as the wind went through,” says Roger Holmes, editor of the town’s Star Edge newspaper.

“I’ve lived in this town for over 30 years, and I’ve never seen a wind storm like that come through.”

Dry, blustery conditions had already gripped the Wainwright area in the days leading up to the deadly blaze.

Environment Canada issued separate wind warnings for the region Wednesday, which remained in effect into early Thursday. The Weather Network and news outlets, including Global News, forecast a cold front crossing Alberta on Saturday with powerful winds.

“It was well advertised days in advance. Computer models knew there would be winds gusting 80 to 100 kilometres an hour,” said Global News meteorologist Anthony Farnell.

The area was also in an extended dry spell.

Weather records show Wainwright had received just 3.5 millimetres of rain this October, with no significant rainfall. The last substantial rainfall was on Sept. 7, when approximately 23.5 millimetres fell, roughly six weeks earlier.

By Saturday, wildfire danger across much of southern Alberta, including Wainwright, was rated “extreme,” according to provincial data and the Canadian Wildland Fire Information System.

That appears to contradict an internal memo issued Sunday by the military’s Strategic Joint Staff (SJS), which rated the fire risk as low.

It is unclear whether the memo referred to broader fire-weather conditions or the risk posed by the exercise.

Nasa satellite data show possible fire activity at CFB Wainwright at two different times Saturday.

The first detections came at 12:17 p.m., when Nasa’s Landsat 8 satellite identified 59 possible fire hotspots across an area roughly 1.6 kilometres wide.

More than two and a half hours later, at 2:49 p.m., a second satellite system, Viirs, detected additional hotspots in the area.

Landsat can detect smaller fires with greater precision, while Viirs provides more frequent observations. The timestamps reflect when the satellites passed over the area, rather than when the fires began.

The detections do not establish the size of the fire, exactly when it began or whether it was the same blaze that later turned deadly.

Wildfire researcher Mike Flannigan said the fire likely started “at least half an hour before that, maybe even hours before that,” for satellites to detect it.

Within an hour, powerful winds were sweeping through the Edmonton region, where the international airport reportedly recorded a gust of 117 kilometres an hour around 1 p.m. Residents described massive dust clouds, property damage and power outages.

Around the same time in Wainwright, conditions were comparatively calm, with temperatures hovering around a balmy 20 C and winds moving at approximately 15 kilometres an hour.

But at 2:15 p.m., Environment Canada issued a wind warning for the Lloydminster region, which includes Wainwright, forecasting gusts of up to 100 kilometres an hour.

By 3 p.m., weather records show, temperatures at the base had climbed above 23 C — before plunging more than 10 degrees in an hour.

Relative humidity was also falling, creating what fire scientists call “crossover fire conditions”, when the temperature in degrees Celsius exceeds the relative humidity percentage.

A cold front can also swing the wind abruptly, dramatically changing how a fire spreads, she explained.

“It means that the flank or side of your fire can suddenly become the head of the fire.”

Around 3 p.m., Environment Canada extended its wind warning in a separate alert, with forecasters expecting gusts up to 90 kilometres an hour. But strong winds alone would not necessarily halt military training, said retired Col. Ryan Jurkowski, director of the Conference of Defence Associations.

“In my 30 years of training with the Canadian Armed Forces for infantry training, wind has never been a factor.”

He said he’d trained with higher gusts, and that inclement weather “adds to the value of the training.”

By 4 p.m., Environment Canada data showed gusts at CFB Wainwright reaching 48 kilometres an hour. The agency also recorded an 82-kilometre-an-hour gust that day, though its public data does not say when. Environment Canada did not respond to a request for clarification.

“That wind was so strong, and it was blowing me over trying to carry my baby and the cats,” says Madison Keller, who lives on the edge of the military base.

Her father called to warn her about an approaching fire, she said, but within moments, it was upon her. She scrambled to gather her one-year-old baby, pets and a bag of essentials and fled.

“It just came out of nowhere. No noise, besides the wind. That’s all we heard was wind.”

As the winds shifted, Rutland said, the once-contained fire became a fast-moving inferno.

“I spoke to my commander on the ground last night and this morning, and he said within 30 seconds to a minute, they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them.”

Wildfire experts say that kind of speed would be extraordinary.

Flannigan said grass fires typically spread at about one-tenth the speed of the wind, while Beverly says that even under extreme conditions, Canada’s fire-behaviour prediction system might forecast a grass fire spreading at around 20 kilometres an hour.

But Rutland’s account suggests the Wainwright fire was moving between 60 and 120 kilometres an hour — several times faster than those estimates.

“If the fire was spreading at the rate that they described, it’s not impossible, but it would be on record as the fastest moving fire ever recorded in Canada,” says Beverly, adding that such speeds have been recorded in rural Australia grass fires and during the 2023 Hawaii wildfires.

Brian MacDonald, who advised then-defence minister Peter MacKay in 2008, said it was “fairly routine” for military exercises to continue even when a fire was burning nearby, provided it was considered safe.

“There’s usually a detailed meteorological report that’s provided, but of course those are often imperfect, and the imperative is to continue on with the mission,” he said.

Locals confirmed the base was known for fires.

Wainwright resident Annette Nesbitt said plumes of smoke rising above the base rarely caused alarm.

“We say that the base was on fire again, but it is always on fire… you don’t think anything of it.”

She did not hear an explosion, as has been widely reported. Neither did several other residents Global News interviewed. Some heard loud “booms,” but said that’s common near the base. “We’re used to hearing the guns, you don’t think anything of it,” Nesbitt said.

“You go to sleep hearing that sound, and the joke is – if something serious happened, how long would it take us to realize?”

This isn’t the first time a fire on an Alberta military base has spread out of control.

In September 2017, a grass fire broke out as soldiers at CFB Suffield were destroying an unexploded artillery shell. Fuelled by dry conditions and strong winds, it scorched across roughly 36,000 hectares, destroyed a ranch, killed more than 160 cattle and forced dozens of residents to evacuate.

The military subsequently pledged to improve its firefighting and fire-prevention procedures.

What sparked the deadly Wainwright fire remains unanswered, with politicians, community leaders and military officials largely unwilling to speculate while the investigation continues.

Rutland offered few details about the possible cause, other than ruling out any involvement of oil and gas infrastructure or “outside interference.”

“There was a multitude of ordnance moving through the Wainwright training area yesterday: grenade launcher, grenades, small arms, ammunition. Quite frankly, it could have been any of that or none of it,” he said.

But beyond what ignited the flames, the 50 investigators deployed to Wainwright face another question: whether the deaths and injuries could have been avoided.

Retired Canadian Armed Forces Maj.-Gen. Denis Thompson cautioned against drawing conclusions before the investigation is complete, but said one question remains central.

“The real question here is, was this a preventable accident or incident? Or was it non-preventable?”

Hours later, a grass fire overtook soldiers during a live-fire exercise at the base, about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, killing four members of the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) and injuring 39, 19 of them critically.
The military says a sudden shift in wind turned a fire it believed was contained into a deadly one.
“The fire was a kilometre away when the wind shifted. It is not normal for a fire to move a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds,” said Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division.
But satellite imagery reviewed by Global News and weather records reveal warning signs around four hours before the blaze expanded.
Forecasters had also flagged unusually powerful winds days earlier.

Satellite data from Nasa’s Fire Information for Resource Management System (Firms) detected 59 possible fire hotspots across an area roughly 1.6 kilometres wide at CFB Wainwright at approximately 12:20 p.m. Saturday. Global News could not independently confirm whether it was the same fire that turned fatal.

Mike Flannigan, a wildfire researcher at Thompson Rivers University, said the data definitively showed at least one fire burning on the base roughly four hours before the tragedy, although he could not rule out multiple fires.
To be detectable by satellite, he said, it likely started “at least half an hour before that, maybe even hours before that.”
The detections do not show the fire’s size, when it began, or whether the blaze that later turned deadly was the one detected.
The Office of the Canadian Forces Provost Marshal declined to answer questions from Global News about the event, as the investigation is ongoing and requires co-operation from multiple agencies.

As the afternoon wore on, strong-wind forecasts escalated into Environment Canada warnings, while warm, dry conditions and an approaching cold front created what wildfire experts call a potentially lethal combination.

“This was just a confluence of really extreme conditions that all played out at the exact moment when they had an active fire in the area,” says Jen Beverly, an associate professor of wildland fire at the University of Alberta.
Rutland said at a press conference Sunday that a fire burned on the base “for several hours,” but training continued “for a certain amount of time” because commanders believed the fire was contained.

“The weather for the majority of the day was well within standard procedures, well below 50 kilometres,” he added. “This was uncommon, rapid, and I certainly hadn’t seen anything like it. Certainly we train in all types of conditions because you don’t know where you’re going to operate.”

Three former senior military officers interviewed by Global News said training exercises often continue while a fire burns nearby, provided the base’s Range Control deems it safe. They also said strong winds alone wouldn’t necessarily be grounds to suspend training.

The Wainwright area is consistently windy, partly because of its exposed prairie landscape. Environment Canada records from nearby Lloydminster – the closest available long-term climate data – show prevailing westerly winds for most of the year, with stronger average winds outside the summer months.

The area was also in an extended dry spell.

By Saturday, wildfire danger across much of southern Alberta, including Wainwright, was rated “extreme,” according to provincial data and the Canadian Wildland Fire Information System.

Nasa satellite data show possible fire activity at CFB Wainwright at two different times Saturday.

Within an hour, powerful winds were sweeping through the Edmonton region, where the international airport reportedly recorded a gust of 117 kilometres an hour around 1 p.m. Residents described massive dust clouds, property damage and power outages.

By 3 p.m., weather records show, temperatures at the base had climbed above 23 C — before plunging more than 10 degrees in an hour.
Relative humidity was also falling, creating what fire scientists call “crossover fire conditions”, when the temperature in degrees Celsius exceeds the relative humidity percentage.
A cold front can also swing the wind abruptly, dramatically changing how a fire spreads, she explained.
“It means that the flank or side of your fire can suddenly become the head of the fire.”

stories.title: 'Is this a joke?': Cruise ship heading for the Bahamas rerouted to Nova Scotia instead
stories.summary: About 5,000 passengers aboard a Royal Caribbean cruise ship expecting to visit the Bahamas Tuesday will instead make port in Halifax, N.S.
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A cruise ship carrying 5,000 passengers that embarked from New Jersey is heading to Nova Scotia, not Nassau as they thought, because of heavy weather at sea.

Royal Caribbean’s Oasis of the Seas left Cape Liberty, N.J., ON Sunday, diverting course from its original itinerary of Florida, then the Bahamas, to sail instead for Halifax, where passengers will spend 24 hours of their seven-day cruise. It’s not clear where the ship will go next, but it’s about a three-day sail to the Bahamas from Nova Scotia and the cruise is due back on Sunday.

“The funny thing is I was on board Vision of the Seas in September, and it was supposed to go to Canada, but it was rerouted to the Caribbean because of a storm and now I have the opposite happening,” passenger Debra DelCamp wrote in a message to the National Post.

“I don’t think it’s a big deal; It’s cruise life. For first-time cruisers, I can understand it being confusing or upsetting, but for regulars it’s just cruising.”

The saddest story she has heard about the itinerary swap was from a family aboard the Oasis of the Seas who had planned to scatter their late father’s ashes while the 362-metre-long cruise ship was in the Bahamas.

“It was to celebrate their father’s last trip on Oasis that actually went to Nassau,” DelCamp said. “So, they were very sad to be releasing ashes in Canada.”

Another passenger, David Hess of Ephrata, Penn., heard about the itinerary swap after boarding Oasis of the Seas.

“We mostly packed summer clothes, tank tops, booty shorts,” Hess wrote on social media. “My question is: is it as warm in Canada as the Bahamas?”

Daisy Mungin from Greenville, S.C., responded: “I’m on the boat with you,” she said. “It’s freezing.”

Passenger Nicole Borowicz-Byler seemed taken aback by the destination swap.

“Instead of the Bahamas it now says we’re going to Canada,” she wrote on social media. “Is this a joke?”

Passenger Mikayla Iverson wrote that she’d driven eight hours to board the ship. “Now I’ve gotta go buy something warm to wear.”

Cruise ships are regular visitors to the Port of Halifax, which saw 184 of them stop in the N.S. capital last year, carrying a total of about 357,000 passengers.

The accidental N.S. tourists, who are slated to land in the province Tuesday evening just before sunset, will have lots on offer once they get to Halifax, according to Giacomo Bruno, director of sales and marketing with Ambassatours Gray Line, which organizes outings for visiting cruise ships.

“We’re offering the Harbour Hopper Tour (#1 boat tour in Halifax); tours to Georges Island National Historic Site, bus tour to Peggy’s Cove, a Waterfront Walking Tour and trips to McNabs Island,” Bruno said in an email.

“If folks didn’t pack for the cold, we have a charming shop on the waterfront where we sell East Coast Lifestyle … Tall Ship Silva hoodies and full zip sweatshirts, and Harbour Hopper Tours sweaters.”

Halifax Mayor Andy Fillmore was practically effusive about this week’s unplanned stop for the sun-seeking cruisers aboard Oasis of the Seas.

“To the 5,000 visitors who packed their swimsuits for the Bahamas but woke up headed for Nova Scotia — welcome to Halifax!” Fillmore said in an email to the National Post.

“You May be come-from-aways, but we’re delighted you’re here.”

The ship is slated to arrive Tuesday evening and stay in Halifax for most of Wednesday. The weather forecast calls for cloudy skies both days and highs between 13 C and 15 C while the Oasis of the Seas is in port. Meanwhile, the temperature in sunny Nassau Tuesday was 28 C.

“We can’t promise you tropical temperatures, but we can promise you a warm welcome — with zero chance of sunburn,” Fillmore said.

“So, trade the flip-flops for Blundstones, and the palm trees for pine trees. Grab a toque, find a good bowl of seafood chowder, and explore our wonderful local restaurants, pubs, and shops. paragraphs: A cruise ship carrying 5,000 passengers that embarked from New Jersey is heading to Nova Scotia, not Nassau as they thought, because of heavy weather at sea.

Royal Caribbean’s Oasis of the Seas left Cape Liberty, N.J., ON Sunday, diverting course from its original itinerary of Florida, then the Bahamas, to sail instead for Halifax, where passengers will spend 24 hours of their seven-day cruise. It’s not clear where the ship will go next, but it’s about a three-day sail to the Bahamas from Nova Scotia and the cruise is due back on Sunday.

“The funny thing is I was on board Vision of the Seas in September, and it was supposed to go to Canada, but it was rerouted to the Caribbean because of a storm and now I have the opposite happening,” passenger Debra DelCamp wrote in a message to the National Post.
“I don’t think it’s a big deal; It’s cruise life. For first-time cruisers, I can understand it being confusing or upsetting, but for regulars it’s just cruising.”

The saddest story she has heard about the itinerary swap was from a family aboard the Oasis of the Seas who had planned to scatter their late father’s ashes while the 362-metre-long cruise ship was in the Bahamas.
“It was to celebrate their father’s last trip on Oasis that actually went to Nassau,” DelCamp said. “So, they were very sad to be releasing ashes in Canada.”
Another passenger, David Hess of Ephrata, Penn., heard about the itinerary swap after boarding Oasis of the Seas.
“We mostly packed summer clothes, tank tops, booty shorts,” Hess wrote on social media. “My question is: is it as warm in Canada as the Bahamas?”
Daisy Mungin from Greenville, S.C., responded: “I’m on the boat with you,” she said. “It’s freezing.”
Passenger Nicole Borowicz-Byler seemed taken aback by the destination swap.
“Instead of the Bahamas it now says we’re going to Canada,” she wrote on social media. “Is this a joke?”
Passenger Mikayla Iverson wrote that she’d driven eight hours to board the ship. “Now I’ve gotta go buy something warm to wear.”
Cruise ships are regular visitors to the Port of Halifax, which saw 184 of them stop in the N.S. capital last year, carrying a total of about 357,000 passengers.

The accidental N.S. tourists, who are slated to land in the province Tuesday evening just before sunset, will have lots on offer once they get to Halifax, according to Giacomo Bruno, director of sales and marketing with Ambassatours Gray Line, which organizes outings for visiting cruise ships.

“We’re offering the Harbour Hopper Tour (#1 boat tour in Halifax); tours to Georges Island National Historic Site, bus tour to Peggy’s Cove, a Waterfront Walking Tour and trips to McNabs Island,” Bruno said in an email.

“If folks didn’t pack for the cold, we have a charming shop on the waterfront where we sell East Coast Lifestyle … Tall Ship Silva hoodies and full zip sweatshirts, and Harbour Hopper Tours sweaters.”
Halifax Mayor Andy Fillmore was practically effusive about this week’s unplanned stop for the sun-seeking cruisers aboard Oasis of the Seas.
“To the 5,000 visitors who packed their swimsuits for the Bahamas but woke up headed for Nova Scotia — welcome to Halifax!” Fillmore said in an email to the National Post.
“You May be come-from-aways, but we’re delighted you’re here.”

The ship is slated to arrive Tuesday evening and stay in Halifax for most of Wednesday. The weather forecast calls for cloudy skies both days and highs between 13 C and 15 C while the Oasis of the Seas is in port. Meanwhile, the temperature in sunny Nassau Tuesday was 28 C.
“We can’t promise you tropical temperatures, but we can promise you a warm welcome — with zero chance of sunburn,” Fillmore said.

“So, trade the flip-flops for Blundstones, and the palm trees for pine trees. Grab a toque, find a good bowl of seafood chowder, and explore our wonderful local restaurants, pubs, and shops. And tell them the Mayor sent you! Who knows — you might just discover that the best part of your Caribbean cruise was Canada.”

stories.title: Alberta separatists vow to fight on after referendum loss: 'Tonight isn't the finish line'
stories.summary: Alberta separatists advocates Mitch Sylvestre , Jeffrey Rath, Keith Wilson and others aren't giving up their fight following a referendum loss.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Canada

'We have awakened something in this province, and that spirit isn't going anywhere,' Alberta Prosperity Project CEO Mitch Sylvestre told supporters at a watch party

Alberta Prosperity Project CEO Mitch Sylvestre, right, speaks with a supporter during a referendum watch party in downtown Edmonton. When it started looking like his side would lose on the separatism question, he said he was "not happy."Photo by Megan Albu /AFP via Getty Images

The results of Monday’s Alberta referendum question on separation from Canada won’t be official for more than a week, but all indications are that the separatist movement was handed a sound defeat.

As the earliest numbers showed about 76 per cent in favour of remaining in Confederation, a figure that hasn’t changed much as of 10 a.m. MT, separatist leader Jeffrey Rath expressed optimism about the political movement and re-emphasized the need to take control of the United Conservative Party of Alberta from Premier Danielle Smith, whom he said conspired with “fake news” and the “entire Canadian political establishment” to campaign against independence.

“It’s time to have a serious discussion as to whether or not a supermajority of the (UCP) want to continue to be led by a federalist who’s in bed with Naheed Nenshi, Mark Carney, Rachel Notley, and the rest of the socialists and globalists that have literally been ruining this province and ruining this country,” Rath told Global News late Monday night at a downtown Edmonton pizza parlour.

During his interview, the self-described “constitutional lawyer” and co-founder of the Alberta Prosperity Project (APP) estimated that, by night’s end, anywhere from 600,000 to 700,000 people will have voted in favour of starting the formal process of Alberta seceding from Canada. Elections Alberta, with 78 per cent of polls reported, counted 458,923 as of 10 a.m. Official results are due on Thursday, Oct. 29.

Rath said supporters of independence won’t be swayed from their cause.

“We roll up our sleeves and we work harder because that’s who we are as people,” he said.

As for Smith, she said on Xthat she was “very pleased” with the initial results on the separation question and promised to address the province at 6:45 p.m. local time on Tuesday, “to discuss the results of all referendum questions for which results are available, and where our province goes from here.”

With roughly 40% of polls reporting, nearly one in four votes cast have gone to Option 2. Many will see tonight as a catastrophic setback for Alberta’s independence movement. I don’t. What we just witnessed was a grassroots movement stand against the combined weight of… pic.twitter.com/ghdixy1AzT — Rise Of Alberta (@RiseOfAlberta) October 20, 2026

During a short but passionate concession speech shared by The Orchard late Monday night, APP co-founder and CEO Mitch Sylvestre said “Alberta has changed” and “there is no going back.”

“They can underestimate us. They can throw every obstacle imaginable in our way, and believe me, they have, but they cannot stop what has already started. Tonight isn’t the finish line,” he said.

“It’s another chapter in something much bigger than any one of us. We have awakened something in this province, and that spirit isn’t going anywhere.”

Sylvestre also addressed UCP co-founder and former Alberta premier Jason Kenny, a staunch opponent of the separatist movement, who last week said supporters of separatism were facing a post-referendum reckoning.

“We certainly don’t need lectures from those who have already underestimated us once before,” Sylvestre said.

The true reckoning, he said, is a group of Albertans that are “organized, integrated, and not putting up with the corruption and the failure.”

He told the BBChe was “not happy” about the results and the CBCthat he’s “never been a good loser.”

After Kenny posted on X Monday that secession talk only pushed election-deciding “mainstream centre-right voters” away from conservative parties towards the NDP, Republican Party of Alberta leader Cameron Davies, another fierce separatism advocate, countered that they’re gravitating because conservatives are “acting and governing like liberal lite.”

“Fake conservatives are kryptonite for any real conservative movement,” he wrote.

This is the consequence of “Conservatives” acting and governing like liberal lite. Fake conservatives are kryptonite for any real conservative movement. Fixed it for ya bubba. https://t.co/60u8V1BuNc — Cameron Davies (@Realcamdavies) October 20, 2026

In Calgary, Let Alberta Decide founder Keith Wilson, formerly of the 2022 Freedom Convoy, noted that at least a quarter “feel that Alberta needs to be treated better, that Alberta can do better.”

“So tonight concludes a campaign, but the conversation about Alberta’s future in Canada and our place in Canada and our role in Canada will continue,” he said in a video shared on X.

David Parker, founder of conservative group Take Back Alberta, called Monday’s result “bleak.”

“Independence feels far away and we should not pretend this was not a defeat,” he wrote on X,“however, it changes nothing about the reality of the circumstances Albertans find themselves in.”

Cory Morgan, founder of Pathway to Independence, said it’s not the Ucp’s role to become a separatist party. He said a single advocacy group should lead the effort and that the recent campaign was hurt by not collectively addressing voters.

“We had six or seven different groups speaking throughout the campaign. You don’t run a general election that way; it would just be a dog’s breakfast,” he said.

Meanwhile, as the results were taking shape, pro-separation MLA Jason Stephan (Red Deer-South), announced on X that he would not seek re-election in next year’s provincial general election.

“The status quo is not the right way for Albertans. Empty words and platitudes do not make it otherwise,” he wrote in an open letter. “Some say they want Unity, but their actions say otherwise. Does fearmongering, name calling labelling, and gaslighting produce unity?”

Dear Friends, The Alberta provincial election will be in one year. By such time, I will have served as MLA for over 8 years and I will not be seeking re-election. Thank you to for supporting my efforts to seek freedom and prosperity for Albertans, a blessed land that we love. pic.twitter.com/qjJseYPxI5 — Jason Stephan (@AlbertaNumber1) October 20, 2026

stories.title: Seven taken to hospital after Oxford collision
stories.summary: The lone occupant of an SUV and the six occupants of the minivan were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A collision in South-West Oxford sent seven occupants out of two vehicles to hospital Monday afternoon, according to police.

Oxford OPP along with Oxford County Fire and Oxford County Paramedic Services, responded to a two-vehicle collision at the intersection of Foldens Line and Clarke Road at about 2 p.m. on Monday.

Police said a sport utility vehicle and a minivan collided at the intersection.

The lone occupant of the SUV and the six occupants of the minivan were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

A 32-year-old driver from the minivan has been charged with careless driving under the Highway Traffic Act.

Police did not release the identities of those involved.

stories.title: Canadian man who stole Las Vegas flamingo convicted of animal cruelty
stories.summary: During the trial, defence lawyer Josh Tomsheck told jurors in a Nevada court that Fairbarn deeply regretted the 'bad decisions' he made while intoxicated.
stories.author: Katie Scott
stories.content:
A Canadian tourist was convicted of animal cruelty charges Monday for snatching a flamingo named Peachy from its enclosure at the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino on March 3.

Prosecutors said it was a malicious prank while a lawyer for tourist Mitchell Fairbarn said it was drunken foolishness not meant to harm the bird, according to The Associated Press.

Fairbarn, 34, was seen on security camera around 5 a.m. on March 3, hopping a fence to get inside the flamingo habitat. He had been charged after taking the 27-year-old Chilean flamingo from the habitat and carrying the bird to his hotel room.

Peachy was injured during the incident and the flamingo’s treating veterinarian said the bird had seven to eight missing feathers, broken shafts and blood loss that were consistent with trauma. She said that Peachy needed weeks of pain medication, antibiotics and anti-inflammatories after the incident.

Since the incident, the flamingo has been doing all right physically but is more anxious and nervous when being evaluated, said Peachy’s veterinarian, Tiffany Moore, medical director of Lone Mountain Animal Hospital.

During the trial, defence lawyer Josh Tomsheck told jurors in a Nevada court that Fairbarn deeply regretted the “bad decisions” he made while intoxicated.

A charging document, viewed by the Las Vegas Review-Journal , alleges that Fairbarn “did willfully, unlawfully, maliciously, and feloniously torture or unjustifiably maim or mutilate an animal kept for companionship or pleasure.”

Global News has not independently viewed the charging document.

Fairbarn testified that he spent March 2 drinking and gambling and estimated that he had consumed between 30 to 40 beers before arriving at the flamingo habitat around 5 a.m, Klas Las Vegas reported .

He claimed that he was drunk and sleep-deprived before taking the bird.

Fairbarn said he took the bird as a “silly pranky joke.”

Prosecutors showed surveillance video, photos and Snapchat videos showing Fairbarn smiling and grabbing the flamingo by the neck.

Video showed the bird squawking while Fairbarn handled it and prosecutors said Peachy felt pain when it was pulled by its feet.

Las Vegas police responded to the scene after security staff reported someone had taken the flamingo. When Peachy was located, it was missing seven to eight feathers, had blood on its feathers and injuries to its wings, authorities said.

“Did you ever, at any time, have any malicious intent or desire?” his lawyer asked. “Did you intend to kill?”

“No,” Fairbarn replied.

Taking the bird was “dumb” and “fueled by drunkenness,” Tomsheck said.

“He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn’t have touched a bird, shouldn’t have taken Peachy inside,” Tomsheck added. “The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions.”

Fairbarn said he was in Las Vegas for Con Expo, “global construction show that happens every three years,” where he was asked to be “one of the representatives from Canada,” according to Kcbd .

After about five hours of deliberations, jurors returned convictions on felony and misdemeanor animal cruelty counts against Fairbarn.

Fairbarn’s sentencing hearing is set for Dec. 1 and he remains under house arrest pending the hearing.

The Ontario man faces up to four years in prison for the felony and possibly six more months for the misdemeanor conviction, according to The Associated Press.

Nevada animal rights advocate John Waudby, who recently helped strengthen the state’s animal cruelty laws, said he believes justice was delivered on Peachy’s behalf.

“I hope this sends a message to anybody else that wants to mess with our animals, that you’re not going to do it in Nevada,” he said outside the courtroom after Monday’s verdict.

—With files from The Associated Press

Chamber president and CEO Deborah Yedlin says Albertans have delivered a clear message that they want to be at the national table and help shape Canada’s prosperity.

stories.title: Ontario to allow over-the-counter hearing aids for sale in the province
stories.summary: Toronto - Ontario is planning to make over-the-counter hearing aids available in the province for people with mild hearing loss.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The government says a legislative change set to be included in the fall economic update later this year will enable the devices to be used in Ontario.

Health Minister Sylvia Jones says it will give Ontarians more choice and flexibility to get the hearing support they need, when and where they need it.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Image 9Image 10

Health Canada has issued medical device licences for some wireless earbuds that have built-in hearing aid capabilities, but Ontario law currently bans selling a hearing aid unless it is prescribed by a doctor or audiologist.

Following an update to the law and some regulatory changes, manufacturers of in-ear headphones and earbuds with built-in hearing aid capabilities will be able to turn on these features in devices for sale in Ontario.

The government says the new measure doesn’t replace or impact existing hearing aid prescriptions and coverage.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

stories.title: Canadian man who took Peachy the flamingo from Las Vegas hotel found guilty of animal cruelty
stories.summary: Prosecutors said it was a malicious prank while a lawyer for the tourist insisted it was drunken foolishness not meant to harm the bird
stories.author: Jessica Hill
stories.content:
A Canadian man was convicted of animal cruelty charges Monday for snatching a flamingo named Peachy from its enclosure at an iconic Las Vegas hotel. Prosecutors said it was a malicious prank while a lawyer for the tourist insisted it was drunken foolishness not meant to harm the bird.

Prosecutors said tourist Mitchell Fairbarn hurt and frightened the 27-year-old Chilean flamingo when he took it from its habitat at the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino and carried the squawking bird to his room March 3. Defense attorney Josh Tomsheck told jurors at trial in a Nevada court that the man deeply regretted the “bad decisions” he made while intoxicated.

After about five hours of deliberations, jurors returned convictions on felony and misdemeanour animal cruelty counts against the Ontario, Canada, man.

Fairbarn remains under house arrest pending a sentencing hearing set for Dec. 1. He faces up to four years in prison for the felony and possibly six more months for the misdemeanour conviction. Following the verdict, he declined to comment as he left the courtroom with his wife. He showed no visible emotion.

His lawyer also had no comment.

Since the incident, the flamingo has been doing all right physically but is more anxious and nervous when being evaluated, said Peachy’s veterinarian, Tiffany Moore, medical director of Lone Mountain Animal Hospital.

Prosecutors told jurors earlier that Fairbarn willfully caused the bird physical pain, noting feathers were found on the hotel floor. Video showed the bird squawking while Fairbarn handled it and prosecutors said Peachy felt pain when it was pulled by its feet.

Video played at the trial showed Fairbarn holding the flamingo in an elevator and carrying it down a hotel hallway at the famous hotel. The Flamingo is one of the oldest hotels on the Las Vegas Strip, and its well-known flamingo habitat also features hummingbirds, turtles, koi and other species.

Las Vegas police responded to the scene after security staff reported someone had taken the flamingo. When Peachy was located, it was missing seven to eight feathers, had blood on its feathers and injuries to its wings, authorities said.

Taking the bird was “dumb” and “fuelled by drunkenness,” the defence attorney Tomsheck said. But he added that his client never intended any harm to the bird, a key element in the felony charge.

“He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn’t have touched a bird, shouldn’t have taken Peachy inside,” Tomsheck said. “The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions.”

Fairbarn could be seen in court at one point with head lowered, hands covering his eyes.

The man had received death threats after taking the flamingo, and he was unable to leave the U.S. when his father died while Fairbarn was awaiting trial, said Clark County prosecutor Haley Willming. While those events were unfortunate, the prosecutor said, “none of that would have happened had he not done what he did, had he not made the choices he made.”

Jurors began deliberating shortly before midday after closing arguments Monday morning.

Nevada animal rights advocate John Waudby, who recently helped strengthen the state’s animal cruelty laws, said he believes justice was delivered on Peachy’s behalf.

“I hope this sends a message to anybody else that wants to mess with our animals, that you’re not going to do it in Nevada,” he said outside the courtroom after Monday’s verdict.

“I hope this sends a message to anybody else that wants to mess with our animals, that you’re not going to do it in Nevada,” he said outside the courtroom after Monday’s verdict.

content_blocks.text: A Canadian man was convicted of animal cruelty charges Monday for snatching a flamingo named Peachy from its enclosure at an iconic Las Vegas hotel. Prosecutors said it was a malicious prank while a lawyer for the tourist insisted it was drunken foolishness not meant to harm the bird.

Prosecutors said tourist Mitchell Fairbarn hurt and frightened the 27-year-old Chilean flamingo when he took it from its habitat at the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino and carried the squawking bird to his room March 3. Defense attorney Josh Tomsheck told jurors at trial in a Nevada court that the man deeply regretted the “bad decisions” he made while intoxicated.
After about five hours of deliberations, jurors returned convictions on felony and misdemeanour animal cruelty counts against the Ontario, Canada, man.
Man remains under house arrest awaiting sentencing

Fairbarn remains under house arrest pending a sentencing hearing set for Dec. 1. He faces up to four years in prison for the felony and possibly six more months for the misdemeanour conviction. Following the verdict, he declined to comment as he left the courtroom with his wife. He showed no visible emotion.
His lawyer also had no comment.

Since the incident, the flamingo has been doing all right physically but is more anxious and nervous when being evaluated, said Peachy’s veterinarian, Tiffany Moore, medical director of Lone Mountain Animal Hospital.

Prosecutors told jurors earlier that Fairbarn willfully caused the bird physical pain, noting feathers were found on the hotel floor. Video showed the bird squawking while Fairbarn handled it and prosecutors said Peachy felt pain when it was pulled by its feet.

Video played at the trial showed Fairbarn holding the flamingo in an elevator and carrying it down a hotel hallway at the famous hotel. The Flamingo is one of the oldest hotels on the Las Vegas Strip, and its well-known flamingo habitat also features hummingbirds, turtles, koi and other species.
Peachy was missing some feathers after being taken

Las Vegas police responded to the scene after security staff reported someone had taken the flamingo. When Peachy was located, it was missing seven to eight feathers, had blood on its feathers and injuries to its wings, authorities said.
Taking the bird was “dumb” and “fuelled by drunkenness,” the defence attorney Tomsheck said. But he added that his client never intended any harm to the bird, a key element in the felony charge.

“He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn’t have touched a bird, shouldn’t have taken Peachy inside,” Tomsheck said. “The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions.”
Fairbarn could be seen in court at one point with head lowered, hands covering his eyes.

The man had received death threats after taking the flamingo, and he was unable to leave the U.S. when his father died while Fairbarn was awaiting trial, said Clark County prosecutor Haley Willming. While those events were unfortunate, the prosecutor said, “none of that would have happened had he not done what he did, had he not made the choices he made.”
Jurors began deliberating shortly before midday after closing arguments Monday morning.
Animal rights advocate says justice was delivered
Nevada animal rights advocate John Waudby, who recently helped strengthen the state’s animal cruelty laws, said he believes justice was delivered on Peachy’s behalf.
“I hope this sends a message to anybody else that wants to mess with our animals, that you’re not going to do it in Nevada,” he said outside the courtroom after Monday’s verdict.

stories.title: Travelling to France? Make sure you read Canada’s updated travel advice first
stories.summary: Canada is urging travellers to France to avoid demonstrations as French authorities impose curfews to deal with violent protests and rioting.
stories.author: Daniel Otis
stories.content:
Canada is urging travellers to France to avoid demonstrations as French authorities impose curfews to deal with violent protests and rioting.

On Monday, Global Affairs Canada updated its travel advice for France amid nationwide demonstrations , which began in September with students protesting school conditions. Those protests have since swelled into a broader movement targeting issues like the rising cost of living.

With some demonstrations leading to vandalism, looting, arson and violent clashes with police, French authorities have responded with tear gas, water cannons and localized curfews.

Global Affairs Canada is now urging travellers to France to avoid areas where demonstrations are taking place and to follow local curfew orders, which are currently in place in parts of Paris such as the Place de la République square and around the Les Halles food market.

We have updated our travel advice for #France due to ongoing demonstrations and local curfews. More details here: https://t.co/tA5PyGcwyR pic.twitter.com/edVUKzDJ3z — Travel.gc.CA (@TravelGoC) October 19, 2026

Other restrictions on gatherings, such as curfews for minors, are also in effect in cities like Lyon, Marseille, Nice and Lille.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu credited the “targeted curfews” with helping maintain calm overnight into Tuesday, and warned that local authorities are considering whether to impose similar measures for a further night.

“Check with local authorities to determine whether you are in an area subject to a curfew,” Global Affairs Canada advises. “Even peaceful demonstrations can turn violent at any time.”

Canada is also advising travellers to France to monitor local media for the latest information and follow the instructions of local authorities.

“Be prepared to adjust your travel plans in the event of disruptions,” Global Affairs Canada says. “Expect heightened security measures and an increased police presence.”

Canada has long advised travellers to France to “exercise a high degree of caution” due to the potential threat of terrorism.

More than 2,000 people were arrested this past weekend, with at least two deaths and reports of serious injuries, including two people who lost their hands.

With files from CNN

stories.title: Quebec lieutenant-governor sitting out ceremony swearing in ministers
stories.summary: QUÉBEC - Quebec's lieutenant-governor has agreed to sit out the swearing-in ceremony for the new Parti Québécois ministers, at the request of the premier-designate.
stories.author: Patrice Bergeron The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Under the constitution, ministers must swear an oath before the lieutenant-governor, who represents the British monarch at the legislature and officially names ministers at the premier’s recommendation.

But a PQ spokesperson says Manon Jeannotte accepted Paul St-Pierre Plamondon’s request that she not participate in Wednesday’s ceremony.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Image 9Image 10

The government’s general secretary will preside over the ceremony, and Jeannotte will sign appointment documents at her office immediately after.

St-Pierre Plamondon has said he wants to abolish the monarchy in Quebec and pledged on the campaign trail to stop the province’s funding of the lieutenant-governor’s office.

He had also suggested that legal experts would evaluate how the role of lieutenant-governor, who also enacts all laws, could be entrusted to another entity.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published October 20, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Is Canada in an ‘affordability crisis’? Conservative motion heads to a vote
stories.summary: The opposition motion calls on the House of Commons to “officially recognize that: (a) the Liberals have been in power for 11 years; and (b) Canada is in an affordability crisis.”
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
A Conservative motion to declare that Canada is an affordability crisis will face a vote in the House of Commons on Tuesday.

The motion, brought by Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre , will come up for a vote later in the day on the floor of the House of Commons.

The opposition motion calls on the House of Commons to “officially recognize that: (a) the Liberals have been in power for 11 years; and (b) Canada is in an affordability crisis.”

MPs are expected to vote on the motion at roughly 3 pm Eastern, shortly after question period ends.

Canada’s annual inflation rate rose to 3.1 per cent in September as war in the Middle East continued to drive up gasoline prices, but economists say easing core inflation suggests higher energy costs have yet to spread widely throughout the economy.

Statistics Canada released the latest consumer price index report on Monday, which said the acceleration in headline inflation was led by a 27.8 per cent spike in gasoline prices last month compared with a year earlier, despite the switch to the less expensive winter gas blend.

Excluding gasoline, however, consumer prices increased 2.2 per cent year-over-year in September after a 2.4 per cent rise in August.

–With files from Canadian Press

stories.title: High turnout caused referendum delays for some Indigenous voters: officials
stories.summary: Elections Alberta says it delivered additional ballots to several Indigenous communities after unexpectedly high turnout caused voting delays during Monday’s referendum.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Elections Alberta says it delivered additional ballots to several Indigenous communities after unexpectedly high turnout caused voting delays during Monday’s referendum .

Siksika First Nation was one of several communities affected Monday, Chief Samuel Crowfoot said. Voting was extended by more than 90 minutes due to high turnout.

He’s requesting a formal explanation of how Elections Alberta allocated polling staff, ballots and other resources.

“There are barriers when it comes to carrying out these civic functions in rural communities,” Crowfoot said.

Elections Alberta spokesperson Kevin Duncan told Global News Tuesday the agency relied on historical data for ballot distribution.

Some communities eventually required multiple ballot deliveries because turnout exceeded expectations, he added.

“We’re seeing this as a bit of a good news story. We’re seeing high voter turnout in these areas,” Duncan said.

In total, 106 polling stations across Alberta had to remain open later Monday after delays prevented them from opening on time, Duncan said. Most of the delays lasted 10 to 15 minutes, but some were longer. The last voting station closed at 10:41 p.m. MT.

“We’re very impressed with how quickly the team was able to react.”

Duncan said more than 47,000 workers were on hand to help at the 1,400 polling stations across Alberta on Monday.

“As you can imagine, popping up 1,400 locations for a one-day event is no small task,” he said.

Unofficial results showed 10,607,881 responses had been recorded across the referendum’s 10 questions as of 8:30 a.m. MT Tuesday. Elections Alberta said 1,356,873 advance and special ballots were cast from Oct. 13 to Oct. 17.

stories.title: 33 military members injured in fire remain in hospital
stories.summary: Ottawa — Defence Minister David McGuinty says 33 members of the Canadian Armed Forces remain in hospital after a deadly fire swept through a training ground at the military base in Wainwright, Alta., ON Saturday.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — Defence Minister David McGuinty says 33 members of the Canadian Armed Forces remain in hospital after a deadly fire swept through a training ground at the military base in Wainwright, Alta., on Saturday.

McGuinty was in Wainwright on Monday, where he visited both the base and CAF members who are recovering in a local hospital.

The minister said he will not comment on the condition of those in hospital out of respect for their privacy.

More coming.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: QuickQuotes: Leaders react to Alberta referendum results to remain in Canada
stories.summary: Ottawa — Albertans voted overwhelmingly to stay in Canada on Monday in a historic referendum vote.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
A voter enters a polling station to cast their vote in the Alberta referendum in Calgary, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Jeff McIntosh THE Canadian Press

By The Canadian Press

Posted October 20, 2026 10:41 am.

Last Updated October 20, 2026 10:56 am.

Ottawa — Albertans voted overwhelmingly to stay in Canada on Monday in a historic referendum vote.

In early returns, about three in four Albertans said yes to Confederation, while about one in four said they wanted the province to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving.

The separation question was one of 10 put to Albertans. The other nine focused on immigration and the Constitution.

Here’s what some Canadian leaders are saying.

“Thank you, Alberta! I’m very pleased to see the initial results from Elections Alberta show widespread support for remaining in Canada. Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada.

“Thank you to all Albertans who took time to vote on these critically important referendum questions.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith

“It’s a great day for Canada … I’m thrilled that Albertans have chosen unity. They’ve chosen to build together. They’ve chosen to continue to take care of each other, to move forward together with purpose, high ambition.

“I’d like to thank all of the volunteers who supported the election, of course those who campaigned on all sides, the electoral volunteers who were still counting some of the votes, above all, Albertans for turning out in numbers, participating in the democratic process.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney

“At a time when our country is under threat and when we need to come together as Canadians, this result represents a clear rejection of the politics of division.

“Well over one million Albertans came together to give us something all too rare these days: a moment of hope.

“We know things are tough in Alberta, from health care to the cost of living, to the embattled education system and so much more … But as so many Albertans have shown us, we don’t fix our problems by turning on each other.”

NDP Leader Avi Lewis

“Canada is stronger with Alberta as part of it, and last night’s results show the overwhelming majority of Albertans agree with this. Many Nova Scotians have strong ties to Alberta, either having worked there or with friends and family going to their province to help build up their industry.

“Here in Nova Scotia, we’ll keep doing our part to develop our own natural resources, create opportunities and contribute to a stronger Canada.”

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canada urges travellers to avoid demonstrations as France grapples with rioting
stories.summary: Canada is urging travellers to France to avoid demonstrations as French authorities impose curfews to deal with violent protests and rioting.
stories.author: Daniel Otis
stories.content:
Canada is urging travellers to France to avoid demonstrations as French authorities impose curfews to deal with violent protests and rioting.

On Monday, Global Affairs Canada updated its travel advice for France amid nationwide demonstrations , which began in September with students protesting school conditions. Those protests have since swelled into a broader movement targeting issues like the rising cost of living.

With some demonstrations leading to vandalism, looting, arson and violent clashes with police, French authorities have responded with tear gas, water cannons and localized curfews.

Global Affairs Canada is now urging travellers to France to avoid areas where demonstrations are taking place and to follow local curfew orders, which are currently in place in parts of Paris such as the Place de la République square and around the Les Halles food market.

We have updated our travel advice for #France due to ongoing demonstrations and local curfews. More details here: https://t.co/tA5PyGcwyR pic.twitter.com/edVUKzDJ3z — Travel.gc.CA (@TravelGoC) October 19, 2026

Other restrictions on gatherings, such as curfews for minors, are also in effect in cities like Lyon, Marseille, Nice and Lille.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu credited the “targeted curfews” with helping maintain calm overnight into Tuesday, and warned that local authorities are considering whether to impose similar measures for a further night.

“Check with local authorities to determine whether you are in an area subject to a curfew,” Global Affairs Canada advises. “Even peaceful demonstrations can turn violent at any time.”

Canada is also advising travellers to France to monitor local media for the latest information and follow the instructions of local authorities.

“Be prepared to adjust your travel plans in the event of disruptions,” Global Affairs Canada says. “Expect heightened security measures and an increased police presence.”

Canada has long advised travellers to France to “exercise a high degree of caution” due to the potential threat of terrorism.

More than 2,000 people were arrested this past weekend, with at least two deaths and reports of serious injuries, including two people who lost their hands.

With files from CNN

stories.title: Alberta referendum vote to remain is ‘great result for Canada,’ Carney says
stories.summary: Albertans have opted to remain part of Canada — decisively voting to reject the idea of holding a formal referendum on separatism.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Albertans voting decisively not to pursue separation was a “great result for Canada,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday.

Carney said he was “thrilled that Albertans have chosen unity.”

“They’ve chosen to build together. They’ve chosen to continue to take care of each other, to move forward together with purpose,” Carney said.

He spoke with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith on the phone on Tuesday morning, Carney said.

The “first focus” of the call was the fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and the supports that both governments can provide for the victims and families affected by the fire.

“Then we turn to the referendum and moving forward in the spirit of cooperative federalism, including on issues of immigration, other common priorities of the federal government, the provinces,” Carney said.

The nation’s focus must now be on questions of affordability, safety and immigration, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said on Tuesday.

stories.title: Carney says Alberta’s choice of unity is ‘a great result’ for Canada
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney says it was "a great result for Canada" when Albertans chose unity in a referendum on Monday.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks about the incident at CFB Wainwright as he rises in the House of Commons in Ottawa, Monday, Oct. 19, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Adrian Wyld

By Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

Posted October 20, 2026 10:09 am.

Last Updated October 20, 2026 10:34 am.

Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney says it was “a great result for Canada” when Albertans chose unity in a referendum on Monday.

Carney says he spoke to Alberta Premier Danielle Smith about the results this morning.

In the historic referendum, voters chose in overwhelming numbers to remain in the country that made Alberta a province 121 years ago.

In early returns, about three-quarters of Albertans said yes to Confederation, while one-quarter said they wanted the province to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving.

Carney says he and Smith also talked about additional support for people affected by the tragic fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta before turning to the referendum results.

He told reporters they discussed moving forward in the spirit of co-operative federalism, including on the issue of immigration.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

— With files from Jack Farrell in Edmonton

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canada’s PBO slashes economic forecasts, warns debt will rise
stories.summary: Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down at the end of August followed by a new round of U.S. tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The Parliamentary Budget Office is trimming its outlook for economic growth for this year and next amid new U.S. tariffs and Canadian countermeasures.

The federal budget watchdog says it now projects real gross domestic product growth of 0.9 per cent for this year and 1.5 per cent in 2027.

The forecast is down from an estimate in June for growth of 1.1 per cent and 1.6 per cent, respectively.

Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. broke down at the end of August followed by a new round of U.S. tariffs and Canadian counter-tariffs.

The PBO says it also now projects a budgetary deficit of $63.3 billion for the 2026-27 fiscal year which will peak at $70.2 billion in 2027-28.

It says, relative to its June outlook, the deficits are $3 billion higher per year on average over 2026‑27 to 2030‑31, as new spending measures more than offset stronger revenues.
