stories.title: Albertans split in early returns on remaining 9 referendum questions
stories.summary: Edmonton - While Albertans roundly rejected separation in Monday’s referendum, results were decidedly closer in early returns on nine other questions.
stories.author: Jack Farrell The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - While Albertans roundly rejected separation in Monday’s referendum, results were decidedly closer in early returns on nine other questions.

Premier Danielle Smith also polled Albertans on five questions on immigration and four seeking a mandate to work with other provinces to change the Constitution and wrest more power from Ottawa.

The immigration questions asked whether Alberta should have more say on who comes to the province to work and whether it’s time to put more limitations — and perhaps introduce fees — on some who seek access to health care and education.

With votes still being counted Tuesday morning, the yes side was leading on all of the immigration questions with more than 55 per cent of votes. The strongest response was the question around requiring proof of citizenship to vote in provincial elections, with more than 63 per cent of those who voted saying yes.

Smith has said immigration is a benefit but must be economically sustainable. Critics have called the questions anti-immigrant dog-whistling.

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack said Monday that not only does Alberta need to move on from separation, it should also ditch the immigration questions.

“Edmontonians are the ones most directly impacted by those five questions, and I don’t want our neighbours to feel like they’re not welcome in our city,” Knack said.

“They are welcome in our city no matter who they are, no matter what they believe in, no matter any of that.”

At a polling station in Calgary, voters were split.

Jamie Fisher said she supports all nine. “I don’t think it’s been fair (to Alberta) for a really long time, and I think a lot of people need to really hear that message,” she said.

Amneet Mann characterized some of the questions as anti-immigrant.

“I just don’t think that’s what this country stands for,” she said. “I think it’s crazy that we’re here and we have to make that known.”

The constitutional questions asked Albertans for a blessing to pursue talks with other provinces on gaining control from Ottawa and abolishing the Senate.

Early results showed the yes option leading in most of the constitutional questions as well, though the largest lead — on the Senate question — was only 53 per cent in favour. The only question where the no option was winning was on whether provinces should be allowed to opt out of federal programs “intrude on provincial jurisdiction,” such as health care and Education. Fifty-one per cent of the counted ballots said no Tuesday morning.

Smith said those issues are pressing. Critics have called them posturing.

Smith said she voted to stay in Canada but needed a yes to the nine questions to get a mandate to bargain with Prime Minister Mark Carney. Her government commissioned a $4-million advertising campaign urging Albertans vote yes to the nine.

The nine became a passive-aggressive dance between Smith and Carney as the campaign wound down, with each publicly poking the other in the eye.

Last week, Carney barnstormed the province to rally support for federalists and was mobbed by cheering, back-patting selfie-seekers. On Thursday, he leveraged the opportunity and popularity in Smith’s metaphorical backyard of Calgary to publicly urge Albertans to reject the nine questions.

Smith scrambled to pivot the narrative. A day later, at a joint event in a Red Deer brewery, she pointedly handed Carney her government’s explanatory referendum booklet to get him get up to speed on the nine issues.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

— With files from Dayne Patterson in Calgary
paragraphs: Edmonton - While Albertans roundly rejected separation in Monday’s referendum, results were decidedly closer in early returns on nine other questions.
Premier Danielle Smith also polled Albertans on five questions on immigration and four seeking a mandate to work with other provinces to change the Constitution and wrest more power from Ottawa.

The immigration questions asked whether Alberta should have more say on who comes to the province to work and whether it’s time to put more limitations — and perhaps introduce fees — on some who seek access to health care and education.

With votes still being counted Tuesday morning, the yes side was leading on all of the immigration questions with more than 55 per cent of votes. The strongest response was the question around requiring proof of citizenship to vote in provincial elections, with more than 63 per cent of those who voted saying yes.
Smith has said immigration is a benefit but must be economically sustainable. Critics have called the questions anti-immigrant dog-whistling.
Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack said Monday that not only does Alberta need to move on from separation, it should also ditch the immigration questions.
“Edmontonians are the ones most directly impacted by those five questions, and I don’t want our neighbours to feel like they’re not welcome in our city,” Knack said.
“They are welcome in our city no matter who they are, no matter what they believe in, no matter any of that.”
At a polling station in Calgary, voters were split.
Jamie Fisher said she supports all nine. “I don’t think it’s been fair (to Alberta) for a really long time, and I think a lot of people need to really hear that message,” she said.
Amneet Mann characterized some of the questions as anti-immigrant.
“I just don’t think that’s what this country stands for,” she said. “I think it’s crazy that we’re here and we have to make that known.”
The constitutional questions asked Albertans for a blessing to pursue talks with other provinces on gaining control from Ottawa and abolishing the Senate.

Early results showed the yes option leading in most of the constitutional questions as well, though the largest lead — on the Senate question — was only 53 per cent in favour. The only question where the no option was winning was on whether provinces should be allowed to opt out of federal programs “intrude on provincial jurisdiction,” such as health care and Education. Fifty-one per cent of the counted ballots said no Tuesday morning.
Smith said those issues are pressing. Critics have called them posturing.

Smith said she voted to stay in Canada but needed a yes to the nine questions to get a mandate to bargain with Prime Minister Mark Carney. Her government commissioned a $4-million advertising campaign urging Albertans vote yes to the nine.
The nine became a passive-aggressive dance between Smith and Carney as the campaign wound down, with each publicly poking the other in the eye.

Last week, Carney barnstormed the province to rally support for federalists and was mobbed by cheering, back-patting selfie-seekers. On Thursday, he leveraged the opportunity and popularity in Smith’s metaphorical backyard of Calgary to publicly urge Albertans to reject the nine questions.

Smith scrambled to pivot the narrative. A day later, at a joint event in a Red Deer brewery, she pointedly handed Carney her government’s explanatory referendum booklet to get him get up to speed on the nine issues.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.
— With files from Dayne Patterson in Calgary

stories.title: 'Very much an open question': Carney's West Coast pipeline project could run into legal pitfalls
stories.summary: The pipeline, called Pacific Link, is the first project to be designated within the national interest under the government's Bill C-5.
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal government has promised to have shovels in the ground in the less than a year on the construction of a new pipeline to the West Coast, but lawyers and legal academics are warning the project could face legal challenges in court.

The pipeline, called Pacific Link, is the first project to be designated within the national interest under the federal government’s Bill C-5, also known at the Building Canada Act.

The legislation allows Cabinet to give projects in the national interest a fast-tracked regulatory process.

Robin Junger, counsel on Indigenous law and the environment at McMillan LP, said he is anticipating court challenges on two fronts: the Crown’s duty to consult under Section 35 of the Constitution Act and the federally legislated United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (Undrip).

“They passed a law that talks about consulting First Nations before they designate a project in the national interest, and then the statute talks about consulting First Nations and development of conditions,” said Junger.

“But that’s a different way of approving projects than previously; I’ll say it’s at best untested, and whether that’s going to complicate potential legal challenges is very much an open question,” he added.

Junger said the federal government could end up reviewing the major projects legislation if there is uncertainty there.

Prime Minister Mark Carney announced the national interest designation of Pacific Link earlier this month, promising the country will remain one of high standards, but not necessarily slow decisions.

The newly formed Major Projects Office undertook consultations with over 130 Indigenous communities between July 3 to Sept. 18, before the designation was announced. The MPO will begin its review of the project in early 2027, with public hearings held by the commission of the Canada Energy Regulator. The MPO is expected to finalize a conditions document by Sept. 1, 2027.

First Nations have been clear that they view Bill C-5 as a violation of the Undrip. In July, Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse-Nepinak said that fast-tracking projects will not come at the expense of First Nations’ rights.

“A one-year timeline, principally designed to attract investment, subordinates the honour of the Crown to commercial imperatives,” she said, during her opening remarks at the Afn’s annual meeting.

A note published by Osler, Hoskin & Harcourt LLP last December warned that the consultation process under Bill C-5 could be challenged in court.

“An accelerated BCA (Building Canada Act) process May result in legal challenges where Indigenous consultation is perceived to be truncated or otherwise inadequate to fulfill the federal government’s obligations,” the report said, adding that proponents can mitigate these risks by consulting early, proactively and responsively to Indigenous communities.

“However, if a project is designated as an (National Interest) Project and faces Indigenous opposition, there is a risk a court will find that Crown consultation prior to designation of the (National Interest) Project was inadequate,” the report added.

Dwight Newman, professor of law at the University of Saskatchewan, said there is ample case law about the duty to consult, which the courts have made clear does not give Indigenous communities final say on whether a project moves forward.

However, the federally legislated Undrip has added an extra layer of uncertainty, which was first passed by the federal government in 2021. This is because Undrip includes Free, Prior and Informed Consent (Fpic), which allows Indigenous communities to say no to a project development.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser told reporters last year that Undrip does not allow “a blanket veto power” to Indigenous communities, but later apologized for his comments after criticism, noting that speaking about Undrip in that way makes an assumption that Indigenous people and the federal government are working against each other.

Newman said the federally legislated Undrip does not go as far as the one in British Columbia, where it has become an provincial election issue, but is still having an impact on case law across the country.

Newman said a recent Federal Court of Appeal decision last Friday, in the case of Canadian Nuclear Laboratories and the Kebaowek First Nation in Quebec, has determined that Undrip does not change the duty to consult.

“The lower court in that case had said that the duty to consult turned into free, prior, and informed consent because Canada adopted the UN Declaration Act, and the Federal Court of Appeal has overturned that reasoning, and they’ve said the duty to consult doctrine hasn’t changed,” said Newman.

However, the case could go to the Supreme Court of Canada, which means the issues surrounding Undrip are not finalized.

Junger said it’s hard to say how Undrip will court challenges going forward.

“Is the federal government going to rescind the Undrip Act, or is it going 60 miles an hour into a brick wall?”

“Or am I wrong? Those are all possibilities, but they are the possibilities, and that’s separate from the duty to consult,” he added.

Newman, like Junger, noted that the court challenges could also come in the initial phase of consultations that took place prior to the national interest designation.

Heather Exner-Pirot, senior fellow at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, said the federal government would have already run a risk assessment on the likelihood of court challenges facing the project and are preparing accordingly.

“I think everyone knew that there would be court challenges,” she said. “I think it was anticipated, and they prepared for it, especially on the designation process.”

That's a different way of approving projects than previously ... and whether that's going to complicate potential legal challenges is very much an open question

Last week, Major Projects Office CEO Dawn Farrell had a candid moment with the BC Assembly of First Nations, noting that the frustrations over lack of consultations on the Pacific Link project made her feel “like Canada is never going to work” according to a report by the Canadian Press.

Farrell said members of her team had “very, very big scars” while working on the Trans Mountain Expansion Project.

“The projects that we have to deliver out of our office have to achieve your rights. We have to make sure that we go through your processes,” Farrell said.

“We can’t just make stuff up. The courts will just come and overturn the projects and we’ll be like Canada’s always been, 10, 15 years, dragging stuff around in the ditch and not getting it done and wasting time and money and resources, and your time and your people’s resources. We can’t keep doing that.”

Exner-Pirot said the federal government has learned its lesson from the court challenges against TMX, with the final case dismissed in 2020.

The decision from the Federal Court of Appeal concluded that “consultation means that Canada consider and address the rights claimed by Indigenous peoples in a meaningful way” but cannot be used to create a “de facto veto right.”

Exner-Pirot said the federal government has also learned from its court losses, including in the case of Enbridge’s Northern Gateway Project, which ultimately led to the federal government’s decision not to move forward.

“There’s a lot more knowns this time,” she said. “And regulators are conservative, and they are slow, but part of it is because they’re hyper aware that the durability of the approval once they do give it must be airtight, and it’s a disaster for a regulator’s decision to be overturned because the regulator did not meet the Crown’s obligations.”

However, Exner-Pirot admitted that Undrip certainly could complicate matters in the courts, noting that Undrip was not federal law during the TMX court decision in 2020.

Newman said ultimately no project development is without legal risk, and the federal government has decided this pipeline is worth facing those pitfalls.

“It would be difficult to say there are no legal risks because there are some legal risks there, but sometimes governments have to take legal risks, and they’re saying this is in the national interest, and they need to make some decisions in the national interest,” said Newman.

“And sometimes there are legal risks attached to doing that, but they’re making the decision that they’re going to do that,” he added.

Newman, like Junger, noted that the court challenges could also come in the initial phase of consultations that took place prior to the national interest designation.

Heather Exner-Pirot, senior fellow at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, said the federal government would have already run a risk assessment on the likelihood of court challenges facing the project and are preparing accordingly.
“I think everyone knew that there would be court challenges,” she said. “I think it was anticipated, and they prepared for it, especially on the designation process.”
That's a different way of approving projects than previously ... and whether that's going to complicate potential legal challenges is very much an open question

content_blocks.text: Last week, Major Projects Office CEO Dawn Farrell had a candid moment with the BC Assembly of First Nations, noting that the frustrations over lack of consultations on the Pacific Link project made her feel “like Canada is never going to work” according to a report by the Canadian Press.
Farrell said members of her team had “very, very big scars” while working on the Trans Mountain Expansion Project.
“The projects that we have to deliver out of our office have to achieve your rights. We have to make sure that we go through your processes,” Farrell said.

“We can’t just make stuff up. The courts will just come and overturn the projects and we’ll be like Canada’s always been, 10, 15 years, dragging stuff around in the ditch and not getting it done and wasting time and money and resources, and your time and your people’s resources. We can’t keep doing that.”
Exner-Pirot said the federal government has learned its lesson from the court challenges against TMX, with the final case dismissed in 2020.

The decision from the Federal Court of Appeal concluded that “consultation means that Canada consider and address the rights claimed by Indigenous peoples in a meaningful way” but cannot be used to create a “de facto veto right.”

Exner-Pirot said the federal government has also learned from its court losses, including in the case of Enbridge’s Northern Gateway Project, which ultimately led to the federal government’s decision not to move forward.

“There’s a lot more knowns this time,” she said. “And regulators are conservative, and they are slow, but part of it is because they’re hyper aware that the durability of the approval once they do give it must be airtight, and it’s a disaster for a regulator’s decision to be overturned because the regulator did not meet the Crown’s obligations.”
However, Exner-Pirot admitted that Undrip certainly could complicate matters in the courts, noting that Undrip was not federal law during the TMX court decision in 2020.
Newman said ultimately no project development is without legal risk, and the federal government has decided this pipeline is worth facing those pitfalls.

“It would be difficult to say there are no legal risks because there are some legal risks there, but sometimes governments have to take legal risks, and they’re saying this is in the national interest, and they need to make some decisions in the national interest,” said Newman.
“And sometimes there are legal risks attached to doing that, but they’re making the decision that they’re going to do that,” he added.

stories.title: Wainwright, Alta., residents grieving but resilient after tragic fire on army base
stories.summary: Wainwright - Residents of a central Alberta town are grieving after a vicious fire killed four men and injured dozens more at a nearby military base, but living alongside soldiers preparing for battle has built up a deep stoicism and resilience in the community.
stories.author: David Baxter and Bill Graveland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Wainwright - Residents of a central Alberta town are grieving after a vicious fire killed four men and injured dozens more at a nearby military base, but living alongside soldiers preparing for battle has built up a deep stoicism and resilience in the community.

“It’s heartbreaking. My heart goes out to the families but we’ll bounce back,” said Sharon Pashko, 79, whose uncle was once commander of CFB Wainwright.

Pashko said the community, about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, takes care of its own and should be proud.

“We’ve gone above and beyond and I’m very proud of Wainwright residents,” she added.

The brother of Shaun Farrell and a friend of Morgan Wong, two of four who died on Saturday, shared memories of the soldiers.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre has been meeting with constituents in the town, which is in his Battle River-Crowfoot riding. He said while many unanswered questions remain, people are coping.

“I’m just amazed how resilient and strong the people are. Nobody’s breaking. Everyone’s just putting their head down and they’re doing their jobs. It’s the best of Canada,” he said.

“They’re obviously heartbroken. They see the loss of these brilliant young men in the springtimes of their lives but at the same time they bounce back and they keep working to support the living.”

Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the base has always been a part of the community.

“It’s a part of us and we’re a part of it. It’s a symbiotic relationship,” he said.

Despite the temporary closure of the local polling station for Alberta’s referendum, a steady stream of voters continued to cast ballots Monday.

“A couple of friends of mine from church are in the military and I’ve heard, last night, that they were actually both in Latvia right now,” Dustin Degenhardt said after voting.

“I’m grateful that they’re safe, but at the same time I know hearts are here too.”

Degenhardt said the tragedy didn’t affect how he voted and sees the two as separate issues. Other residents shared that view, while some said the shadow of the fire loomed over their decision.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

stories.title: Advance voting in B.C. election is down compared to 2024
stories.summary: The number of ballots cast in the first three days of advance voting in the British Columbia election is down about 8 per cent compared to 2024.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The number of ballots cast in the first three days of advance voting in the British Columbia election is down about 8 per cent compared to 2024.

Elections BC says there were about 440,000 votes cast from Friday to Sunday, compared to almost 480,000 for the first three days of advance voting last election, which set a record for total advance turnout.

stories.title: Alberta voters reject push for separation referendum
stories.summary: Preliminary results show 76% backed remaining in Canada, while 24% supported holding a binding referendum
stories.author: Nathan VanderKlippe
stories.content:
Alberta has decided to remain in Canada, with voters in the province emphatically rejecting an effort by separatists to pursue a permanent rupture with the country.

Roughly 75 per cent of Albertans voted in favour of staying in Canada and 25 per cent for a binding referendum, according to preliminary results from Elections Alberta, which had counted ballots from 83 per cent of voting locations by 10 a.m. MT (noon ET) on Tuesday.

It marked the failed culmination of decades of effort by disaffected Albertans who have demanded a chance to create their own independent country.

“I’m very pleased to see the initial results from Elections Alberta show widespread support for remaining in Canada,” Alberta Premier Danielle Smith wrote late Monday on social media. “Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney promised a future in which “Albertans and all Canadians will move forward together with renewed purpose and high ambition.”

“Canada is so much greater than the sum of its parts,” he wrote in a statement. “Now it is our opportunity to take all that we have been given as Canadians – and we have been given the greatest country in the world – and make our country better for all of us.”

Thomas Lukaszuk, who led Forever Canadian, which campaigned for a remain vote, told a rally late Monday night that “Alberta will not be the weak link in Confederation. We Albertans are as proud to be Canadians as any other Canadians across the country.”

Public-opinion surveys had long shown that a large majority of Albertans support preserving Confederation and the province’s 121-year history as part of Canada.

The Prime Minister, in urging Albertans to remain, had appealed to the strength of a country united and called on shared memories of patriotic pride. Separatist leaders demanded rupture, promising an independent Alberta would deliver better fortunes and decisions unfettered by people outside the province.

Separatists had mounted a vocal campaign that garnered significant attention both in this country and south of the border.

On Monday night, the results brought dejection to an event hosted by the pro-independence Alberta Prosperity Project, where supporters who were gathered at The Parlour, an Edmonton bar, voiced their displeasure with expletives when the first results were released.

But leaders of the movement had already begun to pivot, describing new ways to foment separation.

“You have to get involved in government,” said APP leader Mitch Sylvestre.

Lawyer Jeff Rath, who has also helped lead APP, renewed threats to unseat Premier Smith through a party leadership vote.

“The next phase for us moving forward is an institutional phase where we move forward to take control back of our party, which is the United Conservative Party of Alberta,” he said. “And we will form government. Period.”

Ballots for the 10-question referendum were being counted by hand, and early results included smaller numbers of votes for the nine questions outside the one related to secession. The full count is likely to take two days to complete.

The referendum drew great numbers of Albertans. Even before voting centres opened Monday, more than 1.3 million people had cast ballots, 43 per cent of those eligible to vote, according to Elections Alberta.

Many more came out on Monday. In Edmonton, turnout surpassed expectations for Barbara Schmidt, an Elections Alberta officer who worked at multiple polling stations, each with lengthy queues of voters.

For some, it was a moment years in the making.

“If we can get free of the rest of Canada, I’ll be the happiest man on Earth,” said Roy Mears, 76.

He began questioning Alberta’s place in Canada in the 1970s. He persisted in his beliefs through the National Energy Program, the controversial imposition of federal power on Alberta’s energy resources. In 2015, when Justin Trudeau won election as a Liberal prime minister, Mr. Mears founded a Facebook group called The Republic of Western Canada.

“If we don’t separate, we’re screwed. I mean, the immigration’s killing us,” he said on Monday as he voted in the town of Vulcan, Alta.

Albertans voted in community centres, schools, hotels, golf clubs, a Hindu temple, sports complexes, churches and outposts of the Royal Canadian Legion, with neighbours and colleagues making ballot choices that would steer their homes toward radically different futures.

“I love Canada. We need Canada. We need the whole of it, not just part of it,” said Carol Shaw, who moved to Alberta from Britain in 1981. She voted in Gleichen, a small railroad hamlet east of Calgary, where more than a dozen people arrived as morning temperatures dipped below freezing.

Some came determined to stand not merely against Alberta independence but against the fracturing of Canada at a time when U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened annexation.

“There’s people that would like to join the U.S. – it’ll be over my dead body,” said Leslie Leckie, a retired snowplow and cable ferry operator. On Monday morning, he put on a pink hat emblazoned with a maple leaf, arriving to vote struggling to comprehend how it had to come to this.

“This is foolishness. As people, can we not get together? Can we not negotiate?”

When Ms. Smith first proposed a nine-question referendum, she said she was seeking a “mandate” from Albertans. Critics have accused her of seeking to mollify xenophobic factions in her own party, while proposing constitutional amendments that Alberta itself has no power to enact.

The addition of the 10th question, ON a possible vote for secession, has carried considerably more consequence, prompting competing displays of patriotism across the province on referendum day. In Edmonton, a man rollerbladed over the North Saskatchewan River on the Walterdale Bridge, holding aloft a hockey stick attached to a giant Canadian flag, waving through the wind.

Albertans have voted in droves to stay in Canada. The result was satisfying for the pro-Canada movement, but separatists say it's just the beginning.

The Canadian Press

Near Cochrane, drivers sounded their horns at two friends who stood beside a highway flying large Alberta flags in favour of the separatist cause.

At the Royal Canadian Legion in Sundre, Delena Barker, a retired accountant and union leader, enthusiastically voted yes to all the referendum questions and to taking steps toward separation. She said she would also vote yes in a future secession ballot.

Ms. Barker moved to Alberta from Toronto 15 years ago.

“We’re a different type of people,” she said, “and I say ‘we’ now because I feel I’m an Albertan.”

In Wainwright, the eastern town reeling from a deadly weekend grass fire that killed four military members at a nearby base, voters marked ballots near a memorial of bouquets that has grown around the town’s war memorial.

“In the service of Canada,” one of the plaques read.

“I hope everyone is doing all right, the best they can,” said local resident Brandon Barss.

“And I hope this vote goes in the way of not needing another referendum.”

The results of the referendum will reflect separatist sentiment, although only partly. Some voted against remaining in Canada, even if they had no real intention of seeking independence in a secession vote.

In Edmonton, Sheila Taylor said she had been “a fence-sitter,” not sure which side she’d vote for. On Monday, she chose to support a binding separation vote.

“Ultimately, for me, it became a decision of just saying that I’m okay with Prime Minister Mark Carney doing whatever he wants with the rest of the country – but just leave us in Alberta alone and out of it, please,” she said.

James Wocknitz, a retired drilling rig worker in Vulcan, was among those who signed a petition demanding a referendum. Yet he remains skeptical that the province could ever achieve independence.

“People think this is about leaving. It’s about leverage. It’s about getting the ability to have a say,” Mr. Wocknitz said.

Others, though, questioned the damage done by a referendum that has brought to the fore disagreements that could leave wounds for generations to come.

In Calgary, Mayor Jeromy Farkas recounted a question he was asked during a recent elementary school visit to City Hall.

“I have never felt my heart so broken as when one of the children asked me, ‘Am I a real Canadian?’”

That is a question, he said, that “no child should ever have to ask.”

The results of the referendum will reflect separatist sentiment, although only partly. Some voted against remaining in Canada, even if they had no real intention of seeking independence in a secession vote.
In Edmonton, Sheila Taylor said she had been “a fence-sitter,” not sure which side she’d vote for. On Monday, she chose to support a binding separation vote.

“Ultimately, for me, it became a decision of just saying that I’m okay with Prime Minister Mark Carney doing whatever he wants with the rest of the country – but just leave us in Alberta alone and out of it, please,” she said.
James Wocknitz, a retired drilling rig worker in Vulcan, was among those who signed a petition demanding a referendum. Yet he remains skeptical that the province could ever achieve independence.
“People think this is about leaving. It’s about leverage. It’s about getting the ability to have a say,” Mr. Wocknitz said.
Others, though, questioned the damage done by a referendum that has brought to the fore disagreements that could leave wounds for generations to come.
In Calgary, Mayor Jeromy Farkas recounted a question he was asked during a recent elementary school visit to City Hall.
“I have never felt my heart so broken as when one of the children asked me, ‘Am I a real Canadian?’”
That is a question, he said, that “no child should ever have to ask.”

stories.title: Alberta votes in referendum to stay in Canada. A timeline on how we got here
stories.summary: Edmonton — Albertans voted overwhelmingly Monday to remain in Canada in a referendum, writing a new chapter in longstanding debate on relations with the rest of the nation.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By The Canadian Press

Posted October 20, 2026 2:37 am.

Last Updated October 20, 2026 5:18 am.

Edmonton — Albertans voted overwhelmingly Monday to remain in Canada in a referendum, writing a new chapter in longstanding debate on relations with the rest of the nation.

Here’s a look at some key events:

1980 — The federal government ignites widespread alienation in Alberta with the National Energy Program, which keeps domestic oil prices below world levels to promote Canadian energy security and increase the federal share of oil revenues. Alberta views it as an unjustified attack and a federal money grab. The issue is later settled, but discontent with Ottawa continues.

1982 — Separatism enjoys a brief heyday. Gordon Kesler of the Western Canada Concept Party wins a provincial byelection in central Alberta on a separatist platform. Later that year in the general election, he loses a spot in the legislature. The party receives 12 per cent of the vote but no seats.

2019 — The anti-Ottawa mood ramps up as the United Conservative Party under Jason Kenney wins power in Alberta, capitalizing on discontent over federal rules and policies deemed to impair Alberta’s ability to create wealth, particularly in oil and gas. Premier Kenney fights for more independence from Ottawa but remains a staunch advocate for the province staying in Confederation.

2022-23 — Kenney is replaced by Danielle Smith, who wins government in the 2023 election on a platform of further asserting independence from Ottawa. Unlike Kenney, Premier Smith, while stressing her preference for a “sovereign Alberta within a united Canada,” refuses to characterize separatists as fringe extremists, saying they have valid grievances that deserve to be aired.

April 28, 2025 — Mark Carney and the Liberals defeat the federal Conservatives to win a minority government.

May 5, 2025 — Smith announces a panel to discuss Alberta’s future in Canada. She says her government won’t itself put separation on a ballot but would honour a successful citizen petition seeking such a vote. At the same time, her government takes steps to eventually pass rules to lower thresholds for citizen-led petitions.

June 2025 — Former Alberta Progressive Conservative deputy premier Thomas Lukaszuk launches a “Forever Canadian” petition to affirm the province stays in Canada. It eventually collects more than 400,000 names — enough to validate the petition. But by the spring of 2026, the petition is tied up in a legislature committee as Smith questions whether Lukaszuk gathered the names for a referendum or as a trigger for a vote among legislature members.

January 2026 — Mitch Sylvestre of the separatist Alberta Prosperity Project is given the green light by election officials to launch a petition asking whether Alberta should leave Canada. Months later, the petition is deemed successful, having gathered about 223,000 signatures.

Feb. 19, 2026 — Smith announces nine referendum questions about immigration and constitutional concerns will be put to Albertans in an Oct. 19 referendum.

May 13, 2026 — An Alberta Court of King’s Bench judge quashes the separatist petition, ruling Smith’s government didn’t properly consult First Nations as required in the Constitution. Smith later promises to challenge the ruling, and it remains in legal limbo.

May 21, 2026 — Smith announces a 10th referendum question asking whether Alberta should stay in Canada or hold a binding vote on separation. Smith cites the legal uncertainty of the court decision on the separatist petition as the driving force, saying it unduly deprives thousands of Albertans of having a say. Smith later cites Lukaszuk’s petition, too, as a reason. She says both show hundreds of thousands of Albertans want the issue decided.

Sept. 10, 2026 — The Alberta government launches a $4-million advertising campaign for the referendum and urges citizens to vote to stay in Canada. The move comes as polls suggest a broad majority of Albertans want to stay.

Sept. 14, 2026 — Smith’s UCP loses a byelection to the Opposition NDP in their conservative stronghold of Calgary Shaw. Critics across the political spectrum say the referendum was a factor in punishing Smith’s UCP. Her office says the party lost due to right-centre vote splitting.

Sept. 16, 2026 — Smith’s government publishes a report it commissioned from the University of Calgary to determine what fiscal challenges and benefits an independent Alberta could see. It estimates an initial five-year price tag of $50 billion to $170 billion, noting that figures could swing sharply depending on factors outside Alberta’s control.

Oct. 16, 2026 — Carney wraps up a two-day barnstorming tour of Alberta, urging people to vote to stay in Canada. Carney and Smith sing O Canada, tap a keg and have a beer at a Red Deer brewery at a pro-Canada event.

Oct. 17, 2026 — Advance voting closes. Elections Alberta reports 1.3 million Albertans — about 43 per cent of eligible voters — have already cast a ballot.

Oct. 19, 2026 — Albertans vote by a wide margin to stay in Canada.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Alberta referendum voters reject separatism, choose to stay in Canada
stories.summary: Most of the province of Alberta has rejected a formal referendum on separatism and would rather remain part of Canada.
stories.author: Karen Bartko
stories.content:
Most of the province of Alberta has rejected a formal referendum on separatism and would rather remain part of Canada.

Elections Alberta began releasing the referendum results late Monday night, and by midnight around 76 per cent of Albertans voted to remain part of Canada without any further deliberation.

The separatism question asked voters if Alberta should remain in Canada or if the provincial government should begin the legal process of holding a future binding referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada.

As of midnight, the votes were as follows:

Remain: 883,641 Hold second referendum/Leave: 278,062 Total: 1,163,148

By law, officials must count all votes by hand within 48 hours. Question 10 — about separation — is being counted first.

Early results were supposed to start being released at 8 p.m. MT — only once the final ballot is cast and all polling stations are closed — but several locations opened late on Monday, pushing back that timeline by more than three hours.

The referendum asked residents 10 government-initiated questions, though public and political attention largely focused on the question asking Albertans whether they want to remain in Canada or proceed with a binding referendum on leaving Confederation.

The referendum, announced Feb. 19, initially included nine questions pertaining to immigration and the Constitution. The question on independence, added back in May by Premier Danielle Smith , is the tenth that voters were asked to mark an X on .

The separation question was added after Smith said she disagreed with the ruling of a Court of King’s Bench judge that quashed a separatist petition in May , saying the provincial government had a duty to consult with First Nations before Stay Free Alberta was allowed to gather signatures.

She said because the proposed referendum would not “directly trigger separation,” the court ruling would not apply.

Interest in the outcome of the referendum was high even before Monday’s official voting day.

More than 1.35 million votes were cast in both last week’s advance polls and by special mail-in ballots — a significant increase over the roughly 810,000 who voted that way in the 2023 provincial election.

The use of special ballots increased tenfold in the referendum compared to that election, with a total of 519,082 mail-in ballots received by Elections Alberta by the cut-off date.

The results reflect more than half a year of polling, which since the beginning of 2026, has consistently shown about 70 per cent of Albertans want the province to remain in Canada .

In January, an Ipsos poll found about three in 10 residents supported independence , but a deeper dive revealed that when faced with the costs and consequences, only half of those interested in separatism were truly committed to following through.

Grievances in Alberta towards the federal government are not new.

The nuanced disgruntlement harkens back decades: Alberta farmers feeling shortchanged by the monopoly the Canadian Wheat Board had over crop prices and their sales, anger at how Pierre Trudeau’s National Energy Program decimated jobs and investment in the province’s oil and gas sector in the 1980s, and more recent grievances over the Justin Trudeau government’s policies on energy investment and public health restrictions during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Smith’s United Conservative Party never campaigned on holding a separation vote in the 2023 provincial election, but Smith has said some Albertans’ anger with the state of affairs under former Liberal prime minister Justin Trudeau has boiled over into hundreds of thousands signing petitions for and against Confederation.

She has said a referendum was necessary to resolve the matter once and for all.

Smith has said repeatedly that if the vote went the way polling has suggested for months, she expected everyone to accept it and move on . Leaders of the independence movement contest that.

The remaining nine questions surround immigration and constitutional issues.

The immigration questions ask Albertans whether the province should have more say over who comes to the province to work and whether it’s time to put more limitations — and potentially introduce fees — on some who arrive seeking health care and education.

The constitutional questions ask Albertans to bless talks with other provinces to wrest power from the federal government and abolish the Senate

Smith has said the first nine questions are meant to give the province leverage in negotiations with Ottawa.

The premier has also said she voted to stay in Canada, but she needs a yes on the remaining nine questions to get a mandate to bargain for a better deal with Carney.

Carney came to Alberta last week to rally pro-Canada forces and to agree to disagree with Smith. He urged Albertans to reject the nine remaining questions.

Elections Alberta hired more than 48,000 workers to count ballots, which is happening around the clock.

The results of those nine questions should be completed and announced by Wednesday. Officials will count ballots in order from question one to nine. Timelines depend on location closing times and voter turnout.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: The latest developments on the Alberta referendum
stories.summary: Edmonton - Albertans have voted in a historic referendum.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - Albertans have voted in a historic referendum.

There are 10 questions on the ballot, with the key one asking whether the province should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

The other nine questions focus on immigration and the Constitution.

Here are the latest developments (all times Mountain):

Prime Minister Mark Carney says the results show it’s time for Albertans and Canadians to move forward with renewed purpose.

Carney says Albertans made a clear choice for unity and to work to help each other.

He says the country is so much greater than the sum of its parts.

Jeff Rath of the pro-independence Alberta Prosperity Project says the fight is not over.

Rath says his movement dominated the conversation in the last year and they have shown Albertans the benefits of independence.

Thomas Lukaszuk, leader of the Forever Canadian campaign, says the referendum results send a strong message to the world: “Don’t mess with Canada.”

He says if U.S. President Donald Trump is watching, he should be worried about his mid-terms because Canada isn’t up for grabs.

Lukaszuk also says those who voted in favour of separation shouldn’t be ignored.

He says they have concerns and deserve to be listened to.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says she’s pleased to see the early results in the referendum on separation.

She says Albertans have shown widespread support for keeping the province in Canada.

And she says they have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada.

She says she’ll address the results of all 10 referendum questions, and where the province goes from here, in a televised address on Tuesday night.

Albertans have voted to reject a referendum on separation.

With just over one million votes counted, or one-third of eligible voters, about 76 per cent voted for the province to stay in Canada.

About 24 per cent voted for a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

Albertans are anxiously waiting for results in the vote on whether the province should stay in Canada.

The last polling station was set to close just after 10 p.m.

However, Elections Alberta says one is still open outside Calgary.

It says it’s waiting on confirmation that all voting locations are closed.

Before most polls closed, a voice in Premier Danielle Smith’s caucus calling for a separation referendum announced he won’t run for re-election next year.

Jason Stephan says on social media that eight years as a legislature member is enough and that he did his best to speak the truth.

He says Canada continues to badly lag behind other developed countries.

Stephan represents the riding of Red Deer South for the United Conservative Party.

All polls are now closed in Alberta’s separation referendum.

Most polling stations closed two hours earlier at 8 p.m.

About 100 out of the 1,400 stayed open late because they didn’t open on time in the morning due to various issues.

Elections Alberta says voting results can start being reported.

About 1.3 million voters cast ballots by mail or at advance polls.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

stories.title: Albertans vote to remain in Canada, rejecting push for separation
stories.summary: The deadly fire at CFB Wainwright on Saturday cast a shadow over Monday’s vote, and a bitter federalist-separatist split leaves lingering questions about unity.
stories.author: Stephanie Taylor
stories.content:
Edmonton — A turbulent campaign that pitted federalists against separatists over Alberta’s future in Canada ended with the remain side securing an overwhelming victory.

With votes still being counted on Tuesday morning, about 76 per cent of Albertans voted to remain in Canada and roughly 24 per cent backed a second binding referendum on leaving the country.

At a watch party in Edmonton hosted by the federalist group “Forever Canadian,” a crowd of fewer than 100 jumped to its feet, hugging, cheering and waving Canadian flags as the call was made.

“Canada, Canada, Canada,” the crowd chanted.

The projections came before Elections Alberta had released complete official results. More than 100 polling stations that opened late stayed open past the scheduled closing time, delaying the count until after midnight.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said on X that she would address Albertans Tuesday at 8:45 p.m. Eastern time regarding the results “and where our province goes from here.”

“I’m very pleased to see the initial results from Elections Alberta show widespread support for remaining in Canada. Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada,” Smith wrote.

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Mark Carney issued a statement celebrating the results, saying the province had “made a clear choice” in Monday’s vote.

“Above all, Albertans chose Canada.”

He said that while all of the results have not yet been counted, “the defining question of separation” has been decided and victory for the federalist camp means that the country can now return to the job of advancing Canada “with renewed purpose and high ambition,” referring to his government’s agenda of increasing international trade and developing infrastructure, mining and energy projects across the country.

He said that Canada was “unleashing our full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta at its core.”

While federalists celebrated Monday’s victory, many were quick to note that 23 per cent of Albertans choosing the option to hold a vote on separation was not something to cheer about.

“I was hoping it would be like 85 per cent,” Dee Winn, a volunteer with the “Forever Canadian” campaign, told the Star as the early results came in.

Amid the cheers and applause, Thomas Lukaszuk, who spearheaded the federalist group, told the crowd those voters could not be ignored.

“These are Albertans. These are Canadians,” he said from the stage, adding that something had to be done to address what was driving their anger and frustration.

“We cannot go on like this.”

Before the polls even closed, Mitch Sylvestre, a key separatist leader, told a crowd of volunteers and other independence supporters gathered at a nearby Edmonton bar that their movement had become something that was not going to disappear.

“Alberta has changed,” he said.

Monday’s vote took place under the shadow of tragedy after four people were killed and 39 others injured when extreme winds pushed an already burning fire onto troops conducting exercises at CFB Wainwright on Saturday.

Polls opened as scheduled, with some voters in Wainwright worried about what would happen to the base, an integral part of the community’s identity and economy, should Alberta one day separate from Canada.

“This is a federal town,” said Greg Granger, who works in IT at CFB Wainwright.

Elsewhere, the polarization that has taken hold across the province during the referendum campaign was on full display.

Olivia Hughes, an Edmonton resident living with disabilities, walked to a polling station at an Anglican church in the city on Monday, wondering, “Why the f—- do I have to be out here?”

Besides contemplating the impact secession would have on her quality of life, she said: “I’m a Canadian, I’m not just an Albertan.”

“I would like to remain a Canadian, so that’s why I’m here.”

Others arrived feeling fed up.

“I think we’ve been screwed over by the other provinces,” said fellow Edmonton voter Bill Lewis, who cast his ballot at a polling station in one of the city’s strip malls for the option to begin the process of holding a future vote to leave Canada.

“I think our money should stay here instead of us getting nothing and the other provinces getting it all.”

A record-breaking 1.3 million Albertans had already cast their ballots through advance polls or by mail, comprising 43 per cent of the province’s eligible voters.

How Alberta came to this moment is a mix of historic grievance, COVID-fuelled populism and a premier who was unwilling to close the door on separatists.

While Western alienation is nothing new in the country’s largest oil-producing province, successive public opinion polls suggested an uptick in the sentiment after the election of Prime Minister Mark Carney, whose victory was viewed by some as another blow to the deep-blue Conservative province.

Anger had been brewing for years during the tenure of former prime minister Justin Trudeau, whose environmental policies were viewed by many in the province as stymying resource development. Even before that, the Trudeau name triggered distrust among some Albertans, who remembered the legacy of the long-dismantled National Energy Program introduced by his father, former prime minister Pierre Trudeau.

But while Carney has sought to reset relations with Alberta, working with Premier Danielle Smith to advance a new million-barrel-a-day oil pipeline to the West Coast and overhauling federal regulatory processes with the goal of getting more major energy and infrastructure projects off the ground, another movement was brewing in the province.

Independence organizers who entered Alberta’s political arena through opposition to COVID-19 pandemic measures got to work pushing for a referendum.

Sylvestre, the owner of a sporting goods store in Bonnyville, Alta., spent the dead of winter travelling the province collecting 300,000 signatures for a petition under provincial citizen-initiative rules to trigger a referendum on leaving Canada.

Lukaszuk, a former deputy premier in a Progressive Conservative government, was busy collecting tens of thousands of signatures for his own “Forever Canadian” initiative under the same provincial rules in response to the separatist push.

Things came to a head this May when an Alberta judge quashed the separatist petition over concerns about the failure to properly consult First Nations.

One evening in late May, Smith addressed Albertans to announce that her United Conservative Party government would add an independence question to a previously decided set of nine referendum questions focused on taking greater control over immigration and pursuing constitutional reforms such as abolishing the Senate.

That sparked criticism from all corners. Carney called the referendum a “dangerous bluff.” Other premiers panned the move, while federalists in Alberta mobilized supporters who wanted to remain in Canada to turn out and vote, warning that separatism remained a minority view but a vocal and highly motivated one.

Independence leaders also expressed ire at Smith, particularly over her public support for remaining in Canada, viewing it as a betrayal of her party base, where support for independence is popular.

ByMegan Ogilvie Health Reporter

As news broke that victims of the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright could overwhelm Alberta’s hospitals, Ontario burn specialists were trying to figure out how they could help.

Though details were still sparse, they knew the high stakes and brutal demands of treating dozens of patients with severe burns.

Patients in critical condition would likely need to be intubated and put on a breathing machine. Those with the most extensive and deepest burns would need urgent surgeries, ideally within 24 to 72 hours. Hospitals could run out of dressings and other supplies, including their stockpiles of frozen donor skin.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Image 10Image 11Image 12Image 13

“It’s a unique type of trauma,” said Dr. Alan Rogers, a burn surgeon at the Ross Tilley Burn Centre at Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre.

“Any burn centre, in any province, could be overwhelmed with the numbers that we believe are injured in this accident. Even five severely burned patients could overwhelm available resources at any one time.”

Rogers said burn centres across Canada have offered help to their colleagues in Alberta, with some specialists volunteering to travel.

He said Sunnybrook, the largest burn centre in Canada, has the capacity to take in several Alberta patients, and noted that the burn team has readied two operating rooms, checked their supplies of dressing materials and ensured the hospital’s skin bank has sufficient supply.

“We stand ready to help as much as we possibly can,” Rogers said.

The fire killed four soldiers and injured dozens, including 19 in critical condition.It’s not yet clear what help Alberta hospitals might need; an initial “Code Orange” calling for hospitals to free up beds for a mass casualty event was later called off. The province has two dedicated burn centres, one in Edmonton and one in Calgary.

In a statement, Sunnybrook said its teams are in close touch with provincial and federal officials and have offered “any support needed to help those injured by the fire.”

“As of right now, we have not been asked to take any patients but stand ready to do so,” the hospital said.

Ontario’s Ministry of Health confirmed Monday afternoon that Alberta has not requested assistance but that Premier Doug Ford has stated the province “stands ready to help with the recovery efforts however we can.”

Dr. Marc Jeschke, a burn surgeon and director of the burn program at Hamilton Health Sciences, Ontario’s other primary burn centre, said his hospital has also offered help to Alberta colleagues, including patient transfers.

He said Canada has 46 specialized beds for burn patients across 17 hospitals, with 14 at Sunnybrook and 10 in Hamilton, and that centre directors know each other and want to help.

“We told (Alberta colleagues) we’re here to support you,” said Jeschke, vice-president of research and innovation at Hamilton Health Sciences.

Patients with severe burns to more than 20 per cent of their total body surface area are “among the sickest patients in hospital” and need specialized care to survive, Jeschke said. He called burns to more than 40 to 60 per cent of a patient’s body “catastrophic.”

Severely burned patients may need ventilation and intensive care, along with multiple surgeries, and often spend months recovering in hospital, Jeschke said. He noted burns are extremely painful and that severe burns are life-threatening due to their high risk of infection.

Some patients, Jeschke said, can take years to recover due to extensive skin grafting surgeries that lead to scarring and require intensive rehabilitation.

“There’s no guarantee that you will ever be the same,” he said. “Which is what makes it so sad that so many people were involved in this tragedy.”

Rogers said the extent, depth and location of a patient’s burns will determine their treatment, while other trauma and inhalation injuries also play a role. He said deep burns often require skin grafting but that surgeons may use donated cadaver skin to temporarily replace burned tissue.

Much like organ donation, people can donate their skin after they die. Rogers said skin retrieved from a deceased person is screened for infection and quality, then processed and stored in antimicrobial fluid before it is cryopreserved.

Sunnybrook’s skin bank, which Rogers said the hospital uses almost every day, typically has about 90,000 square centimetres of skin onsite. He said that’s about enough to cover the entire body five times, though most patients don’t require that much.

Rogers called donor skin “life saving” because it allows for burn specialists to treat severe burns over multiple surgeries as they wait for patients to be stable enough to use their own skin for grafting. He noted skin grafting “creates a new wound that has to heal.”

Though the goal is to help patients, and their families, get through the burn injury as smoothly as possible, Rogers said many will spend months in hospital.

“It’s not just the injury itself, but its treatment … it can be a very traumatic process.”

Megan Ogilvie is a Toronto-based health reporter for the Star. Follow her on X: @megan_ogilvie or reach her via email: mogilvie@thestar.ca.

stories.title: More than half of Canadian toddlers get too much screen time — but this Toronto family is an outlier
stories.summary: New research shows more than half country’s infants, toddlers and preschoolers exceed national screen-time guidelines.
stories.author: Kerry Gillespie
stories.content:
Em Skublics plays with their two-year-old daughter who is limited to 1 hour of TV a week.

New research shows more than half of the country’s infants, toddlers and preschoolers exceed national screen-time guidelines.

Oct. 20, 2026

New subscriber benefit!

Copied to clipboard

A gifted article has been claimed.

Out of gifts for the month

Unfortunately you've used all of your gifts this month. Your counter will reset on the first day of next month.

Nick Lachance/Toronto Star[](http://www.thestar.com/news/gta/a-toronto-mom-keeps-their-two-year-old-almost-entirely-screen-free-here-is-their-weekly-rule-and-exceptions/article_511c4add-426d-421e-8ebf-a73ece7d0ea4.html)

ByKerry Gillespie Health Reporter

Em Skublics introduced Friday night family movies when their daughter turned two. It’s really half-movie night because, even if Mary Poppins is singing “Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious,” the TV is turned off after one hour.

The rest of the time, she gets no screen time. No TV while mom is cleaning up. No iPad while waiting in a restaurant. No phone to distract her in a long line.

“When I describe this, most parents are shocked,” Skublics said. “They say, ‘Wow — this is parenting in hard mode’ or ‘you’re really choosing to make this difficult.’ But I see it more like a tradeoff that will pay off in her development.”

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Image 15Image 16

Despite increasing awareness of the detrimental impacts of screens on young children, the Toronto family is an outlier. New research released Tuesday shows that more than half of Canadian infants, toddlers and preschoolers spend more time on screens than health guidelines recommend.The national guidelines call for zero screen time under age two, and no more than an hour a day, on average, for kids two to four.

of infants met recommendation of zero screen time.

of toddlers met recommendation of zero screen time for children under 2 or no more than 1 hour/day, on average, for children aged 2 years.

of preschoolers met recommendation of no more than 1 hour/day of screen time, on average.

of infants met recommendation of at least 30 minutes/day of tummy time, on average.

of toddlers met recommendation of at least 180 minutes/day of physical activity at any intensity, on average.

of preschoolers met recommendation of at least 180 minutes/day of physical activity, of which at least 60 minutes/day was moderate-to-vigorous, on average.

Source: 2026 Participaction Report Card

Toronto Star graphic

The report, from ParticipAction — a national non-profit that conducts research and promotes health and active living — also found that only one in four children under five meet the 24-hour movement guidelines, which cover physical activity, sleep and screen time combined. That 25 per cent is actually the best Canada manages at any age: the organization’s previous report cards show that as kids grow older, they miss age-specific guidelines on physical activity, screens and sleep in even greater numbers.

This 2026 report card is the first time Canada has done this kind of reporting on infants, toddlers and preschoolers — and it is leading the way on this research globally, said Leigh Vanderloo, ParticipAction’s scientific director.

She hopes this first look at what’s happening in the early years shows parents and policymakers alike that efforts to boost sport and recreation for children and increase protections from online harms and devices need to start earlier.

Historically, the youngest children have received less research attention and public funding than school-aged children, but this age group is also the most malleable when it comes to instilling healthy habits that, hopefully, last a lifetime, she said.

“It’s alarming to see just how many kids straight from birth are already on screens.”

And given that the screen data is based on parental surveys, it likely underestimates how much screen time kids are actually getting because there’s a social bias to “overestimate how active we are and underestimate how engaged in screens we are,” Vanderloo said. Still, it’s the best data available and will serve as a benchmark to track progress over time, she said.

“We see that very few kids are actually getting the right amount of movement, sleep, play and non-screen-based recreation time for optimal development.”

The report cites research showing active play aids brain and body development, while screen time can hinder focus, memory and learning in young children.

Skublics read a lot about the detrimental effects of screens on children, especially infants and toddlers, before committing to such strict limits on screens.

Skublics knows allowing more screen time could make daily life just a little easier, but sees the impact a screen has on their daughter.

“She’s kind of like a zombie,” Skublics said.

“It’s a little jarring to watch as a parent, because I have a very engaged, very talkative, interactive daughter. And as soon as the TV is on, it’s like nothing else exists. She just sits there with her eyes glued to the screen, like she’s being hypnotized. You can’t talk to her. You won’t get a question out of her. You won’t get an answer out of her.”

Still, Skublics, who works outside the home as a marketing manager, already sees the cracks forming.

“She’s started to gain more awareness around us using our phones. If I take a picture of her now, she’ll ask to see it … so there’s little gateway moments where she sees a screen for like 30 seconds. I do wonder, as that continues, if it’s going to be harder to keep saying no.”

And harder still when she starts having playdates with friends.

“As she starts to understand what’s normal in other households, I’m probably going to get a lot more pushback.”

The family rules do break down every month or two when it’s time for a haircut.

Skublics’s daughter hates it and tends to thrash around while the scissors are near her eyes, so she gets a “Bluey” episode on Mom’s phone.

“That’s my one breaking of the rule,” Skublics said. “I think this is the one time where putting her in zombie mode is actually safer.”

Kerry Gillespie is a Toronto-based health reporter for the Star. Reach her via email: kgillespie@thestar.ca.

Despite increasing awareness of the detrimental impacts of screens on young children, the Toronto family is an outlier. New research released Tuesday shows that more than half of Canadian infants, toddlers and preschoolers spend more time on screens than health guidelines recommend.The national guidelines call for zero screen time under age two, and no more than an hour a day, on average, for kids two to four.
How the youngest are faring
of infants met recommendation of zero screen time.
of toddlers met recommendation of zero screen time for children under 2 or no more than 1 hour/day, on average, for children aged 2 years.
of preschoolers met recommendation of no more than 1 hour/day of screen time, on average.
of infants met recommendation of at least 30 minutes/day of tummy time, on average.
of toddlers met recommendation of at least 180 minutes/day of physical activity at any intensity, on average.
of preschoolers met recommendation of at least 180 minutes/day of physical activity, of which at least 60 minutes/day was moderate-to-vigorous, on average.
Source: 2026 Participaction Report Card
Toronto Star graphic

The report, from ParticipAction — a national non-profit that conducts research and promotes health and active living — also found that only one in four children under five meet the 24-hour movement guidelines, which cover physical activity, sleep and screen time combined. That 25 per cent is actually the best Canada manages at any age: the organization’s previous report cards show that as kids grow older, they miss age-specific guidelines on physical activity, screens and sleep in even greater numbers.

This 2026 report card is the first time Canada has done this kind of reporting on infants, toddlers and preschoolers — and it is leading the way on this research globally, said Leigh Vanderloo, ParticipAction’s scientific director.

She hopes this first look at what’s happening in the early years shows parents and policymakers alike that efforts to boost sport and recreation for children and increase protections from online harms and devices need to start earlier.

Historically, the youngest children have received less research attention and public funding than school-aged children, but this age group is also the most malleable when it comes to instilling healthy habits that, hopefully, last a lifetime, she said.
“It’s alarming to see just how many kids straight from birth are already on screens.”

And given that the screen data is based on parental surveys, it likely underestimates how much screen time kids are actually getting because there’s a social bias to “overestimate how active we are and underestimate how engaged in screens we are,” Vanderloo said. Still, it’s the best data available and will serve as a benchmark to track progress over time, she said.
“We see that very few kids are actually getting the right amount of movement, sleep, play and non-screen-based recreation time for optimal development.”
The report cites research showing active play aids brain and body development, while screen time can hinder focus, memory and learning in young children.
Skublics read a lot about the detrimental effects of screens on children, especially infants and toddlers, before committing to such strict limits on screens.
Skublics knows allowing more screen time could make daily life just a little easier, but sees the impact a screen has on their daughter.
“She’s kind of like a zombie,” Skublics said.

“It’s a little jarring to watch as a parent, because I have a very engaged, very talkative, interactive daughter. And as soon as the TV is on, it’s like nothing else exists. She just sits there with her eyes glued to the screen, like she’s being hypnotized. You can’t talk to her. You won’t get a question out of her. You won’t get an answer out of her.”
Still, Skublics, who works outside the home as a marketing manager, already sees the cracks forming.

“She’s started to gain more awareness around us using our phones. If I take a picture of her now, she’ll ask to see it … so there’s little gateway moments where she sees a screen for like 30 seconds. I do wonder, as that continues, if it’s going to be harder to keep saying no.”
And harder still when she starts having playdates with friends.
“As she starts to understand what’s normal in other households, I’m probably going to get a lot more pushback.”
The family rules do break down every month or two when it’s time for a haircut.
Skublics’s daughter hates it and tends to thrash around while the scissors are near her eyes, so she gets a “Bluey” episode on Mom’s phone.
“That’s my one breaking of the rule,” Skublics said. “I think this is the one time where putting her in zombie mode is actually safer.”
Kerry Gillespie is a Toronto-based health reporter for the Star. Reach her via email: kgillespie@thestar.ca.

stories.title: New study sheds light on inequities in breast cancer survival rates
stories.summary: A new study published in Clinical Breast Cancer has identified inequities in outcomes among women with HER2-negative breast cancer. The study from London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute…
stories.content:
Uncategorized October 20, 2026

A new study published in Clinical Breast Cancer has identified inequities in outcomes among women with HER2-negative breast cancer. The study from London Health Sciences Centre Research Institute (Lhscri), Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre, and Ices suggests that socioeconomically disadvantaged women had poorer outcomes compared to other women.

Funded through the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) credit program, the retrospective study analyzed public Ontario health data available through Ices from 10,634 women with stage one to three HER2-negative breast cancer who underwent surgery followed by chemotherapy. Researchers grouped patients into five socioeconomic levels based on the average income of their geographic area and followed them for a median of 5.5 years. Despite access to universal health care in Ontario, the study found persistent gaps in care and outcomes.

Breast cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related deaths worldwide. The most common subtype, HER2-negative breast cancer, accounts for about 80% of cases and is characterized by cancer cells that do not have high levels of the HER2 protein.

Overall, catching breast cancer early could mean better outcomes as the cancer is more likely to be found before it grows or spreads to other parts of the body. When the cancer is smaller and still contained, surgery is more effective and, in many cases, chemotherapy May be omitted. However, when the tumour is considered high risk, chemotherapy is more likely to help eliminate any remaining cancer cells and improve a patient’s chances of survival.

“The key is to detect this type of cancer early when we are more successful with surgery and chemotherapy can often be avoided,” says Dr. Danilo Giffoni, lead author on the study, Scientist at Lhscri, and Oncologist at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC). “However, we found that patients that are socioeconomically disadvantaged are presenting with much more advanced disease, which means they require the most aggressive forms of chemotherapy.”

The study found that survival differed based on income level, revealing gaps that persist long after diagnosis. Five years after being diagnosed, 91.3 per cent of women from the lowest‑income areas were alive, compared with 94 per cent of women from the highest‑income areas. Nearly nine out of every 100 women in the lowest‑income group died within five years, compared to about six out of every 100 women in the highest‑income group.

The differences began early in the cancer journey.

Women from lower‑income neighbourhoods were less likely to be diagnosed at an early stage, when treatment is often more effective. A total of 15.8 per cent of women from lower-income neighbourhoods were diagnosed at stage one (the earliest stage), compared to 22.1 per cent of women from higher‑income areas. They were also more likely to have larger tumours and more locally-advanced disease at the time of diagnosis.

“These are factors known to be associated with poorer outcomes and early differences in care can shape the entire course of treatment and recovery,” says Dr. Giffoni.

The study also observed gaps throughout care. It was found that women from lower‑income areas were more likely to have other chronic health conditions, which can complicate cancer treatment and increase the risk of side effects. They were also more likely to receive more toxic chemotherapy drugs, such as anthracycline‑based treatments.

Even after accounting for age, stage of cancer, and other medical conditions, the difference remained: women in the highest-income neighbourhoods had a 35 per cent lower risk of death over the study period compared with those in the lowest-income neighbourhoods.

“The research highlights how social and economic factors continue to shape health outcomes and that a universal health system alone cannot eliminate inequities,” says Dr. Giffoni.

The findings also raise important questions about the factors driving these disparities, while also pointing to opportunities for future action.

“Now that we have clear evidence these inequities exist, my hope is to better understand where they come from,” says Dr. Giffoni. “That insight could help inform strategies to ensure disadvantaged groups have the same access to high-quality care as everyone else within our universal health-care system.”

Dr. Maureen Trudeau, retired Oncologist at Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre and study collaborator, says the research also reinforces the importance of expanding access to screening and education.

“Equitable access to care starts with equitable access to information,” she says. “By strengthening education about breast cancer screening and making resources available in multiple languages, we can help ensure women across diverse communities are able to access the care and support they need.”

stories.title: Fatal motor vehicle collision
stories.summary: London, ON (October 20, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Frontline Division, with the assistance of members of the Road Safety Section, are investigating a fatal motor vehicle collision that occurred early this morning in the Old South area.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 20, 2026) –Members of the London Police Service Frontline Division, with the assistance of members of the Road Safety Section, are investigating a fatal motor vehicle collision that occurred early this morning in the Old South area.

At approximately 1:20 a.m., emergency crews responded to the 600-block of Upper Queen Street in relation to a serious single motor vehicle collision.

A female passenger was transported to hospital with life-threatening injuries. She has since died as a result of her injuries.

The male driver of the vehicle was arrested at the scene and remains in custody.

The investigation is in its early stages and remains ongoing.

Upper Queen Street is currently closed between Chiddington Avenue and Ferndale Avenue while members of the Road Safety Section continue their investigation. Members of the public are asked to avoid the area and use an alternate route. The roadway is expected to remain closed for an undetermined period.

More information will be provided as appropriate.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously toLondon Middlesex Crime Stoppers.
