stories.title: Sentiment improved, but new tariffs weigh on business outlook: BoC report
stories.summary: Ottawa — The Bank of Canada's latest outlook survey suggested that business sentiment improved on average in the third quarter, although concerns remained about rising costs and the war in the Middle East.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Bank of Canada’s latest outlook survey suggested that business sentiment improved on average in the third quarter, although concerns remained about rising costs and the war in the Middle East.

However, about three-quarters of the interviews with businesses for the survey took place before trade talks between Canada and the United States broke down at the end of August and new Canadian counter-tariffs were announced.

It says after the trade talks broke down, firms cited new U.S. tariffs on some goods and Canadian counter‑tariffs as factors weighing on their outlooks.

The Bank of Canada says inflation expectations have risen alongside the new tariffs and the recent increase in energy prices.

“The tariffs are also dampening business sentiment, weakening outlooks for exports and investment, and putting upward pressure on costs and prices,” the bank said in its report.

The business outlook survey was conducted by in-person, video and phone interviews from Aug. 6 to Sept. 2.

The bank said that at the time of the survey, a lessening of the drag from both trade tensions and geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East helped firms report better sales outlooks than in the second quarter.

The outlook survey said that roughly half the firms planned to continue passing some or all cost increases on to customers and that for several firms, those plans reflected somewhat improved demand and efforts to make up for past margin compression. At the same time, more companies than in the previous quarter said competitive pressures continue to limit their ability to increase prices.

The report also noted that business investment intentions eased slightly, but remained robust with improvements in demand conditions supporting investment plans overall.

In a separate report, also done mostly before the trade talks broke down, the Bank of Canada says its Canadian survey of consumer expectations found long-term inflation expectations rose to match those for the short term.

The consumer report also says consumers reported better financial health than in the previous quarter, though high prices and economic uncertainty continue to weigh on Canadians.

The reports comes ahead of the Bank of Canada’s next interest rate decision and monetary policy report set to be released on Oct. 28.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Inquest into death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet hears from police
stories.summary: A coroner's inquest into the death of a Toronto woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in her home is hearing from one of the officers called to the incident.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A coroner’s inquest into the death of a Toronto woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in her home is hearing from one of the officers called to the incident.

Const. Shane Beaudoin told the inquest into Regis Korchinski-Paquet’s death that he volunteered to serve as backup when dispatch put out a high-priority call for an assault involving knives on May 27, 2020.

He says he met an officer from a different division outside the building and the two of them went up together after a resident let them in.

Beaudoin says there was a lot of information coming at them and it was hard to know who the primary aggressor was, and the fact that it was a family dispute made matters “more murky.”

He says he heard before arriving that Korchinski-Paquet had experienced seizures earlier in the day, but only learned about postictal delirium through the inquest.

An agreed narrative read at the inquest last week said Korchinski-Paquet had a history of seizures from epilepsy and often experienced confusion, “physically and verbally abusive behaviour,” and temporary amnesia afterward.

A neurologist who did not treat her but examined her records testified that Korchinski-Paquet on several occasions showed symptoms in keeping with postictal delirium or postictal psychosis — both altered mental states that can follow seizures.

stories.title: Man charged in hit-and-run crash that left woman dead in Vaughan, Ont.
stories.summary: Vaughan - Police say they have identified and charged the alleged driver of a van that struck a woman whose body went undiscovered on the roadside for two days in Vaughan, Ont.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vaughan - Police say they have identified and charged the alleged driver of a van that struck a woman whose body went undiscovered on the roadside for two days in Vaughan, Ont.

York regional police say the woman was walking on Pine Valley Drive around 8:30 p.m. on Oct. 4 when she was hit by a vehicle that then left the scene.

stories.title: Peel police break up ‘violent criminal network’ behind luxury car thefts
stories.summary: Peel Regional Police say they’ve broken up a “violent criminal network” that was linked to carjackings and luxury vehicle thefts.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Peel Regional Police say they’ve broken up a “violent criminal network” that was linked to carjackings and luxury vehicle thefts across the Greater Toronto Area.

Det. Sgt. Earl Scott told reporters Monday that 10 people are facing a total of 128 charges in connection to Project High Guard, an eight-month-long investigation that began in March.

Police allege the group was behind 21 carjackings and high-end vehicle thefts between June 2025 and April 2026 in the GTA.

“Some of these events left victims with severe injuries,” Scott said.

“The identified culprits brandished knives, firearms and utilized violent physical assaults during the carjackings.”

As an example, police played a video of a carjacking that occurred in Brampton last summer. The video shows a suspect attacking a driver of a Rolls Royce outside a business to take control of the car. The victim was left with injuries as a result of the attack, Scott said.

The network itself included people who would target vehicles, some who coordinated robberies, some who carried them out, as well as, recruiters who targeted youth. The network was also made up of individuals responsible for coordinating the sales of stolen cars, Scott said.

Of the 10 people arrested, two were youths, he added. Some of the charges they all face include participating in a criminal organization, robbery, conspiracy to commit robbery and failure to comply with release orders.

Police conducted a series of raids across the region on Sept. 3 and seized 15 stolen vehicles worth $1.4 million as well as weapons, drugs and vehicle reprogramming devices, Scott said. One of the vehicles seized was heading out for export at the Port of Montreal.

“The 10 people we’ve arrested, we believe that they are the ones responsible for this network,” Scott said.

“These networks will utilize a variety of different people. They have contacts through social media, through friends and simply put, they’re looking for profit. They’ll put out an opportunity to make money into their networks that they know and recruit people for a specific job.”

Chief Nishan Duraiappah said vehicle thefts across Peel Region are down more than 50 per cent since peaking in 2023 and have dropped 10 per cent year-to-date in 2026.

The investigation remains ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Stellantis workers hand Unifor leaders a strike mandate amid stalled talks
stories.summary: Union, automaker remain at an impasse over plans to sell idled Brampton, Ont., plant
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Unifor’s Stellantis Stla-N workers have voted overwhelmingly in favour of a strike, empowering the union to call a work stoppage while contract talks have hit an impasse over the automaker’s plans to close and sell its plant in Brampton, Ont.

The automaker and the union began collective bargaining in August, but Unifor walked away from the table on Sept. 11, after Stellantis NV confirmed it has a preliminary agreement to sell its idled Brampton plant to Roshel Inc., a maker of armoured vehicles.

There have been no formal talks since then.

Unifor, which represents more than 9,000 Stellantis workers in Canada, said on Monday that 97 per cent of votes cast were for a strike. “While we now have a mandate, that does not automatically mean a strike will occur,” Unifor said in a statement, adding the union is not in a legal strike position.

A strike or employer lockout cannot occur for 17 days after the conciliator issues a statement, known as a no-board report, at the request of either party, saying that talks are deadlocked. Neither side has requested the report.

A work stoppage would include the company’s Windsor plant, which makes minivans and Dodge muscle cars, and the casting plant in Toronto.

As of Monday, more than 6,400 workers at the Windsor plant are on a layoff for three weeks. Stellantis blames the layoffs, which also took place during a two-week shutdown in September, ON U.S. tariffs and declining sales.

“Stellantis continues to evaluate and adjust its manufacturing operations in response to evolving market conditions, including consumer demand and the impact of tariffs,” said LouAnn Gosselin, a spokeswoman for the company.

Unifor is pushing Stellantis to reverse plans to sell the Brampton plant. The company shifted planned production of the Jeep Compass to Belvidere, Ill., after the U.S. announced 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian-made cars last year. The factory northwest of Toronto employed more than 3,000 people when it closed for retooling in 2023, and has about 2,200 people on layoff.

In addition to reviving the Brampton plant, the union is seeking production and employment security at the Windsor and Toronto plants. Unifor is pushing Stellantis to accept the wage package won in summer negotiations with Ford and General Motors.

Canadian workers at the other Detroit-based automakers approved three-year contracts that provide 3-per-cent raises in each year of the deal. Over the life of the new agreements, senior hourly wages rise to about $50.50 for production workers and about $62.70 for skilled tradespeople.

A strike or employer lockout cannot occur for 17 days after the conciliator issues a statement, known as a no-board report, at the request of either party, saying that talks are deadlocked. Neither side has requested the report.
A work stoppage would include the company’s Windsor plant, which makes minivans and Dodge muscle cars, and the casting plant in Toronto.

As of Monday, more than 6,400 workers at the Windsor plant are on a layoff for three weeks. Stellantis blames the layoffs, which also took place during a two-week shutdown in September, ON U.S. tariffs and declining sales.

“Stellantis continues to evaluate and adjust its manufacturing operations in response to evolving market conditions, including consumer demand and the impact of tariffs,” said LouAnn Gosselin, a spokeswoman for the company.

Unifor is pushing Stellantis to reverse plans to sell the Brampton plant. The company shifted planned production of the Jeep Compass to Belvidere, Ill., after the U.S. announced 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian-made cars last year. The factory northwest of Toronto employed more than 3,000 people when it closed for retooling in 2023, and has about 2,200 people on layoff.

In addition to reviving the Brampton plant, the union is seeking production and employment security at the Windsor and Toronto plants. Unifor is pushing Stellantis to accept the wage package won in summer negotiations with Ford and General Motors.

Canadian workers at the other Detroit-based automakers approved three-year contracts that provide 3-per-cent raises in each year of the deal. Over the life of the new agreements, senior hourly wages rise to about $50.50 for production workers and about $62.70 for skilled tradespeople.

stories.title: Teams scrambling after two Winnipeg arenas shut down
stories.summary: Winnipeg junior and minor hockey teams lost hundreds of ice time after two arenas were shut down for repairs as the season gets underway.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
Some Winnipeg junior and minor hockey teams have lost hundreds of hours of ice time after two arenas were shut down for repairs as the season gets underway.

Terry Sawchuk arena was closed due to structural issues with eight to ten of its beams needing repair. The city says it is exploring different timelines for repairs. The West Kildonan Memorial Community Centre is also closed for gas detection system, exhaust fans, and relief vent piping work, which is estimated to take months to complete and will not be open for this hockey season.

Barry Bonni, the president of River East Royal Knights, said he and his players are frustrated about the short notice.

“They (the players) are saying ‘do we have a game? Where’s the game? What time is the game? What’s going on?’ We’re saying ‘we don’t know. We don’t know. We’re scrambling for ice time’,” said Bonni, who founded the Royal Knights in 1981. “It affects our whole organization, our whole league, and every team we’re playing. We’re playing all over the place now instead of our own area.”

Derek German, Seven Oaks Minor Hockey Association President, said he is concerned that with practice time being cut, player development will be halted.

Watch the video above for the full story.

stories.title: Oro-Medonte mayoral candidate’s son injured in CFB Wainwright fire
stories.summary: In a post on Facebook, Cathy Keane posted that her eldest son was among those 39 injured in the blaze.
stories.author: Dilshad Burman
stories.content:
The son of an Oro-Medonte, Ont., mayoral candidate was critically injured in the fatal fire at CFB Wainwright on Saturday that claimed the lives of four soldiers and injured dozens of others.

In a post on Facebook, Cathy Keane confirmed that her eldest son was among the 39 injured in the blaze.

“As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family,” she wrote, adding that she will be travelling to Alberta and will not be able to continue door-knocking for the remainder of the campaign.

“I want residents to know that I am still in the race for Mayor of Oro-Medonte, and I stand by my commitment to our friends, families and neighbours more than ever. My belief in this community and the future we can build together has not changed,” she said.

In the post she also encouraged community members to read about her platform in the pinned posts on her Facebook page, with the hope that it will “help residents understand my priorities and the commitments I have made to our township as online voting continues.”

She ended her statement saying, “Right now, I ask for your understanding as our family navigates an incredibly difficult and uncertain time. We are grateful for the kindness and support of our friends and community. Please hold your loved ones a little tighter tonight.”

The blaze is believed to have ignited as a result of ongoing training exercises with live munitions and started as a grass fire roughly a kilometre away from where soldiers were training for an upcoming deployment to Latvia in 2027.

According to Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division, leaders were aware of the fire but it was not deemed a threat initially. However, sudden strong winds sent flames across the Prairie landscape in seconds, ripping through the training area.

The Armed Forces confirmed early Sunday that there’s no indication that the fire was the result of terrorist activity.

stories.title: Former broadcaster Pamela Wallin resigns from Senate
stories.summary: Ottawa — Pamela Wallin, a former broadcaster who was appointed to the Senate by former prime minister Stephen Harper, has resigned.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Pamela Wallin knows her decision to resign from the Senate on Monday came as a surprise to some — but to her, she said, it “just felt like the right time” to move on after 17 years.

“I know people are always surprised when somebody walks away, but we all know our time,” Wallin said in an interview.

The news broke on Monday morning after a note was sent to senators from the Senate clerk and Wallin’s biography on the Senate website was changed to list her as a former member.

She said she chose not to telegraph what she called a very personal decision to step down, adding a recent change in the government’s assisted dying policies gave her the closure she needed.

Justice Minister Sean Fraser announced last week that the government will amend the Criminal Code to allow people to make advance requests for medical assistance in dying, also known as Maid.

Wallin has long advocated for advance directives after watching her mother’s long struggle with Alzheimer’s disease.

She’s been an outspoken supporter of Maid and served on multiple parliamentary committees that have studied the issue in recent years.

“I just think there are so many people in that situation that want to have some control and some sense of choice in the way that they leave, add some dignity to their departure,” she said.

Wallin said she leaves the Senate convinced that the institution is a “core part of our democracy,” although she believes the provinces should have much more say over who is appointed to represent them.

Albertans were voting Monday in a referendum that included a question about whether the government should work with other provinces to amend the Constitution to abolish the unelected Senate.

Wallin said that “until somebody comes up with some other genius idea,” the Senate is a critical way to ensure checks on the partisan House of Commons.

“The Senate itself is the only body that puts a second pair of eyes on crucial legislation, and our process is much more thoughtful and much more in-depth than the House has the opportunity to engage in,” she said.

Wallin’s time in the Senate followed a trail-blazing career as a journalist.

Wallin became a household name after being named co-host of Canada AM in 1981. She was tapped to lead CTV’s Ottawa bureau in 1985 — making her the first woman to head a national television news bureau in Canada — and was the producer and host of the network’s flagship political show Question Period.

She broke ground again in 1992 when she became the first woman to co-anchor a nightly news show in Canada — CBC’s Prime Time News.

Wallin had surgery for colorectal cancer in 2001 but continued a tour to promote her book at the time.

In 2002, she was named consul general to New York, just months after the 9/11 attacks, and served in that role for more than four years.

She was made an officer of the Order of Canada in 2007 and was appointed to the Senate in 2009 by Prime Minister Stephen Harper.

She became a key figure in the 2013 Senate expenses scandal after an audit found about $140,000 of the $500,000 in travel expenses she had billed to the Senate were improper because they were related to her work on corporate boards.

In May 2013, Harper’s chief of staff asked her to leave the Conservative caucus in the Senate.

During an interview with The National that year, Wallin apologized and said she did not “deliberately set out to use the system or abuse the system.”

She attributed the mistakes to carelessness in dealing with mounds of paperwork and said she didn’t pay enough attention to her expense filings.

In September, when she repaid some $150,000 — including interest — a defiant Wallin called out what she described as a “lynch mob” mentality in the Senate.

She was suspended without pay from the Senate in November 2013 over disallowed expenses, along with Mike Duffy and Patrick Brazeau.

Her Senate suspension was lifted when Parliament was dissolved for the 2015 election.

On Monday, Wallin said she had no interest in reliving that time but said the reforms that followed the expense scandal were necessary.

She has recently been a member of the Canadian Senators Group.

Speaking on behalf of the group, Sen. Flordeliz Osler said in a media statement that Wallin spent her career “asking difficult questions, challenging conventional thinking, and standing firmly behind her convictions.”

“From breaking barriers in Canadian journalism to representing Canada on the international stage and advocating passionately for the rights and dignity of Canadians in the Senate, she has never been one to shy away from difficult conversations,” said Osler.

“Her independence, determination and unmistakable voice have left a lasting mark on public life in Canada.”

Wallin, who is from Wadena, Sask., represented her home province in the Senate. She is two years shy of the mandatory retirement age of 75.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

Sarah Ritchie, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Stellantis workers give union authorization to strike as talks with automaker stalled
stories.summary: Stellantis workers in Canada have voted to give their union a mandate to strike. Unifor says 97.3 per cent of members who took part in the vote over the weekend were in favour of authorizing a potential strike. The union is not yet in a legal strike position as neither it nor Stellantis have requested […]
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Toronto — Stellantis workers in Canada have voted to give their union a mandate to strike.

Unifor says 97.3 per cent of members who took part in the vote over the weekend were in favour of authorizing a potential strike.

The union is not yet in a legal strike position as neither it nor Stellantis have requested a “no board” report, which is one of the steps necessary under labour law required for a job action.

Unifor, which represents more than 9,000 Stellantis workers in Canada, said it still believes there is a path to reaching a new collective agreement with Stellantis “so long as the company honours its commitments and does right by its workers.”

“Strike action is always a last resort, but we will not back down and accept a deal that weakens Stellantis’ footprint within Canada’s auto industry due to broken commitments that further cause devastation for our members, families and communities that rely on good union auto jobs,” said James Stewart, Unifor’s Stellantis master bargaining chairperson.

The previous collective agreement between Stellantis and the union expired Sept. 20 without the two sides coming to terms on a new tentative deal.

The union’s bargaining committee and the company are at an impasse over several key issues, including job security and the future of the idled Brampton, Ont., assembly plant Stellantis wants to sell.

In response to the Unifor vote, Stellantis spokesperson LouAnn Gosselin reiterated the company’s previous statement that it hopes to return to the bargaining table.

“Stellantis remains committed to bargaining in good faith and is prepared to continue discussions toward a negotiated agreement that recognizes the contributions of our employees while supporting the long-term competitiveness of our Canadian operations,” she said.

Talks came to a standstill on Sept. 11 when Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with defence contractor Roshel for a potential sale of the Brampton facility.

More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the Brampton plant when it halted operations in 2023.

The facility had been slated to be retooled for Jeep production, a process that began early in 2024, before the company paused the plan in early 2025. It later announced it was moving production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois, leaving the plant idled indefinitely.

The union has written to federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly urging the government to block the potential sale and clarify whether the MOU breached Stellantis’ previous commitments to Ottawa.

Unifor ratified new collective agreements with Ford Motor Co. and General Motors in Canada during the summer, as part of its pattern bargaining process with each of the Detroit Three.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Live updates: Polls open across Alberta in historic referendum vote
stories.summary: Polling stations are open from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. MT, and Elections Alberta expects substantial turnout
stories.author: Globe staff
stories.content:
I just got an email from Vern Yu, the president and CEO of AltaGas. A vocal proponent for the Remain side leading up to the referendum, Yu said often that Alberta’s future is strongest within Canada, and Canada is stronger with Alberta helping to lead it.

He said he’s thankful that Albertans have chosen to stay within Canada.

“Seeing the results come in, I’m optimistic about the opportunities ahead and confident in what we can achieve together,” Yu said.

“Here in Alberta, we have world-class resources, innovative businesses, talented people, and tremendous opportunities ahead of us. Now, it’s time to get to work.”

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe says he’s glad Albertans voted overwhelmingly to stay in Canada, but the grievances of people living in the Prairies must still be addressed.

“There is still work to be done on improving how Western Canada is treated by Ottawa. But Canada is worth that effort,” Moe said in a social media post on Tuesday.

“Saskatchewan will continue to work with Alberta to make our provinces stronger within a united Canada.”

Good morning, friends. It’s Emma Graney here, The Globe’s energy reporter, based in Calgary.

Reaction to yesterday’s vote for Alberta to remain in Canada continues to flood my inbox – this time in the form of two political adversaries and former Alberta premiers who joined forces to campaign for the Remain side and co-chair Stronger Together.

From the conservative side, Jason Kenney said in a statement that at a historic time of unstable market access, businesses know there’s no advantage in cutting off reliable customers and neighbours.

“These results amplify the fact that Albertans remain overwhelmingly united that we’re better off with Canada, especially when we partner and help set a win-win economic agenda with the rest of the federation. That’s who Alberta is and will always be.”

And from the NDP, Rachel Notley said that small businesses have been battered by years of economic barriers, and the layer of added uncertainty caused by the referendum was unwelcome for folks thinking of starting a business.

“I know many Alberta businesses and possible investors are counting on this question being settled once-and-for-all. As we move forward, let’s commit to delivering that finality for them,” she said.

– Stephanie Levitz

Prime Minister Mark Carney says the outcome of the Alberta referendum question on secession was “a great result for Canada.”

He said Tuesday morning that he had a long call with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith to talk about how Ottawa and the province can move forward in the spirit of co-operative federalism.

Carney also spoke on Parliament Hill about the preliminary results on the nine referendum questions that did not relate to separation, suggesting Albertans want more control over immigration and noting Ottawa has already brought down the number of people allowed into the country in recent years.

He said what happens next on immigration policy will require discussions with the provinces.

The federal government tables an annual plan for immigration every fall, with the next one expected within weeks.

Voters in Alberta also appear to be in favour of certain constitutional reforms, but Carney is suggesting there are steps that should be taken first before going that route.

Carney is gathering with his cabinet for their regular weekly meeting on Tuesday. He has no other public events on his agenda for the day.

Hello, I’m Maura Forrest, a Quebec correspondent for The Globe based in Montreal.

Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is not planning to make a public statement about the results of the Alberta referendum, according to spokesperson Alexandre Tanguay.

St-Pierre Plamondon, who will be sworn in as premier on Wednesday after winning an Oct. 5 provincial election, has promised to hold a third referendum on independence in Quebec, though not before 2029.

The Parti Québécois leader has acknowledged having contact with the Alberta separatist movement, though the party’s official position is to stay out of Alberta’s business.

Opposition Liberal Leader Charles Milliard is the only one of the province’s major party leaders to have commented on the results as of Tuesday morning. “The results reflect a desire to come together and work to build Canada rather than divide it,” he said in a social media statement.

Andre Harpe, a farmer and chair of the Canadian Canola Growers Association, said Tuesday he is “very relieved” about the referendum result.

Alberta is the second largest producer of canola, Canada’s most lucrative crop, and a vote in favour of a binding referendum would have added uncertainty for an industry already grappling with complex trade challenges, he said. “We don’t need anything else to disrupt our exports and our living.”

Roger Chevraux, a farmer and director at Alberta Canola, agrees that a vote for separation would have been bad for Canadian agriculture.

But he is concerned that Ottawa will return to its “long history” of ignoring issues faced by Albertans.

In January, Carney inked a deal with Beijing that would permit a select number of Chinese-made electric vehicles to enter Canada at a reduced tariff rate in exchange for lowered levies on Canadian Canola exports. Under the government of former prime minister Justin Trudeau, a decision to impose a 100-per-cent tariff on Chinese-made electric vehicles had provoked tariffs on canola.

“I think Carney made that deal because he was worried about Alberta,” said Chevraux.

Federal NDP Leader Avi Lewis is holding a news conference Tuesday morning in Ottawa to share his reaction to the referendum.

He says he is heartened that Albertans have voted to stay in Canada.

But he says the frustrations that fuelled the separatist debate won’t disappear now that the referendum is over. Lewis says fixing the challenges in Alberta requires people working together, not turning on each other.

The NDP has one seat in the province: the riding of Edmonton-Strathcona, held by Heather McPherson.

Lewis paid tribute to McPherson’s efforts to fight for national unity and to raise questions in the House of Commons about potential foreign meddling in the referendum campaign.

The NDP Leader says more light must be shed on whether American-aligned operatives were involved with the Leave side.

The Business Council of Alberta is joining a chorus of industry voices welcoming the result of the referendum question on separation.

Council president Adam Legge said he is “delighted” by voters’ decision that Alberta should remain a province of Canada. He said in a statement on Tuesday that voting to stay allows Alberta to continue to build on its economic strengths.

“It is now time to move forward and get Alberta focused on generating prosperity and opportunity through economic expansion, job creation, innovation and education,” said Legge. “Enough time has been lost to this referendum. There’s much work to do.”

– Stefanie Marotta

Hi, I’m Stefanie Marotta, a business reporter at The Globe and Mail. I cover Canadian banks and the industry’s regulators.

Now that Bay Street has spent the early hours of the morning absorbing Alberta’s decision to remain in Canada, I’m chasing industry reaction.

Bank of Nova Scotia chief executive officer Scott Thomson said the result of the vote demonstrates that Canadians “see something worth building together,” even during periods of strain.

“I am more optimistic today than I have been in years,” Thomson said in a statement. “There is growing recognition of the province’s importance to Canada’s economic future, and new momentum behind the projects needed to realize its potential.”

Thomson spent much of his career in Alberta and around its natural resources sector. He previously served as CEO of construction equipment dealer Finning International Inc. – its Canadian headquarters is in Edmonton – and, before that, as chief financial officer of Calgary-based Talisman Energy Inc.

Alberta boasts the second-largest share of Canada’s $1.1-trillion project inventory over the next decade, according to research from the Scotia Growth Institute. With an additional estimated $120-billion in upstream oil and gas development capital related to Pacific Link and LNG opportunities, Alberta would make up the largest share, Thomson said.

Ottawa’s efforts to accelerate project timelines are having an impact, he told The Globe last month.

The “emotionally charged” question of whether Alberta should separate from Canada has been answered, TD chief economist Beata Caranci said in a Tuesday morning report, but that “does not end the conversation.”

“A non-trivial share of Albertans supported separation and their concerns May linger,” she said. “Businesses and investors will be looking for evidence of enduring certainty. This should be the case for the next five years.”

Her five-year timeline is based on the provincial legislation that allowed the referendum to take place, which prohibits similar proposals for five years following an unsuccessful vote.

But Caranci warned that “with a relatively low voter threshold that enables the question to come back on the ballot, investors will be looking for signs on whether Alberta risks a perpetual five-year cycle of constitutional uncertainty.”

The five-year window “affords time to rebuild broader investor confidence that a predictable backdrop is here to stay,” she said. “From an economic lens, this is particularly important when courting investment in large capital projects where the timeframe from proposal to operation spans multiple government election cycles.”

According to a survey conducted by the Alberta Chamber of Commerce, 44 per cent of businesses in the province said the separation debate was affecting their operations, with many indicating investments or projects had been delayed, scaled back or cancelled.

“With the results of the vote, some delayed investment decisions May now move forward,” Caranci said.

Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston issued a statement on X pointing to residents’ many links to Alberta.

“Canada is stronger with Alberta as part of it, and last night’s results show the overwhelming majority of Albertans agree with this,” he said.

“Many Nova Scotians have strong ties to Alberta, either having worked there or with friends and family going to their province to help build up their industry. Here in Nova Scotia, we’ll keep doing our part to develop our own natural resources, create opportunities, and contribute to a stronger Canada.”

Newfoundland and Labrador Premier Tony Wakeham is “delighted” that Alberta has voted to remain a part of Canada.

Speaking to reporters at the techNL Summit in St. John’s on Tuesday morning, Wakeham said his province has always had a “strong connection with Alberta.”

“We joke sometimes that there is as many people from Newfoundland and Labrador living in Alberta as there is living in our province,” he said. “I will say this, that as a country, I think we have more that unites us than divides us, and in my year in this position I have come to recognize that. I am very delighted from the results.”

Asked to respond to the fact that roughly one in four Albertans voted in favour of a separation vote, Wakeham said that was a result of “frustration.”

“There is always frustration with government and how governments work. That is always a challenge,” he said. “Nothing is perfect, and so we have to find ways to keep moving forward and improve the lives of people, whether they are in our own province or in another province.”

Referring to U.S. President Donald Trump, Wakeham added: “Right now, we have a president south of the border who has declared an economic war on us. And what we are seeing is more opportunity than ever for people in Canada to invest in Canada and to talk about what we have to offer the world.”

The business community can breathe easy after Albertans voted to stay in Canada, says the Calgary Chamber of Commerce.

Chamber president Deborah Yedlin said in a statement early on Tuesday that the concerns around the debate on separation have not disappeared overnight, but there is now an opportunity to address them through Canada-wide relationship-building.

“The results provide much needed certainty for businesses to move forward with hiring, planning and investing for the future, allowing us to turn the page and focus our collective energy on the economic opportunities ahead,” she said.

“Alberta’s economic success has been built on more than a century of trade relationships, shared infrastructure and strong connections with partners across Canada. At a time of growing global competition and trade uncertainty, Albertans have delivered a clear mandate: we want to be at the table, helping shape Canada’s prosperity and ensuring our province’s contributions and potential are fully recognized.”

Good morning from Calgary, where the sun is still sleeping. I’m Alanna Smith. I usually cover health for The Globe and Mail, but today I’m going back to my roots to cover Alberta politics.

The headline, for those of you just waking up, is that Albertans have voted overwhelmingly to stay in Canada.

Preliminary results from Elections Alberta as of 7 a.m MT show more than 1.37 million Albertans, or roughly 76 per cent, supported staying in Canada, while more than 438,000, or 24 per cent, elected to launch the legal process to hold a second referendum on secession.

Early results indicate voters in Calgary and Edmonton threw their weight behind Confederation at a rate outpacing their rural counterparts.

While we are still waiting for the results of the other nine questions on topics including immigrants’ access to social programs, judicial appointments and constitutional issues, here are five key takeaways from Monday’s vote to get your morning started. Expect another long day in Alberta politics.

Market reaction to the Alberta referendum results Tuesday “is likely to be more of a sigh of relief,” according to Bank of Montreal chief economist Doug Porter.

In an email, Porter noted the Canadian dollar is strengthening a bit more than other currencies against the U.S. dollar today, though he said this can also be attributed to growing expectations that the Bank of Canada will raise interest rates, possibly as soon as next week.

When he was in Calgary last week, he said the business community wasn’t really that interested in discussing the referendum, “perhaps in part because the polls were so consistent.”

“If anything, the No side fared a bit better than expected,” Porter said.

“And while the issue is unlikely to completely fade away, I suspect the markets will believe the future timeline is long enough that any concerns over uncertainty won’t blunt the investment outlook.”

Clear victory for the federalist side in Alberta’s referendum “removes the worst-case scenario,” according to Brian Clow, but the separatists did well enough to win ongoing relevance.

Clow was deputy chief of staff and Canada-U.S. relations lead in the office of former prime minister Justin Trudeau. In an e-mail, he said the fact that roughly one in four Albertans voted in favour of leaving Canada “can’t be ignored.”

“It’s going to stay a factor in Alberta and national politics for a long time,” he said.

“And there will continue to be voices in the U.S. who would like nothing more than a fractured Canada. The vote is settled, but I expect some Americans will keep stirring the pot. We should be clear-eyed about that.”

Clow, who was directly involved in negotiating the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement on continental free trade, said at a time when Canada is again negotiating with Washington and trying to diversity trade, “a united front matters.”

“Our trading partners were watching, and last night’s vote strengthens Canada’s hand,” he said.

Alberta’s vote to remain in Canada is “unambiguously constructive” for the country’s plans to build massive energy infrastructure projects, according to a Royal Bank of Canada analyst.

As energy producers, utilities and the federal and Alberta governments launch projects that include a new pipeline from the oil sands to Vancouver and an expansion of West Coast natural gas export facilities, RBC analyst Maurice Choy said in a report that Alberta’s decision to remain a province removed “a tail risk that has cast a modest shadow over the sector for certain investors.”

“A unified Canada preserves the legal, regulatory, and financial frameworks that have underpinned the long-dated, contracted/regulated cash flows that have defined much of the sector’s investment thesis,” said Mr. Choy.

“The vote also reinforces Canada’s positioning as a jurisdiction capable of attracting the competitive capital to develop its energy export infrastructure – a critical requirement as global demand for the country’s energy products remains structurally supportive,” the analyst added.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has set a target of $1-trillion in investment in Canada over the next five years, and recently hosted a summit in Toronto to pitch potential projects to many of the world’s largest asset managers.

American outlets are reporting the referendum results through the lens of what it means for President Donald Trump’s trolling of Canada as the 51st state and Alberta secessionists’ attempts to gain U.S. support for independence.

The New York Times published its first story about Monday’s referendum result at 1:47 a.m. ET on Tuesday. Reporter Ian Austen, who is normally based in Ottawa but is in Edmonton for the results, led off his coverage by stating citizens of the “oil-rich Western province” decided to reject “a campaign to try to separate.”

CNN chimed in two hours later with a story that also opened with a reference to Alberta’s vast oil reserves and said the province “rejected the pathway to secession and will remain part of Canada, landing a definitive blow to a fringe but loud campaign which sought support from the US.”

At the Washington Post, the online headline for referendum coverage read: “Alberta voters reject a move toward independence from Canada.” The story appears well down the Post’s home page, next to a feature on the latest instalment of the Victoria’s Secret fashion show.

Fox News, which is regular viewing for more than a third of Americans, had no mention of the Alberta vote on its website’s home page as of 8:30 a.m. on Tuesday.

The Times, which has 13 million subscribers globally, featured a quote from Thomas Lukaszuk, a former provincial politician behind the Forever Canadian campaign. The Times said when the results were first reported, Lukaszuk targeted President Trump by saying the vote “will send a very strong message to the rest of the world: Don’t mess with Canada.”

Mark Little, chief executive officer of Suncor Energy Inc. from 2019 through 2022, said Alberta’s decision to remain in Canada is “very positive” for the province.

Commenting on Alberta Premier Danielle Smith’s LinkedIn post announcing victory for the federalist side, Little added there is still “lots of work to do to achieve Alberta’s full potential in Confederation! Let’s go!!”

Good morning from Ottawa, where the sun is slowly coming up over Parliament Hill. I’m Stephanie Levitz and I cover politics for The Globe.

This morning, NDP Leader Avi Lewis – whose party holds one seat in Alberta – is scheduled to respond to the Alberta referendum results at a 9:30 news conference.

About an hour later, Prime Minister Mark Carney convenes his cabinet for their regular Tuesday meeting.

Carney has already issued a statement about the results of the vote on separation.

But he and his cabinet are likely to be peppered with questions on how Ottawa will respond to the results of the other nine questions on yesterday’s ballot, especially those about immigration reform.

When it comes to currency markets, oil prices matter more than the results of an Alberta referendum that was largely in line with expectations.

The Canadian dollar is gaining strength on Tuesday morning against its U.S. counterpart, but the fossil fuel-linked Norwegian krone is slightly stronger.

“Albertans delivered a solid rejection of separation in yesterday’s referendum. This result and firm oil prices are lifting the Canadian dollar 0.4 per cent this morning,” said a report by Shaun Osborne, chief FX strategist at Bank of Nova Scotia, and FX strategist Eric Theoret.

The Scotiabank team also pointed out the krone is up by 0.45 per cent, and is the top performer among the major currencies so far on Tuesday.

In a statement on X, Ontario Premier Doug Ford welcomed Alberta’s referendum result , calling it decisive and vowing to build new pipelines to the province.

“Alberta voters have overwhelmingly chosen a stronger, more prosperous future for their province by remaining in Canada,” the Premier said.

“I’m thrilled by the decisive support Albertans have shown for the country we all love. Now it’s up to the rest of Canada to deliver on our commitment to Alberta by building new pipelines, unlocking our natural resources and unleashing the prosperity that will protect the future of Canadians from coast to coast to coast.”

Ford has been touting his concept, unveiled last year alongside Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, for a Northern Shield pipeline that would carry oil 3,300 kilometres from Alberta east to Ontario, without crossing into the U.S. as current routes do.

Ontario has signed memorandums of understanding to explore the idea with Alberta and Saskatchewan, but not Manitoba, which has so far declined to participate. There is no cost estimate or private-sector backer for the idea, which is subject to a feasibility study. But Ford has said Ontario taxpayers could put up the cash for the project.

Hi, I’m Jameson Berkow, capital markets reporter here at The Globe.

Corporate Canada is no doubt breathing a sigh of relief this morning as Albertans have made their desire to remain part of Canada clear.

However, the margin of federalist victory might concern some executives, who were broadly hoping for a more crushing separatist defeat.

I’ll be gathering reaction from business leaders across the country and sharing it here throughout the day.

Good morning. I am Andrew Willis, a business reporter based in Toronto.

As the country awoke to news of Albertans’ strong vote to remain in Canada, the first messages from business leaders were a reminder that national unity takes work.

Looking to the future, Canadian Chamber of Commerce chief executive Candace Laing put out a statement that began: “Alberta has clearly chosen to remain in Canada and commit to our shared future. Businesses, workers and communities can feel more confident with this result.”

“A strong Canada means that we need to make sure every part of our federation knows their essential value and that they feel valued and understood by the whole country,” she said.

“Alberta is central to economic security and opportunity in Canada and we must now turn our attention squarely to the needed work to collaboratively build a stronger, resilient, united economy from coast to coast to coast,” said Laing, who grew up in Saskatchewan and was an executive at fertilizer producer Nutrien, one of the country’s largest exporters.

With the separation question settled, Alberta is in the process of counting the nine other referendum questions on immigration and constitutional issues that Premier Danielle Smith put on the ballot.

Some of the questions propose various measures centred around taking more control over immigration. Several of the constitutional questions ask voters if they support the provincial government working with other provinces toward constitutional amendments that would give them greater control over judicial appointments and how they spend federal money.

The results of those votes are too early or close to call, with millions more ballots to be counted.

Elections Alberta has said final results for these questions would come much later than the separation question.

Being a separatist means being an optimist. Take Tanya Clemens, one of the leaders of Let Alberta Decide. On Monday night, before Elections Alberta’s early results confirmed that the federalists prevailed, Clemens said she believed her side would come out on top.

“There was such an opportunity in front of us, that I believe that Albertans had so many grievances with Ottawa, that this was the big opportunity to be able to resolve some of those,” she said. “Even if you weren’t supporting independence, I really think this was an opportunity to solve those grievances.”

Clemens said she believes in independence, but there is a chance Alberta Premier Danielle Smith could win her back now if she can turn the referendum results into a bargaining chip with Ottawa, though it would take opening the Constitution to redistribute power, revamp the Senate and address Alberta’s grievances over equalization.

If Smith can, in fact, turn the referendum into a negotiating tool, Clemens thinks the United Conservative Party leader has a shot at healing the party’s wounds. Perhaps, she said, if Smith extracts concessions from Ottawa, the separatists in the party will see value in staying in the country.

Mitch Sylvestre and Jeff Rath started doing interviews shortly after the first results were released. By then, the crowd at the Alberta Prosperity Project event at The Parlour in downtown Edmonton had started to thin out.

Asked how he was doing, Sylvestre said, “not great,” but said he’s not surprised by the result.

Sylvestre said the referendum was his first option to try moving forward his agenda. Now, he’s looking at what he’s viewed as the second option.

“You have to get involved in government. That’s the different way,” he said, though he added he believes an independence party would have slim chances of winning a general election.

Rath continued his threats to unseat Premier Danielle Smith through a party leadership vote. “The next phase for us moving forward is an institutional phase where we move forward to take control back of our party, which is the United Conservative Party of Alberta,” Rath said. “And we will form government. Period.”

When asked whether he accepts the result as representing the will of Albertans, Rath replied, “It’s the result tonight following a campaign where everything was stacked against us.”

Voter turnout at a handful of First Nations communities surpassed Elections Alberta’s expectations, the agency said late Monday evening.

Elections Alberta delivered extra ballots to five First Nations, and three of those received multiple shipments, according to agency spokeswoman Michelle Gurney.

Samson Cree Nation, Ermineskin Cree Nation and Louis Bull Tribe – three of the four communities at Maskwacis in central Alberta – received multiple deliveries, Gurney said in a statement.

The Blood Tribe near Lethbridge, Alta., and Whitefish Lake First Nation #459, about 400 kilometres north of Edmonton, also received extra ballots, Gurney said.

“Each voting location receives the ballots we believe they will need based on our data, as well as a ‘buffer’ in case they have additional electors at those locations,” she said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says the referendum results will allow the province and country to move forward together.

“On Oct. 19, Albertans made a clear choice. They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other,” he wrote in a statement published shortly after midnight MT.

“Above all, Albertans chose Canada.”

Carney campaigned in Alberta last Thursday and Friday, capping each day with major rallies – one in Calgary and one in his hometown of Edmonton. The Prime Minister last had a front-row seat to a referendum as governor of the Bank of England in 2016 when the United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union.

“Canada is securing new trade partners around the world, fast-tracking major, nation-building projects in every part of the country, and unleashing our full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta at its core,” Carney wrote in the statement.

Keith Wilson and Tanya Clemens, the leaders of the Let Alberta Decide campaign, took to a small riser in a small room to address a small crowd shortly after midnight.

“Alberta can do better,” Wilson told about a dozen separatist supporters at the Alt Hotel in Calgary, after major news organizations declared the federalist victory in the referendum question on separation.

“Tonight concludes a campaign but the conversation about Alberta’s future in Canada, and our place in Canada, and our role in Canada will continue,” Wilson said. “As we continue this discussion, we will see how we can unleash the power of this province, the wealth of this province, to build not just a prosperous future for our children, but actually help all of Canada.”

The referendum sparked a discussion about the province’s place in Confederation, he said, noting Alberta’s concerns began a century ago.

“Alberta is treated differently,” Wilson said. For too long, he said, Albertans have felt like they’ve been held back by forces in Ottawa, and the province does not have “true democratic representation” because Canada has a legislative body driven by population and lacks a “functioning Senate.”

He noted the final results of the separation question have not been tallied, but about 1 in 4 eligible voters who cast a ballot indicated they want to change Alberta’s relationship with the rest of Canada.

“At least a quarter of Albertans feel that Alberta needs to be treated better, that Alberta can do better,” Wilson said.

Thomas Lukaszuk, the leader of Forever Canadian, said he’s proud of being an Albertan tonight.

“We have shown with this result that we all want to belong to Canada,” the former MLA told the crowd at his pro-unity group’s watch party in Edmonton, closing out for the night.

“I know not all the results are here yet, but at least we know where we stand on this important day.”

But Lukaszuk said it is important to continue a meaningful dialogue with the smaller percentage that voted in favour of separation.

“We cannot go on like this,” he said of separatists. “Some of the issues they have raised are legitimate. And we must make sure we use common language to speak with them, to keep talking to them. As Canadians and Albertans, we cannot go on fighting with each other like this. I don’t want to see us doing another referendum like this ever again.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says she’s “very pleased” with early results on the separation question.

“I’m very pleased to see the initial results from Elections Alberta show widespread support for remaining in Canada,” Smith wrote in a social-media post at 11:49 p.m. MT Monday.

“Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada. Thank you to all Albertans who took time to vote on these critically important referendum questions.”

The Premier said she will be addressing Albertans live at 6:45 p.m. on Tuesday to “discuss the results of all referendum questions for which results are available, and where our province goes from here.”

Smith was not made available to take questions from reporters at any media events or watch parties on Monday.

Albertans have voted to remain in Canada in a referendum that exposed deep grievances within some corners of the province and tested national unity.

The Canadian Press projected the victory for the pro-Canada side at about 11:30 p.m. Mountain Time. As of now, more than 76 per cent of voters have endorsed remaining in Canada with 25 per cent of polls reporting, according to preliminary results on Elections Alberta’s website. The other option – to start the process to hold a binding referendum – has 24 per cent support.

Results on the nine other referendum questions are still coming in.

The small crowd at the pro-unity watch party in Edmonton erupted in loud applause and cheers upon hearing the CBC decision desk making a call that a strong majority of Albertans have voted to remain in Canada.

“Canada! Canada! Canada!” the crowd of about 30 or so people chanted, as CBC anchor Adrienne Arsenault’s live telecast was heard loudly in the Polish Hall at 11:12 p.m. MT Monday night.

Elections Alberta is finally reporting results after the last polls closed late this evening.

The first tally shows nearly 77 per cent of voters have chosen to remain in Canada and roughly 23 per cent voting for a second, binding separation referendum.

Nineteen per cent of locations have reported so far.

Evening, night owls. You May be wondering when Elections Alberta plans to start reporting results.

Elections Alberta just informed me that they’re waiting to confirm that the last polls have closed. Unofficial results will start to roll in when they confirm. Counters have been tallying mail-in and advance ballots since 5 p.m.

Newlyweds Raelene and William Diaz both voted in favour of separation, despite desiring different outcomes.

“I’m actually a federalist in disguise,” Ms. Diaz said, pulling out of her purse a lanyard decorated with Canadian flags. Canadians rescued her grandparents in the Netherlands during the Second World War.

“I obviously carry a sense of national pride from hearing their stories,” she said. “I definitely didn’t take my vote lightly.”

But Alberta has tried various tactics to better its place in Confederation, without luck, Ms. Diaz, 25, said. “This is one more method of making sure our voice actually gets heard this time, and so I’m gonna go for it, I’m going to vote for this.”

She voted for Option 2 – the preferred choice of separatists and those who want Alberta to use support for separation as a bargaining chip with Ottawa.

The pair, who worked together in conservative politics, attended Let Alberta Decide’s referendum watch party Monday evening.

Her husband is more definitive in his secessionist sentiment. He grew up in Quebec and moved to Alberta in 2023. “I see the complete cultural difference between eastern Canada and Western Canada,” he said. “We are a unique, distinct nation. We look at things in a different way than Quebeckers do.”

The pair deal with their differences on separation – however narrow – by turning to what they have in common.

“We have Christ,” Mr. Diaz said. “We have the same Christian values. And ultimately, that’s our goal. To see Alberta, preferably Canada, to see Alberta go back to a Judeo-Christian nation. To see it go back to its biblical roots Canada was founded on.”

One of the last polling stations still open in Alberta, at Westminster School in Edmonton, has now closed for voters after two delays.

Alberta Chief Electoral Officer Gordon McClure had authorized a voting extension in Westminster, requiring it to close at 10 p.m. MT because the site had opened later than scheduled on Monday morning. While most other late-opening polls extended their hours by only 10 or 20 minutes, Westminster remained open for more than two extra hours.

Elections staff and the supervisor at Westminster told me that their late opening occurred because Elections Alberta sent the station 10 ballot boxes instead of their required 30 this morning.

Then, just before 10 p.m. MT, it was extended by 10 more minutes due to a last minute rush of voters.

Now that the final polling stations are closing, voting data will begin to trickle in. However, the results will be slow to arrive. Elections Alberta has said that final results are not expected until around at least 2 a.m. MT.

Good evening again from the NDP supporter party in downtown Calgary, where Opposition Leader Naheed Nenshi just told reporters that he is extremely annoyed that he has to be here tonight.

“I did not have ‘save Canada’ on my summer to-do list,” he said, sporting a Maple Leaf lapel pin and a red and white pocket square. “I wanted to talk about health care and the economy and education and the cost of living.”

The party tonight is to thank volunteers who helped rally the Remain vote, Nenshi said, adding that he was “uplifted by the fact that people really want to save the country.”

We don’t have any results yet, but Nenshi said anything above 75 per cent for the Remain side means the separatist vote is what it was in 1980.

“Every other premier of Alberta has said to the separatists, ‘Try winning an election.’ Only this one has given them everything they wanted and given them the dream of their lifetimes to have a referendum,” he said.

Thomas Lukaszuk was an MLA in Alberta from 2010 to 2014. He was part of the former Progressive Conservative Party of Alberta, whose membership voted in 2017 to merge with the Wildrose Party, forming the United Conservative Party, often called the UCP. Premier Danielle Smith has been the Ucp’s leader since 2022.

On Monday night, Lukaszuk did not mince words when speaking about Smith and her party’s agenda.

Lukaszuk has been campaigning as leader of the citizen-led pro-unity group Forever Canadian, which is hosting a watch party for Alberta’s referendum. He is starkly against “another useless referendum on this separation nonsense after tonight,” he said.

Smith said this month that she will not hold another referendum on Alberta separation, should the majority of her province vote to remain in Canada. But Lukaszuk said he doesn’t believe her.

“Because what exactly is a win with this vote? She gets to decide that,” he said. ”She gets to make that call to say, ‘okay, fine, 70 per cent is enough for me to not do this again.’ But what if she tries it again anyway? Who’s to stop her?”

I’m at the pro-Canada federalist watch party in Edmonton’s Polish Hall, where it’s been a far cry from the crowds that showed up to their rallies across the province in recent weeks.

Just over an hour after the first polls closed in Alberta, a live jazz band here is playing hits such as the Pink Panther theme song. But in front of them is an audience of barely a few dozen supporters.

There are more reporters, photographers and videographers here than voters supporting the pro-unity cause with the group Forever Canadian, which arranged this event. Forever Canadian has held several other well-attended events recently, including one with Prime Minister Mark Carney in Edmonton that drew a crowd of more than 5,000 people this past Friday.

Volunteers for Forever Canadian are tying the lack of attendees on Monday night to results being so late on a weeknight. “People are tired of this, and they’ve done their job by going out to vote for pro-unity,” said former MLA Thomas Lukaszuk, the leader of Forever Canadian.

Jason Stephan, the only United Conservative Party caucus member to publicly say he voted for a binding secession referendum, announced tonight that he won’t be seeking re-election in the next provincial election.

“It is time to step back. I will not be seeking re-election,” Stephan wrote in a letter he posted to social media – barely 45 minutes before the first polls closed. He didn’t say what motivated his decision.

The MLA for Red Deer-South said last month that he was voting for a second, binding separation referendum. Stephan argued that a separation referendum “puts Ottawa on notice,” while voting to remain in Canada “affirms the status quo, a nation in decline, dragging Alberta down with it.”

It triggered a major political headache for Premier Danielle Smith, who has said she would vote to remain in Canada. She responded saying she welcomes a variety of opinions in her party. (Most UCP MLAs have been tight-lipped on how they would vote on the separation question.)

Stephan didn’t mention the referendum in his Monday night letter. He wrote: “The status quo is not the right way for Albertans. Empty words and platitudes do not make it otherwise. Some say they want Unity, but their actions say otherwise.”

Michelle Plante, decked out in black cowboy boots bedazzled with rhinestones, has been working with the Let Alberta Decide team since it opened its doors as a third-party advertiser with Elections Alberta.

“It’s time that decisions are made locally,” she said in an interview at the Let Alberta Decide referendum watch party in a small conference room at the Alt Hotel in Calgary’s downtown. “All of our decisions are made on the other end of the country and they affect every aspect of our lives.”

She favours fully cutting ties with the rest of Canada, but would settle for increased leverage in negotiating more power for the province.

“I would take that. And how did Quebec achieve that? By doing this.”

Plante worries the debate over separation will be stifled if the federalists come out on top in Monday’s referendum.

“The conversation – it needs to stay going,” she said. “Option 1 shuts that conversation down. It says: ‘We’re good with everything. We like the cost of living. We like the taxes we pay. We like equalization.’”

Greetings from The Palomino Smokehouse in downtown Calgary, where roughly 150 NDP supporters and MLAs have gathered for a watch party.

It’s 8:45 p.m. MT. The vibe is upbeat, the beers are flowing, the CBC broadcast is silent on big screens in favour of classic rock tunes for the time being (currently When I’m With You by Sheriff is belting through the bar). Most folks are wearing some kind of pro-unity attire – think Team Canada hockey jerseys, flashing Maple Leaf earrings and the kind of red getups you otherwise only tend to see on July 1. Above me, a large stuffed bison head on the wall has fixed me with a glassy stare.

Opposition Leader Naheed Nenshi is expected to arrive at roughly 9 p.m. MT, his team tell me. He’ll address supporters around 10:15 p.m. MT, when results are due to start coming in.

Extended voting ended quietly at a polling station in Calgary, west of downtown, at A.E. Cross School in Glenbrook. The polling station was one of more than 100 in the province that had extended hours on Monday after a delayed opening. A.E. Cross closed at 8:20 p.m., and like most of the polling stations that were open later than planned, it was a relatively modest extension after the official 8 p.m. end of voting. The A.E. Cross station was slow to open because of a sick staffer.

Amanda Burgener, the site supervisor for Elections Alberta, said the polling station was busy in the morning and saw a steady trickle through the day. But it was slower than she thought it might be, and she noted the high advance voting numbers.

Most polls have closed across the province as we move deeper into the 8 p.m. hour. As we reported earlier, however, the last poll is now expected to close at 10 p.m. MT. Votes won’t be reported until then.

That will start the slow roll toward getting a final result. Elections Alberta told us months ago to expect a final result on the separation question between 2 and 4 a.m. MT.

Alberta polling stations have begun to close as scheduled at 8 p.m. MT, but this one will be the last to close at 10 p.m. MT.

There are dozens of locations closing late due to delays opening on Monday morning, which is causing first results to be pushed back.

Hello again! Live, from Let Alberta Decide’s referendum watch party.

This separatist faction is home to lawyer Keith Wilson and farmer Tanya Clemens, who tried to appeal to Alberta’s separatist-curious crowd as more palatable representatives of the secessionist movement than Mitch Sylvestre and Jeff Rath.

This group pushed hard on the idea that voting for Option 2 – to kickstart the legal process to have a second, binding referendum on leaving – would give Alberta leverage over Ottawa. It wouldn’t mean really leaving because that commitment would come later, they argued.

Howdy, and good evening. I’m at The Parlour, a restaurant in downtown Edmonton where supporters with the Alberta Prosperity Project have gathered for referendum night.

People are mixing and mingling. CBC and Global News’s referendum coverage are playing on the TVs above me. Jeffrey Rath, the separatist leader who organized meetings with the U.S. State Department earlier this year, just arrived.

Mitch Sylvestre, chief executive of the pro-independence Alberta Prosperity Project, has two words for how he’s feeling: “Relieved. Peaceful.”

But Sylvestre is already casting doubt on the integrity of the referendum. Leaning against the bar, he told me the presence of mail-in ballots “never sat well with me” and will “tarnish the results here.” Nearly 520,000 Albertans voted by mail in the referendum.

The gun-store owner told me that the fight for a binding independence referendum isn’t over after tonight if the results don’t go his way. He won’t say what that will entail; he’s joining a group of separatist leaders for breakfast.

“If we win, then we go to a referendum. But if we don’t win, then we have to figure out how we get to a referendum.”

Hi, I’m Amir Salehi, a freelance photojournalist who primarily works with The Globe and Mail. I was driving around the Elbow Drive area in Calgary today, looking for signs related to the referendum, when I spotted Evan Saunter riding his scooter with a Canadian flag.

I immediately honked to get his attention, and once I caught up with him, he happily agreed to let me take his photo.

Afterward, Saunter was very friendly and energetic and talked about how much he loves Canada. He told me he was born and raised in Calgary, and supports “unity with everyone.”

“We share much more than what divides us,” he said.

The polling station at Westminster School in Edmonton is one of more than 100 sites that will remain open to voters later than planned, Elections Alberta says.

But staff at the station in the west-central neighbourhood of Glenora did not know they had to remain open until 10 p.m. MT instead of 8 p.m. because Elections Alberta had not told them of the change.

They learned the news around 5 p.m. when a Globe and Mail reporter (me!) showed up, the elections supervisor said.

Elections Alberta issued a press release around 4 p.m, stating that Chief Electoral Officer Gordon McClure authorized the extension at dozens of stations. “Late openings were due to various issues that have been resolved,” the release stated without providing details about the issues.

While most polls extended their hours by only 10 or 20 minutes , Westminster is the only one to remain open for two extra hours.

Howdy, Carrie Tait here. I am one of The Globe and Mail’s reporters in Calgary. I will be hanging out with a separatist faction that will set up camp in Calgary to watch the results roll in tonight.

But first, I had a quick chat with one of the group’s ideological foes: Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas, who views this exercise in direct democracy as harmful, both socially and economically. The questions, he said, demand nuance, but the only answers available are yes or no.

He is frustrated at the overall process, not just the separation question, or the cluster of questions about immigration, or the ones focused on constitutional reforms.

He illustrated his point by recounting a question a student, probably in Grade 5 or 6, asked him when spending the week at city hall on a school program.

“I have never felt my heart so broken as when one of the children asked me – quote, unquote: ‘Am I a real Canadian?’” Farkas said. “No child should ever have to ask.”

G’day again, Emma Graney in Calgary here.

In Australia, my homeland, we have a tradition called the “Democracy Sausage.” Because our elections are on Saturdays and voting is compulsory, the community buildings that typically host polling stations use elections as fundraising events. Alongside bake sales, you’ll find sausage sizzles – the Aussie culinary delicacy of a barbecued sausage on a slice of white bread, slathered in tomato sauce (translation: ketchup).

I tell you this because a Calgary bar, Bottlescrew Bill’s, is stimulating democracy by awarding a free beer to those who turn up with an “I voted!” sticker.

“We want to encourage dialogue and conversation, because it matters,” said co-owner Geoff Allan. “In Calgary, there’s historically a pretty low voter turnout. If this is going to get people out, we’re happy to encourage it.”

While Democracy Sausages would be the perfect accompaniment to free beer, they are, alas, not on tonight’s menu.

At 4 p.m. in Olds, a town of about 10,000 people an hour north of Calgary, a steady stream of voters strolled in and out of the Regional Exhibition building. Signing in and casting a ballot took about 10 minutes.

Arlene Graham immigrated to Canada from the Philippines in the mid-1990s when she was 24. She has lived in Olds for several decades and works as an educational assistant at a local school.

She voted to take a step towards separation, but did so to register her frustrations with the federal government, she said.

“It’s just hearing the voice of the people, that they’re fed up,” Graham said.

“I don’t agree with separation but I guess if it comes to that, if the government doesn’t change, then I will be leaning towards that.”

Elections Alberta says dozens of polls will stay open later than expected tonight, pushing back when the first results will be reported to 10 p.m. MT.

Voting was scheduled to close at 8 p.m., but Elections Alberta says more than 100 voting locations will stay open later because of delays opening the polls. A statement from Elections Alberta says Chief Electoral Officer Gordon McClure has authorized the extension under the Election Act.

“Late openings were due to various issues that have been resolved,” Elections Alberta said in a statement.

While most poll locations have extended their hours by only 10 or 20 minutes, one poll in Edmonton will remain open until 10 p.m.

That means we won’t receive first results until after 10 p.m., as no results can be reported until all polling stations have closed. Elections workers will start hand-counting from mail-in and advance voting at 5 p.m.

Sheila Taylor, 60, said she’s not a separatist, though she voted in favour of that option on Monday.

“I definitely think I’m in the minority here in Edmonton voting that way today, especially in this urban area. But I know a lot of people are frustrated, and they want their voices to be heard,” she said outside a downtown polling station.

“With this high price of living, no jobs available because of immigration being so high, and just so many other problems under Carney’s federal government, what kind of future are we giving our grandchildren if we allow things to be the way they are right now?”

Leading up to voting day, Taylor said she had been “a fence-sitter,” not sure which side she’d vote for.

“Ultimately, for me, it became a decision of just saying that I’m okay with Prime Minister Mark Carney doing whatever he wants with the rest of the country – but just leave us in Alberta alone and out of it, please,” she said.

Barbara Schmidt, an Elections Alberta officer who has been working at multiple polling stations in Edmonton, said Monday’s turnout in the city is much larger than she’d expected.

“I have seen steady streams of people and long lines at each of the polls I’ve been to so far,” she said late afternoon at the downtown All Saints’ Anglican Cathedral.

“I don’t know numbers yet, but it’s been very, very busy everywhere in the city today, even with so many people doing advance voting.”

Across Calgary’s north side, voters are quietly filing inside polling stations where there are few lines to speak of. There’s more energy on the roadways where vehicles are buzzing past with Canadian or Alberta flags and on front lawns where signs pledging allegiance to either group are displayed proudly.

In the community of Saddleridge, 36-year-old Mandy Sidhu quickly cast her vote inside a local high school.

She’s voted against separation but had varied answers for the other nine questions on topics regarding such issues as immigration and health care. Sidhu said she’s been put off by separatist supporters who have loudly voiced their opinions without giving mind to people with opposing views.

“I feel like they’re just deciding for themselves. They don’t really care what we’re thinking,” she said. “I just don’t think it’s fair that they’re separating us.”

– Nathan VanderKlippe

“People think this is about leaving,” says James Wocknitz, 64.

They’re wrong, he says: “It’s about leverage.”

Wocknitz has retired from a career working on drilling rigs. He favours the idea of an independent Alberta – he was among those who signed a petition demanding a referendum. He moved from B.C. three decades ago, but grew angry when he learned about the billions of dollars in transfer payments from Alberta that are sent to other provinces every year.

“That was probably the turning point for me, when I heard about that,” he said.

He is nonetheless skeptical of independence ever being achieved, in part because he has little faith the rest of Canada would allow Alberta to leave.

Maybe, he said, independence isn’t even necessary.

“If we get negotiating leverage, then all that’s moot,” he said. “That’s what we want. We want to be listened to.”

Delena Barker, a retired accountant and union leader from Toronto, moved to Alberta 15 years ago and has lived in the town of Sundre for the past decade.

At the local Royal Canadian Legion, she enthusiastically voted yes to all the referendum questions and to take steps toward separation. She would also vote yes in a future secession ballot. To her mind, Ottawa has way too much power and all provinces should fight for more independence.

“The federal government has become a dictator and it’s time for the West to quit supporting Eastern Canada,” Barker said outside the legion on a sunny autumn afternoon.

Thinking of her years back east, she said there’s a distinct character to Alberta and Albertans.

“We’re a different type of people,” she said, “and I say we now because I feel I’m an Albertan.”

Brooke Healy has many childhood memories at the Royal Canadian Legion in Vulcan, Alta. It’s where the family gathered for birthdays. It’s where they came to remember her grandfather’s military service. And on Monday, it’s where she came to vote to remain in Canada.

She couldn’t help but think of her grandfather as she marked her ballot.

“There’s been many instances in history where we have come together despite differences in culture and religion,” she said. “To separate that would be a loss.”

As a younger woman, “I was very much more like with the Wexit movement,” she said, referring to a Western secessionist movement.

But Healy, 22, is preparing to become a teacher and her studies of Canadian history have changed her thinking.

Unity, she says, does not mean conformity – and she hopes Ottawa will do a better job of listening to provincial concerns.

Nonetheless, “unity as a country only makes us stronger.”

G’day, everyone. I’m Matthew Scace with The Globe’s Alberta bureau, coming to you from Edmonton. A few readers have sent us questions about today’s referendum – particularly around the nine other referendum questions and the size of Alberta’s electorate.
