MIDDLESEX COUNTY (October 19, 2026) –Middlesex County is proud to be celebrating Local Government Week and the important role municipal government plays in building strong communities.

This week, Middlesex County will highlight the people, partnerships, and services key to its success. Through essential services like infrastructure, housing, paramedic services, long-term care, and community supports, Middlesex County staff are focused on making our communities great places to call home.

"Local Government Week is an opportunity to recognize the essential role we have in supporting residents," said Middlesex County Warden Sue Clarke. "Local governments are working tirelessly to build strong, vibrant, and welcoming communities now and into the future.”

Middlesex County serves a large and diverse geographic area, supporting communities across the region by collaboration with local municipalities, community organizations, and the provincial and federal governments.

Residents are encouraged to take this opportunity to learn more about local government and the services provided by Middlesex County. Join us on our social media channels each day this week to learn more our services and initiatives.

Middlesex County is an innovative, well-run organization offering high-value programs and services to the best community in which to live, visit, and do business in Southwestern Ontario. The County serves a vibrant, growing community of 81,700 people and offers a great place to call home, offering exceptional lifestyle, a wide variety of local attractions, and wonderful sense of community.

MEDIA CONTACT:

Middlesex County Media Relations Legislative Services Division mediarelations@middlesex.ca

Middlesex County is a great place to call home. Our modern telecommunications infrastructure, excellent health and social services, retail shopping, recreation facilities, beautiful landscapes and great people, make Middlesex the place to be!

stories.title: Are our drug laws making things worse?
stories.summary: A look at the politicization of harm reduction efforts and how initiatives like Dulf could be the solution to B.C.'s drug crisis.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
A B.C. Supreme Court judge found that a section of Canada’s Controlled Drug and Substances Act was unconstitutional, and gave Ottawa six months to fix it.

The ruling came after a pair of drug activists, Eris Nyx and Jeremy Kalicum, were convicted on drug trafficking charges after their downtown Vancouver compassion club, DULF, was raided by police in 2023. Their charges have since been stayed.

Host Maria Kestane speaks to Michelle Gamage, a health reporter from The Tyee , and Dr. Dan Small, a medical anthropologist with the University of British Columbia, to discuss the politicization of harm reduction efforts, and how initiatives like DULF could be the solution to B.C.’s drug crisis.

stories.title: Manitoba grieves with CFB Wainwright after deadly fire
stories.summary: Several Manitoba politicians are offering their condolences to those who were killed and seriously injured at Canadian Forces Base in Wainwright on Saturday.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
Manitoba politicians are offering their condolences to those who were killed and seriously injured at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on Saturday.

Four people were killed and dozens of others injured after a grass fire ignited during a live-fire training exercise and rapidly spread in high winds. Flags at CFB Winnipeg and federal buildings across the province were lowered to half-mast Sunday.

Premier Wab Kinew called the fire is a terrible tragedy and said his heart goes out to everyone affected.

“Manitoba stands ready to help in any way we can,” Kinew said in a social media post.

Jeff Fawcett, mayor of Brandon, said the loss is felt across the nation. He described Brandon as a “military city” because of its proximity to CFB Shilo.

Fawcett said some people from CFB Shilo could be deployed to Wainwright or have connections to the base, as cross-training is common.

Watch the video above for the full story.

stories.title: Lasting impact expected from historic Alberta referendum, regardless of result
stories.summary: Alberta electors are to also weigh in on nine other questions on policies linked to immigration and possible constitutional reforms.
stories.author: Devon Dekuyper
stories.content:
Albertans cast their ballots Monday in a historic referendum that could have lasting effects on the political landscape, regardless of the vote’s results.

Among the 10 questions on the ballot was one that asked whether Albertans preferred to remain a part of Canada or to begin the process of holding a binding referendum on separation.

“I don’t think most people really want to separate,” said Brayden Temple, a Calgary-Shaw voter. “But it’s time to get our voices heard a bit more here in Alberta.”

Although he is optimistic about a recent slate of pipeline-related announcements, he said he wanted the province to have the power to reject any federal regulations on energy companies to attract more investment.

“If we could get rid of some of that, which I think is what the Conservatives’ goals kind of are, that would be good because we’re a resource nation, right?” said Temple who works in health care but whose father, he added, worked in the oil and gas sector.

The other nine questions relate to policies related to immigration and potential changes to the Constitution.

For Rexall Sillito, who graduated high school last year, maintaining status quo is the wiser choice.

“I mostly voted in immigration favour, as some people moving to Canada do need help coming here and they kind of need that head start,” Sillito. But he feels the referendum itself isn’t a wasted exercise. Instead it’s a way to roar at Ottawa to snatch up some benefits it wouldn’t have otherwise had.

“Quebec did that once, and that’s how Quebec got so many benefits that a bunch of the other provinces don’t have,” Sillito said.

However, that doesn’t mean the Alberta should yank all of Ottawa’s power to hold the province accountable

Elections Alberta has recorded strong turnout for mail-in ballots and advance polls. Those who have yet to cast their ballot were told to vote as early as they can Monday and to anticipate lineups. However, several polling stations in Calgary’s south were relatively quieter with little to no line ups.

Betty Evans stopped by Riverside School in northeast Calgary on Monday, curious to see how busy the polling station was.

Evans, who had already cast her ballot by mail, said an election officer told her voters had lined up before the polls opened Monday morning, but that the station had been relatively quiet since.

For Evans, voting in the referendum felt like an important action. Having already voted by mail, a process she described as “pretty simple,” Evans said she is now eager to see the results.

Polls are open from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m., but complete results for all referendum questions aren’t likely to come before Wednesday evening. Elections Alberta is required to have all ballots hand-counted within 48 hours of polls closing, but with 10 questions on separate ballots — making this the largest referendum in Canada’s history — the task will be monumental.

Question 10 — the separation question — will be counted first, followed by questions one through nine in order.

Emily Faye, an agronomist, spent several weeks researching those questions to make up her mind.

“I’ve just been making my own decision of which way I want to vote, rather than what my friends say or what my family says or whatever that might be,” she told Postmedia.

Eventually, she realized the referendum was her opportunity to tell Ottawa “we’re not going to be a pushover anymore, and it’s not about Alberta leaving Canada. It’s about the West having more say in this country.”

That means taking back control over immigration and federal funding, even though some of them would require agreement from the majority of the country’s provinces.

“We produce a lot of Canada’s economy over here, and we get forgotten about when it comes to a federal election because by the time Toronto votes, it’s already decided, right?” said Faye, whose family hails from Saskatchewan.

While legislation requires vote officials to complete the count within the 48-hour timeframe, there aren’t any legislated penalties or consequences if the deadline isn’t met, Elections Alberta spokesperson Maia Hanrahan said.

“We’re expecting to meet that requirement, and that’s why we’ve put out the call for so many ballot counters,” she said. “Regardless, though, we’ll be completing that count regardless of how long it takes.”

As of Friday, 47,000 workers have been hired, but Elections Alberta originally set a target of 60,000 additional workers.

The counting of mail-in and advance vote ballots will begin at 5 p.m. Monday, but no results will be published until all voting stations have closed, said Hanrahan.

Voting stations are scheduled to close at 8 p.m., but May stay open longer to accommodate anyone queued at that hour, she said.

“That result site will wait to be published until all locations are confirmed as closed.”

Over the course of the five-day advance vote period, 837,791 ballots were cast, Elections Alberta said, while the agency added it has received and processed 519,082 mail-in or special ballots. The 1,356,873 total represents a turnout of 43.1 per cent.

The 2023 general election saw a 60.5 per cent turnout rate in total, with 1,764,915 valid ballots cast. Just over half were cast on election day, while 757,453 ballots were cast during advance voting and 51,351 were by special ballot.

Elections Alberta has yet to release a cost for the referendum.

Mount Royal University political science professor Lori Williams said that while the turnout has been promising so far, it’s difficult to predict how it will translate to Monday’s vote.

“It’s hard to game out what people looking at those numbers might decide about whether it’s worth the trouble to stand in the line to vote or not,” she said. “Some are saying it suggests 85 per cent turnout, but I think it’s a bit early to tell.”

Some advance voters have reported their wait to only be minutes long, while others have been in line for hours.

“So much is unprecedented here that we just don’t know,” she said. “I see really good signs of commitment, people who think it’s important enough to stand in line. I just don’t know if the final numbers will be sufficient to actually reflect the will of the full range of Albertans or not.”

MRU public policy professor Duane Bratt said there have been elections in the past with high turnout at the advance poll, but no overall impact on total turnout.

“It just shows that people want to vote when they want to vote,” he said. “But when you calculate the degree of the advance polls combined with the mail-in votes with what Elections Alberta is projecting, this could have one of the largest voter turnouts in an Alberta election in decades.”

There are 10 questions on the referendum, nine of which, the province said, came from the recommendations from the Alberta Next panel hosted last year, which aimed to hear from Albertans about how the province’s sovereignty could be enhanced within a united Canada.

The panel consisted of 10 public town hall meetings across the province and one online meeting, attended by a total of more than 5,000 Albertans, who were then surveyed.

Three additional online surveys were conducted, each polling 1,000 Albertans. The resulting report made seven recommendations , which included holding a referendum on the province increasing control of immigration and looking into several constitutional amendments.

The report also recommended a referendum on establishing an Alberta Pension Plan to replace the Canada Pension Plan for Albertans, but that question is not on Monday’s ballot.

Of the nine questions, five are immigration-related, and four are regarding constitutional changes .

The 10th question on separation was prompted by a citizen-led petition asking the province to hold a referendum on separation and another asking for the government to reject separatism , which together garnered around 700,000 signatures.

However, despite the petitions meeting the signature threshold, a court decision ruled that a binding referendum on separation couldn’t be held without first undergoing a consultation process with First Nations.

Instead, the province added question 10 as it reads on the ballot, which asks voters whether Alberta should remain in Canada, or whether the province should begin the legal process of holding a binding referendum to leave Confederation.

Recent polls have found that support for the latter option ranges anywhere from 22 to 33 per cent, but the outcome will likely come down to turnout.

If option one wins, he said, the margin will make a big difference in how the separatist movement responds.

“The other possibility is that the party splits, the separatists get kicked out, they form their own party,” she said. “Do we then have Wildrose and Progressive Conservative again, and all of the implications of that?”

Speaking at an event in Calgary Friday, former premier and UCP co-founder Jason Kenney suggested the party should purge itself of separatists , while Smith herself did not address this point.

As far as the other nine questions go, there’s some speculation as to how the results will be leveraged.

“You could have a situation where (Smith) continues to go forward on some of these things, even if they are defeated,” Bratt said.

Question five, for example, asks about a requirement for proof of citizenship to vote, but the province is already adding citizenship to drivers’ licences.

“Are they going to reverse course?” Bratt said. “They’re going to interpret the results how they want.”

Such an outcome wouldn’t be unprecedented. When the province held a referendum on switching to permanent daylight time in 2021, 50.2 per cent voted no. However, more recently, the Alberta government implemented permanent daylight time anyway.

Williams added that the province already has the power to act on the first five questions without a referendum vote, and the four constitutional questions would require buy-in from other provinces regardless of the vote’s outcome.

“This is one of the reasons why people are wondering why the questions are on the referendum, because the province has power to do these things or doesn’t have power to do these things, and this vote isn’t going to make any difference,” she said.

“This is not grassroots democracy,” Bratt added. “All of the questions were chosen by the government. Why are we talking about immigration and not pensions or data centres? The government made that choice. The government wrote the questions.”

Among the 10 questions on the ballot was one that asked whether Albertans preferred to remain a part of Canada or to begin the process of holding a binding referendum on separation.
“I don’t think most people really want to separate,” said Brayden Temple, a Calgary-Shaw voter. “But it’s time to get our voices heard a bit more here in Alberta.”

Although he is optimistic about a recent slate of pipeline-related announcements, he said he wanted the province to have the power to reject any federal regulations on energy companies to attract more investment.

“If we could get rid of some of that, which I think is what the Conservatives’ goals kind of are, that would be good because we’re a resource nation, right?” said Temple who works in health care but whose father, he added, worked in the oil and gas sector.
The other nine questions relate to policies related to immigration and potential changes to the Constitution.
For Rexall Sillito, who graduated high school last year, maintaining status quo is the wiser choice.

“I mostly voted in immigration favour, as some people moving to Canada do need help coming here and they kind of need that head start,” Sillito. But he feels the referendum itself isn’t a wasted exercise. Instead it’s a way to roar at Ottawa to snatch up some benefits it wouldn’t have otherwise had.
“Quebec did that once, and that’s how Quebec got so many benefits that a bunch of the other provinces don’t have,” Sillito said.
However, that doesn’t mean the Alberta should yank all of Ottawa’s power to hold the province accountable

Elections Alberta has recorded strong turnout for mail-in ballots and advance polls. Those who have yet to cast their ballot were told to vote as early as they can Monday and to anticipate lineups. However, several polling stations in Calgary’s south were relatively quieter with little to no line ups.
Betty Evans stopped by Riverside School in northeast Calgary on Monday, curious to see how busy the polling station was.
Evans, who had already cast her ballot by mail, said an election officer told her voters had lined up before the polls opened Monday morning, but that the station had been relatively quiet since.
For Evans, voting in the referendum felt like an important action. Having already voted by mail, a process she described as “pretty simple,” Evans said she is now eager to see the results.

Polls are open from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m., but complete results for all referendum questions aren’t likely to come before Wednesday evening. Elections Alberta is required to have all ballots hand-counted within 48 hours of polls closing, but with 10 questions on separate ballots — making this the largest referendum in Canada’s history — the task will be monumental.
Question 10 — the separation question — will be counted first, followed by questions one through nine in order.
Emily Faye, an agronomist, spent several weeks researching those questions to make up her mind.
“I’ve just been making my own decision of which way I want to vote, rather than what my friends say or what my family says or whatever that might be,” she told Postmedia.

Eventually, she realized the referendum was her opportunity to tell Ottawa “we’re not going to be a pushover anymore, and it’s not about Alberta leaving Canada. It’s about the West having more say in this country.”
That means taking back control over immigration and federal funding, even though some of them would require agreement from the majority of the country’s provinces.

“We produce a lot of Canada’s economy over here, and we get forgotten about when it comes to a federal election because by the time Toronto votes, it’s already decided, right?” said Faye, whose family hails from Saskatchewan.

While legislation requires vote officials to complete the count within the 48-hour timeframe, there aren’t any legislated penalties or consequences if the deadline isn’t met, Elections Alberta spokesperson Maia Hanrahan said.

“We’re expecting to meet that requirement, and that’s why we’ve put out the call for so many ballot counters,” she said. “Regardless, though, we’ll be completing that count regardless of how long it takes.”
As of Friday, 47,000 workers have been hired, but Elections Alberta originally set a target of 60,000 additional workers.
The counting of mail-in and advance vote ballots will begin at 5 p.m. Monday, but no results will be published until all voting stations have closed, said Hanrahan.
Voting stations are scheduled to close at 8 p.m., but May stay open longer to accommodate anyone queued at that hour, she said.
“That result site will wait to be published until all locations are confirmed as closed.”

Over the course of the five-day advance vote period, 837,791 ballots were cast, Elections Alberta said, while the agency added it has received and processed 519,082 mail-in or special ballots. The 1,356,873 total represents a turnout of 43.1 per cent.

The 2023 general election saw a 60.5 per cent turnout rate in total, with 1,764,915 valid ballots cast. Just over half were cast on election day, while 757,453 ballots were cast during advance voting and 51,351 were by special ballot.
Elections Alberta has yet to release a cost for the referendum.
Mount Royal University political science professor Lori Williams said that while the turnout has been promising so far, it’s difficult to predict how it will translate to Monday’s vote.

“It’s hard to game out what people looking at those numbers might decide about whether it’s worth the trouble to stand in the line to vote or not,” she said. “Some are saying it suggests 85 per cent turnout, but I think it’s a bit early to tell.”
Some advance voters have reported their wait to only be minutes long, while others have been in line for hours.

“So much is unprecedented here that we just don’t know,” she said. “I see really good signs of commitment, people who think it’s important enough to stand in line. I just don’t know if the final numbers will be sufficient to actually reflect the will of the full range of Albertans or not.”
MRU public policy professor Duane Bratt said there have been elections in the past with high turnout at the advance poll, but no overall impact on total turnout.

“It just shows that people want to vote when they want to vote,” he said. “But when you calculate the degree of the advance polls combined with the mail-in votes with what Elections Alberta is projecting, this could have one of the largest voter turnouts in an Alberta election in decades.”

stories.title: How Embark is getting Canadians to rethink RESPs, rebuilding trust in the process
stories.summary: Embark has established itself as a key player in a niche financial service, handling education savings for around 425,000 kids, which amounts to $6.5-billion in assets under management
stories.author: Andrew Seale
stories.content:
It’s a critical time for Canada’s economy and its business community. The country needs innovation and growth more than ever, yet businesses across a wide range of industries are facing trade disruptions, rising costs and technological change, among other challenges. This series profiles forward-thinking Canadian companies that are growing their markets by re-examining their business practices and trying new things.

Toronto-based Embark Student Corp. is streamlining education savings with its online platform and simplified onboarding. The challenge is convincing Canadians to care.

Registered education savings plans (RESPs) are a grossly underutilized investment vehicle, says Andrew Lo, chief executive officer of Embark. Only 43 per cent of parents or caregivers have an Resp for their child, according to data from the Financial Consumer Agency of Canada.

“There’s a lack of awareness,” says Mr. Lo. “It’s not well-advertised and it’s complicated to onboard.”

RESPs allow parents to contribute up to $50,000 per child in a tax-sheltered account, collecting investment growth and earning 20 per cent of their annual contributions in grant money through the government’s Canada Education Savings Grant (Cesg). Grants are capped at $500 per year and $7,200 over the account’s lifetime.

Embark has established itself as a key player in this niche financial service, handling education savings for around 425,000 kids, which amounts to $6.5-billion in assets under management.

The company has focused on digitizing the process, including identity verification, the opening of virtual accounts, registering accounts with the Canada Revenue Agency and streamlining the withdrawal process. Embark also connects with Employment and Social Development Canada to ensure eligible low-income Canadians can tap into the Canada Learning Bond, an additional $2,000 incentive for education savings.

Mr. Lo says it’s a disruption of the in-person process offered by the banks. “Any eligible family can open an Resp account in eight minutes.”

Despite this simplified, digital-first approach, Mr. Lo says it’s a challenge to get Canadians to think of contributing to RESPs. It’s also been a challenge for Embark to win their trust.

Originally founded in 1965 as University Scholarships of Canada, Embark has gone through a series of name changes over the years, including Knowledge First Financial. During that time, the company faced legal action, such as a March 2014 settlement with the Ontario Securities Commission regarding compliance and sales supervision deficiencies. The company also faced a 2021 Quebec Superior Court class-action lawsuit over enrolment and early termination fees that named Knowledge First Financial alongside several other high-profile children’s education funds and was settled in July 2025.

Mr. Lo, who previously ran Kanetix (now Rates.CA), an insurance and financial products comparison site, joined Knowledge First Financial in 2023, helping the company rebrand to Embark a few months later. He says the change reflects a shift in how the company works with families. “We pivoted the sales model from advisor-based to digital direct-to-consumer,” he says.

At its peak, the company had around 1,500 investment advisors. Today it has about 30 licensed advisors, less than a third of the business’s 150 employees. Mr. Lo says earning trust amidst any lingering reputational challenges requires transparency.

“Families should understand exactly what they’re paying and why before they commit, with no surprises down the road,” he says. “It also means giving them more choice so their plan can adapt as their circumstances change.”

Jessica Moorhouse, a certified financial counsellor and author of Everything but Money: The Hidden Barriers Between You and Financial Freedom, says it can be challenging for a fintech like Embark to rebuild trust once it’s been broken. “They did a really good rebrand – they have a lot of resources on their blog that are pretty well written,” says Ms. Moorhouse.

But Embark needed to do that to erase all the negative press they had for a very long time, she adds.Ms. Moorhouse says Embark is competing with a growing crop of digital-first solutions offering RESPs, as well as the limited bandwidth of new parents struggling to balance costs and responsibilities.

“A lot of families are struggling to pay rent and/or pay for groceries… they also have to save for retirement, and that can be a priority over saving for their kid’s university education,” she says.

Like Mr. Lo, Ms. Moorhouse says there’s a lack of understanding about how RESPs can be used.

“People are under the impression an Resp is just meant to be used for university, but it actually pays for a lot of different post-secondary, like trade schools,” she says. “There are other options.”

Kevin Oulds is very familiar with how difficult it can be to bring Canadians to the table for financial matters. As co-founder of online estate planning platform Willful, he says it’s an ongoing hurdle.

“There’s a lot of overlap between our audiences,” says Mr. Oulds of Embark. “We both face the same challenges of, how do you get someone to do something they should do, but don’t have to?”

Mr. Oulds says Willful views it as an education challenge rather than a sales challenge. Early on, the company pivoted its focus to educating Canadians about the importance of having a will.

“We believe that once we’ve convinced you having a will is something that you need to do, Willful will be the easiest and best way to do it,” says Mr. Oulds.

But that digital experience also needs to be backed by strong customer relationship management. “[You] have to have a human touch to it and be available to have a real conversation on the phone,” he says. “That’s really helped people who were unsure, unaware of where to start and what to do.”

Mr. Oulds also points to the importance of partnerships when it comes to building trust. (Willful has partnered with Embark in the past to cross-promote their offerings).

Mr. Lo says digital marketing is a key part of Embark’s pivot. The brand advertises on social media and Google as well as YouTube, streaming platforms and television. But it’s also about meeting parents where they are, he says. “We sponsor both local and major sports like the CFL. We’re on the rink boards at all the kids’ arenas.”

Trust takes time to rebuild, but Mr. Lo sees Canadians’ underutilization of RESPs as a business opportunity.

“350,000 kids are born in Canada every year; I’d love to open that many accounts every year,” he says. “My aspiration is to get that through awareness and efficiency in our digital platform – it’s getting there, but it’s just going to take a little bit of time.”

stories.title: Students are paying the price for Ontario’s neglect of private colleges
stories.summary: After years of weak oversight, the sector is rife with problems
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
The rot in the private career college sector has become so bad that the Ontario government had to pause loan payments to students while the provincial police decide if it will launch a criminal probe. The halt of loans to students at all private career colleges is a drastic step that could have been avoided with proper provincial oversight.

The funding pause is now unavoidable, but the Ministry of Colleges, Universities, Research, Excellence and Security needs to work quickly to restore loans and fulfil its duty to provide proper oversight to the sector. Its lax oversight is harming students and legitimate private career colleges, which provide valuable career training in specialized sectors.

Adults with lower socioeconomic backgrounds and newcomers to Canada often choose private career colleges as a practical way to secure better jobs and salaries. The halting of Osap funds has pulled the rug out from underneath for many who are already attending programs and don’t know if they will have the money to continue.

The province’s freeze on loans followed an audit of the Ontario Student Assistance Program at private postsecondary institutions. The audit identified serious concerns, such as inadequate student validations, high concentrations of Osap applications from the same geographic locations, and the involvement of immigration firms. Government documents filed in court suggest that third parties May have been completing student coursework.

For years, Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservative government ignored warnings in the sector. A 2021 Auditor-General report found that the ministry hadn’t effectively carried out its regulatory activities to meet its primary objective of protecting private career college students, and didn’t ensure colleges were providing quality, up-to-date education. The report found the ministry hadn’t met its own target of inspecting all colleges within three years.

A 2023 follow up to the report found that only 35 per cent of the actions recommended had been fully implemented. Another auditor-general report this year documented the shocking state of Ontario’s truck driving schools, finding that some students completed programs without taking the required training. Twenty-five per cent of these colleges were never inspected by the ministry.

With little oversight in recent years, it’s hardly surprising that some private career colleges could become vehicles for suspicious grants and loans. This issue specifically was flagged to the provincial government by an industry association as early as Jan. 2023.

Ballooning Osap costs in recent years should have set off alarm bells at Queen’s Park. Earlier this year, Premier Doug Ford said the financial aid program was “unsustainable.” The government eliminated grants entirely for students at private career colleges, following Ottawa’s 2025 elimination of federal grants for students attending for-profit institutions due to “integrity issues.” Ontario also reduced grants for students at publicly funded universities and colleges, leaving them mostly reliant on loans.

However, over the last decade, the grants given to students at public institutions have been fairly stable. It was the grants at private career colleges that soared, making up 40 per cent of Osap grants in the 2024-25 academic year. Students at all Ontario institutions are being impacted by the problems at a small number of private colleges.

Osap loans need to be restored quickly to students at legitimate colleges. People’s futures are on the line, and they shouldn’t have to pay the price for the lack of scrutiny of bad actors. The government has said third-party financing will be available – it should ensure it is accessible and affordable.

Private career colleges are an important part of the education mix, but the sector requires significantly more oversight to function properly. Ontario needs to get control of the sector by greatly increasing inspections and enforcement, ensuring that all activities are legitimate and that students have good outcomes. Institutions not following the rules should be shut down, and in cases of fraud, criminal charges should be pursued.

It’s simplistic to view private postsecondary institutions as bad and publicly funded ones as good. Just like students at public institutions, private college students deserve high standards and reliable access to financing. Private colleges have a key role to play in career training, and with proper oversight, confidence in the sector can be restored.

The halt of loans to students at all private career colleges is a drastic step that could have been avoided with proper provincial oversight.

The funding pause is now unavoidable, but the Ministry of Colleges, Universities, Research, Excellence and Security needs to work quickly to restore loans and fulfil its duty to provide proper oversight to the sector. Its lax oversight is harming students and legitimate private career colleges, which provide valuable career training in specialized sectors.

Adults with lower socioeconomic backgrounds and newcomers to Canada often choose private career colleges as a practical way to secure better jobs and salaries. The halting of Osap funds has pulled the rug out from underneath for many who are already attending programs and don’t know if they will have the money to continue.

The province’s freeze on loans followed an audit of the Ontario Student Assistance Program at private postsecondary institutions. The audit identified serious concerns, such as inadequate student validations, high concentrations of Osap applications from the same geographic locations, and the involvement of immigration firms. Government documents filed in court suggest that third parties May have been completing student coursework.

For years, Doug Ford’s Progressive Conservative government ignored warnings in the sector. A 2021 Auditor-General report found that the ministry hadn’t effectively carried out its regulatory activities to meet its primary objective of protecting private career college students, and didn’t ensure colleges were providing quality, up-to-date education. The report found the ministry hadn’t met its own target of inspecting all colleges within three years.

A 2023 follow up to the report found that only 35 per cent of the actions recommended had been fully implemented. Another auditor-general report this year documented the shocking state of Ontario’s truck driving schools, finding that some students completed programs without taking the required training. Twenty-five per cent of these colleges were never inspected by the ministry.

With little oversight in recent years, it’s hardly surprising that some private career colleges could become vehicles for suspicious grants and loans. This issue specifically was flagged to the provincial government by an industry association as early as Jan. 2023.

Ballooning Osap costs in recent years should have set off alarm bells at Queen’s Park. Earlier this year, Premier Doug Ford said the financial aid program was “unsustainable.” The government eliminated grants entirely for students at private career colleges, following Ottawa’s 2025 elimination of federal grants for students attending for-profit institutions due to “integrity issues.” Ontario also reduced grants for students at publicly funded universities and colleges, leaving them mostly reliant on loans.

However, over the last decade, the grants given to students at public institutions have been fairly stable. It was the grants at private career colleges that soared, making up 40 per cent of Osap grants in the 2024-25 academic year. Students at all Ontario institutions are being impacted by the problems at a small number of private colleges.

Osap loans need to be restored quickly to students at legitimate colleges. People’s futures are on the line, and they shouldn’t have to pay the price for the lack of scrutiny of bad actors. The government has said third-party financing will be available – it should ensure it is accessible and affordable.

Private career colleges are an important part of the education mix, but the sector requires significantly more oversight to function properly. Ontario needs to get control of the sector by greatly increasing inspections and enforcement, ensuring that all activities are legitimate and that students have good outcomes. Institutions not following the rules should be shut down, and in cases of fraud, criminal charges should be pursued.

It’s simplistic to view private postsecondary institutions as bad and publicly funded ones as good. Just like students at public institutions, private college students deserve high standards and reliable access to financing. Private colleges have a key role to play in career training, and with proper oversight, confidence in the sector can be restored.

stories.title: Report traces alleged Muslim Brotherhood influence in Canada
stories.summary: “Under the radar, Canada is being infiltrated,” says founder and director of the Institute for the Study of Global Antisemitism and Policy.
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
stories.content:
A new report alleges that the Muslim Brotherhood is infiltrating Canadian institutions through various non-profit organizations and universities, a trend that it frames as part of a broader transnational ideological strategy.

In a sprawling 200-page study, the Institute for the Study of Global Antisemitism and Policy (Isgap) argues that, through an organized campaign of pro-Palestinian activism and anti-Islamophobia rhetoric, the Brotherhood and other groups are helping to foment antisemitism in Canada. The organizations, the report alleges, are often funded through highly sophisticated financial channels that run through Qatar, and have embedded themselves in some of Canada’s biggest universities.

“Under the radar, Canada is being infiltrated,” said Charles Small, founder and director of Isgap.

The report comes after the New York-based Isgap’s separate study last year, which asserted that the Muslim Brotherhood was systematically influencing various U.S. institutions, and called for the group to be designated as a terrorist organization. (Days later, the Trump administration indeed said it would designate certain chapters of the Brotherhood as global terrorists.)

The Muslim Brotherhood is a movement that began in Egypt in the 1920s and, at its root, seeks to establish core Islamic values as a foundation for society. Today, the group has multiple chapters spread across the Middle East, each with differing compositions and objectives.

Various Middle Eastern nations, including Egypt and Saudi Arabia, have outlawed the Brotherhood and designated it a terrorist organization. Canadian lawmakers have faced pressure domestically to also designate the group as such.

The Isgap report argues that the Muslim Brotherhood seeks to embed pro-Islamism into Canadian life primarily through “entryism,” or the act of changing institutions — cultural, governmental, educational, or others — from within.

Canada, with its preference for multicultural ideals and lax immigration laws, is particularly susceptible to such efforts, Small said. While the report cites Canadian organizations that avoid the more radical Muslim Brotherhood values, it asserts that many such charities and advocacy groups push specific transnational interests, often under the guise of inclusivity, Pro-Palestine activism or efforts to combat “Islamophobic” ideas.

“The Muslim Brotherhood manipulates and uses these democratic principles and our cultural institutions in a way that allows them to enter into our society, to enter into higher education, to enter into the Muslim community, to create mosques and civic organizations that are radicalized,” Small said.

Researchers in France have raised similar concerns recently about the Muslim Brotherhood’s entryism there, warning that it threatens to undermine the country’s secular identity. British authorities have raised similar alarms about the group, but so far have done little to stem its influence. Internal Muslim Brotherhood texts like the 1991 “Explanatory Memorandum,” the Isgap argues, explicitly outline plans to reshape Western society, including Canada, from within.

The Isgap report cites groups like the Canadian Muslim Public Affairs Council (Cmpac) and The Canadian-Muslim Vote (Tcmv), which it says have become organs for mobilizing muslim voting bases in Canada. Those groups, it says, have been “employing a targeted riding strategy across 60 to 80 federal constituencies where the Muslim population approaches or exceeds the margin of victory,” in which they back candidates specifically on their Palestine and Islamophobia positions.

Cmpac’s executive director, Khaled al-Qazzaz, was former foreign affairs secretary to former Egyptian president Mohamed Morsi, and the former president of the Brotherhood’s political arm in Egypt in 2011 and 2012. The Isgap report indicates that a 2024 CRA filing by Tcmv lists a board member who was formerly the head of another Canadian organization with alleged past ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, although the organization has repeatedly denied those allegations.

In response to National Post’s questions about the report’s allegations of Cmpac’s connection to the Muslim Brotherhood, the organization dismissed those claims outright, saying it has “no ties with any foreign entity.”

“The Isgap report lacks credibility and is full of biased claims that makes it more of an Islamophobic propaganda piece than research,” it said. “Cmpac is a non-for-profit Canadian organization that advocates for civil liberties and against Islamophobia in Canada.”

The Cmpac spokesperson said also that the organization was “very concerned about rising anti-semitism, Islamophobia and hate in Canada,” and said it is a domestically-funded non-profit group.

“Cmpac relies entirely on Canadian funds from individuals, private granting organizations and events’ sponsorship. Cmpac does not receive any funds from any foreign entity.”

The Cmpac said Al-Qazzaz had worked for “one year as a staffer in the first democratically-elected government of Egypt, working on Egypt’s new human rights agenda and the development of Egypt’s new foreign policy vision.” Al-Qazzaz served as Morsi’s foreign affairs minister before he was arrested and imprisoned in 2013 alongside others who were alleged to be aligned with the Morsi government. Al-Qazzaz was never charged, but was held in the maximum-security Tora Prison for nine months before he returned to Canada in 2016.

In response to National Post’s request for comment, a lawyer representing Tcmv called the Isgap report “inflammatory” and said it was calling on the organization to retract its assertions.

“Tcmv has sent a Notice of Libel to Isgap seeking a retraction and apology for these allegations,” Jeff Saikaley, partner at law firm Caza Saikaley, said in an email. “Tcmv will consider any republication of these allegations to be defamatory and will take appropriate legal action should this occur.”

We don’t understand the ideology, the goals, the religious worldview of the Brotherhood, what the strategic and military or philosophical underpinnings are

On its website, the Tcmv calls itself “a national, non-partisan charity empowering Canadian Muslims through civic engagement and education” that says it does not “endorse parties, tell you how to vote, lobby politicians, or preach religion.”

In his response to National Post, Saikaley said Tcmv’s mandate was to “empower Canadian Muslims through civic education, political engagement, and leadership, fostering an informed and active community that contributes to Canada’s democracy. That means encouraging everyone, including our community, to get involved in Canada’s democratic system.” Saikaley said that Tcmv has not targeted between 60 and 80 ridings in an effort to mobilize Muslim voters, as the Isgap report said, but said it “encouraged all Canadians, including all Canadian Muslims, to get out and vote.”

The report also highlights a handful of universities — the University of Toronto, University of Waterloo and Toronto Metropolitan University — where “consistent concerns are identified.” Those include what Isgap sees as limited foreign funding disclosures, a lack of disclosure on intellectual property contracts and the “use of campus environments as platforms for sustained mobilization, coalition-building, and narrative development,” among other things.

The report finds that Qatari financing activities, particularly through its soverign Qatar Investment Fund (QIF) or Qatar National Research Fund (Qnrf), have increasingly backed Canadian university programs that often have limited disclosure rules overseeing them. It lists numerous examples of Qatari-backed research projects into strategic fields like smart grids, carbon systems and secure communications. Many of the specific research arrangements at TMU, Waterloo and University of Toronto, for example, don’t disclose details around matters like intellectual property rights, data access or contractual terms, the Isgap report said.

Further, many Canadian campuses have become hotbeds for pro-Palestine sentiments, with leadership at those same universities often opting to actively silence pro-Israel events, the report alleges.

In response to the National Post’s questions, a University of Toronto spokesperson confirmed that the institution has received 11 research grants worth a total of $1.76 million from the Qnrf over the last decade, focused on projects ranging from whiplash trauma to “geobiological process in the sabkhas of Qatar.” The $1.76 million in grants, the spokesperson points out, is a mere 0.01 per cent of the $13.3 billion the university and its partner hospitals have recieved over the same period.

“The university is not subject to foreign influence via research awards, donations or partnerships,” the spokesperson said in an email. “The university has robust policies that protect the academic integrity of the institution and safeguard research independence and autonomy, and all partnerships and funding agreements comply with these policies and with Canadian laws and regulations.” The spokesperson, who declined to identify themselves, said the report’s claims that University of Toronto campus groups and student push anti-Israel ideas are “without merit.”

University of Waterloo spokesperson Anne Galang said the institution did not independently verify the Isgap’s claims (the report said it has received $3.8 million on five projects from various Qatari backers), but said U of W has set out clear principles to guide its international research partnerships.

“We are committed to safeguarding research, and we comply with Canadian government research security requirements,” Galang said in an email.

Toronto Metropolitan University did not respond to National Post’s questions.

Some Muslim Brotherhood groups are clearly not violent, they are clearly not terrorists

Muslim groups in Canada have repeatedly claimed that allegations of their ties to extremist groups are themselves an example of Islamophobia.

The Isgap report names the Muslim Association of Canada (MAC) as a key example of how it says non-profit and other organizations based in Canada can advance ideologies or interests sympathetic to the Muslim Brotherhood’s cause.

It cites the Canada Revenue Agency’s preliminary audit of the MAC, in which the financial regulator alleged that some of Mac’s activities “appear to be in furtherance of the Muslim Brotherhood organization,” and also that many of the charity’s activities were not explicitly charitable in nature.

While the final result of the audit was never publicized, the Cra’s initial 150-page assessment was later released. In that assessment, reviewed by National Post, the CRA drew from financial records and correspondences between 2011 and 2015 that the CRA had indicated some of Mac’s top leaders were actively involved in activities of the Egyptian chapter of the Muslim Brotherhood. It also details how the CRA alleged that members of the Egyptian and other chapters of the Brotherhood could immediately become MAC members upon coming to Canada. In its assessment, the CRA also said the MAC had expanded its real estate property holdings from $12 million in 2006 to more than $51 million by 2015, enough that the federal agency took the position that the expansion was of an unstated or non-charitable purpose. These things, the agency said, often were in direct contradiction to the group’s claims.

“There appears to be a significant difference between what the [MAC] represents it stands for and the activities that it appears to conduct,” The CRA stated.

MAC, for its part, had argued that the CRA had conflated its support for The Muslim Brotherhood founder, Hassan al-Banna, and the explicit goals of the wider Brotherhood as an organization.

“The Isgap report is nothing more than recycled Islamophobic tropes dressed up as research,” The MAC said in an email. “It is a biased, unsubstantiated hit piece that relies on discredited allegations that were themselves challenged by the Ontario Superior Court for their apparent bias. It amplifies narratives designed to fuel Islamophobia and sow division within Canadian society.”

The group did not speak specifically to any alleged connections between the MAC and Muslim Brotherhood that the CRA initially raised in its preliminary findings. However, the MAC said in its email that those alleged Brotherhood connections were “were dismissed from the Cra’s final conclusion.” The MAC did not have its charitable status removed following the audit, and continues to operate today.

The MAC had initially sought to block the Cra’s audit through the Ontario Superior Court in 2023, but the lawsuit was ultimately rejected. While Justice Markus Koehnen was sympathetic to some of the Mac’s arguments , he ruled that the court should not be intervening in the audit process.

The Isgap report calls for several policy changes, including greater oversight of academic partnerships with foreign entities at universities; giving financial auditors more powers to review non-profits and charities; and greater transparency for foreign funding to universities.

Small said that Canada culturally is blind to entryism from foreign interests including by the Muslim Brotherhood, in part because the general population is largely unfamiliar with those entities’ geopolitical aims.

“In the West — in Canada, but in other Western democratic countries — we don’t really understand what the Muslim Brotherhood is,” Small said. “It sounds like a benevolent organization. It’s a nice name, (but) we don’t understand the ideology, the goals, the religious worldview of the Brotherhood, what the strategic and military or philosophical underpinnings are, and they have mastered us.”

In Canada, the government has not yet acted on efforts from third parties to designate the Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist organization. That is largely because it is difficult to differentiate the current-day activities and mandates of various Muslim Brotherhood chapters.

While some divisions of the Brotherhood are “undeniably” terrorist outfits, many others are clearly not, Thomas Juneau, a Middle East researcher and professor at the University of Ottawa’s Graduate School of Public and International Affairs, told National Post earlier this year.

“Some Muslim Brotherhood groups are clearly not violent, they are clearly not terrorists,” Juneau said at the time.

In 2025, the U.S. government designated the Lebanon, Jordan and Egypt chapters of the Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist entity, saying that they “support violence and destabilization campaigns that harm their own regions, United States citizens, and United States interests,” according to the White House’s executive order.

Following the Oct. 7 attack on Jewish civilians, “the military wing of the Lebanese chapter of the Muslim Brotherhood joined Hamas, Hezbollah, and Palestinian factions to launch multiple rocket attacks against both civilian and military targets within Israel,” the executive order said.

The organizations, the report alleges, are often funded through highly sophisticated financial channels that run through Qatar, and have embedded themselves in some of Canada’s biggest universities.
“Under the radar, Canada is being infiltrated,” said Charles Small, founder and director of Isgap.

The report comes after the New York-based Isgap’s separate study last year, which asserted that the Muslim Brotherhood was systematically influencing various U.S. institutions, and called for the group to be designated as a terrorist organization. (Days later, the Trump administration indeed said it would designate certain chapters of the Brotherhood as global terrorists.)

content_blocks.text: The Muslim Brotherhood is a movement that began in Egypt in the 1920s and, at its root, seeks to establish core Islamic values as a foundation for society. Today, the group has multiple chapters spread across the Middle East, each with differing compositions and objectives.

Various Middle Eastern nations, including Egypt and Saudi Arabia, have outlawed the Brotherhood and designated it a terrorist organization. Canadian lawmakers have faced pressure domestically to also designate the group as such.

stories.title: Sunny start to the week in London region
stories.summary: London will see a sunny start to the week, according to Environment Canada.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
London will see a sunny start to the week, according to Environment Canada.

Monday will see sunshine with fog in the morning, which will let up as the morning progresses. A high of 18 C is expected.

Overnight, skies will remain clear, but the temperature will drop to 3 C.

Tuesday will bring more sunshine with a high of 18 C, low of 1 C.

Here’s a look at the rest of the week:

Wednesday: Sunny. High 17 C, low 1 C.

Thursday: Sunny. High 18 C, low 5 C.

Friday: Sunny. High 14 C, low 2 C.

stories.title: Canada must tackle our crisis in major project delivery
stories.summary: The high cost of building in the country means that we’re getting less for our scarce resources
stories.author: Matti Siemiatycki
stories.content:
Matti Siemiatycki is a professor of geography and planning and the director of the Infrastructure Institute at the University of Toronto.

Ever since he became Prime Minister, Mark Carney has been fond of the phrase, “We can give ourselves far more than any foreign government can take away.”

Truer words have not been spoken when it comes to improving Canada’s record of constructing major projects.

The future of this country is being diminished because of how much it costs to build big things, and how often they go terribly off the rails.

At a time when building ambitious major projects is central to diversifying the economy, weathering the trade war, and bolstering sovereignty, there is a lot riding on improving how big projects are built.

The numbers, as they stand, are gruesome.

According to Statistics Canada , non-residential building construction prices rose 14 per cent in the six years before the pandemic started in 2020.

In the six years since, construction prices have risen 45 per cent, double the general rate of inflation. For the biggest projects, the rising costs are even more extreme.

In the transit sector, a study by the University of Toronto’s School of Cities shows that Canada is among the most expensive jurisdictions in the Oecd to build new transit projects. Subway construction costs in Toronto went from $200-million per kilometre in 2001 to upward of $2.2-billion for the new Ontario line.

A similar pattern has taken place with the Montreal Metro .

The high cost of building means that in Canada we get less infrastructure for our scarce resources than our peers. In other words, it costs more to build less, which has real world consequences.

In Ontario, Mississauga’s new mega-hospital is estimated to cost $13.9-billion to build and maintain over the course of its lifespan, around two-and-a-half times more per square foot than the Humber River Regional Hospital in 2011, after adjusting for inflation. This means we can afford fewer new hospital beds and operating rooms across the health care system, for a whole lot more money.

And the challenge is not just for governments who have many priorities and limited budgets, but for private investors that Canada is boldly trying to attract. Investors will be well aware of energy projects like the Woodfibre LNG project near Squamish that rose in cost by 73 per cent, or the Coastal GasLink pipeline which ballooned from $6.2-billion to $14.5-billion.

Turning the pitch that Mr. Carney made at September’s Canada Investment Summit into real investments in ports, transmission lines, wind farms and natural resource developments requires certainty that projects can be built as proposed.

Otherwise, investors May view attractive investment opportunities as potential quagmires that are not worth the risk.

This long-standing problem has been highly resistant to change. Of course, there is a need to prune Canada’s thicket of regulations and speed up approvals that in some cases can take decades.

But that is only part of the problem. The company that led the development of the Coastal GasLink pipeline, TC Energy, reported in 2023 that cost-escalation pressures during construction were the result of skilled labour shortages, poor contractor performance and disputes, and weather-related challenges. These are the same types of problems that plague public sector projects.

Brute-force solutions like forcing projects through the planning and construction process at warp speed, conducting rushed Indigenous engagement, and outsourcing as much as possible to the private sector and contractors have failed.

Major projects are complex systems that succeed through deliberate, detailed design and engagement, to then build quickly. Measure twice, cut once.

Studies of successful major project delivery show that they benefit from structures that encourage the building of trust, relationships, and collaboration between the various public- and private-sector parties. Strong leadership fosters a culture of teamwork, problem solving and innovation. This enables the decisiveness that allows major projects to proceed quickly.

Recently, the federal government announced a $150-million investment to advance AI safety, recognizing that the risk is existential.

The same level of urgency and investment is necessary to tackle Canada’s crisis of major project delivery, which threatens the country’s prosperity, national unity and sovereignty.

We can give ourselves so much by lowering the cost and improving the predictability of building big things.

stories.title: Separatists, federalists make final push ahead of Alberta referendum vote
stories.summary: Polls have shown respondents are more likely to say they prefer to remain in Canada, but separatists have mounted a vocal campaign
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Albertans vote Monday on whether to remain in Canada or begin the process of pursuing separation, the culmination of a campaign that has divided the province and transfixed the country.

Premier Danielle Smith announced in May that she would use a previously planned referendum on a range of other issues to also ask Albertans to weigh their future in this country. The question asks whether Alberta should remain in Canada or the province should start the process to have a second, yes-or-no vote on separating into its own country.

The separatist and federalist camps made their final pitches in duelling rallies at the Alberta legislature in Edmonton over the weekend, part of a last-minute push that also saw Prime Minister Mark Carney make several stops in the province late last week urging Albertans to vote to remain in Canada.

At the federalist event on Sunday, leader Gil McGowan led the crowd in a moment of silence for victims and first responders at Alberta’s Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, where a fire had killed four service members the night before.

He said fellow Canadians responded to the call for help when it came.

“That’s why we are stronger together in one Canadian federation,” Mr. McGowan said to cheers and applause.

A day earlier, more than a thousand people gathered on the legislature grounds, many dressed in blue and waving Alberta flags, to cap off the separatist campaign.

Supporters were bused in from across the province to hear speeches from leaders imploring people to get out and vote. Lawyer Keith Wilson, one of several prominent voices who have emerged in the campaign, predicted that whatever happens on Monday, the separatist movement is here to stay.

“We’re going to get stronger. We’re going to get smarter. We’re going to get more clear,” he said.

The push for independence has dominated Alberta politics for well over a year, with petition drives by the federalist and separatist camps gathering signatures from hundreds of thousands of residents.

It has inflamed debate about national unity at a time when the country’s sovereignty is also being challenged by the trade policy and rhetoric of the Trump administration in the United States. And Monday’s vote takes place just two weeks after Quebec’s provincial election brought a separatist government to power there.

Multiple polls of Albertans have shown respondents are much more likely to say they prefer to remain in Canada, but separatists mounted a vocal campaign as they criss-crossed the province holding town halls and other events.

The turnout for advanced and mail-in ballots has been significant. Elections Alberta data show about 43 per cent of eligible voters had cast ballots before Monday. The most recent referendum in the province in 2021, which asked whether the equalization system should be cancelled and if the province should stop switching between standard and daylight saving time, had an overall turnout of just 39 per cent.

Federalists such as former Alberta premier Jason Kenney have warned voters in the province who support remaining in Canada that they must make sure to vote rather than becoming complacent.

In a speech in Calgary last Thursday night, Mr. Carney said the referendum “comes at the worst possible time,” pointing to what he described as a more dangerous and divided world.

Ms. Smith, who joined the Prime Minister at an event in Red Deer, Alta., ON Friday, also urged Albertans to choose Canada, citing the promise of a new bitumen pipeline to the West Coast as proof that the country can work for the province.

While the Premier has come under fire for not being vocal enough about her support for federalism, she has made it clear in recent days that she would vote to stay in Canada.

Separatists have dismissed Ms. Smith’s argument that her thawing relationship with Mr. Carney shows Ottawa can be a generous partner for the province. Independence leaders have spent the better part of the past year telling supporters that secession is the only way to free the province from the demands of the federal government, which they argue undermine Alberta’s prosperity.

More than a million residents have so far voted by mail or at advance polls, and Elections Alberta is expecting turnout to be significantly higher than in most elections.

Polls across the province will open Monday from 9 a.m. until 8 p.m., with results expected late into the night or early Tuesday morning.

The referendum also asks nine other questions on proposals to limit some non-permanent residents’ access to social services, charge them fees for health care and education, and other constitutional changes such as abolishing the federal Senate.

With reports from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Army likely to probe CFB Wainwright fire using board of inquiry
stories.summary: Process has come under scrutiny over transparency, as hearings and findings are not automatically made public
stories.author: Lindsay Jones, Colin Freeze
stories.content:
The army is expected to investigate the fire at the Canadian Forces base in Wainwright, Alta., in which four soldiers were killed and 39 people injured, through a process known as a board of inquiry, which can compel evidence and is designed to make recommendations to prevent similar incidents.

Boards of inquiry are used to investigate everything from misconduct involving Canadian Forces personnel to suicides and fatal incidents such as the one in Alberta. But they have come under criticism for a lack of transparency, particularly because neither the board’s hearings nor the final report and recommendations are automatically made public.

University of Ottawa law professor Ret. Colonel-Maître Michel W. Drapeau said it’s “absolutely essential” that the Forces and the federal government allow public and media access to the board of inquiry into the Wainwright fire.

“Those members’ fatalities and those who are injured are our sons and daughters, and husbands and wives, so we the public have an interest to find out what happened and hopefully to find out also what measures May be taken to prevent recurrence,” Mr. Drapeau said.

“Four deaths is significant and there May be more. I think the public has a right to know.”

Mr. Drapeau said he’s represented families and military members at boards of inquiry, witnessing their frustration at having to wait five or six years to see the report and recommendations, which in many cases are abridged or redacted.

The Department of National Defence said a fire fanned by high winds moved quickly into a training area at CFB Wainwright around 4 p.m. on Saturday.

A fire marshal team will determine the cause of the fire, while the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service, an independent investigative unit of the military police, and RCMP working alongside local military police, are also investigating what happened, said Major-General Wade Rutland, Commander of 1st Canadian Division.

Maj.-Gen. Rutland declined to say whether the report’s findings would eventually be made public. He also cautioned that the process would not be quick.

“With this amount of casualties and complexities, it’s not going to take a day or a week,” Maj.-Gen. Rutland said, referring to when board of inquiry would convene.

A board of inquiry, usually made up of three members, can depose witnesses to testify under oath. It’s purely investigative and designed to make recommendations, not find fault, said Ret. Master Seaman Gordon Scott Campbell, a military lawyer.

Mr. Scott said he expects the Canadian government to make the board of inquiry report public, as it eventually did for the 2004 submarine fire aboard Hmcs Chicoutimi, which killed one man and injured nine others, though it took intense political pressure and calls for transparency.

“Ultimately, Parliament became involved. Here, as I’ve heard there have been multiple deaths, I would anticipate probably it will be made public in the end,” he said.

The circumstances of a tragedy at CFB Valcartier in 1974 that killed six teenaged reservists were almost never made public. Ultimately, a Quebec coroner held a full inquiry which found criminal liability, Mr. Scott said.

Former Canadian Armed Forces reservist Gerry Fostaty was an 18-year-old reservist at CFB Valcartier when he witnessed a horrific explosion that injured nearly 100 teenagers – killing six of them. And for decades, he said, he was told to never discuss what he saw.

“It was a passive cover up for sure – they told us not to speak about it, and then they ignored it,”Mr. Fostaty said. But many years later he ignored orders and published As You Were: The Tragedy at Valcartier.

The 2011 book is an eyewitness account of how CAF officials were teaching military tactics by passing around a box of inert “dummy” munitions to a group of 14 and 15 year old cadets jammed into a barrack.

But a live grenade was inadvertently in the mix – and it exploded.

“These guys are sitting shoulder to shoulder on the floor, you know, cross-legged,” Mr. Fostaty said in an interview on Sunday. He said he saw horrific deaths and injuries that altered people’s lives forever on that day.

In 1968, seven CAF paratroopers were killed when they drowned in the Ottawa River. The paratroopers jumped off of a transport aircraft expecting to land on the base near Ottawa. Instead, unexpected gusts of wind carried 22 of them into the nearby river, where they were tangled up and weighted down by their chutes. Rescuers saved most of the men, but seven drowned.

In 1988, military officers training on explosives were blowing a five-metre-deep hole at CFB Chilliwack, near Vancouver. Six of them died when the bomb detonated unexpectedly.

The next year, in 1989, a Canadian C-130 transport aircraft with 18 people abroad crashed in Alaska en route to a Canada-U.S. military training exercise. Seven soldiers were killed on impact and two later died in hospital. The nine-death tragedy occurred as the Hercules crashed just short of the runway at U.S. base at Fort Wainwright, which is near Fairbanks.

“Four deaths is significant and there May be more. I think the public has a right to know.”

Mr. Drapeau said he’s represented families and military members at boards of inquiry, witnessing their frustration at having to wait five or six years to see the report and recommendations, which in many cases are abridged or redacted.
The Department of National Defence said a fire fanned by high winds moved quickly into a training area at CFB Wainwright around 4 p.m. on Saturday.

A fire marshal team will determine the cause of the fire, while the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service, an independent investigative unit of the military police, and RCMP working alongside local military police, are also investigating what happened, said Major-General Wade Rutland, Commander of 1st Canadian Division.
Maj.-Gen. Rutland declined to say whether the report’s findings would eventually be made public. He also cautioned that the process would not be quick.
“With this amount of casualties and complexities, it’s not going to take a day or a week,” Maj.-Gen. Rutland said, referring to when board of inquiry would convene.

A board of inquiry, usually made up of three members, can depose witnesses to testify under oath. It’s purely investigative and designed to make recommendations, not find fault, said Ret. Master Seaman Gordon Scott Campbell, a military lawyer.

Mr. Scott said he expects the Canadian government to make the board of inquiry report public, as it eventually did for the 2004 submarine fire aboard Hmcs Chicoutimi, which killed one man and injured nine others, though it took intense political pressure and calls for transparency.
“Ultimately, Parliament became involved. Here, as I’ve heard there have been multiple deaths, I would anticipate probably it will be made public in the end,” he said.

The circumstances of a tragedy at CFB Valcartier in 1974 that killed six teenaged reservists were almost never made public. Ultimately, a Quebec coroner held a full inquiry which found criminal liability, Mr. Scott said.

Former Canadian Armed Forces reservist Gerry Fostaty was an 18-year-old reservist at CFB Valcartier when he witnessed a horrific explosion that injured nearly 100 teenagers – killing six of them. And for decades, he said, he was told to never discuss what he saw.

“It was a passive cover up for sure – they told us not to speak about it, and then they ignored it,”Mr. Fostaty said. But many years later he ignored orders and published As You Were: The Tragedy at Valcartier.

The 2011 book is an eyewitness account of how CAF officials were teaching military tactics by passing around a box of inert “dummy” munitions to a group of 14 and 15 year old cadets jammed into a barrack.
But a live grenade was inadvertently in the mix – and it exploded.

“These guys are sitting shoulder to shoulder on the floor, you know, cross-legged,” Mr. Fostaty said in an interview on Sunday. He said he saw horrific deaths and injuries that altered people’s lives forever on that day.

In 1968, seven CAF paratroopers were killed when they drowned in the Ottawa River. The paratroopers jumped off of a transport aircraft expecting to land on the base near Ottawa. Instead, unexpected gusts of wind carried 22 of them into the nearby river, where they were tangled up and weighted down by their chutes. Rescuers saved most of the men, but seven drowned.
In 1988, military officers training on explosives were blowing a five-metre-deep hole at CFB Chilliwack, near Vancouver. Six of them died when the bomb detonated unexpectedly.

The next year, in 1989, a Canadian C-130 transport aircraft with 18 people abroad crashed in Alaska en route to a Canada-U.S. military training exercise. Seven soldiers were killed on impact and two later died in hospital. The nine-death tragedy occurred as the Hercules crashed just short of the runway at U.S. base at Fort Wainwright, which is near Fairbanks.

stories.title: 3-D digital twins of Scott and Shackleton’s last ships show minute details of sunken wrecks
stories.summary: Upcoming exhibition will give visitors a close look at both wrecks
stories.author: Marie Woolf
stories.content:
The wrecks of the last ships of famed explorers Sir Ernest Shackleton and Capt. Robert Falcon Scott have been replicated using 3-D imagery in minute detail, creating “digital twins” to preserve them for posterity.

The 3-D digital replicas, created by knitting together tens of thousands of images captured on the ocean floor during an expedition this summer, are to be unveiled Wednesday at the Royal Canadian Geographical Society’s Ottawa headquarters for viewing by the public. And the replicas will later be made available to schools across the country.

In 2024, the Rcgs discovered the wreck of Sir Ernest Shackleton’s last ship, Quest – on which the renowned polar explorer died suddenly during an Antarctic voyage in 1922 – at a depth of 390 metres , off the coast of Newfoundland and Labrador.

This summer, an international expedition led by the Rcgs went back to view the wreck up close in the Labrador Sea and, using a remotely operated vehicle, captured the first clear images of the sunken vessel. A three-man team – including Rcgs chief executive John Geiger – became the first to directly set eyes on the historic wreck through the portholes of a submersible. (The mini-submarine they used was the same one that in 1986 captured the first pictures of the Titanic, which sank off the coast of Newfoundland in 1912.)

The Canadian-led Rcgs expedition then set sail to waters off Greenland’s coast to survey Terra Nova, the last vessel of famed Antarctic explorer Capt. Scott, who perished with his entire team while returning from a much-vaunted expedition to the South Pole in 1912.

During the Second World War, Terra Nova was chartered to carry supplies to Greenland. The ship, built in Dundee, Scotland, and launched in 1884, was damaged in 1943 while at sea and was deliberately sunk after the crew were rescued.

Digital twins of both wrecks, as well as models being made of them, will preserve them for posterity, Mr. Geiger said.

The expedition used photogrammetric technology from Voyis Imaging, a company based in Waterloo, Ont., to capture detailed portraits of both ships. Tens of thousands of high-resolution images of the shipwrecks have now been knitted together “into a complete lucid picture” of both vessels, he said.

The Rcgs has also made a film of the expedition and a gallery of still photographs, including underwater images of the wrecks, for the exhibition.

“These wrecks are going to eventually disappear – they’re deteriorating, and there will come a point where they won’t exist at all,” Mr. Geiger said. “They’ll just have been subsumed into the seabed. And so what we’ve been able to do is capture – almost as if in amber – this moment, what these ships are like today.”

The Rcgs-led expedition, which included the non-profit Massachusetts-based Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, found that Quest had suffered considerable damage when she sank. Her masts were down, her nameplate – which dated back to Shackleton’s last expedition – was lost and the vessel was covered in sea life and abandoned fishing nets.

After the explorer’s death aboard the ship, it was used in several daring adventures, including helping to rescue a Danish crew marooned on ice floes off the coast of Greenland, Mr. Geiger said, speaking from London last week, where he was launching a book he wrote about Shackleton.

According to Mr. Geiger’s book, Quest, Shackleton’s Last Ship and the End of the Heroic Age, the vessel was chosen in 1930 by 23-year-old British Arctic explorer Gino Watkins to investigate the feasibility of an air route linking London with Winnipeg, via several hops from Scotland to the Faroe Islands, Iceland, Greenland and to Baffin Island.

After its career as an exploration vessel ended, Quest returned to its original vocation as a sealing ship. It sank off the coast of Labrador after suffering damage in 1962.

Mr. Geiger said Terra Nova, found in waters at a depth of 179 metres, off the coast of Greenland, was “a much more beautiful ship than Quest, which was a small, kind of stubby little workman-like vessel.”

The Terra Nova wreck was also better preserved than Quest, and the expedition discovered navigation equipment used during Capt. Scott’s ill-fated expedition to the Antarctic. Although Terra Nova’s hull had split in two, its original rudder, propeller, two masts, as well as its wheel and ceramic mugs abandoned by its crew when she sank in 1943, were visible.

Mr. Geiger said “the imagery is absolutely striking” and will be closely studied, including to gain more insight into the sea creatures that have made them their homes.

He said the 3-D images are “extremely powerful” and make the viewer “feel like you’re basically swimming over the wrecks.”

Editor’s note: A photo cutline in an earlier version of this article misspelled Royal Canadian Geographical Society. This version has been corrected.
