stories.title: House of Commons holds moment of silence over Wainwright tragedy
stories.summary: The House of Commons held a moment of silence today after a deadly fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright left four Canadian soldiers dead and sent dozens to hospital with injuries.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The House of Commons held a moment of silence on Monday to honour the dead and wounded after a ferocious fire ripped through Canadian Forces Base Wainwright’s training grounds in Alberta on Saturday.

The main party leaders dropped their usual partisan tone as each expressed condolences to the deceased and concern for the injured.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said members of Parliament are “united in grief” over a tragedy that touches every corner of the country.

“In a few weeks, Canadians will gather at cenotaphs across the country, including the one in Wainwright, to remember those who have sacrificed so we can live freely. This year, we will carry more names with us,” Carney told the House.

“To their friends and families, to their colleagues, to the people of Wainwright, please know that you have the entire nation at your side.”

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre — who on Monday was back in his Alberta riding, which includes the military base — delivered his remarks to the Commons by video.

He told the House he had personally met one of the deceased — Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23. Poilievre described him as “strong, handsome, polite” and a “real gentleman.”

He also acknowledged the tireless efforts of the firefighters and soldiers who faced great risks while attempting to save their colleagues from danger.

“Here on the ground in Wainwright, we are hearing third-hand accounts of unimaginable heroism. Soldiers running towards danger,” Poilievre said. “Can you imagine the courage it takes to see fire and run towards it to help your comrades?”

Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet said the “cost of service should never be this high.”

“All Quebecers, I am certain, are with you and by your side today,” he said in French.

Defence officials have said 84 members of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were in a training area of CFB Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton, when disaster struck Saturday.

Strong and sudden winds sent flames from a nearby grass fire racing across the Prairie landscape, stopping soldiers in their tracks and sending 39 of them to hospital — 19 in critical condition.

The dead are Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Goulding of North Vancouver and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C.

Defence Minister David McGuinty said people have been lining up to donate blood, bring meals to first responders and open their homes to those grieving.

Canadian Blood Services encouraged those who want to help by donating blood to do so in the coming days and weeks.

“We are closely monitoring the needs of patients and hospitals in Alberta and will continue to work with health system partners to ensure those needs are met,” the non-profit said in a post on its website.

CFB Wainwright is 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton. It is one of Canada’s busiest military bases and is used mainly to train soldiers and prepare units for combat operations.

Canada’s military has said the grass fire was known about well beforehand but, at roughly a kilometre away, was not considered a threat.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division, told reporters on Sunday the 84 members of 3rd Battalion were engaged in two exercises at the time.

Most were throwing hand grenades on a range, while 10 soldiers were simulating an attack on an enemy.

What happened next was an anomaly, he said.

“I spoke to my commander on the ground. He said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them,” he said at the Sunday news conference.

Medical personnel from neighbouring areas, including Saskatchewan, were called in. Some were seen parachuting into the base. Alberta health officials invoked a critical Code Orange, a call for hospitals to find staff and free up beds to handle a mass casualty incident. That has since been called off.

Rutland said there will be a full investigation and there’s a lot for it to consider. Did the fire move that quickly because of the wind? Did it move unseen through foliage, surprising the soldiers? Was it both?

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith confirmed at the news conference that many of the injured have serious burns. Hospitals in Edmonton, Calgary and Red Deer are treating the wounded.

Flags on provincial and federal buildings have been lowered to half-mast to pay tribute to the deceased.

The tragedy comes as Albertans head to the polls Monday for a referendum that, among other things, asks whether Alberta should remain part of Canada or should hold a second, binding vote on leaving.

McGuinty said those affected were soldiers and reservists from across the country.

“This loss reaches communities in every province,” he said.

Asked what she makes of the reaction by those across the country, Smith said Alberta has a long and proud history of supporting the Canadian Armed Forces.

Shortly after Alberta was brought under Confederation in 1905, thousands of residents enlisted in the military to fight in the First World War, Smith said.

“We were very honoured to have been able to assist at a terrible time for the Armed Forces. And we’re very honoured as well now to be giving all of those soldiers who are injured the very best care,” she said.

“And I think we’re all very, very hopeful for a full recovery of everyone.”

stories.title: Albertans head to polls in historic referendum on whether they want to stay in Canada
stories.summary: Edmonton - Albertans head to the polls today for an historic vote on whether they want to stay in Canada.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Edmonton - O Canada, Alberta is staying put.

In a historic referendum Monday, voters marked their ballots in overwhelming numbers to remain in the country that made Alberta a province 121 years ago.

In early returns, about 76 per cent of Albertans said yes to Confederation, while 24 per cent said they wanted the province to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving.

Both Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Prime Minister Mark Carney lauded the result.

“Thank you, Alberta!” Smith wrote on social media.

“Albertans have voted for a stronger Alberta in a united Canada.”

Smith said she would give a TV address Tuesday night to detail where the province goes from here.

Carney said in a statement: “Albertans made a clear choice. They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other.”

“Canada is so much greater than the sum of its parts.”

At watch parties and rallies, pro-Canada supporters cheered, and those fighting for a new deal were glum but resolute.

“Don’t mess with Canada!” Thomas Lukaszuk, a prominent leader and organizer of the pro-Canada forces, said to cheers at the Polish Hall in Edmonton’s downtown.

About eight blocks away, a rally for separatists at a restaurant fell quiet as the numbers rolled in.

“We’re not going anywhere,” said Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project.

“We’ve dominated the conversation in the last year. We’ve been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we’re going to continue moving forward.”

Alberta joins Quebec in putting the question of sovereignty to its citizens. Quebec has had two votes dating to 1980. In 1995, Quebec voted to stay in Confederation by a razor-thin 50.58 per cent.

The separation question was one of 10 put to Albertans. The other nine focused on immigration and the Constitution. They were also being counted Monday, but the early results came in slower and with closer margins.

The overall turnout was impressive, with more than 1.3 million votes cast earlier in mail-in ballots and at advance polls.

Smith, who said she voted to stay in Canada, promised a simple 50 per cent plus one majority would carry the day and that there would be no followup referendum for the rest of her United Conservative Party government’s mandate.

Christina Fielder, a supporter at the Forever Canadian party, said Alberta is in the same place it was before the referendum and hopes the separatist debate is done.

“They were thumped,” she said. “I hope that they’ll accept that, because they are not the majority. We are.”

At a polling station in Edmonton, Shawn Campbell said he voted for a binding separation referendum — even though he doesn’t want the province to separate and doesn’t believe it ever will.

“It sends a message to Ottawa that Albertans are not happy.”

The voting completes a winding process that began in May, when Smith called the referendum.

Debate turned some neighbours against neighbours. It disrupted public events.

The Alberta flag morphed into a disputed de facto banner for those who want to separate.

There were rallies and speeches, sign wars, stacks of policy documents, analyses and warnings of economic apocalypse should Alberta try to go its own way.

Smith had to explain why her caucus and party is for Canada while allowing separatists to remain in the fold. She said the party stands for Confederation but also welcomes diverse points of view.

Smith and her UCP didn’t campaign on a separation vote in the 2023 provincial election, and it didn’t seek a renewed popular mandate before calling the referendum. Instead, Smith said, her hand had effectively been forced.

She said Albertans’ long-standing simmering resentment with Ottawa boiled over during the administration of former Liberal prime minister Justin Trudeau.

She said policies undercutting resource development, along with unfair equalization policies and federal intrusion on provincial rights, compelled hundreds of thousands of Albertans to sign citizen-led petitions both for and against staying in Canada.

A referendum, she said, was a necessary pressure release valve and a way to settle the matter once and for all.

She walked a line on the issue. She professed love for a “sovereign Alberta within a united Canada.” However, over the last two years, her government has rewritten laws and lowered thresholds that helped power the petition calling for a vote on separation.

When that petition was ultimately bogged down in court this spring, Smith announced the referendum anyway.

The Opposition NDP, among other critics, has said this is the true reason for the referendum.

They say separatism has long been — and still is — a fringe sentiment in Alberta. They accuse Smith of squeezing the bellows on the embers of separation, fanning them into flames to save her job.

They say she has become captive to the influential separatist wing of her party and that the referendum is about keeping them in the fold and dissuading them from tossing her out in a party confidence vote, as was done to her predecessor Jason Kenney.

Kenney, a co-founder of the UCP, has said separatists have no place in the party and that after the referendum, the party faces a “reckoning.”

The next Alberta election is set for October 2027, and the overarching question is whether the whiff of separatism will cling to Smith and her UCP.

Smith has fences to mend.

Two UCP constituency associations have reportedly backed calls for an early leadership review ahead of the party’s annual general meeting in November.

There’s also resentment among some separatists over the wording of the referendum question. Critics have derided it as little more than a referendum on a referendum.

Others resent Smith for calling the vote on Alberta’s future in Canada while simultaneously declaring she will vote to keep the province in Confederation.

There are signs the government’s popularity has taken a hit. The UCP has bled support to the NDP in recent public opinion surveys. Last month, the UCP lost a byelection in its Calgary-Shaw stronghold.

On Monday, Rath said Smith, too, would face a reckoning.

“We are the UCP,” he said. “Jason Kenney, we’ve already kicked out. He’s no longer the leader because of what he did during COVID.

“Danielle,” he said, “is going to be running into the same thing.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

— With files from Fakiha Baig and Aaron Sousa

Smith said she would give a TV address Tuesday night to detail where the province goes from here.
Carney said in a statement: “Albertans made a clear choice. They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other.”
“Canada is so much greater than the sum of its parts.”
At watch parties and rallies, pro-Canada supporters cheered, and those fighting for a new deal were glum but resolute.
“Don’t mess with Canada!” Thomas Lukaszuk, a prominent leader and organizer of the pro-Canada forces, said to cheers at the Polish Hall in Edmonton’s downtown.
About eight blocks away, a rally for separatists at a restaurant fell quiet as the numbers rolled in.
“We’re not going anywhere,” said Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project.
“We’ve dominated the conversation in the last year. We’ve been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we’re going to continue moving forward.”
Alberta joins Quebec in putting the question of sovereignty to its citizens. Quebec has had two votes dating to 1980. In 1995, Quebec voted to stay in Confederation by a razor-thin 50.58 per cent.

The separation question was one of 10 put to Albertans. The other nine focused on immigration and the Constitution. They were also being counted Monday, but the early results came in slower and with closer margins.
The overall turnout was impressive, with more than 1.3 million votes cast earlier in mail-in ballots and at advance polls.

Smith, who said she voted to stay in Canada, promised a simple 50 per cent plus one majority would carry the day and that there would be no followup referendum for the rest of her United Conservative Party government’s mandate.
Christina Fielder, a supporter at the Forever Canadian party, said Alberta is in the same place it was before the referendum and hopes the separatist debate is done.
“They were thumped,” she said. “I hope that they’ll accept that, because they are not the majority. We are.”
At a polling station in Edmonton, Shawn Campbell said he voted for a binding separation referendum — even though he doesn’t want the province to separate and doesn’t believe it ever will.
“It sends a message to Ottawa that Albertans are not happy.”
The voting completes a winding process that began in May, when Smith called the referendum.
Debate turned some neighbours against neighbours. It disrupted public events.
The Alberta flag morphed into a disputed de facto banner for those who want to separate.
There were rallies and speeches, sign wars, stacks of policy documents, analyses and warnings of economic apocalypse should Alberta try to go its own way.
Smith had to explain why her caucus and party is for Canada while allowing separatists to remain in the fold. She said the party stands for Confederation but also welcomes diverse points of view.

Smith and her UCP didn’t campaign on a separation vote in the 2023 provincial election, and it didn’t seek a renewed popular mandate before calling the referendum. Instead, Smith said, her hand had effectively been forced.
She said Albertans’ long-standing simmering resentment with Ottawa boiled over during the administration of former Liberal prime minister Justin Trudeau.

She said policies undercutting resource development, along with unfair equalization policies and federal intrusion on provincial rights, compelled hundreds of thousands of Albertans to sign citizen-led petitions both for and against staying in Canada.
A referendum, she said, was a necessary pressure release valve and a way to settle the matter once and for all.

She walked a line on the issue. She professed love for a “sovereign Alberta within a united Canada.” However, over the last two years, her government has rewritten laws and lowered thresholds that helped power the petition calling for a vote on separation.
When that petition was ultimately bogged down in court this spring, Smith announced the referendum anyway.
The Opposition NDP, among other critics, has said this is the true reason for the referendum.
They say separatism has long been — and still is — a fringe sentiment in Alberta. They accuse Smith of squeezing the bellows on the embers of separation, fanning them into flames to save her job.

They say she has become captive to the influential separatist wing of her party and that the referendum is about keeping them in the fold and dissuading them from tossing her out in a party confidence vote, as was done to her predecessor Jason Kenney.
Kenney, a co-founder of the UCP, has said separatists have no place in the party and that after the referendum, the party faces a “reckoning.”
The next Alberta election is set for October 2027, and the overarching question is whether the whiff of separatism will cling to Smith and her UCP.
Smith has fences to mend.
Two UCP constituency associations have reportedly backed calls for an early leadership review ahead of the party’s annual general meeting in November.
There’s also resentment among some separatists over the wording of the referendum question. Critics have derided it as little more than a referendum on a referendum.
Others resent Smith for calling the vote on Alberta’s future in Canada while simultaneously declaring she will vote to keep the province in Confederation.

There are signs the government’s popularity has taken a hit. The UCP has bled support to the NDP in recent public opinion surveys. Last month, the UCP lost a byelection in its Calgary-Shaw stronghold.
On Monday, Rath said Smith, too, would face a reckoning.
“We are the UCP,” he said. “Jason Kenney, we’ve already kicked out. He’s no longer the leader because of what he did during COVID.
“Danielle,” he said, “is going to be running into the same thing.”

stories.title: Statistics Canada set to release September inflation figures
stories.summary: Ottawa — Statistics Canada is set to report inflation data for September today.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Canada’s annual inflation rate rose to 3.1 per cent in September as war in the Middle East continued to drive up gasoline prices, but economists say easing core inflation suggests higher energy costs have yet to spread widely throughout the economy.

Statistics Canada said Monday the acceleration in headline inflation was led by a 27.8 per cent spike in gasoline prices last month compared with a year earlier, despite the switch to the less expensive winter gas blend.

Excluding gasoline, however, consumer prices increased 2.2 per cent year-over-year in September after a 2.4 per cent rise in August.

BMO chief economist Douglas Porter said while soaring gasoline prices are pushing inflation above the Bank of Canada’s target, underlying price pressures remain relatively contained.

“The fact that a lot of measures of core inflation are holding steady at around two per cent suggests that the run-up in prices really is not spreading far and wide beyond the gasoline pump,” he said in an interview.

“Overall inflation actually came in a just a little bit lower than what had been expected and there were lots of somewhat encouraging developments.”

Economists had broadly expected inflation to accelerate to 3.2 per cent last month, up from three per cent in August, putting pressure on the Bank of Canada ahead of its next interest rate decision on Oct. 28.

Yet Porter said the consumer price index report on its own “does nothing to advance the case for interest rate hikes.”

The latest Statistics Canada inflation data showed moderation in grocery prices, with food purchased from stores up 1.7 per cent in September. That is the smallest yearly increase since May 2024.

Driving the slowdown was a 2.9 per cent drop in prices for fresh vegetables, while sugar and confectionery items fell 2.7 per cent.

Beef prices rose at a slower pace in September, up 8.7 per cent compared with an 11 per cent increase in August.

Despite the year-over-year slowdown, prices for groceries have jumped 33 per cent since September 2020.

September brought the yearly update to tuition fees, which rose 2.4 per cent following a 1.7 per cent increase in 2025, Statistics Canada said.

Even though most tourism-related sectors saw normal seasonal price drops, ticket prices for flights surged 19.4 per cent in September, primarily because of escalating jet fuel costs.

Meanwhile, September saw a wide divergence in inflation between regions.

For example, inflation for all three Maritime provinces was above five per cent amid heating oil spikes. The agency said fuel oil and other fuels surged 57.8 per cent in September, hitting consumers hard in Atlantic Canada where many homes are heated with oil.

Inflation in Ontario came in at 2.5 per cent in September, the lowest in the country.

Porter said the wide gaps reflect deep differences in housing markets, as well as the downward pressure on central Canada due to trade issues with the United States.

“We’ve got some really extreme regional variations across the country, and it’s showing up in the inflation numbers,” he said.

Statistics Canada said measures of core inflation, which offer a clearer picture of underlying price trends by filtering out big price swings, eased slightly last month.

The agency’s so-called CPI-trim, which excludes the biggest price increases and decreases, fell to 1.8 per cent year-over-year in September from 1.9 per cent in August. CPI-median, a measure of the midpoint of price changes across goods and services, declined to 1.9 per cent from two per cent.

Andrew Grantham, senior economist with Cibc Capital Markets, said in a client note that the “hawkish tone” of Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem’s comments over the weekend had raised market expectations of an interest rate hike later this month.

But the inflation report “suggests that there is little rush and policymakers can take more time to assess how U.S. trade relations and the impact of new tariffs develop before raising rates,” Grantham said.

During a media roundtable from Thailand on Saturday, Macklem warned that persistently high energy prices were increasing the risk of broader inflation and that the central bank was prepared to raise rates if necessary.

He said the prevailing message from his peers at the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok was that the global economy has been performing better than expected in the face of ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine, sweeping trade disruptions and higher borrowing costs from rising bond yields.

But Macklem also said that resilience is increasingly “under strain” as shocks like the Middle East conflict persist and drive up energy prices.

Some of those sources of resilience — like releasing global oil reserves — are being depleted, he said.

“You can only release strategic energy, oil reserves so many times, but that has helped contain this energy price shock,” Macklem said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

Brett Bundale, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Air Canada blamed 'dynamic pricing' for their $274 overcharge. Now, the airline says it was a 'technical glitch’
stories.summary: Retired teacher Michael Pogor is glad he kept meticulous records of his Air Canada ticket odyssey. The airline told the Advocate he will be getting a refund.
stories.author: Diana Zlomislic
stories.content:
When Michael Pogor sat down a few weeks ago to choose airline seats for a pre-booked trip to Europe, the retired high school math and computer science teacher did something most of us don’t bother to do: He kept a record.

Air Canada’s website showed the selection fee for each standard seat cost $56.75. Pogor checked the price with his wife, Linda, a sign language interpreter, and the couple they’re travelling with later this month. Then he selected eight seats: four for the flight out and four for the flight home.

Before moving to the payment page, he snapped screenshots and a video of his selections. One screenshot, time-stamped 8:51 p.m., shows seat 43J listed as a standard seat at $56.75.

By his math, the total cost would come to $454 plus tax. Less than a minute after selecting the seats, he entered his credit card number and hit submit.

No receipt arrived. Worried the payment didn’t process, Pogor checked his credit card account online. There was a pending charge from Air Canada for $728, or $91 a seat.

He called the airline at 9 p.m. A recorded message warned of a two-hour wait, so he tried again at midnight. He reached an agent at 2 a.m.

The agent told him $91 was the correct seat-selection fee and that it was non-refundable.

Michael Pogor took screenshots of his Air Canada seat selections for his group’s upcoming trans-Atlantic flight. That’s how he caught a $274 overcharge, which the airline later called a technical glitch.

When Pogor offered to share his screenshots, he said the agent declined and noted “dynamic pricing” accounted for the difference. That the price changed between the moment he picked the seats and the moment he paid and failed to notice.

Gabor Lukacs, founder of Canadian advocacy group Air Passenger Rights, took issue with the “dynamic pricing” explanation.

“What I’m finding more troubling here,” Lukacs said, “is that they are using the buzzword of ‘dynamic pricing’ as a way of trying to make the passenger go away.”

Pogor shared his screenshots and video with me and I passed them on to Lukacs.

“The screenshot is very strong evidence that the passenger did not authorize a higher amount,” said Lukacs. He added that a fee charged without the customer’s authorization cannot be declared non-refundable.

Air Canada spokesperson Sean Davidson told the Star the company reviewed Pogor’s case and “confirmed the discrepancy resulted from a technical glitch. We apologize and will be contacting the customer directly to process a refund.”

Seat selection prices, he added, are fixed by route and aircraft type and do not fluctuate. The price displayed includes all applicable taxes.

“Any suggestion by Mr. Lukacs that Air Canada deliberately charged the customer a different price,” Davidson said, “is categorically false and defamatory.”

The Star shared Air Canada’s response with Lukacs.

“The fact that Air Canada failed to immediately correct/reverse the charges when the passenger contacted their call centre, and instead Air Canada put forward a … ‘dynamic pricing’ explanation,” said Lukacs, “shows that this was not a glitch.”

“A reasonable seller/merchant,” he added, “would have taken corrective measures at the very first opportunity.”

Lukacs also flagged a common mistake in Pogor’s own math. Pogor had assumed tax would be added on top of the seat fee.

“There is no tax on air transportation services between Canada and Europe ,” Lukacs confirmed, adding Pogor should have paid $454 — $274 less than what he was charged.

Pogor knew he could cancel within 24 hours but he didn’t. He worried he’d lose the seats he had chosen for his group, seats he was happy to pay $454 for.

Getting his money back has been its own ordeal.

When Pogor tried to file a refund request through Air Canada’s online form, the field for his home province wouldn’t accept “Ontario.” There was a drop-down menu for U.S. states but not for Canadian provinces. He tried dozens of times, even restarted his computer.

When Air Canada’s receipt landed in his inbox several days after his Oct. 6 purchase, he noticed another oddity.

The $728 pending transaction had been split into eight separate charges of $91 each.

“I have to apply for eight separate refunds,” Pogor said.

He suspects the kludgy online form and split charges are barriers meant to wear customers down.

He eventually submitted his complaint and refund request after logging into Air Canada’s website through an “incognito” browser, which seemed to fix the problem he was having with the drop down menu for selecting his home province.

Air Canada’s Davidson said customer calls are routed to the first available agent at call centres across the country, adding they were unable to reproduce the error Pogor encountered with the online form.

Pogor hadn’t heard back.

“If they showed a fee of $91, I can make an informed decision about whether I’m willing to pay that,” Pogor said. “If I took it on faith, booked just two seats and not checked my credit card statement, I might not have noticed.”

After publication, Pogor confirmed Air Canada had refunded him $273, $1 less than what he was owed. In an email to the Star, Air Canada attributed the shortfall to a rounding error and promised to refund the additional dollar.

Pogor said he hopes his experience will urge others to be more diligent about keeping records and checking their account balances.

“There’s no way on the face of the earth that I’m the first person this has happened to,” he said. “They make it so difficult to contact them to make this point.”

Keldon Bester, executive director of the Canadian Anti-Monopoly Project, suspects an error rather than a scheme is at play here. What happens next, he says, is the real problem.

“I tend to think this is probably an error,” he said, “and then it becomes an extreme pain because it gets sucked up into the same customer service black hole that so many complaints do.”

Consumers can protect themselves by staying vigilant and keeping records like Pogor did, Bester said. “We shouldn’t have to do that.”

Pogor, who moved from Toronto to Fonthill in the Niagara Region during the pandemic, is still looking forward to the trip, which marks a milestone birthday and his travel companions’ 40th wedding anniversary.

Update — Oct. 19, 2026

Post publication, Air Canada initially refunded Pogor $273, $1 less than what he was owed. The airline later attributed the shortfall to “a rounding error” and noted it would refund the additional dollar.

stories.title: Why are candidates running for trustee in Ontario's most unusual election?
stories.summary: The Oct. 26 vote raises questions about what candidates can promise, and what those elected can actually accomplish.
stories.author: Isabel Teotonio
stories.content:
The morning bell is about to ring at Father Serra Catholic School, but parents hurrying to drop off their kids stop in the drizzle to shake hands with a trustee seeking re-election.

“How is everything going?” asks Markus de Domenico, who’s running to represent this Etobicoke ward in the city’s Catholic board. As he stands in front of the school, handing out campaign postcards, parents raise various concerns, including when the area’s new high school will open, with one father calling it “the number one local issue.”

“We’re not being told — the public’s not being told,” says de Domenico, adding he plans to hold a public demonstration to press for answers. “We’re going to shake the tree.”

But how much influence will Toronto trustees have beyond shaking the tree? With both Toronto school boards under provincial supervision and trustees stripped of decision-making powers, the Oct. 26 municipal election raises questions about what candidates can promise voters, and what those elected can actually accomplish.

A governance revamp has left trustees with limited roles. While a Tdsb trustee is hesitating to run again, others say they can still be constructive.

The issue extends beyond the eight Ontario boards currently under provincial control . Recent legislation has dramatically narrowed the role of trustees provincewide. Although once responsible for overseeing budgets, setting policy direction, and participating in central collective bargaining, their role now focuses primarily on parent and student advocacy.

While the effects of supervision, and recent legislation, are difficult to measure in this election, the numbers are notable: Fewer candidates are running provincewide, compared with the previous two election cycles.

“Trustees have been turned into a complaints department, with no powers to fix any problem ,” says Myer Siemiatycki, professor emeritus of politics and public administration at Toronto Metropolitan University.

“We are in totally new ground,” he says, in these elections.

Outside Father Serra school, a mother tells the Star these are indeed unusual elections, but it won’t discourage her from voting.

“If you have the right person in place they can actually do a lot,” she says. “I think it makes this election that much more important to go out and make sure you’re picking someone who has an active voice in the community.”

De Domenico, who served two terms and was chair of the Toronto Catholic District School Board when the province stepped in, says he can still help parents navigate the system. (While trustees at Catholic boards under supervision retain authority on denominational matters, they otherwise have no powers and cannot deal directly with staff, who now report to the supervisor.)

“I get calls every day still .... I advise parents as best I can because I know how the system works. ... What we’re seeing is we don’t have a parent voice. There are no public board meetings. The parents can’t advocate for their kids other than to phone a number.”

His sole challenger for Tcdsb Ward 2, Sara Concordia, says even with reduced powers, parents need a strong voice, especially when it comes to protecting Catholic education and holding the board accountable.

Tcdsb trustee candidate Markus de Domenico outside Father Serra Catholic School in Etobicoke earlier this month. De Domenico, who was board chair when the province stepped in to reduce trustee powers, says he can still help parents navigate the system.

“We will have limited authority, but we still should be representing our communities,” she says, noting her priorities include adequate resources and textbooks for classrooms, along with air conditioning in schools, both of which she fought for while on parent council at her daughter’s school.

Tasha Kheiriddin, who is running in Ward 7 of the Toronto District School Board, says key issues for voters include class size, school safety, technology use and a “frustration that they feel that their voices are not in the conversation.”

Among the common refrains she’s heard on the doorstep are: “I didn’t know I could vote for trustees. I thought the province got rid of them.” Others are more pointed, saying: “What are you actually going to do, because the trustees are not sitting?”

To that, she typically responds that yes, powers have been curtailed, but when supervision lifts she wants to be “one of the people there to make positive change.”

Beginning in 2025 and continuing into early 2026, the province took control of eight school boards, citing concerns that included growing deficits, depleting reserves and financial mismanagement. All remain under supervision: Thames Valley, Toronto’s public and Catholic boards, Ottawa-Carleton, Peel’s public and Catholic boards, Near North and York Catholic.

Education Minister Paul Calandra has warned it could take years before trustees in those boards regain their governance roles, saying he’ll hand back power once he’s confident the individual boards are being well-run.

It’s not only supervision that is changing the voting landscape, but also new legislation. Bill 33, the Supporting Children and Students Act , became law in November 2025, giving the province expanded powers to investigate and take over boards facing financial or governance issues. It also requires boards to reinstate the controversial school resource officer program if the local police service offers it.

Tasha Kheiriddin, right, who is running for Tdsb trustee in Ward 7, says she often hears questions along the lines of “What are you actually going to do, because the trustees are not sitting?”

Months later, Bill 101, the Putting Student Achievement First Act, went further. Reforms included capping the number of trustees at Ontario boards at 12 — a move only affecting the Tdsb , which previously had 22 wards — and cutting their annual honorarium to a maximum of $10,000, down from roughly $25,000 at the Tdsb. The legislation also created a new CEO who leads the budget process — and if the CEO and trustees cannot agree, the minister has the final say. English public and Catholic trustee associations were also stripped of their central bargaining role.

Siemiatycki suspects supervision, and new legislation, has had a chilling effect on people wanting to run for trustee.

“I think definitely that this reduction in the scope of power and honorarium for school trustees is a major factor in bringing about a significant reduction in the number of individuals prepared to take on this position to run for office,” he said.

The minister’s press secretary says the suggestion that holding school boards accountable prevents trustees from representing their communities is “categorically false.”

Markus de Domenico says part of what trustees can do right now is “shake the tree.”

“Trustees have repeatedly said they are elected to represent parents, protect public education and ensure students receive the education they deserve, and they remain fully able to do so under the Putting Student Achievement First Act,” said Emma Testani in a statement.

She said the legislation ensures board resources are spent on student success, “by restricting unnecessary trustee spending, strengthening financial oversight, introducing qualified professional leadership, and putting safeguards in place to prevent the kind of dysfunction that has plagued some school boards.”

Patrick Daly, executive director of Ontario Catholic School Trustees’ Association, thinks the new legislation might have actually “inspired,” rather than discouraged, some people to run, noting “the vast majority of people who run, and stay, as Catholic trustees do so because they see it as a vocation.”

The Ontario Public School Boards’ Association says interest in the position remains high. For instance, Toronto’s public board has 77 candidates, with eight incumbents seeking re-election — and no acclamations. (The city’s Catholic board has 31 candidates, including seven incumbents seeking re-election — there are two acclamations.)

While the role and responsibilities of trustees have changed, Opsba says they help set a board’s direction, ask questions about how public resources are used and keep local priorities in view.

“Public education and your children and youth are too important to be solely governed at a distance from Queen’s Park,” it says.

Siemiatycki says that by limiting trustees to an advocacy role, the province May have inadvertently created space for them to become stronger critics of provincial education policy.

“Rather than eroding and minimizing the voice and role of trustees, there is a possibility — depending on how trustees want to exercise the role that’s now open to them — for a far greater public presence and voice by school trustees,” he says. “They May actually become amplified voices for the direction of public education in Ontario.”

“How is everything going?” asks Markus de Domenico, who’s running to represent this Etobicoke ward in the city’s Catholic board. As he stands in front of the school, handing out campaign postcards, parents raise various concerns, including when the area’s new high school will open, with one father calling it “the number one local issue.”
“We’re not being told — the public’s not being told,” says de Domenico, adding he plans to hold a public demonstration to press for answers. “We’re going to shake the tree.”

But how much influence will Toronto trustees have beyond shaking the tree? With both Toronto school boards under provincial supervision and trustees stripped of decision-making powers, the Oct. 26 municipal election raises questions about what candidates can promise voters, and what those elected can actually accomplish.
A governance revamp has left trustees with limited roles. While a Tdsb trustee is hesitating to run again, others say they can still be constructive.

The issue extends beyond the eight Ontario boards currently under provincial control . Recent legislation has dramatically narrowed the role of trustees provincewide. Although once responsible for overseeing budgets, setting policy direction, and participating in central collective bargaining, their role now focuses primarily on parent and student advocacy.

While the effects of supervision, and recent legislation, are difficult to measure in this election, the numbers are notable: Fewer candidates are running provincewide, compared with the previous two election cycles.

“Trustees have been turned into a complaints department, with no powers to fix any problem ,” says Myer Siemiatycki, professor emeritus of politics and public administration at Toronto Metropolitan University.
“We are in totally new ground,” he says, in these elections.
Outside Father Serra school, a mother tells the Star these are indeed unusual elections, but it won’t discourage her from voting.

“If you have the right person in place they can actually do a lot,” she says. “I think it makes this election that much more important to go out and make sure you’re picking someone who has an active voice in the community.”

De Domenico, who served two terms and was chair of the Toronto Catholic District School Board when the province stepped in, says he can still help parents navigate the system. (While trustees at Catholic boards under supervision retain authority on denominational matters, they otherwise have no powers and cannot deal directly with staff, who now report to the supervisor.)

“I get calls every day still .... I advise parents as best I can because I know how the system works. ... What we’re seeing is we don’t have a parent voice. There are no public board meetings. The parents can’t advocate for their kids other than to phone a number.”

Monday, October 19, 2026

Highbury Avenue between Florence Street and Beattie street will experience lane restrictions starting today until Thursday, October 22. These temporary lane restrictions are to allow for emergency sewer repairs in the area and prevent future deterioration.

Drivers and pedestrians are encouraged to plan ahead and allow extra time when travelling through the area.

Drivers should follow signs and directions from crews.

Please check theLondon Transit Commission website for the most up-to-date information on bus schedules and detours.

For more information about construction projects in London, visit theRenew London map.

stories.title: York Street downtown reopens to traffic as construction is nearly complete
stories.summary: Old underground utilities and infrastructure have been replacedYork Street between Wellington Street and Colbo
stories.content:
York Street between Wellington Street and Colborne Street has reopened to vehicle traffic as the York Street Infrastructure Renewal Project nears completion. This construction project has upgraded underground utility services and increased water, stormwater, and sewer capacity to support future growth in the downtown.

"York Street is an important corridor in our downtown, but beneath the road was some of London’s oldest infrastructure,” says Ashley Rammeloo, Director, Water, Wastewater, and Stormwater. “We’ve now reached a major milestone for the project and have reopened the road to traffic. The improvements we’ve constructed will help reduce the risk of flooding, watermain breaks, and sewer backups, and ensure our infrastructure can continue to support our growing city.”

A key component of the project was the removal of old combined sewers. Combined sewers carry both stormwater and wastewater through a single pipe. Separating these systems helps prevent stormwater and wastewater from mixing, reducing the risk of basement flooding and sewer overflows while decreasing the amount of stormwater entering the sanitary sewer system.

The project also replaced the watermain underground, improved the road and sidewalk, upgraded the intersection, and installed new traffic signals. Improvements were made along Wellington Street and to the underpass where concrete was repaired and the road was replaced. The project also involved collaborating with London Hydro to coordinate and upgrade hydro utilities underground.

The York Street Infrastructure Renewal Project is one of several sewer improvements that the City has undertaken in recent years to separate sewers downtown. Together, these projects help support the health of the Thames River while renewing critical infrastructure, improving the road for people walking and traveling, and enhancing downtown streetscapes.

The City thanks residents and businesses for their patience throughout construction. Some finishing touches for the project will continue this fall, but this work does not require a full road closure.

For more information about construction projects in London, visit the Renew London map .

stories.title: CFB Wainwright fire: Star readers send condolences to families and the injured
stories.summary: After four Canadian Armed Forces members were killed and dozens more injured, readers shared messages of sympathy and support.
stories.author: Paige Oldfield
stories.content:
When a fast-moving grass fire swept through a training exercise at CFB Wainwright on Saturday, four members of the Canadian Armed Forces were killed and 39 patients were taken to hospital, 19 of them in critical condition.

Star readers have responded with grief, gratitude and well wishes for the families and the injured. Here’s what you had to say:

These comments have been edited for clarity and length.

“There are moments when words simply cannot express the sorrow. Four young Canadian soldiers have lost their lives, so many others are fighting for theirs, and families across our country are facing unimaginable heartbreak. My deepest condolences to those who have lost loved ones, and my heartfelt hopes for the recovery of the injured. Canada mourns with you and stands with you in our prayers.” — Lisa

“Heart is broken for all involved. I know that these words seem ‘empty’, but they truly have my thoughts and my heart is with them.” — Patricia

“A heartbreaking tragedy. The loss of these four young men and the critical injuring of so many others is a loss to all of Canada. Whatever the answers are, we shall mourn them and honour them for their service. My heart is so heavy for their family and friends. 💔” — Chris

“May their souls rest in eternal peace. Condolences to the families. May the injured recover soon.” — Amin

“I feel so moved by this. My deep condolences and prayers go to the injured and the grieving families. I keep thinking about how I would feel if it was my child.” — Rosa

stories.title: Weekend shooting
stories.summary: London, ON (October 19, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Major Crime Section are investigating a shooting that took place over the weekend in the south end of the city.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (October 19, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service (LPS) Major Crime Section are investigating a shooting that took place over the weekend in the south end of the city.

On Sunday, October 18, 2026, at approximately 1:30 a.m., police responded to a report of gunshots in the area of Fennell Crescent and Ernest Avenue. While officers were responding, a second call was received regarding a motor vehicle collision in the area of Bradley and Ernest avenues.

Officers located evidence of a shooting on Fennell Crescent and a short time after the original call, an adult male injured in the shooting attended hospital.

Through the course of the investigation, officers determined that the vehicle involved in the nearby collision was also involved in the shooting. Three individuals, two males and one female, who were seen fleeing the vehicle prior to police arrival have not been located.

Investigators believe the victim was targeted, and he remains in hospital in fair condition.

Investigators are asking anyone who was in the area of Fennell Crescent and Ernest Avenue, or Ernest and Bradley avenues, between 1:20 and 1:40 a.m., and May have dash-cam footage, residential or business video surveillance, or information that could assist with the investigation, to contact police.

The Major Crime Section continues to actively investigate this incident with specialized support from across the London Police Service. The investigation remains in its early stages, and more information will be provided as appropriate.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670 or Crime Stoppers at 1-800-222-Tips (8477). Information can also be sent in online anonymously to London Middlesex Crime Stoppers .

stories.title: Brother of CFB Wainwright fire victim demands answers
stories.summary: The Canadian military’s national investigation service is now leading a probe into the incident, Mark Carney says.
stories.author: Alex Ballingall
stories.content:
Ottawa—Serious questions remain about the blaze that killed four soldiers and injured dozens more during a live-fire training exercise at CFB Wainwright on Saturday, as Prime Minister Mark Carney promises the military will lead a thorough investigation to find out how the tragedy happened.

Following a moment of silence Monday in the House of Commons, the prime minister said Parliament was “united in grief” over the incident in Alberta that has prompted anger and a demand for answers from the brother of one of the soldiers who died.

Carney said the “original cause” of the fire is still unknown, but that it was burning during the exercises and “jumped nearly a kilometre in less than a minute” amid “ferocious winds.” The Canadian military’s national investigation service is now leading a probe into the incident, Carney said, with 50 investigators on the ground and support from the RCMP.

Moments later, as he left the Commons, Carney told reporters he was “absolutely” comfortable with the military leading the investigation of a disaster that occurred during its own exercises.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says he will get the answers to "what caused this terrible tragedy," after a grass fire erupted at CFB Wainwright in Alberta on Oct. 17, killing four people and injuring 39 more, 19 of them critically. (Oct. 19, 2026)

“We will give them all the resources that they need,” Carney said. “We will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy as expeditiously and transparently as necessary.”

In an interview with the Star on Monday, the brother of Pte. Shaun Farrell of Saskatchewan, one of the victims, demanded answers from the Canadian military and said he didn’t understand why there weren’t more precautions to prevent the disaster.

“The Canadian Army killed my brother, and they killed those three other men as well,” Bryan Farrell said.

“They died for nothing.”

Appearing Monday evening on CBC, Canada’s top soldier Gen. Jennie Carignan said several investigations are currently looking into what happened: one led by the military’s investigation service, another through Alberta’s chief medical examiner with support from military police and the RCMP, while the armed forces’ fire marshal is also probing the incident.

The military will also strike a formal “board of inquiry” that will include a “panel of experts” to see if the military should change its safety protocols and regulations after the disaster, Carignan said.

She added that it’s too soon to say whether the exercises should have proceeded given the conditions at the time, which included high winds and a burning brushfire, but that preliminary findings suggest reports of explosions as the blaze spread were from another part of the training exercise, further away from the fire.

“We need to train,” Carignan said, pointing to the military’s Nato commitments in Latvia, where soldiers from the base were slated to be deployed.

“There are some risks as well that we need to take when we are training.”

Meanwhile, the House of Commons suspended the day’s sitting after Carney and party leaders addressed Parliament to offer expressions of shared grief.

During his speech in the House, Carney spoke of the four soldiers killed — Farrell, from Prince Albert, Sask.; Sgt. Morgan Wong, from Edmonton; Pte. Aidan Goulding, from North Vancouver; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, from Langley, B.C. — as “sons, brothers, partners, friends, young men with bright futures who chose to serve our country and who died in that cause.”

The Canadian Armed Forces has identified the four soldiers who died in a fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta. Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division, says the service members were from British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta. (Oct. 18, 2026)

Carney spoke of each man’s commitment and service, with Wong preparing for a second tour in Latvia, where the Canadian military is leading a Nato force to deter further Russian aggression in the Baltic. Farrell and Lykkemark, both of Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, were also “best friends, seldom seen apart,” Carney said.

“To their friends, to their families, to their colleagues, to the people of Wainwright, please know that you have the entire nation at your side.”

Addressing the House remotely from Wainwright, where the military base is part of his own riding, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said he recalls meeting Goulding, one of the soldiers killed.

“I remember meeting him. Strong, handsome, polite, a real gentleman,” Poilievre said, sending prayers to those injured badly with burns, and thanked first responders who fought the blaze and are providing care to soldiers in hospital.

“All these heroes must be exhausted,” Poilievre said. “They’ve lived a horror story. And yet, as I travel around town and the municipal district, none of them are breaking.

“Pray for the fallen, pray for the victims, pray for their families, pray for all of the people in and around Wainwright.”

Yves-François Blanchet, the Bloc Québécois leader, offered condolences in English to the families of those killed and said, “The price of service should never be so high.”

New Democrat MP Gord Johns said Canada’s “first responsibility is to those whose lives are forever changed” by the incident, while Green MP Elizabeth May told the House that “questions of how this happened will sit with us until we get answers.

“But today is not that day,” May said.

“We owe it to those who died, and to their loved ones, and to those who are injured and wounded to get those answers and take on board those lessons so this could never happen again.”

On Sunday, after a chaotic night with few details of what happened, Carney said the fire represented one of the worst peacetime tragedies on Canadian soil for the country’s military.

Officials, meanwhile, described in a briefing to journalists how a grass fire ignited inside the training area at the military base and spread quickly in “uncommonly strong winds” as multiple types of exercises were going on at the same time.

Speaking to reporters in Edmonton on Sunday, Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland said officials do not believe the fire was linked to any of the area’s oil and gas infrastructure, or any “outside interference” during the training exercises.

“I spoke to my commander on the ground last night and this morning, and he said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire,” Rutland said. “And then there was a fire right on top of them.”

The investigation will include questions about why they didn’t see the fire coming, he added, including analysis of the terrain, field conditions, foliage and more, “because it all plays into what happened.”

The major-general also said it is not yet clear whether weapons being used during training were linked to the fire. The exercises included grenades, grenade launchers, and other arms and ammunition, he said, stating that “any of that or none of it” could have contributed to what happened.

He also said that “initial impressions” from investigators were that oil and gas infrastructure in the area was not damaged.

“This is why we’re getting that fire marshal team on the ground, because we’ve got to check what caused it,” Rutland said.

“It could be a multitude of things.”

Following a moment of silence Monday in the House of Commons, the prime minister said Parliament was “united in grief” over the incident in Alberta that has prompted anger and a demand for answers from the brother of one of the soldiers who died.

Carney said the “original cause” of the fire is still unknown, but that it was burning during the exercises and “jumped nearly a kilometre in less than a minute” amid “ferocious winds.” The Canadian military’s national investigation service is now leading a probe into the incident, Carney said, with 50 investigators on the ground and support from the RCMP.
Moments later, as he left the Commons, Carney told reporters he was “absolutely” comfortable with the military leading the investigation of a disaster that occurred during its own exercises.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says he will get the answers to "what caused this terrible tragedy," after a grass fire erupted at CFB Wainwright in Alberta on Oct. 17, killing four people and injuring 39 more, 19 of them critically. (Oct. 19, 2026)
“We will give them all the resources that they need,” Carney said. “We will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy as expeditiously and transparently as necessary.”

In an interview with the Star on Monday, the brother of Pte. Shaun Farrell of Saskatchewan, one of the victims, demanded answers from the Canadian military and said he didn’t understand why there weren’t more precautions to prevent the disaster.
“The Canadian Army killed my brother, and they killed those three other men as well,” Bryan Farrell said.
“They died for nothing.”

Appearing Monday evening on CBC, Canada’s top soldier Gen. Jennie Carignan said several investigations are currently looking into what happened: one led by the military’s investigation service, another through Alberta’s chief medical examiner with support from military police and the RCMP, while the armed forces’ fire marshal is also probing the incident.

The military will also strike a formal “board of inquiry” that will include a “panel of experts” to see if the military should change its safety protocols and regulations after the disaster, Carignan said.

She added that it’s too soon to say whether the exercises should have proceeded given the conditions at the time, which included high winds and a burning brushfire, but that preliminary findings suggest reports of explosions as the blaze spread were from another part of the training exercise, further away from the fire.
“We need to train,” Carignan said, pointing to the military’s Nato commitments in Latvia, where soldiers from the base were slated to be deployed.
“There are some risks as well that we need to take when we are training.”
Meanwhile, the House of Commons suspended the day’s sitting after Carney and party leaders addressed Parliament to offer expressions of shared grief.

During his speech in the House, Carney spoke of the four soldiers killed — Farrell, from Prince Albert, Sask.; Sgt. Morgan Wong, from Edmonton; Pte. Aidan Goulding, from North Vancouver; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, from Langley, B.C. — as “sons, brothers, partners, friends, young men with bright futures who chose to serve our country and who died in that cause.”

The Canadian Armed Forces has identified the four soldiers who died in a fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta. Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division, says the service members were from British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta. (Oct. 18, 2026)

Carney spoke of each man’s commitment and service, with Wong preparing for a second tour in Latvia, where the Canadian military is leading a Nato force to deter further Russian aggression in the Baltic. Farrell and Lykkemark, both of Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, were also “best friends, seldom seen apart,” Carney said.
“To their friends, to their families, to their colleagues, to the people of Wainwright, please know that you have the entire nation at your side.”
Addressing the House remotely from Wainwright, where the military base is part of his own riding, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said he recalls meeting Goulding, one of the soldiers killed.

“I remember meeting him. Strong, handsome, polite, a real gentleman,” Poilievre said, sending prayers to those injured badly with burns, and thanked first responders who fought the blaze and are providing care to soldiers in hospital.
“All these heroes must be exhausted,” Poilievre said. “They’ve lived a horror story. And yet, as I travel around town and the municipal district, none of them are breaking.
“Pray for the fallen, pray for the victims, pray for their families, pray for all of the people in and around Wainwright.”
Yves-François Blanchet, the Bloc Québécois leader, offered condolences in English to the families of those killed and said, “The price of service should never be so high.”

New Democrat MP Gord Johns said Canada’s “first responsibility is to those whose lives are forever changed” by the incident, while Green MP Elizabeth May told the House that “questions of how this happened will sit with us until we get answers.
“But today is not that day,” May said.
“We owe it to those who died, and to their loved ones, and to those who are injured and wounded to get those answers and take on board those lessons so this could never happen again.”

stories.title: The victims of CFB Wainwright: What we know about the four soldiers killed in military training fire
stories.summary: Four Canadian soldiers killed in a fast-moving fire during a training exercise in Alberta over the weekend are being remembered by their families and communities as tributes pour in from across the country.
stories.author: Samm Mohibuddin; Aajah Sauter
stories.content:
The fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright broke out Saturday afternoon, about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton. Four soldiers were killed and 39 were injured with 19 of those in critical condition.

The soldiers were participating in live-fire training when a grass fire, fuelled by powerful winds, swept across the training area. Military officials said the fire travelled about a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds, overtaking a section of the training range.

The Canadian Armed Forces identified those killed as Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark.

The Canadian Armed Forces has identified the four soldiers who died in a fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta. Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division, says the service members were from British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta. (Oct. 18, 2026)

All four were serving with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, based in Edmonton, although Wong was a reservist attached to the battalion.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, during his speech in the House of Commons, spoke of the young soldiers as “sons, brothers, partners, friends — young men with bright futures who chose to serve our country and who died in that cause,” stating that the friends, families and colleagues of the victims “have the entire nation at their side.”

As investigators examine what caused the fire, families, friends and fellow soldiers are remembering the lives of those who died.

Here is what we know about them so far.

Sgt. Morgan Wong, from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment based at Edmonton, serving with 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry is shown in an undated handout photo. Wong died during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright on Saturday, Oct. 17.

Morgan Wong, a 26-year-old reservist from Edmonton, balanced his military service with a career in finance and a commitment to volunteering.

Wong joined the Canadian Armed Forces in 2017 and served with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment. He was attached to the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry when the fire occurred.

A graduate of the University of Alberta, Wong earned a Bachelor of Commerce degree and certificates in real estate and civic-military leadership.

He had worked as a financial analyst and manager with the Alberta government for four years and volunteered with St. John Ambulance.

In a family statement reported by The Canadian Press, relatives remembered Wong as someone who could always be counted on and enjoyed staying active and spending time with loved ones.

Wong previously served in Latvia from October 2024 and June 2025, and was preparing for another deployment to Europe.

The 49th Battalion Loyal Edmonton Regiment Association offered condolences to his family and fellow soldiers following the tragedy.

Pte. Shaun Farrell, from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton is shown in an undated handout photo published to social media. Farrell died during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026.

Shaun Farrell, a 23-year-old from Prince Albert, Sask., served with the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

Fateh Nanouh, who is also stationed at CFB Wainwright, met Farrell in September during basic training where the two shared a brotherly kinship.

“He was a really, really smart guy when it comes to fighting,” said Nanouh.

In a short Facebook post Sunday, Farrell’s mother shared a photo of her son, relaying the news of his death and expressed gratitude for love and support “during this incredibly difficult time.”

“Love you, my darling child,” she posted.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said flags in the province will be lowered to half-mast in Farrell’s memory.

“Shaun was a young man full of promise who chose to serve his country. His loss will be felt deeply by his family, friends, fellow service members, and all who knew him,” Moe said in a statement.

“To Shaun’s family, to the families of the other fallen service members, and to everyone carrying the weight of this loss today, please know that Saskatchewan stands with you, and that you are in our prayers in the difficult days ahead.”

Pte. Aidan Goulding, from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, is shown in an undated handout photo. Goulding died during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026.

Aidan Goulding, a 23-year-old from North Vancouver, also served with the 3rd Battalion.

Addressing the House by video from Wainwright, where the military base is part of his own riding, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said he recalls Goulding.

“I remember meeting him. Strong, handsome, polite, a real gentleman.”

In a statement reported by The Canadian Press, his family said he was an exceptional athlete who became a mechanic after high school. He later quit to join the army.

He planned to eventually work for special operations and eventually Csis, according to a statement from his mother, Sonia Monk, and his older brother Wylder Goulding. They said he loved his adopted army family and looked forward to his deployment in Latvia.

“He was the guy that kept people’s spirits up, a contagious laugh and a cheeky smile, he took the role in the army seriously, and our family and his dear friends have suffered a great loss.”

“Before he went to basic training,” the statement read, “he said, ‘I know I have one life to live, and I’m gonna make the best out of it.’ That was our Aidan.”

Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, is shown in an undated handout photo published to social media. Lykkemark died during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026.

Hayden Lykkemark was from Langley, B.C., and served alongside Goulding, Farrell and Wong in the same battalion.

Some of those who knew the 19-year-old described him as “fun” and someone who never got mad. “He always solved problems for other people,” said Nanouh, who served with his friends Lykkemark and Farrell.

“He was always the person to talk to when you needed something.”

Nanouh said Lykkemark’s dream was to become a sailor, describing him as “more of a sea type of guy.”

B.C. Premier David Eby acknowledged Lykkemark and Goulding in a social media post. “In this moment of profound heartbreak, as British Columbians and Canadians, let’s wrap our arms around their families, supporting them and joining in the mourning of this horrible tragedy,” he said.

On Monday, the Vancouver-area Langley Rugby Club acknowledged the death of Lykkemark in a social media post, who they say was a former Langley Secondary School student.

The post read that Lykkemark will be remembered as a “valued member” of the Langley community, who joined the Canadian Armed Forces after graduating.

“He was a dedicated student, athlete, teammate, and friend who made a positive impact on those around him. Whether on the rugby field, in the classroom, or among his peers, Hayden was known for his character, determination, and willingness to support others,” read the post.

Sgt. Morgan Wong, from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment based at Edmonton, serving with 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry is shown in an undated handout photo. Wong died during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright on Saturday, Oct. 17.
Morgan Wong, a 26-year-old reservist from Edmonton, balanced his military service with a career in finance and a commitment to volunteering.
Wong joined the Canadian Armed Forces in 2017 and served with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment. He was attached to the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry when the fire occurred.
A graduate of the University of Alberta, Wong earned a Bachelor of Commerce degree and certificates in real estate and civic-military leadership.
He had worked as a financial analyst and manager with the Alberta government for four years and volunteered with St. John Ambulance.
In a family statement reported by The Canadian Press, relatives remembered Wong as someone who could always be counted on and enjoyed staying active and spending time with loved ones.
Wong previously served in Latvia from October 2024 and June 2025, and was preparing for another deployment to Europe.
The 49th Battalion Loyal Edmonton Regiment Association offered condolences to his family and fellow soldiers following the tragedy.

Pte. Shaun Farrell, from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton is shown in an undated handout photo published to social media. Farrell died during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026.
Shaun Farrell, a 23-year-old from Prince Albert, Sask., served with the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
Fateh Nanouh, who is also stationed at CFB Wainwright, met Farrell in September during basic training where the two shared a brotherly kinship.
“He was a really, really smart guy when it comes to fighting,” said Nanouh.
In a short Facebook post Sunday, Farrell’s mother shared a photo of her son, relaying the news of his death and expressed gratitude for love and support “during this incredibly difficult time.”
“Love you, my darling child,” she posted.
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said flags in the province will be lowered to half-mast in Farrell’s memory.
“Shaun was a young man full of promise who chose to serve his country. His loss will be felt deeply by his family, friends, fellow service members, and all who knew him,” Moe said in a statement.

“To Shaun’s family, to the families of the other fallen service members, and to everyone carrying the weight of this loss today, please know that Saskatchewan stands with you, and that you are in our prayers in the difficult days ahead.”

Pte. Aidan Goulding, from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, is shown in an undated handout photo. Goulding died during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026.
Aidan Goulding, a 23-year-old from North Vancouver, also served with the 3rd Battalion.
Addressing the House by video from Wainwright, where the military base is part of his own riding, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said he recalls Goulding.
“I remember meeting him. Strong, handsome, polite, a real gentleman.”
In a statement reported by The Canadian Press, his family said he was an exceptional athlete who became a mechanic after high school. He later quit to join the army.

He planned to eventually work for special operations and eventually Csis, according to a statement from his mother, Sonia Monk, and his older brother Wylder Goulding. They said he loved his adopted army family and looked forward to his deployment in Latvia.
“He was the guy that kept people’s spirits up, a contagious laugh and a cheeky smile, he took the role in the army seriously, and our family and his dear friends have suffered a great loss.”
“Before he went to basic training,” the statement read, “he said, ‘I know I have one life to live, and I’m gonna make the best out of it.’ That was our Aidan.”

Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, is shown in an undated handout photo published to social media. Lykkemark died during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright on Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026.
Hayden Lykkemark was from Langley, B.C., and served alongside Goulding, Farrell and Wong in the same battalion.

Some of those who knew the 19-year-old described him as “fun” and someone who never got mad. “He always solved problems for other people,” said Nanouh, who served with his friends Lykkemark and Farrell.
“He was always the person to talk to when you needed something.”
Nanouh said Lykkemark’s dream was to become a sailor, describing him as “more of a sea type of guy.”

B.C. Premier David Eby acknowledged Lykkemark and Goulding in a social media post. “In this moment of profound heartbreak, as British Columbians and Canadians, let’s wrap our arms around their families, supporting them and joining in the mourning of this horrible tragedy,” he said.
On Monday, the Vancouver-area Langley Rugby Club acknowledged the death of Lykkemark in a social media post, who they say was a former Langley Secondary School student.
The post read that Lykkemark will be remembered as a “valued member” of the Langley community, who joined the Canadian Armed Forces after graduating.

“He was a dedicated student, athlete, teammate, and friend who made a positive impact on those around him. Whether on the rugby field, in the classroom, or among his peers, Hayden was known for his character, determination, and willingness to support others,” read the post.

stories.title: The 4 soldiers killed in fast-moving fire at CFB Wainwright
stories.summary: A look at the Canadian Armed Forces members who died during a training exercise in Alberta
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Four Armed Forces members were killed when a fast-moving fire overwhelmed soldiers during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton, ON Saturday. Dozens of others were injured, with 39 still in hospital on Sunday.

Here’s a look at the four who died:

Farrell, a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, was from Prince Albert, Sask.

In a social media post, his mother asked for privacy as the family navigates “this profound loss.”

“We want to thank everyone for your love, support, and prayers during this incredibly difficult time,” said Patricia Farrell.

She also posted a photo of her smiling son in uniform, standing by a pickup truck. “Love you my darling child.”

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said flags in the province would be lowered to half-mast in Farrell’s memory.

“Shaun was a young man full of promise who chose to serve his country. His loss will be felt deeply by his family, friends, fellow service members, and all who knew him,” Moe said in a statement.

“To Shaun’s family, to the families of the other fallen service members, and to everyone carrying the weight of this loss today, please know that Saskatchewan stands with you, and that you are in our prayers in the difficult days ahead.”

The 23-year-old, of North Vancouver, was also a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

His family said he was an exceptional athlete and, after high school, became a mechanic.

He later quit to join the army.

“Although he was making excellent money and had a good life, he decided he wanted to defend his country. His goal was to work for Special OPs and then onto Csis,” his mother, Sonia Monk, and older brother, Wylder Goulding, said in a statement.

“He was the guy that kept people’s spirits up, a contagious laugh and a cheeky smile, he took his role in the army seriously, and our family and his dear friends have suffered a great loss.”

They said he loved his adopted new army family and was looking forward to peacekeeping in Latvia.

“Before he went to basic training, he said, ‘I know I have one life to live, and I’m gonna make the best out of it.’ That was our Aidan.”

Lykkemark was from Langley, B.C., and with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

B.C. Premier David Eby recognized Lykkemark and Goulding in a social media post.

“In this moment of profound heartbreak, as British Columbians and Canadians, let’s wrap our arms around their families, supporting them and joining in the mourning of this horrible tragedy,” he said.

The 26-year-old from Edmonton was a reservist with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, serving with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

“He was an incredible person who was always there whenever anyone needed him,” his family said in a statement.

“He loved being active and spending time with his friends and family. He was extremely proud to serve with the Canadian Armed Forces.”

They said he earned a bachelor of commerce degree from the University of Alberta, as well as certificates in real estate and civil-military leadership.

He joined the Forces in 2017, and for the last four years worked as a financial analyst and manager with the Alberta government. He also served as a first responder with St. John Ambulance.

He served in Latvia from October 2024 to June 2025, and was preparing for a second tour in Europe.

“We are deeply saddened by the loss of Sergeant Morgan Wong of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, and all those who lost their lives yesterday at Wainwright,” the 49th Battalion Loyal Edmonton Regiment Association said in a social media post.

“Our thoughts and prayers are also with the injured, their loved ones and everyone affected by this tragedy.

“We will remember them.”

The 26-year-old from Edmonton was a reservist with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, serving with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
“He was an incredible person who was always there whenever anyone needed him,” his family said in a statement.
