stories.title: Vancouver elects Canada’s first Green mayor
stories.summary: Pete Fry said dealing with community safety and homelessness are among his priorities
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
The first Green mayor of a major Canadian city says his top priority will be dealing with community safety and moving toward a thoughtful approach to getting people off the streets in Vancouver.

On the campaign trail, Pete Fry pledged to create an office of community safety to co-ordinate police, fire, community services, and land use, as well as a 24/7 nonpolice team for non-emergency calls.

The Greens have also promised to lift a moratorium, introduced by incumbent Ken Sim, ON new supportive housing projects.

“We hear loud and clear from folks that they are struggling with quality of life in the city,” Mr. Fry said in an interview Sunday.

A really big priority is community safety and dealing with “this sort of visible manifestation of poverty and homelessness on our streets. How do we fix that as a society and a city and get away from this really negative narrative.”

It’s been 15 years since Vancouver elected its first Green councillor and Mr. Fry said the city’s party is distinct from its federal and provincial counterparts.

The civic elections came just a week before British Columbians vote in a snap provincial election. The provincial Greens, under new Leader Emily Lowan, advocate for expanded access to pharmaceutical alternatives to street opioids for those who use drugs and to decriminalize possession of street drugs for personal use, among other measures.

But Mr. Fry distanced his civic colleagues from the provincial Green campaign.

“Where we share a lot of values, we’re not aligned on political ideologies necessarily, or mandates. My priority and my team’s priority is to govern Vancouver, and to achieve the best for the city,” he said.

Still, he said that effort will include core Green values like diversity and sustainability and the environment.

“But that isn’t necessarily a bad thing at all,” he said.

Nick Poppell, executive director of the Vancouver Greens, said the party has had a record of being on council, school boards and the parks board.

“So it really wasn’t a hard sell, per se as a Green. What really helped solidify it was Pete Fry being Pete Fry,” he said.

Mr. Fry was born in Dublin to Anglo-Trinidadian parents and moved to Vancouver when he was two. His mother is long-time Vancouver Liberal MP Hedy Fry.

Mr. Fry studied arts and business at Simon Fraser University, before going on to run a publishing house and a clothing import business. He later moved into computer design and for more than 30 years was self-employed as a graphic artist.

He said he first got involved in local politics in 2006 while sitting on a dog strategy task force. But after a friend was killed while walking on a local street, he became active within the community that encompasses Vancouver’s Downtown Eastside. He still lives there.

On Saturday, voters empowered Mr. Fry to deal with this and other issues, electing him over Mr. Sim, who was seeking a second term as Vancouver mayor.

Mr. Fry has been a city councillor in Vancouver since 2018.

Of the 10 councillors elected Saturday, all but one are left of centre. Voters elected four Greens, four from the left-wing Coalition of Progressive Electors, and one from the OneCity. Mr. Sim’s ABC party, which governed from the right of centre, has been reduced to one member of council.

“It’s certainly a council that I think I can work with,” Mr. Fry said.

Michael Geller, a housing commentator, said in an interview that Mr. Fry’s political situation will be clarified after Saturday’s provincial election determines whether there is a partner or rival for advancing his agenda.

The municipal Greens have talked about holding an independent audit of the Vancouver police before any adjustments to the force’s budget. Mr. Fry said Police Chief Steve Rai called him once the votes were in on Saturday to congratulate him.

“The chief and I have a good working relationship and we have always been quite friendly,” he said. “I look forward to connecting with Chief Rai soon to talk about how we can build that relationship.”

Shortly after Mr. Fry’s win was confirmed on Saturday night, his mother said she was thrilled.

“He’s going to make a great mayor,” Hedy Fry, an MP for 33 years, said at the downtown bar where Mr. Fry and his supporters had gathered to watch the election results.

“I don’t think he will be a partisan mayor. He will work with everybody to get the best ideas and move things forward. That’s how he has always been.”

In Surrey, controversial former mayor Doug McCallum, was elected once again. He defeated the incumbent Brenda Locke.

Four years ago, Ms. Locke beat Mr. McCallum after public dissatisfaction at how he had handled a pledge to replace the RCMP with a new municipal police force. Ms. Locke campaigned in 2022 on keeping the RCMP, but the provincial government eventually forced the city to continue on the path for the new force.

stories.title: Here are the 4 soldiers killed in fast-moving fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta
stories.summary: Wainwright — Four Armed Forces members were killed when a fast-moving fire overwhelmed soldiers during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton, ON Saturday. Dozens of others were injured, with 39 still in hospital on Sunday.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By The Canadian Press

Posted October 18, 2026 9:31 pm.

Last Updated October 18, 2026 10:13 pm.

WAINWRIGHT — Four Armed Forces members were killed when a fast-moving fire overwhelmed soldiers during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton, on Saturday. Dozens of others were injured, with 39 still in hospital on Sunday.

Here’s a look at the four who died:

Private Shaun Farrell

Farrell, a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, was from Prince Albert, Sask.

In a social media post, his mother asked for privacy as the family navigates “this profound loss.”

“We want to thank everyone for your love, support, and prayers during this incredibly difficult time,” said Patricia Farrell.

She also posted a photo of her smiling son in uniform, standing by a pickup truck. “Love you my darling child.”

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said flags in the province would be lowered to half-mast in Farrell’s memory.

“Shaun was a young man full of promise who chose to serve his country. His loss will be felt deeply by his family, friends, fellow service members, and all who knew him,” Moe said in a statement.

“To Shaun’s family, to the families of the other fallen service members, and to everyone carrying the weight of this loss today, please know that Saskatchewan stands with you, and that you are in our prayers in the difficult days ahead.”

Private Aidan Goulding

The 23-year-old, of North Vancouver, was also a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

His family said he was an exceptional athlete and, after high school, became a mechanic.

He later quit to join the army.

“Although he was making excellent money and had a good life, he decided he wanted to defend his country. His goal was to work for Special OPs and then onto CSIS,” his mother, Sonia Monk, and older brother, Wylder Goulding, said in a statement.

“He was the guy that kept people’s spirits up, a contagious laugh and a cheeky smile, he took his role in the army seriously, and our family and his dear friends have suffered a great loss.”

They said he loved his adopted new army family and was looking forward to peacekeeping in Latvia.

“Before he went to basic training, he said, ‘I know I have one life to live, and I’m gonna make the best out of it.’ That was our Aidan.”

Private Hayden Lykkemark

Lykkemark was from Langley, B.C., and served with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

B.C. Premier David Eby recognized Lykkemark and Goulding in a social media post.

“In this moment of profound heartbreak, as British Columbians and Canadians, let’s wrap our arms around their families, supporting them and joining in the mourning of this horrible tragedy,” he said.

Sgt. Morgan Wong

The 26-year-old from Edmonton was a reservist with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, serving with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

“He was an incredible person who was always there whenever anyone needed him,” his family said in a statement.

“Our thoughts and prayers are also with the injured, their loved ones and everyone affected by this tragedy.

“We will remember them.”

Private Shaun Farrell
Farrell, a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, was from Prince Albert, Sask.
In a social media post, his mother asked for privacy as the family navigates “this profound loss.”
“We want to thank everyone for your love, support, and prayers during this incredibly difficult time,” said Patricia Farrell.
She also posted a photo of her smiling son in uniform, standing by a pickup truck. “Love you my darling child.”
Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said flags in the province would be lowered to half-mast in Farrell’s memory.
“Shaun was a young man full of promise who chose to serve his country. His loss will be felt deeply by his family, friends, fellow service members, and all who knew him,” Moe said in a statement.

Private Aidan Goulding
The 23-year-old, of North Vancouver, was also a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
His family said he was an exceptional athlete and, after high school, became a mechanic.
He later quit to join the army.

He joined the Forces in 2017, and for the last four years worked as a financial analyst and manager with the Alberta government. He also served as a first responder with St. John Ambulance.

“We are deeply saddened by the loss of Sergeant Morgan Wong of the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, and all those who lost their lives yesterday at Wainwright,” the 49th Battalion Loyal Edmonton Regiment Association said in a social media post.

stories.title: What we know about the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright
stories.summary: Four military members are dead and dozens more have been seriously injured after an explosion and fast-moving fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, in what Prime Minister Mark Carney described as one of the worst tragedies to hit the Canadian Armed Forces during peacetime.
stories.author: Archie Niari
stories.content:
Four military members are dead and dozens more have been seriously injured after a fast-moving fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, in what Prime Minister Mark Carney described as one of the worst tragedies to hit the Canadian Armed Forces during peacetime.

Thirty-nine people were hospitalized, 19 of them in are in critical condition.

The incident occurred at about 4 p.m. local time Saturday at the military base east of Edmonton. Emergency crews rushed to the scene as the fire spread rapidly, prompting a major medical response across the region.

The Canadian Armed Forces says it is still assessing the full extent of the impact.

Live Updates: Officials providing update after ‘fast-moving’ CFB Wainwright fire kills 4 soldiers

Here is what we know so far:

Four military members killed, dozens injured

Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed the deaths and injuries Sunday.

Family members of those killed have been notified, Carney said. Those affected included personnel from military bases across the country, including reservists and soldiers serving with Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

In his remarks on Sunday, Carney described the scale of the tragedy.

“Yesterday afternoon, a violent, fast-moving fire swept through a Canadian Armed Forces base in Wainwright, Alberta. What followed was one of the worst tragedies for the forces in Canadian soil in peace time,” he said.

In a press conference Sunday afternoon, Maj-Gen. L.W. Rutland told reporters that the fire broke out during a training exercise ahead of the soldiers’ deployment to Latvia.

The officials at CFB Wainwright were aware of the fire for several hours before it turned toward the training area, Rutland said. Despite the knowledge, the soldiers continued to carry out their exercises.

CAF officials believe there was no damage to oil and gas infrastructure as a result of the fire, Rutland said.

CFB Wainwright victims identified

The following members were killed during the fire at CFB Wainwright, according to Maj-Gen. L.W. Rutland:

Sergeant Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Alta., from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment based at Edmonton, Alberta serving with 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry

Private Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alta.

Private Aidan Goulding from North Vancouver, B.C., from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alta.

Private Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C., from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alta.

Nearly 40 patients receiving treatment at regional hospitals

The medical response has placed significant demands on hospitals and emergency services in the Edmonton region.

Dr. Sayeh Zielke, the CEO of Acute Care Alberta told reporters 19 people are in critical condition, eight are stable, and 12 are ambulatory and are receiving care for injuries that can be assessed without admission.

Dr. Steve Fisher, an emergency physician at Edmonton’s Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CTV News Edmonton on Sunday that patients had sustained burns of varying severity, with the most seriously affected being treated at the University of Alberta Hospital, which has a burn intensive care unit.

The scale of the response prompted Acute Care Alberta to ask residents to avoid the University of Alberta Hospital emergency department if possible Saturday night, unless they required emergency care.

The agency said “significant resources” were needed from Emergency Health Services and Edmonton-area emergency departments into the night.

Stars Air Ambulance dispatched two air ambulances from Saskatoon and Edmonton. Helicopters and two aircraft also landed at a nearby medical evacuation site as emergency personnel worked to transport and treat the injured.

Soldiers were working with hand grenades: CAF

The 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry and reservists were taking part in high-intensity training ahead of deploymen, Rutland said.

The Charlie Company, or C Company soldiers were throwing hand grenades on a hand grenade range and conducting a section attack, with 10 soldiers attacking a simulated enemy when the fire broke out, he added.

Code Orange lifted after emergency response

A Code Orange is activated when a mass-casualty event places pressure on the health-care system because of a surge in patients. The code remained in effect for more than 10 hours before being lifted shortly before 1 p.m. Sunday.

Investigation underway, terrorism not likely

The Canadian Armed Forces will undertake a board of inquiry to examine the events of Oct. 17, Rutland said.

A spokesperson for National Defence said Sunday there were no indications the incident was the result of terrorist activity.

“As emergency responders continue their work and the situation continues to evolve, the full extent of the impact remains under assessment. Our immediate priority is supporting those affected and notifying next of kin. We will not confirm casualty or injury details until that process is complete,” Laura McIntyre-Grills wrote in a statement to CTV News Edmonton.

“While the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity.”

Retired major-general David Fraser, a CTV military analyst and former commander of Nato forces in southern Afghanistan, described the incident as the worst training tragedy he had witnessed during his military career.

“We are now dealing with the worst tragedy that I’ve seen in my entire career,” Fraser told CTV News Channel.

Fraser, who was previously posted at Wainwright and trained there extensively, said he had seen no indications the incident was anything other than an accident.

He said Canadian military bases have established safety procedures for live-fire and other training exercises. He expects those procedures to remain in place until investigators determine whether changes are needed.

Defence Minister David McGuinty was travelling to Edmonton on Sunday to receive a briefing on the latest developments. He said the Department of National Defence was working closely with Alberta’s government and local authorities.

I am on my way to Edmonton. I will get briefed on the latest developments regarding the terrible incident that occurred at CFB Wainwright. The Department of National Defence continues to work closely with the Government of Alberta and local authorities. Thank you to first… — David McGuinty (@DavidMcGuinty) October 18, 2026

High winds contributed to rapidly spreading fire

The Municipal District of Wainwright said high winds caused the fire to spread rapidly into the surrounding area Saturday.

Officials said the fire crossed the base fence earlier in the day and was being managed south of Wainwright.

Crews faced volatile conditions as parts of Alberta experienced wind gusts of up to 100 km/h. Municipal information officers told CTV News Edmonton late Saturday that the spread was under control.

Rutland told reporters the wind caused the fire to shift towards the training area, and it crossed fire guards before it was contained.

The fire is not believed to be a result of oil and gas infrastructure or outside interference, but the cause is still under investigation.

Video shows fire burning near CFB Wainwright

Video captured from private property about one kilometre from Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on Saturday shows flames burning in the area as smoke billows across the sky.

The footage offers a glimpse of the fire that prompted a major emergency response at the Alberta military base.

Military families urged to seek support

The Edmonton Military Family Resource Centre opened Sunday to support military families affected by the incident.

Families were invited to connect in a safe and supportive space as they dealt with the aftermath.

People needing additional assistance can call the Family Information Line at 1-800-866-4546 for free, confidential support, available 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

Officials have said supporting those affected and notifying next of kin remain immediate priorities

Canadian Blood Services calls for donations

Canadian Blood Services is offering its condolences to those affected by the CFB Wainwright fire and encouraging Canadians to donate blood to help support injured patients.

“Our top priority is ensuring patients in Canada receive the blood and blood products they need. We are closely monitoring the needs of patients and hospitals in Alberta and will continue to work with health system partners to ensure those needs are met,” a media spokesperson wrote in a statement to CTV News Edmonton on Sunday.

The organization said appointments remained available in Alberta and across Canada, adding that donations in the coming weeks would help maintain the national blood supply.

“We are grateful to the many people who have already reached out to ask how they can help. Donating blood is one meaningful way to support patients in Canada, both now and in the weeks ahead. Many appointments are still available throughout Alberta and across Canada, and donations in the coming weeks will help to keep our national inventory strong.”

Political and military leaders offer condolences

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the loss of life and injuries as heartbreaking and said her government was working with federal officials and local authorities.

“The loss of life and injuries are heartbreaking. On behalf of the Government of Alberta, I extend my deepest condolences to the families who have lost loved ones and wish those who have been injured a full recovery. Our thoughts are also with the military personnel, families and colleagues facing uncertainty and grief during this incredibly difficult time,” Smith said.

Alberta is mourning alongside the Canadian Armed Forces and the families, friends and colleagues of those affected by the tragic incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright yesterday. The loss of life and injuries are heartbreaking. On behalf of the Government of Alberta, I… pic.twitter.com/pKIG6vQuPS — Danielle Smith (@ABDanielleSmith) October 18, 2026

Smith said she would travel to Edmonton to meet with provincial ministers and federal officials. The province activated its Emergency Management Cabinet Co-ordination Committee and raised the Provincial Emergency Coordination Centre to Level 3.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford also offered assistance with recovery efforts, saying his province stood “ready to help.”

“As Canadians, let’s come together to support our brave men and women in uniform, who put their lives on the line to protect our freedoms and our country,” Ford said .

Maritime premiers also expressed condolences , noting the close ties between military personnel, their families and communities across Canada.

Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney said the tragedy would be deeply felt in the region surrounding the base.

“If you live in east central Alberta in the Wainwright area, this base is part of your life, “ Kenney told CTV News Channel on Sunday. “You get to know the soldiers and the base staff (is) a very large part of the whole broader community out in that sparsely populated area.”

Kenney said Albertans have a “deep regard for the sacrifices taken by our men and women in uniform.”

Nato’s Military Committee also offered condolences to the families of those killed and wished the injured a full recovery.

On behalf of the Nato Military Committee, we extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the tragedy at CFB Wainwright, and our wishes for a full recovery to all the injured. Wainwright is where Canadian soldiers, and so many… pic.twitter.com/3zdIR9k9g5 — Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone - Nato CMC (@CMC_NATO) October 18, 2026

Community and military personnel await further answers

The tragedy has affected military families and communities well beyond Wainwright, as personnel from bases across Canada were among those involved.

A Barrie-area mayoral candidate, Cathy Keane, said her eldest son was critically injured in the incident. In a social media post Sunday, she said she would travel to Alberta to be with him and her family.

“As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family,” she said.

Election day locations in Wainwright to open as planned

Elections Alberta says voting locations in Wainwright will be opened as planned on Oct. 19, officials told reporters.

Eligible voters in the area will be able to cast their 10 ballots at the Wainwright Communiplex and the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 29 Wainwright.

Pro-Canada rally goes ahead in Edmonton

A pro-Canada rally was held in Edmonton on Sunday and while attendees were focused on the referendum on Monday, the incident in Wainwright was still top of mind. Organizer Gil McGowan said the Wainwright tragedy “hangs like a real dark cloud” over the event.

McGowan, the head of the Alberta Federation of Labour, thanked first responders from around Canada and said it’s a poignant reminder of why Canada is better united.

Albertans are set to vote on Monday whether the province should remain in Canada or if a referendum should be held on separation.

Smith told reporters the upcoming referendum on Monday will go ahead.

With files from The Canadian Press

Fraser, who was previously posted at Wainwright and trained there extensively, said he had seen no indications the incident was anything other than an accident.

He said Canadian military bases have established safety procedures for live-fire and other training exercises. He expects those procedures to remain in place until investigators determine whether changes are needed.

Defence Minister David McGuinty was travelling to Edmonton on Sunday to receive a briefing on the latest developments. He said the Department of National Defence was working closely with Alberta’s government and local authorities.

I am on my way to Edmonton. I will get briefed on the latest developments regarding the terrible incident that occurred at CFB Wainwright. The Department of National Defence continues to work closely with the Government of Alberta and local authorities. Thank you to first… — David McGuinty (@DavidMcGuinty) October 18, 2026
High winds contributed to rapidly spreading fire
The Municipal District of Wainwright said high winds caused the fire to spread rapidly into the surrounding area Saturday.
Officials said the fire crossed the base fence earlier in the day and was being managed south of Wainwright.
Crews faced volatile conditions as parts of Alberta experienced wind gusts of up to 100 km/h. Municipal information officers told CTV News Edmonton late Saturday that the spread was under control.
Rutland told reporters the wind caused the fire to shift towards the training area, and it crossed fire guards before it was contained.
The fire is not believed to be a result of oil and gas infrastructure or outside interference, but the cause is still under investigation.
Video shows fire burning near CFB Wainwright
Video captured from private property about one kilometre from Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on Saturday shows flames burning in the area as smoke billows across the sky.
The footage offers a glimpse of the fire that prompted a major emergency response at the Alberta military base.
Military families urged to seek support
The Edmonton Military Family Resource Centre opened Sunday to support military families affected by the incident.
Families were invited to connect in a safe and supportive space as they dealt with the aftermath.
People needing additional assistance can call the Family Information Line at 1-800-866-4546 for free, confidential support, available 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
Officials have said supporting those affected and notifying next of kin remain immediate priorities
Canadian Blood Services calls for donations
Canadian Blood Services is offering its condolences to those affected by the CFB Wainwright fire and encouraging Canadians to donate blood to help support injured patients.

“Our top priority is ensuring patients in Canada receive the blood and blood products they need. We are closely monitoring the needs of patients and hospitals in Alberta and will continue to work with health system partners to ensure those needs are met,” a media spokesperson wrote in a statement to CTV News Edmonton on Sunday.
The organization said appointments remained available in Alberta and across Canada, adding that donations in the coming weeks would help maintain the national blood supply.

“We are grateful to the many people who have already reached out to ask how they can help. Donating blood is one meaningful way to support patients in Canada, both now and in the weeks ahead. Many appointments are still available throughout Alberta and across Canada, and donations in the coming weeks will help to keep our national inventory strong.”
Political and military leaders offer condolences
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the loss of life and injuries as heartbreaking and said her government was working with federal officials and local authorities.

“The loss of life and injuries are heartbreaking. On behalf of the Government of Alberta, I extend my deepest condolences to the families who have lost loved ones and wish those who have been injured a full recovery. Our thoughts are also with the military personnel, families and colleagues facing uncertainty and grief during this incredibly difficult time,” Smith said.

Alberta is mourning alongside the Canadian Armed Forces and the families, friends and colleagues of those affected by the tragic incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright yesterday. The loss of life and injuries are heartbreaking. On behalf of the Government of Alberta, I… pic.twitter.com/pKIG6vQuPS — Danielle Smith (@ABDanielleSmith) October 18, 2026

Smith said she would travel to Edmonton to meet with provincial ministers and federal officials. The province activated its Emergency Management Cabinet Co-ordination Committee and raised the Provincial Emergency Coordination Centre to Level 3.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford also offered assistance with recovery efforts, saying his province stood “ready to help.”
“As Canadians, let’s come together to support our brave men and women in uniform, who put their lives on the line to protect our freedoms and our country,” Ford said .
Maritime premiers also expressed condolences , noting the close ties between military personnel, their families and communities across Canada.
Former Alberta premier Jason Kenney said the tragedy would be deeply felt in the region surrounding the base.

“If you live in east central Alberta in the Wainwright area, this base is part of your life, “ Kenney told CTV News Channel on Sunday. “You get to know the soldiers and the base staff (is) a very large part of the whole broader community out in that sparsely populated area.”
Kenney said Albertans have a “deep regard for the sacrifices taken by our men and women in uniform.”
Nato’s Military Committee also offered condolences to the families of those killed and wished the injured a full recovery.

On behalf of the Nato Military Committee, we extend our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives in the tragedy at CFB Wainwright, and our wishes for a full recovery to all the injured. Wainwright is where Canadian soldiers, and so many… pic.twitter.com/3zdIR9k9g5 — Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone - Nato CMC (@CMC_NATO) October 18, 2026
Community and military personnel await further answers
The tragedy has affected military families and communities well beyond Wainwright, as personnel from bases across Canada were among those involved.

A Barrie-area mayoral candidate, Cathy Keane, said her eldest son was critically injured in the incident. In a social media post Sunday, she said she would travel to Alberta to be with him and her family.
“As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family,” she said.
Election day locations in Wainwright to open as planned
Elections Alberta says voting locations in Wainwright will be opened as planned on Oct. 19, officials told reporters.
Eligible voters in the area will be able to cast their 10 ballots at the Wainwright Communiplex and the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 29 Wainwright.
Pro-Canada rally goes ahead in Edmonton

A pro-Canada rally was held in Edmonton on Sunday and while attendees were focused on the referendum on Monday, the incident in Wainwright was still top of mind. Organizer Gil McGowan said the Wainwright tragedy “hangs like a real dark cloud” over the event.
McGowan, the head of the Alberta Federation of Labour, thanked first responders from around Canada and said it’s a poignant reminder of why Canada is better united.
Albertans are set to vote on Monday whether the province should remain in Canada or if a referendum should be held on separation.
Smith told reporters the upcoming referendum on Monday will go ahead.

content_blocks.text: Four military members are dead and dozens more have been seriously injured after a fast-moving fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, in what Prime Minister Mark Carney described as one of the worst tragedies to hit the Canadian Armed Forces during peacetime.
Thirty-nine people were hospitalized, 19 of them in are in critical condition.

The incident occurred at about 4 p.m. local time Saturday at the military base east of Edmonton. Emergency crews rushed to the scene as the fire spread rapidly, prompting a major medical response across the region.
The Canadian Armed Forces says it is still assessing the full extent of the impact.
Live Updates: Officials providing update after ‘fast-moving’ CFB Wainwright fire kills 4 soldiers
Here is what we know so far:
Four military members killed, dozens injured
Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed the deaths and injuries Sunday.

Family members of those killed have been notified, Carney said. Those affected included personnel from military bases across the country, including reservists and soldiers serving with Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
In his remarks on Sunday, Carney described the scale of the tragedy.

“Yesterday afternoon, a violent, fast-moving fire swept through a Canadian Armed Forces base in Wainwright, Alberta. What followed was one of the worst tragedies for the forces in Canadian soil in peace time,” he said.
In a press conference Sunday afternoon, Maj-Gen. L.W. Rutland told reporters that the fire broke out during a training exercise ahead of the soldiers’ deployment to Latvia.

The officials at CFB Wainwright were aware of the fire for several hours before it turned toward the training area, Rutland said. Despite the knowledge, the soldiers continued to carry out their exercises.
CAF officials believe there was no damage to oil and gas infrastructure as a result of the fire, Rutland said.
CFB Wainwright victims identified
The following members were killed during the fire at CFB Wainwright, according to Maj-Gen. L.W. Rutland:
Sergeant Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Alta., from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment based at Edmonton, Alberta serving with 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry
Private Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alta.
Private Aidan Goulding from North Vancouver, B.C., from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alta.
Private Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C., from 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, Alta.
Nearly 40 patients receiving treatment at regional hospitals
The medical response has placed significant demands on hospitals and emergency services in the Edmonton region.

Dr. Sayeh Zielke, the CEO of Acute Care Alberta told reporters 19 people are in critical condition, eight are stable, and 12 are ambulatory and are receiving care for injuries that can be assessed without admission.

content_blocks.text: Dr. Steve Fisher, an emergency physician at Edmonton’s Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CTV News Edmonton on Sunday that patients had sustained burns of varying severity, with the most seriously affected being treated at the University of Alberta Hospital, which has a burn intensive care unit.

The scale of the response prompted Acute Care Alberta to ask residents to avoid the University of Alberta Hospital emergency department if possible Saturday night, unless they required emergency care.
The agency said “significant resources” were needed from Emergency Health Services and Edmonton-area emergency departments into the night.

Stars Air Ambulance dispatched two air ambulances from Saskatoon and Edmonton. Helicopters and two aircraft also landed at a nearby medical evacuation site as emergency personnel worked to transport and treat the injured.
Soldiers were working with hand grenades: CAF
The 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry and reservists were taking part in high-intensity training ahead of deploymen, Rutland said.

The Charlie Company, or C Company soldiers were throwing hand grenades on a hand grenade range and conducting a section attack, with 10 soldiers attacking a simulated enemy when the fire broke out, he added.

A Code Orange is activated when a mass-casualty event places pressure on the health-care system because of a surge in patients. The code remained in effect for more than 10 hours before being lifted shortly before 1 p.m. Sunday.

The Canadian Armed Forces will undertake a board of inquiry to examine the events of Oct. 17, Rutland said.
A spokesperson for National Defence said Sunday there were no indications the incident was the result of terrorist activity.

“As emergency responders continue their work and the situation continues to evolve, the full extent of the impact remains under assessment. stories.title: Poilievre urges Canadians to embrace Remembrance Day in wake of CFB Wainwright tragedy
stories.summary: Pierre Poilievre said the suffering around CFB Wainwright can't be overstated, nor should the heroism of soldiers caught in the fire.
stories.author: Bill Kaufmann
stories.content:
Canada

'More than ever, we need to remember the tremendous men and women who carry on the tradition of the armed forces,' the Conservative leader said Sunday

Federal Conservative leader and Battle River—Crowfoot MP Pierre Poilievre speaks outside Wainwright Town Hall on Sunday, accompanied by Mayor Bruce Pugh, at right.Gavin Young/Postmedia

While noting he’s a fiscal hawk, federal Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre said Sunday no expense should be spared in helping CFB Wainwright and its families.

Speaking 24 hours after a windswept blaze killed four Canadian soldiers and wounded dozens of others, the official opposition leader said the suffering in the community can’t be overstated, nor should the heroism of soldiers caught in the fire.

“People who ran towards rather than away from the danger and are now paying a cruel price, fighting for their lives in hospitals,” said Poilievre outside Wainright’s town hall next to a maple leaf flag at half-mast.

“We’re well known for wanting to count every penny the government spends but in this case, we need to show the utmost generosity to the base, its members, its families.”

Poilievre, who’s the local MP for Battle River—Crowfoot, also said Canadians should pay tribute to the victims on Remembrance Day, which will be marked in less than a month.

“More than ever, we need to remember the tremendous men and women who carry on the tradition of the armed forces, who sacrifice everything for all of us,” he said, adding he’ll be briefing the Liberal government on the needs of the grieving community.

Joining Poilievre was Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh, who said the steadfast work of the town’s hospital on Saturday night as a mass casualty event unfolded will remain memorable.

“Those of you who had a chance to stand outside those doors to see the work that goes on inside, it’ll be praised for years,” said Pugh.

“When we speak that there are angels us, you’re witnessing it.”

He said it’s time to return the favour of military personnel in Wainwright by serving them.

stories.title: Former Montreal Canadiens owner George Gillett Jr. built on the club’s rich legacy
stories.summary: The American tycoon’s other sports-related ventures included ski resorts, the Miami Dolphins, the Harlem Globetrotters, a Nascar racing team and the storied Liverpool Football Club
stories.author: Tom Hawthorn
stories.content:
When the Colorado-based interloper George Gillett Jr. purchased hockey’s Montreal Canadiens, many fans feared that he was out to pillage a beloved part of Quebec’s heritage.

The wheeler-dealer, who made – and lost – fortunes from meatpacking, television and professional sports, had earlier sought to purchase at least five other National Hockey League teams.

The availability of hockey’s most successful and prestigious franchise was too good an opportunity to pass. In 2001, he paid US$180-million for an 80.1-per-cent stake in the team, as well as ownership of the 21,273-seat Molson (now Bell) Centre, according to Forbes.

The sale created anxiety and apprehension that the Canadiens – a club as integral to Quebec culture as tourtière, Mon pays and the Fête nationale – would be moved south to the new owner’s native land.

Those fears turned out to be unfounded, as Mr. Gillett’s tenure as owner marked a revitalization of a storied franchise. The owner built on the club’s rich legacy. Like so many introduced to Montreal, he was smitten by the city, handling the hockey team almost as a public trust.

The chaos that critics feared from his ownership did later manifest itself in another business deal, as Mr. Gillett’s participation in a heavily leveraged takeover of the famous Liverpool Football Club of the English Premier League ended with public demonstrations and a forced sale.

Mr. Gillett, who has died at the age of 87, owned parts of several other sports franchises in his career, including football’s Miami Dolphins, a Nascar auto-racing team and the touring Harlem Globetrotters basketball troupe. He described each as a business opportunity, insisting he was “no jock sniffer,” a derogatory term for those who seek to hang out with professional athletes.

He also owned several ski resorts, indulging a personal passion for downhill skiing.

An unorthodox approach to business – his family described him as “a visionary, a disrupter” in a paid death notice – kept him in the headlines for nearly six decades.

Instead of buying low and selling high, he bought high and sold higher.

“The so-called experts have said I’ve paid too much for just about everything I’ve bought, then turn around and say I stole it a couple of years later,” he told the Baltimore Sun in 1986.

His maxim: “Every market has an unexploited niche.”

George Nield Gillett Jr. was born on Oct. 22, 1938, in Racine, Wis., to the former Alyce Herbert and Dr. George Nield Gillett Sr., a physician and surgeon. He grew up on a 1,200-acre farm with 130 head of dairy cows. As a young man, he attended Lake Forest Academy and Amherst College before graduating with a liberal arts degree in 1961 from the Dominican College of Racine. He was rejected by Harvard Business School.

After working in sales for the Crown Zellerbach forest products conglomerate, he became a consultant with McKinsey & Company.

In 1966, he joined Racine land developer Willard (Bud) Keland in buying a minor share in the year-old Dolphins, his own participation approved in part because National Football League commissioner Pete Rozelle mistakenly thought he was from the wealthy Gillette safety-razor family. Mr. Gillett served briefly as the team’s business manager. He would later be thwarted in trying to purchase the Nfl’s Dallas Cowboys, Seattle Seahawks and New Orleans Saints.

Two years later, he sold his share in the football team and joined with two other partners to purchase the Globetrotters, a moribund barnstorming team on the brink of failure after the death of founder Abe Saperstein. More of an entertainment than a sports team, the Trotters were no longer filling arenas with their athletic performances since television made professional basketball readily available.

Mr. Gillett revived the Globetrotters through dramatic marketing, including a Saturday morning animated cartoon on CBS created by Hanna-Barbera in 1970, introducing the team and such stars as Curly Neal and Meadowlark Lemon to a new generation. The cartoon series was the first to air on U.S. television with a predominant cast of Black characters.

Back in his home state, he bought a failing meatpacking plant. He also purchased three small local television stations. A believer in the financial benefits of consolidation, he continued to add to his portfolios, accumulating more stations and meatpacking plants, as well as automobile dealerships and ski resorts, the industry closest to his heart.

He had fallen in love with skiing in 1963 on a visit to a year-old resort in Vail, Colo. He purchased it in 1985, as well as the Beaver Creek ski resort. He skied at Vail for 135 days in his first-year as owner, wearing a name tag that read, “George, Racine, Wisconsin,” speaking frankly with customers, employees and others doing business with the resort.

He expanded Vail until it became the largest single-mountain resort in the United States. He also attracted the Alpine World Ski Championships to the resort in 1989, 1999 and 2015.

In a two-year period, Mr. Gillett became owner of the largest group of television network affiliates in the United States through Gillett Holdings Inc. He owned 17 stations, including several in major markets, generating substantial cash flow. His approach was to allow his radio and television stations to improve their local coverage even as they were more closely scrutinized for savings.

“If you build on quality and commitment to the community,” he told the New York Times in 1988, “the cash flow will follow.”

By then, though, his empire was in deep trouble, as purchases partly financed by junk bonds and notes became precarious and vulnerable following the Black Monday stock-market crash in 1987.

The following recession and junk-bond collapse led to a personal bankruptcy after his holding company defaulted on nearly US$1-billion in loans, and he was stripped of the Vail resort and the television stations. He rebuilt by buying other ski resorts and expanding his ownership of pork and beef processors. As well, he was hired to operate the Vail resort by the new owners.

His fortunes were on the upswing by the time Molson Breweries put hockey’s Canadiens on the market. No bids came from Canadian sources.

Mr. Gillett had recently been frustrated in trying to purchase the NHL’s Colorado Avalanche and basketball’s Denver Nuggets, as well as their shared Pepsi Centre arena, in a partnership including retired quarterback John Elway, so the availability of the Montreal team after several months on the market was a welcome opportunity.

He pledged to bring the franchise back to its former glory.

“Our vision is to restore the franchise as the greatest team in hockey,” he told a news conference in 2001. “Our vision is a 25 th Stanley Cup in Montreal.”

A condition of the sale was that the team was not to be moved.

Mr. Gillett wore a Canadiens sweater in public and was often photographed wearing casual clothes including the team’s crest. The Canadiens’ famed bleu, blanc et rouge logo fit well with an owner who flew the red, white and blue.

The Canadiens were Mr. Gillett’s second NHL franchise. He had earlier been a minor owner of the troubled Oakland Seals in 1968.

While he did succeed in revitalizing the team and its reputation, notably promoting the team’s rich history, especially during centennial celebrations, as well as making peace with an estranged Patrick Roy, the championship remained elusive. In 2009, he sold the team and the arena to three Molson brothers – Geoff, Andrew and Justin – for a reported US$575-million. The club returned to a family ownership originally established in 1957 when the brothers’ grandfather Thomas Molson and great uncle Hartland Molson acquired the Canadian Arena Company.

“The numbers don’t show the pride we had in owning this marvellous asset nor the heartbreak we suffered in selling it,” Mr. Gillett told Forbes magazine, which estimated the financier had pocketed about US$340-million on the deal, money which he desperately needed to shore up his investment in England.

The takeover of Liverpool Football Club faltered when Mr. Gillett fell out with American partner Tom Hicks, known for his leveraged buyouts of such brands as Weetabix and Dr. Pepper. Once again, a global financial crisis, this one in 2008, made it impossible to sustain the cost of loans. Liverpool FC was sold for less than the estimated total debt, and Mr. Gillett was stuck with paying interest on loans for a club which he no longer owned.

His other sports ventures included ownership of Evernham Motorsports, which merged with another team owned by a legendary driver to become Richard Petty Motorsports.

Mr. Gillett died on Sept. 22 at the Highline Place Memory Center in Denver several years after receiving a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease. He leaves the former Rose Dye Foster, his wife of 59 years. He also leaves their sons George (Geordie) Gillett III, Alexander Gillett and Foster Gillett; eight grandchildren; a step-granddaughter; and his 97-year-old stepmother, Ida Gillett. He was predeceased by his parents; a sister, Penelope Ann Harper, who died in 2020, aged 78; and a son, Andrew, who was Foster’s twin brother and who died in 2011, aged 35.

“George Gillett’s passion for the Montreal Canadiens and commitment to the city of Montreal were demonstrated throughout his tenure as owner,” NHL commissioner Gary Bettman said in a statement following Mr. Gillett’s death.

The tycoon once spoke of his legacy at the request of a Baltimore journalist. “All I know,” he said, “is that I want my epitaph to read, ‘He owned the best, not the most.’”

stories.title: B.C. Conservatives platform promises $2.6 B in growth, $10.8B deficit
stories.summary: The British Columbia Conservatives say their platform will create $2.6 billion in new revenue over three years, while shrinking the deficit to $10.8 billion by 2030.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The British Columbia Conservatives say their election platform amounts to restraint, not austerity, and will create $2.6 billion in new revenue over three years, while shrinking the deficit to $10.8 billion by 2030.

The document released Sunday, with related costs, says that if Gross Domestic Product grows by 2.5 per cent in 2027, 2.8 per cent in 2028, and 3.2 per cent in 2029, the province will collect an additional $2.62 billion, compared with the NDP’s own forecast.

But the figures assume that provincial growth would exceed national growth rates. The July forecast from the Bank of Canada projects GDP growth in 2027 to reach 1.4 per cent and 1.8 per cent by 2028.

The latest report from the International Monetary Fund also says that advanced economies would grow by 1.9 per cent next year, while overall growth rates for 2027 would be three per cent. That overall figure includes growth rates for economies like China’s and India’s.

Interim Conservative leader Lorne Doerkson didn’t make himself available after the platform was released on Sunday, but said at an earlier event that he reviewed the document before it was made public.

“I just had a final look at it in the car on the way over here, and it will be open for criticism, I suppose, this afternoon. But it looks really great to me. I’m really excited about the opportunity to certainly attack the deficit and grow the economy in this province.”

The platform says that traditional industries like mining, energy and agriculture are all fundamental to British Columbia’s prosperity.

Conservatives, it says, will quickly restore confidence in these industries, cut red tape, speed up permits for projects, and support more production and processing in B.C. .

It says the net new “revenue from unleashing growth” includes a 15 per cent increase in gas production over the previous forecasts by 2029-2030.

Conservatives say their plan to “supercharge” the economy will bring in new revenue without cutting front-line services or raising taxes, while giving struggling taxpayers and businesses needed relief.

Promised tax cuts, which were announced earlier in the campaign, include raising the provincial basic personal exemption amount from $13,126 to $32,000, and no provincial sales tax on major projects until they start operating, so taxes arrive with revenue.

Starting in 2026, those tax cuts would add up to $11.3 billion by 2030, the platform says.

The Conservatives say they would fully fund health care, and their plan would add new operational spending estimated at $1.42 billion per year, with growth revenue exceeding spending every year.

Doerkson had promised the platform would be out before people had an opportunity to vote.

It was released late Sunday afternoon ahead of the Oct. 24 general vote, although advanced voting began Oct. 16.

The platform says a Conservative government, if elected, would chop spending by freezing outside hiring, cutting consultants, and will review spending on numerous government ministries.

The 71-page platform says the core review would trim about $1.8 billion over four years, while the hiring freeze and attrition of staff outside the front lines would save about $2 billion over the same period.

Doerkson said in a letter introducing his party’s platform that his job would be about making the lives of B.C. residents easier and better.

“I’ll work to get the economy moving, bring your costs down, and create good jobs. I’ll fully fund and protect our health care, and fix the mess David Eby and the NDP have made so that British Columbians aren’t dying on wait-lists or going to closed ERs when they need help.”

The New Democrats say the platform is “packed full of shell games, wildly unrealistic growth projections, and deep health care cuts hidden in plain sight.”

The NDP said in a statement released Sunday that the Conservatives claim they would save $2 billion a year from cuts to the contingencies envelope, but that funds health care caseload pressures and other unavoidable expenses like fighting wildfires.

“Cutting contingencies is a backdoor health-care cut,” it said.

The NDP said in an earlier statement Sunday that Doerkson has a budget gap of $6 billion after announcing items such as a new women and children’s hospital and changing the Massey tunnel replacement from the current plan of a tunnel to a bridge.

It added that the party’s growth claims are unrealistic.

“Doerkson seems to plan to pretend he can, quote, ‘flip a switch’ and make billions of dollars appear out of thin air. It doesn’t work like that,” the NDP says in its statement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Fire risk was low before sudden wind shift sparked deadly base fire: CAF memo
stories.summary: An internal Canadian Armed Forces memo says the fire index was low for a scheduled live-ammunition training exercise Saturday at a base near Wainwright, Alberta, when an “unexpected and sudden wind change” sparked a runaway grass fire that killed four soldiers and seriously injured dozens more. “During training, a grass fire ignited, and strong winds...
stories.author: Charles Rusnell
stories.content:
An internal Canadian Armed Forces memo says the fire index was low for a scheduled live-ammunition training exercise Saturday at a base near Wainwright, Alberta, when an “unexpected and sudden wind change” sparked a runaway grass fire that killed four soldiers and seriously injured dozens more.

“During training, a grass fire ignited, and strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction; the fire shifted toward the personnel on the range and overtook their admin area,” the memo states.

Earlier on Saturday, Environment Canada had issued a high-wind warning for Alberta. Gusts of up to 100 km/h in some parts of the province tipped over semi-trailer trucks and toppled trees.

Issued Sunday by the Strategic Joint Staff (SJS) and obtained by Global News, the memo also said the fire jumped a fire guard and spread outside the base, forcing the evacuation of one family home. The fire has been contained but is still burning.

The SJS directly reports to the chief of defence staff, Canada’s highest-ranking military officer.

The staff memo specifies that the dead and injured are from C or Charlie Company, Third Battalion of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, which is based at Edmonton Garrison.

Four soldiers were killed, another 31 suffered “very serious or serious” injuries, and six to eight others had minor injuries, it said.

Fifteen soldiers were intubated and sent to the University of Alberta and Royal Alexandra hospitals in Edmonton.

The memo cautioned that the situation was “fluid” and “these casualty reporting numbers are considered accurate but May change over time with ongoing assessments of casualty status.”

At a news conference Sunday afternoon, Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland identified the four deceased as Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, and Privates Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver, B.C., and Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C.

Their families have been notified.

Rutland said the training was to prepare the soldiers for a global response task force “ready to move within hours to any hotspot around the world,” and for deployment to Latvia in April and May to bolster the brigade there.

“This was high-intensity combat training with live munitions.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney told a news conference it was one of the worst tragedies on Canadian soil in peacetime.

“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost,” Carney said, adding that, to honour them, flags on all federal buildings will be flown at half-mast.

The Royal Canadian Air Force dispatched seven Griffon helicopters from Edmonton, and one Hercules aircraft from Winnipeg.

Ten search-and-rescue technicians parachuted from the Hercules onto a field in Wainwright, a town of about 6,500 people, about 200 km east of Edmonton, near the Saskatchewan border.

The non-profit charity, Stars, or Shock Trauma Air Rescue Service, dispatched air ambulances from Edmonton and Saskatoon, and nearby towns sent ground ambulances to assist in the transfer of the injured.

Investigators with the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service are en route to Wainwright, and the RCMP have offered investigative support, the memo states, adding that the process of casualty confirmation and next-of-kin notification has begun.

Fifteen soldiers were intubated and sent to the University of Alberta and Royal Alexandra hospitals in Edmonton.
The memo cautioned that the situation was “fluid” and “these casualty reporting numbers are considered accurate but May change over time with ongoing assessments of casualty status.”

At a news conference Sunday afternoon, Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland identified the four deceased as Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, and Privates Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver, B.C., and Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C.
Their families have been notified.

Rutland said the training was to prepare the soldiers for a global response task force “ready to move within hours to any hotspot around the world,” and for deployment to Latvia in April and May to bolster the brigade there.
“This was high-intensity combat training with live munitions.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney told a news conference it was one of the worst tragedies on Canadian soil in peacetime.
“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our armed forces who we have lost,” Carney said, adding that, to honour them, flags on all federal buildings will be flown at half-mast.
The Royal Canadian Air Force dispatched seven Griffon helicopters from Edmonton, and one Hercules aircraft from Winnipeg.
Ten search-and-rescue technicians parachuted from the Hercules onto a field in Wainwright, a town of about 6,500 people, about 200 km east of Edmonton, near the Saskatchewan border.

The non-profit charity, Stars, or Shock Trauma Air Rescue Service, dispatched air ambulances from Edmonton and Saskatoon, and nearby towns sent ground ambulances to assist in the transfer of the injured.

Investigators with the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service are en route to Wainwright, and the RCMP have offered investigative support, the memo states, adding that the process of casualty confirmation and next-of-kin notification has begun.

stories.title: Four Canadian soldiers killed by 'uncommon, rapid' grass fire at CFB Wainwright: officials
stories.summary: A fire broke out at CFB Wainwright in Alberta. Here's all the details we know about the casualties and how it happened.
stories.author: Cindy Tran
stories.content:
Federal and provincial officials on the ground in Edmonton on Sunday afternoon provided an update on the fire that broke out at Canadian Forces Base (CFB) Wainwright which led to four people dying and 39 more injured.

Maj.-Gen. L.W. Rutland, Commander of the 1st Canadian Division battalion, told reporters soldiers were undergoing a preparatory training activity at the CFB Wainwright when a grass fire broke out at 4 p.m. on Saturday. Rutland said the fire began a kilometre away when the wind shifted.

“I spoke to my commander on the ground last night and this morning and he said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them,” Rutland said.

“This was uncommon, rapid and I certainly hadn’t seen anything like it.”

Rutland said despite the forecast for wind conditions, the weather for the majority of Saturday was within standard protocol — well below 50 kilometres.

Within 20 to 30 minutes of the incident being reported, the first evacuation occurred and within less than an hour and a half there were multiple partners on the ground. Rutland described the response as “extremely rapid action” which is by design.

Rutland said parachuters that were flown in were search and rescue technicians part of air force efforts and government efforts to get more capacity on the ground as soon as possible.

The training activity was for the Third Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Infantry for two roles — the Global Response Task Force and to go to Latvia in the spring. Rutland said it was the Charlie Company or “C Company” that was impacted.

There are about 84 soldiers in the C Company in the 350-plus range for the entire battalion, Rutland said.

Rutland said the activity was “high-intensity combat training” with live munitions. He said soldiers were split between throwing hand grenades on a hand grenade range and conducting a “section attack” where 10 soldiers attack a simulated enemy.

The fire moved quickly and struck what is called the administration area of the section attack range — the grenade range was not affected.

The size of the fire has not been determined, but Rutland said range control was aware there was a fire for several hours and were monitoring it.

Rutland said soldiers train for all types of conditions and if protocols needs to change following the ongoing investigation they will. He would not comment on whether not the incident was preventable.

A fire marshal is currently on the ground investigating the cause of the fire. Rutland said the cause is not believed to be related to oil and gas facilities and teams have gone in to ensure the infrastructure is not damage with a preliminary assessment has determined it is not.

During the training exercise on Saturday grenade launchers, grenades and smaller arms ammunition were moving through the training area. Rutland said the cause of the fire could have been any of the listed or none at all.

The cause could be a multitude of things, Rutland said.

Rutland said with the number of casualties — four dead, 39 hospitalized and 19 of whom are in critical condition, along with the complexity it will take nearly a month for the board of inquiry to make a report to the public.

The families of the injured and deceased have all be notified.

Premier Danielle Smith said on Saturday 30 emergency units including 22 ground ambulances and eight aircraft were deployed directly Wainwright with dedicated medical teams across the Edmonton corridor and beyond.

“To handle the sudden surge, code orange protocols were activated at the facilities managing the rapid influx of injured patients,” Smith said.

“An active emergency response was sustained across the system for more than 10 hours, with patients transported and receiving care at facilities across the province.”

There were no armoured vehicles on site as it is a light infantry battalion, but there were trucks, ambulances and light vehicles on site. There is no information on the impact the fire had on vehicles.

The C Company has been moved out of the training area and the rest will move back home for a certain period of time. The remainder of the battalion took a “maintenance day” on Sunday and did not train to allow leadership to determine what will happen in the coming days.

“The rest of the battalion is still slated to go to Latvia, so they will pick up this training and and do it. Whether it’ll be tomorrow at a later date, I can’t say at this minute,” Rutland said.

stories.title: 4 killed in CFB Wainwright fire identified as dozens remain in hospital
stories.summary: Four members died in the incident at CFB Wainwright, with Alberta's premier saying more than three dozen have been injured and are in hospital.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
The Canadian Armed Forces has identified the four service members killed in the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright on Saturday.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland told reporters on Sunday afternoon that Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pvt. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pvt. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver, B.C., and Pvt. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.c., had died. Their families have been notified.

“Our thoughts are with the families and loved ones of those we lost and with the injured members still receiving care,” Rutland said during a news conference. “We stand with the teammates, friends, and units affected by this terrible tragedy. The well-being of our people is our highest priority.”

Dozens more were injured in the incident.

In a post on Facebook, Prince Albert, Sask., resident Patricia Farrell confirmed her son Shaun was among those killed in Saturday’s incident.

“It is with heavy hearts that we share the news that our son, Shaun Farrell, has passed away to be with our heavenly father,” she wrote on Facebook. “We want to thank everyone for your love, support, and prayers during this incredibly difficult time.”

Farrell asked for privacy as the family grieves.

All four members were serving at CFB Edmonton with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Light Infantry, and participating in a training exercise at Wainwright.

“(It was) to prepare for two roles, to become what’s called our global response task force, ready to move within hours to any hotspot around the world,” Rutland said, adding it was also to prepare to go to Latvia in April and May to bolster the brigade there. “So this was high intensity combat training with live munitions.”

Rutland said during the training, a grass fire ignited in the training area. An investigation into the cause of the fire is underway, but uncommonly strong winds caused it to spread rapidly and change direction towards the range administrative area.

Military and civilian emergency services responded to control the fire, which the Municipal District of Wainwright said was being held as of late night Saturday.

Environment Canada had issued a warning of high winds for Alberta earlier in the day, with a windstorm hitting large areas of the province. Gusts reached up to 100 km/h, toppling trees, sending signs flying, and rolling garbage cans down streets.

Asked about the weather conditions, Rutland said forces train in all types of conditions and never know what environment they’ll face. But while the majority of the day saw weather within standard procedures, when the incident occurred the weather “was uncommon, rapid, and I certainly hadn’t seen anything like it.”

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith also spoke at the news conference and provided more details on the dozens of people injured in the incident.

She said 39 patients were being cared for in hospital, and at least 19 were in critical condition.

Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Oro-Medonte, Ont., said in a social media post Sunday morning that her eldest son was among those injured.

“Overnight, our family received the devastating news that our eldest son is among the military personnel critically injured in the incident in Wainwright,” Keane said.

She went on to say while she’s staying in the mayoral race, she was was travelling to Alberta to be with her son and family and would be unable to continue door-knocking for the remainder of the campaign.

“We are grateful for the kindness and support of our friends and community,” Keane said.

Within the past 24 hours, patients were transferred from the Wainwright Health Centre to four facilities, the University of Alberta Hospital, the Royal Alexandra Hospital, the Foothills Medical Centre, and the Red Deer Regional Hospital Centre.

— with files from Global News’ Jeff Semple, Karen Bartko and Ashleigh Stewart
