stories.title: Four dead and dozens more wounded in fire at CFB Wainwright
stories.summary: Ontario mayoral candidate says her son is among the wounded
stories.author: Globe staff
stories.content:
– Matthew Scace

While there are still many questions about what caused yesterday’s tragic fire in Wainwright, Alta., more details are emerging.

A grass wildfire near the base met with sudden winds blowing greater than 130 kilometres per hour, quickly raging out of control in less than a minute, and descended on a group of military members performing a live ammunition exercise.

Four members were killed, and 39 people were injured, many critically.

– The Canadian Press

More information is emerging about the four Armed Forces members killed in the fast-moving fire at CFB Wainwright, and how their loved ones are remembering them.

Private Shaun Farrell

Farrell, a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, was from Prince Albert, Sask.

In a social media post , his mother asked for privacy as the family navigates “this profound loss.”

“We want to thank everyone for your love, support, and prayers during this incredibly difficult time,” said Patricia Farrell.

She also posted a photo of her smiling son in uniform, standing by a pickup truck. “Love you my darling child.”

Private Aidan Goulding

The 23-year-old, of North Vancouver, was also a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

His family said he was an exceptional athlete and, after high school, became a mechanic. He later quit to join the army.

“Although he was making excellent money and had a good life, he decided he wanted to defend his country. His goal was to work for Special OPs and then onto CSIS,” his mother, Sonia Monk, and older brother, Wylder Goulding, said in a statement.

“He was the guy that kept people’s spirits up, a contagious laugh and a cheeky smile, he took his role in the army seriously, and our family and his dear friends have suffered a great loss.”

They said he loved his adopted new army family and was looking forward to peacekeeping in Latvia.

“Before he went to basic training, he said, ‘I know I have one life to live, and I’m gonna make the best out of it.’ That was our Aidan.”

Private Hayden Lykkemark

Lykkemark was from Langley, B.C., and with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

B.C. Premier David Eby recognized Lykkemark and Goulding in a social media post.

“In this moment of profound heartbreak, as British Columbians and Canadians, let’s wrap our arms around their families, supporting them and joining in the mourning of this horrible tragedy,” he said.

Sgt. Morgan Wong

The 26-year-old from Edmonton was a reservist with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, serving with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

“He was an incredible person who was always there whenever anyone needed him,” his family said in a statement.

“He loved being active and spending time with his friends and family. He was extremely proud to serve with the Canadian Armed Forces.”

They said he earned a bachelor of commerce degree from the University of Alberta, as well as certificates in real estate and civil-military leadership.

He joined the Forces in 2017, and for the last four years worked as a financial analyst and manager with the Alberta government. He also served as a first responder with St. John Ambulance.

He served in Latvia from October 2024 to June 2025, and was preparing for a second tour in Europe.

Training at CFB Wainwright in Alberta is “as real as it can be” to prepare soldiers for combat operations, says a retired Canadian Armed Forces major-general.

David Fraser, who spent much of his 30-year-plus military career training at CFB Wainwright, said training can involve up to thousands of people depending on the exercise.

Some exercises are individual, he said, such as a member shooting a rifle at a gun range. Others are known as collective exercises, which involve two or more members.

“They’re progressive,” Fraser said in an interview with The Canadian Press on Sunday. “You start off with one person and you end up at some stage in the game probably with 5,000 or 6,000 people.”

Fraser said training at the base teaches regular and reserve forces to use every weapon in the military’s arsenal, including aircraft. The exercises can involve firing both unloaded and loaded weapons, he said.

He described the exercises as organized and methodical and said something went wrong at CFB Wainwright on Saturday.

“It’s very procedural, it’s complex, it’s detailed to make it as safe as possible,” Fraser said.

– Jana G. Pruden

Residents of Wainwright, Alta., are accustomed to the thunder of artillery fire and detonations from training exercises on the military base next door. It’s so close, sometimes people can feel the walls of their house rattle after an explosion.

While the town of about 7,000 has other industries and military people travelling to Wainwright tend to stay mostly on the base, the two communities are inextricably linked.

On Sunday morning, about two dozen people gathered at Wainwright’s Church of the Nazarene, where some military families occasionally worship, to pray for those killed, injured or otherwise affected by the events on the base.

“It is with heavy hearts and concerned minds, as we think about the tragedy unfolding in our community,” Rev. Ryan Wood told the congregation. “We think of the families of those who have lost their lives, we want to pray for them today in the midst of this terrible loss and grief.”

He also thanked first responders and people from the community and surrounding area “who have been on a horrific scene, who are impacted by the tragedy and the loss that they’ve witnessed.”

Standing at the back of the church, Devon Thiessen was overcome by emotion.

“The impact of yesterday, and hearing about the tragedy and the traumas other people are experiencing, it really made me grateful for what I have,” he said, as tears welled in his eyes.

– Temur Durrani

Private Shaun Farrell from Saskatchewan has been identified as one of the four members of the Canadian Armed Forces who died as a result of the violent fire in Wainwright this weekend.

In Facebook messages to The Globe on Sunday, Farrell’s parents, Roland and Patricia, requested privacy to process the news before commenting further. They did not say how old their son was.

“Love you my darling child,” Patricia wrote in an emotional post on social media, which she provided as a family statement. “We want to thank everyone for your love, support, and prayers during this incredibly difficult time.”

In his remarks to reporters, Major-General Wade Rutland said Farrell was a member of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry. He was from Prince Albert, Sask., and based in Edmonton.

On social media, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said Farrell “was a young man full of promise who chose to serve his country.”

“His loss will be felt deeply by his family, friends, fellow service members, and all who knew him,” Moe said.

Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, speaking to reporters in Wainwright, says he’s hearing about incredible acts of bravery as a devastating fire ripped through the nearby military base.

He said some soldiers ran toward the danger to help and are now paying the price, fighting for their lives in hospital.

He asked Canadians to pray for Wainwright.

Poilievre represents the area as part of the Battle River-Crowfoot riding.

– Andrea Woo

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said that in addition to the four soldiers killed in the fire, 39 people were injured. Of those, she said, 19 people are in critical condition. All patients have been accounted for, and no others are awaiting transport, she said.

“We know that the road ahead, especially for those who are suffering from severe burn injuries, will be long, requiring weeks and months of intensive and specialized care,” Smith said.

She added that Alberta stands with the families of the four who have died.

The four deceased all served with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry (PPCLI), based in Edmonton, Major-General Wade Rutland said.

Maj.-Gen. Rutland said the PPCLI soldiers were doing high-intensity preparatory combat training with live munitions, in advance of deployments to Latvia in April and May to bolster the CAF’s brigade there, when a grass fire ignited and spread rapidly because of uncommonly strong winds.

“They were throwing hand grenades on a hand grenade range and conducting what we call a section attack: 10 soldiers attacking a simulated enemy,” he said.

Maj.-Gen. Rutland said multiple training exercises were under way at the time. The cause of the fire’s ignition is under investigation.

“Certainly, we do not believe this to be as a result of any oil and gas infrastructure, nor any outside interference,” he said.

– Steven Chase

The Department of National Defence has identified the four soldiers who died as a result of the Wainwright fire as:

Sergeant Morgan Wong , from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment based at Edmonton, serving with 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry (from Edmonton)

Private Shaun Farrell , from 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton (from Prince Albert, Sask.)

Private Aidan Goulding , from 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton (from North Vancouver, B.C.)

Private Hayden Lykkemark , from 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton (from Langley, B.C.)

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said that Alberta stands with the families of the four who have died, who came from all over Western Canada.

– Grant Robertson

This weekend’s tragedy is among the worst military training incidents on Canadian soil since the 1988 Slesse Creek accident near Chilliwack, B.C., and the 1993 crash of a military plane at CFB Wainwright.

In June, 1988, six military engineering students were killed during a training exercise at the Slesse Demolition Range at CFB Chilliwack. They died when explosives used to crater a road unexpectedly detonated, according to the Canadian Military Engineers Association.

CFB Wainwright has had other deadly training incidents, including a crash that killed five airmen in July, 1993, when a C-130 Hercules transport plane hit the ground while practising a military cargo drop. Four others were also injured.

In April, 1991, a reserve soldier died and another was injured when an unexploded shell detonated on the base during a live-fire exercise. That same year, eight reservists were injured when an armoured personnel carrier crashed into an embankment.

In June, 2000, Corporal Leslie John Douglas, a British soldier involved in joint training exercises at CFB Wainwright, was killed during a live-ammunition drill.

In November, 2014, Private Steve Allen died and a second soldier was injured when a three-metre lookout tower structure collapsed during training.

And in April, 2017, Sergeant Robert J. Dynerowicz, a veteran of the Afghanistan War, died when the LAV-III vehicle he was commanding crashed on a gravel road on the base. Three other soldiers were also injured.

Acute Care Alberta, the agency that co-ordinates medical services at acute health centres in the province, said Sunday afternoon that all Code Orange activations have been ended.

The emergency alert is issued when an incident causes more casualties than emergency departments or urgent care resources can manage using routine procedures. It was activated Saturday to co-ordinate a response across health care teams and emergency services.

“Regular acute care operations have resumed, under existing high capacity pressures, and some additional localized staffing pressures in the Wainwright and Flagstaff County areas,” Shannon Shimek, executive director of communications for Acute Care Alberta, said in a statement.

As of Sunday, Ms. Shimek said, patients were transferred from Wainwright Health Centre to four facilities: the University of Alberta Hospital, Royal Alexandra Hospital, Foothills Medical Centre and Red Deer Regional Hospital Centre. Care for patients will be intensive and is expected to “add to existing high demand on acute care in Alberta,” she added.

Emergency Health Services Alberta had deployed 30 units into Wainwright, including 22 ground ambulances, six fixed-wing units and two rotary-wing units.

– Steven Chase and Mercedes Stephenson

The blaze at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright began as a smouldering grass fire that was whipped into a “wall of flame” by high winds, early internal military assessments indicate.

The flames then overtook Canadian Armed Forces members who were on a firing range, according to the reports, which were obtained by The Globe and Mail.

It remains unclear what first ignited the grass fire.

Hello, I’m Temur Durrani, a national correspondent for The Globe. Today, I’m in Edmonton helping our team chase more details about the tragic incident at CFB Wainwright.

In his remarks earlier today, Prime Minister Mark Carney mentioned that soldiers training at the base are part of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

The Princess Pats, as they are often called, are an illustrious group within the Canadian Armed Forces. I know them quite well because I’m usually based in Manitoba.

Stories about the Pats are the stuff of legends. The infantry is particularly integrated into the agricultural community around Brandon, Manitoba’s second-largest city, close to where they have a base in Shilo.

Brandon is a hub for the soldiers and their families. The Pats frequently participate in highly attended events there, such as civic parades and Remembrance Day ceremonies.

“Throughout Canada’s history, the Princess Pats have fought for freedom, democracy, human dignity,” Carney said, “in the First World War, in the Second, in Korea, in Afghanistan and during numerous peacekeeping missions over decades.”

– Emma Graney and Jeffrey Jones

Multiple oil and gas producers operate on CFB Wainwright property, but the Alberta Energy Regulator said Sunday it had not received any reports of incidents involving energy infrastructure.

The regulator posted on its website that it is communicating with operators in the area. Under law, energy companies must notify the AER immediately if an incident affects their assets or facilities.

“The AER continues to monitor the situation and has not been engaged by the lead agency or other provincial agencies in any response at this time,” it said.

Companies have produced oil and gas on Canadian Armed Forces bases in Alberta for decades. Production in the Wainwright area began in the 1920s, long before the base was established at the start of the Second World War.

There are 87 active wells on the base, most of them producing natural gas, according to data from the Alberta Energy Regulator.

It’s also home to various natural gas pipelines, including a network owned by Sumerian Oil & Gas Inc., formerly Cleo Energy Corp., that runs through the grounds, along its northern and southern edge and southwest onto non-CFB land.

Sumerian issued a statement Sunday saying that all of its wells, pipelines and facilities – including roughly 300 well licences on the Wainwright training area – were placed under the care of the AER and Orphan Well Association on Oct. 5.

It said it “has not been informed by any authority that its wells or pipelines were involved in the incident.”

Tanya Porter, a long-time Wainwright resident, said she saw a wall of smoke on Saturday, right as strong gusts of wind blew into town.

“I was like, ‘Is that a fire or dust?’ But I didn’t hear any explosion. They were bombing all day,” she said Sunday morning while she and her husband, Bob, picked away at eggs and pancakes at the Wainwright Legion.

Residents of the base town are accustomed to hearing the thunder of artillery fire and detonations from on-base training exercises. The couple said the walls of their house sometimes rattle after explosions.

“You hear explosions but you get used to it,” Bob said. “Like, if you hear the train all day long, by the afternoon or next day, you don’t hear it. The same with them out there shooting away.”

But the constant wail of sirens into the night and crowded airspace was far beyond their definition of ordinary.

“That mass casualty – we’ve never had an experience like that,” Tanya said.

– Carrie Tait

Keith Brower lives just north of CFB Wainwright and said the noise and smoke emanating from the base on Saturday didn’t faze him – at first.

“It didn’t seem unusual because they’ve been bombing out there, or shooting, practising all week long,” he said after Sunday’s service at Wainwright’s Church of the Nazarene. Fire on the base is also common, he said, especially in the spring when the grass is dry.

“We just saw a plume of smoke and it didn’t seem unusual at the time, because we’ve seen it before,” he said. “We’re used to training out there, for sure.”

Tim Valleau coaches the Wainwright Commandos, the local high school football team. He said three or four retired military personnel are also on the coaching staff. The team doctor, Mr. Valleau said, would have been at the hospital Saturday evening.

Mr. Valleau also lives near the base. “We could hear the bombing non-stop, just as a normal, everyday occurrence.”

But his mom told him she heard a “really loud explosion” and saw “the flash of red and knew it was something different.”

Mr. Valleau said the football team was scheduled to play Sunday against Cold Lake, another northeastern Alberta community that is home to a military base.

A vast area of rolling grasslands around the base was charred black, with white-grey smoke still drifting out of stands of trees in the gusting wind on Sunday afternoon.

Wainwright Fire Chief Aime Smyl said about 30 firefighters were still working to put out hot spots in the area. He noted that local fire crews were only responding to fire outside the base, to where the blaze moved into municipal land.

– Globe staff

The winds at CFB Wainwright on Saturday were fierce – and predicted.

Environment Canada data show that strong wind gusts picked up around 2 p.m. and reached a peak at 4 p.m., around the same time the military says the fire started. Hourly data shows gusts of 69 kilometres an hour at that time, with the maximum gust for the day of clocking in at 82 km/h.

Earlier in the day, the weather agency had predicted such weather. Forecasts issued at 5 a.m. and 11 a.m. called for wind gusts of up to 80 km/h in the afternoon.

It was also dry in the region. Environment Canada data show that just 3.5 millimetres of rain had fallen so far in October, with no precipitation at all since last Monday.

Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Oro-Medonte, Ont., said on social media Sunday that her eldest son is among the soldiers injured in the incident, and that the family was on their way to Alberta to be with him.

“Overnight, our family received the devastating news that our eldest son is among the military personnel critically injured in the incident in Wainwright, Alberta, on Saturday,” Ms. Keane posted on Facebook.

“As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family. I will be travelling to Alberta and unable to continue door-knocking for the remainder of the mayoral campaign,” Ms. Keane told the residents of Oro-Medonte. “Right now, I ask for your understanding as our family navigates an incredibly difficult and uncertain time. We are grateful for the kindness and support of our friends and community. Please hold your loved ones a little tighter tonight.”

Doug Shipley, MP for Barrie-Springwater-Oro-Medonte, posted a message of support for the family on his Facebook account.

“A member of a local Oro-Medonte family was critically injured in a tragic incident involving our Canadian Armed Forces at CFB Wainwright last night,” Mr. Shipley said, asking people to “keep her family in your thoughts during this difficult time.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney made a statement from Parliament Hill a day after the fire broke out.

“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our Armed Forces whom we have lost. And I have asked the flags on all federal buildings to be flown at half-mast to honour them,” Mr. Carney said.

He called the incident “one of the worst tragedies that our armed forces have experienced on Canadian soil in peacetime.”

The Prime Minister praised those who fought the fire and rescued victims.

“Military and civilian crews fought this fire throughout the night in some of the worst conditions imaginable, risking their lives to protect their fellow Canadians,” he said.

Mr. Carney said those affected by the fire came from military bases across the country, including reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

“Throughout Canada’s history, the Princess Pats have fought for freedom, democracy, human dignity. In the First World War, in the Second, in Korea, in Afghanistan, and during numerous peacekeeping missions over decades.”

The Prime Minister pledged that Canada would support the victims and their families.

“We will be there for their families for as long as they need. We will care for the injured through every step of their recovery, and we will stand by the women and men of our armed forces as they bear the weight of this loss,” he said.

“They will not carry it alone, because in Canada, we take care of one another.”

On Sunday morning, about two dozen people gathered at Wainwright’s Church of the Nazarene, where some military families occasionally worship, to pray for those killed, injured, or affected by the events the evening prior.

“It is with heavy hearts and concerned minds, as we think about the tragedy unfolding in our community,” Rev. Ryan Wood told the congregation. “We think of the families of those who have lost their lives, we want to pray for them today that in midst of this terrible loss and grief.”

He added: “We think about our first responders, people from our own community and surrounding communities, members of the miliary, who have been on a horrific scene, who are impacted by the tragedy and the lost that they’ve witnessed”

Acute Care Alberta, the agency that coordinates medical services at acute health centres in the province, said a Code Orange had been declared at several ERs “to coordinate a response to an incident that results in multiple severe patients needing care at the same time.”

The agency urged people in Edmonton to avoid going to the emergency department at the University of Alberta hospital so that patients coming from the military base could be prioritized.

Around midnight on Saturday, two bright red flares dropped from the sky before seven Canadian Forces members parachuted onto the football field of the local high school across the street from the Wainwright hospital. They were soon met by a helicopter that touched down to unload medical equipment, including what appeared to be a ventilator that the troops wheeled into the hospital.

Nearby, paramedics loaded two patients on stretchers into waiting ambulances, which then sped off.

By Sunday morning, the scene at the Wainwright Health Centre was quiet. The ambulances that had continued moving patients late into the night were gone.

Access to CFB Wainwright was blocked. At front gate of the base, civilian vehicles filed through a security checkpoint at sunrise.

The Department of National Defence said the incident began after a fire ignited at about 4 p.m. local time Saturday in the training area of the military base, which is located about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton. There’s no evidence so far that the Wainwright fire was caused by terrorism, the department said.
paragraphs: – Matthew Scace
While there are still many questions about what caused yesterday’s tragic fire in Wainwright, Alta., more details are emerging.

A grass wildfire near the base met with sudden winds blowing greater than 130 kilometres per hour, quickly raging out of control in less than a minute, and descended on a group of military members performing a live ammunition exercise.
Four members were killed, and 39 people were injured, many critically.
– The Canadian Press
More information is emerging about the four Armed Forces members killed in the fast-moving fire at CFB Wainwright, and how their loved ones are remembering them.
Private Shaun Farrell
Farrell, a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton, was from Prince Albert, Sask.
In a social media post , his mother asked for privacy as the family navigates “this profound loss.”
“We want to thank everyone for your love, support, and prayers during this incredibly difficult time,” said Patricia Farrell.
She also posted a photo of her smiling son in uniform, standing by a pickup truck. “Love you my darling child.”
Private Aidan Goulding
The 23-year-old, of North Vancouver, was also a member of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
His family said he was an exceptional athlete and, after high school, became a mechanic. He later quit to join the army.

“Although he was making excellent money and had a good life, he decided he wanted to defend his country. His goal was to work for Special OPs and then onto CSIS,” his mother, Sonia Monk, and older brother, Wylder Goulding, said in a statement.
“He was the guy that kept people’s spirits up, a contagious laugh and a cheeky smile, he took his role in the army seriously, and our family and his dear friends have suffered a great loss.”
They said he loved his adopted new army family and was looking forward to peacekeeping in Latvia.
“Before he went to basic training, he said, ‘I know I have one life to live, and I’m gonna make the best out of it.’ That was our Aidan.”
Private Hayden Lykkemark
Lykkemark was from Langley, B.C., and with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
B.C. Premier David Eby recognized Lykkemark and Goulding in a social media post.
“In this moment of profound heartbreak, as British Columbians and Canadians, let’s wrap our arms around their families, supporting them and joining in the mourning of this horrible tragedy,” he said.
Sgt. Morgan Wong
The 26-year-old from Edmonton was a reservist with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, serving with the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
“He was an incredible person who was always there whenever anyone needed him,” his family said in a statement.
“He loved being active and spending time with his friends and family. He was extremely proud to serve with the Canadian Armed Forces.”
They said he earned a bachelor of commerce degree from the University of Alberta, as well as certificates in real estate and civil-military leadership.
He joined the Forces in 2017, and for the last four years worked as a financial analyst and manager with the Alberta government. He also served as a first responder with St. John Ambulance.
He served in Latvia from October 2024 to June 2025, and was preparing for a second tour in Europe.
Training at CFB Wainwright in Alberta is “as real as it can be” to prepare soldiers for combat operations, says a retired Canadian Armed Forces major-general.
David Fraser, who spent much of his 30-year-plus military career training at CFB Wainwright, said training can involve up to thousands of people depending on the exercise.
Some exercises are individual, he said, such as a member shooting a rifle at a gun range. Others are known as collective exercises, which involve two or more members.
“They’re progressive,” Fraser said in an interview with The Canadian Press on Sunday. “You start off with one person and you end up at some stage in the game probably with 5,000 or 6,000 people.”

Fraser said training at the base teaches regular and reserve forces to use every weapon in the military’s arsenal, including aircraft. The exercises can involve firing both unloaded and loaded weapons, he said.
He described the exercises as organized and methodical and said something went wrong at CFB Wainwright on Saturday.
“It’s very procedural, it’s complex, it’s detailed to make it as safe as possible,” Fraser said.
– Jana G. Pruden

Residents of Wainwright, Alta., are accustomed to the thunder of artillery fire and detonations from training exercises on the military base next door. It’s so close, sometimes people can feel the walls of their house rattle after an explosion.
While the town of about 7,000 has other industries and military people travelling to Wainwright tend to stay mostly on the base, the two communities are inextricably linked.

On Sunday morning, about two dozen people gathered at Wainwright’s Church of the Nazarene, where some military families occasionally worship, to pray for those killed, injured or otherwise affected by the events on the base.

“It is with heavy hearts and concerned minds, as we think about the tragedy unfolding in our community,” Rev. Ryan Wood told the congregation. “We think of the families of those who have lost their lives, we want to pray for them today in the midst of this terrible loss and grief.”
He also thanked first responders and people from the community and surrounding area “who have been on a horrific scene, who are impacted by the tragedy and the loss that they’ve witnessed.”
Standing at the back of the church, Devon Thiessen was overcome by emotion.
“The impact of yesterday, and hearing about the tragedy and the traumas other people are experiencing, it really made me grateful for what I have,” he said, as tears welled in his eyes.
– Temur Durrani
Private Shaun Farrell from Saskatchewan has been identified as one of the four members of the Canadian Armed Forces who died as a result of the violent fire in Wainwright this weekend.
In Facebook messages to The Globe on Sunday, Farrell’s parents, Roland and Patricia, requested privacy to process the news before commenting further. They did not say how old their son was.

“Love you my darling child,” Patricia wrote in an emotional post on social media, which she provided as a family statement. “We want to thank everyone for your love, support, and prayers during this incredibly difficult time.”

In his remarks to reporters, Major-General Wade Rutland said Farrell was a member of the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry. He was from Prince Albert, Sask., and based in Edmonton.
On social media, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said Farrell “was a young man full of promise who chose to serve his country.”
“His loss will be felt deeply by his family, friends, fellow service members, and all who knew him,” Moe said.
Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, speaking to reporters in Wainwright, says he’s hearing about incredible acts of bravery as a devastating fire ripped through the nearby military base.
He said some soldiers ran toward the danger to help and are now paying the price, fighting for their lives in hospital.
He asked Canadians to pray for Wainwright.
Poilievre represents the area as part of the Battle River-Crowfoot riding.
– Andrea Woo

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said that in addition to the four soldiers killed in the fire, 39 people were injured. Of those, she said, 19 people are in critical condition. All patients have been accounted for, and no others are awaiting transport, she said.
“We know that the road ahead, especially for those who are suffering from severe burn injuries, will be long, requiring weeks and months of intensive and specialized care,” Smith said.
She added that Alberta stands with the families of the four who have died.
The four deceased all served with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry (PPCLI), based in Edmonton, Major-General Wade Rutland said.

Maj.-Gen. Rutland said the PPCLI soldiers were doing high-intensity preparatory combat training with live munitions, in advance of deployments to Latvia in April and May to bolster the CAF’s brigade there, when a grass fire ignited and spread rapidly because of uncommonly strong winds.
“They were throwing hand grenades on a hand grenade range and conducting what we call a section attack: 10 soldiers attacking a simulated enemy,” he said.
Maj.-Gen. Rutland said multiple training exercises were under way at the time. The cause of the fire’s ignition is under investigation.
“Certainly, we do not believe this to be as a result of any oil and gas infrastructure, nor any outside interference,” he said.
– Steven Chase
The Department of National Defence has identified the four soldiers who died as a result of the Wainwright fire as:
Sergeant Morgan Wong , from the Loyal Edmonton Regiment based at Edmonton, serving with 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry (from Edmonton)
Private Shaun Farrell , from 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton (from Prince Albert, Sask.)
Private Aidan Goulding , from 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton (from North Vancouver, B.C.)
Private Hayden Lykkemark , from 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at Edmonton (from Langley, B.C.)
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said that Alberta stands with the families of the four who have died, who came from all over Western Canada.
– Grant Robertson

This weekend’s tragedy is among the worst military training incidents on Canadian soil since the 1988 Slesse Creek accident near Chilliwack, B.C., and the 1993 crash of a military plane at CFB Wainwright.

In June, 1988, six military engineering students were killed during a training exercise at the Slesse Demolition Range at CFB Chilliwack. They died when explosives used to crater a road unexpectedly detonated, according to the Canadian Military Engineers Association.

CFB Wainwright has had other deadly training incidents, including a crash that killed five airmen in July, 1993, when a C-130 Hercules transport plane hit the ground while practising a military cargo drop. Four others were also injured.

In April, 1991, a reserve soldier died and another was injured when an unexploded shell detonated on the base during a live-fire exercise. That same year, eight reservists were injured when an armoured personnel carrier crashed into an embankment.
In June, 2000, Corporal Leslie John Douglas, a British soldier involved in joint training exercises at CFB Wainwright, was killed during a live-ammunition drill.
In November, 2014, Private Steve Allen died and a second soldier was injured when a three-metre lookout tower structure collapsed during training.

And in April, 2017, Sergeant Robert J. Dynerowicz, a veteran of the Afghanistan War, died when the LAV-III vehicle he was commanding crashed on a gravel road on the base. Three other soldiers were also injured.
Acute Care Alberta, the agency that co-ordinates medical services at acute health centres in the province, said Sunday afternoon that all Code Orange activations have been ended.

The emergency alert is issued when an incident causes more casualties than emergency departments or urgent care resources can manage using routine procedures. It was activated Saturday to co-ordinate a response across health care teams and emergency services.

“Regular acute care operations have resumed, under existing high capacity pressures, and some additional localized staffing pressures in the Wainwright and Flagstaff County areas,” Shannon Shimek, executive director of communications for Acute Care Alberta, said in a statement.

As of Sunday, Ms. Shimek said, patients were transferred from Wainwright Health Centre to four facilities: the University of Alberta Hospital, Royal Alexandra Hospital, Foothills Medical Centre and Red Deer Regional Hospital Centre. Care for patients will be intensive and is expected to “add to existing high demand on acute care in Alberta,” she added.
Emergency Health Services Alberta had deployed 30 units into Wainwright, including 22 ground ambulances, six fixed-wing units and two rotary-wing units.
– Steven Chase and Mercedes Stephenson
The blaze at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright began as a smouldering grass fire that was whipped into a “wall of flame” by high winds, early internal military assessments indicate.
The flames then overtook Canadian Armed Forces members who were on a firing range, according to the reports, which were obtained by The Globe and Mail.
It remains unclear what first ignited the grass fire.
Hello, I’m Temur Durrani, a national correspondent for The Globe. Today, I’m in Edmonton helping our team chase more details about the tragic incident at CFB Wainwright.
In his remarks earlier today, Prime Minister Mark Carney mentioned that soldiers training at the base are part of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.
The Princess Pats, as they are often called, are an illustrious group within the Canadian Armed Forces. I know them quite well because I’m usually based in Manitoba.

Stories about the Pats are the stuff of legends. The infantry is particularly integrated into the agricultural community around Brandon, Manitoba’s second-largest city, close to where they have a base in Shilo.
Brandon is a hub for the soldiers and their families. The Pats frequently participate in highly attended events there, such as civic parades and Remembrance Day ceremonies.

“Throughout Canada’s history, the Princess Pats have fought for freedom, democracy, human dignity,” Carney said, “in the First World War, in the Second, in Korea, in Afghanistan and during numerous peacekeeping missions over decades.”
– Emma Graney and Jeffrey Jones
Multiple oil and gas producers operate on CFB Wainwright property, but the Alberta Energy Regulator said Sunday it had not received any reports of incidents involving energy infrastructure.
The regulator posted on its website that it is communicating with operators in the area. Under law, energy companies must notify the AER immediately if an incident affects their assets or facilities.
“The AER continues to monitor the situation and has not been engaged by the lead agency or other provincial agencies in any response at this time,” it said.

Companies have produced oil and gas on Canadian Armed Forces bases in Alberta for decades. Production in the Wainwright area began in the 1920s, long before the base was established at the start of the Second World War.
There are 87 active wells on the base, most of them producing natural gas, according to data from the Alberta Energy Regulator.

It’s also home to various natural gas pipelines, including a network owned by Sumerian Oil & Gas Inc., formerly Cleo Energy Corp., that runs through the grounds, along its northern and southern edge and southwest onto non-CFB land.

Sumerian issued a statement Sunday saying that all of its wells, pipelines and facilities – including roughly 300 well licences on the Wainwright training area – were placed under the care of the AER and Orphan Well Association on Oct. 5.
It said it “has not been informed by any authority that its wells or pipelines were involved in the incident.”
Tanya Porter, a long-time Wainwright resident, said she saw a wall of smoke on Saturday, right as strong gusts of wind blew into town.

“I was like, ‘Is that a fire or dust?’ But I didn’t hear any explosion. They were bombing all day,” she said Sunday morning while she and her husband, Bob, picked away at eggs and pancakes at the Wainwright Legion.

Residents of the base town are accustomed to hearing the thunder of artillery fire and detonations from on-base training exercises. The couple said the walls of their house sometimes rattle after explosions.
“You hear explosions but you get used to it,” Bob said. “Like, if you hear the train all day long, by the afternoon or next day, you don’t hear it. The same with them out there shooting away.”
But the constant wail of sirens into the night and crowded airspace was far beyond their definition of ordinary.
“That mass casualty – we’ve never had an experience like that,” Tanya said.
– Carrie Tait
Keith Brower lives just north of CFB Wainwright and said the noise and smoke emanating from the base on Saturday didn’t faze him – at first.

“It didn’t seem unusual because they’ve been bombing out there, or shooting, practising all week long,” he said after Sunday’s service at Wainwright’s Church of the Nazarene. Fire on the base is also common, he said, especially in the spring when the grass is dry.
“We just saw a plume of smoke and it didn’t seem unusual at the time, because we’ve seen it before,” he said. “We’re used to training out there, for sure.”

Tim Valleau coaches the Wainwright Commandos, the local high school football team. He said three or four retired military personnel are also on the coaching staff. The team doctor, Mr. Valleau said, would have been at the hospital Saturday evening.
Mr. Valleau also lives near the base. “We could hear the bombing non-stop, just as a normal, everyday occurrence.”
But his mom told him she heard a “really loud explosion” and saw “the flash of red and knew it was something different.”
Mr. Valleau said the football team was scheduled to play Sunday against Cold Lake, another northeastern Alberta community that is home to a military base.
A vast area of rolling grasslands around the base was charred black, with white-grey smoke still drifting out of stands of trees in the gusting wind on Sunday afternoon.

Wainwright Fire Chief Aime Smyl said about 30 firefighters were still working to put out hot spots in the area. He noted that local fire crews were only responding to fire outside the base, to where the blaze moved into municipal land.
– Globe staff
The winds at CFB Wainwright on Saturday were fierce – and predicted.

Environment Canada data show that strong wind gusts picked up around 2 p.m. and reached a peak at 4 p.m., around the same time the military says the fire started. Hourly data shows gusts of 69 kilometres an hour at that time, with the maximum gust for the day of clocking in at 82 km/h.
Earlier in the day, the weather agency had predicted such weather. Forecasts issued at 5 a.m. and 11 a.m. called for wind gusts of up to 80 km/h in the afternoon.
It was also dry in the region. Environment Canada data show that just 3.5 millimetres of rain had fallen so far in October, with no precipitation at all since last Monday.

Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Oro-Medonte, Ont., said on social media Sunday that her eldest son is among the soldiers injured in the incident, and that the family was on their way to Alberta to be with him.

“Overnight, our family received the devastating news that our eldest son is among the military personnel critically injured in the incident in Wainwright, Alberta, on Saturday,” Ms. Keane posted on Facebook.

“As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family. I will be travelling to Alberta and unable to continue door-knocking for the remainder of the mayoral campaign,” Ms. Keane told the residents of Oro-Medonte. “Right now, I ask for your understanding as our family navigates an incredibly difficult and uncertain time. We are grateful for the kindness and support of our friends and community. Please hold your loved ones a little tighter tonight.”
Doug Shipley, MP for Barrie-Springwater-Oro-Medonte, posted a message of support for the family on his Facebook account.

“A member of a local Oro-Medonte family was critically injured in a tragic incident involving our Canadian Armed Forces at CFB Wainwright last night,” Mr. Shipley said, asking people to “keep her family in your thoughts during this difficult time.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney made a statement from Parliament Hill a day after the fire broke out.

“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our Armed Forces whom we have lost. And I have asked the flags on all federal buildings to be flown at half-mast to honour them,” Mr. Carney said.
He called the incident “one of the worst tragedies that our armed forces have experienced on Canadian soil in peacetime.”
The Prime Minister praised those who fought the fire and rescued victims.
“Military and civilian crews fought this fire throughout the night in some of the worst conditions imaginable, risking their lives to protect their fellow Canadians,” he said.
Mr. Carney said those affected by the fire came from military bases across the country, including reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

“Throughout Canada’s history, the Princess Pats have fought for freedom, democracy, human dignity. In the First World War, in the Second, in Korea, in Afghanistan, and during numerous peacekeeping missions over decades.”
The Prime Minister pledged that Canada would support the victims and their families.

“We will be there for their families for as long as they need. We will care for the injured through every step of their recovery, and we will stand by the women and men of our armed forces as they bear the weight of this loss,” he said.
“They will not carry it alone, because in Canada, we take care of one another.”

stories.title: British Columbia NDP Leader Eby asks Green voters to think carefully about vote
stories.summary: Victoria - British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby is appealing to Green voters as the snap election slated for Oct. 24 enters its final week.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - British Columbia NDP Leader David Eby is appealing to Greens for their votes as the provincial election enters its final week, but Green Party Leader Emily Lowan says he is just trying to frighten voters.

Eby said on Sunday that Green supporters should think carefully about their choices, as they prepare to cast their ballots in the Oct. 24 election.

While he respects Lowan, he said she won’t be the premier, and votes for her party could end up electing a Conservative government.

“The message to Green voters is very straightforward,” Eby said. “I have a great deal of respect for their leader, and she’s not going to be the premier next week. The damage that a Conservative government would do would last for generations, and some of it would be impossible to undo.”

Lowan said in a statement the situation is on Eby’s doing.

“David Eby called this snap election two years early,” she said. “Now, he is trying to scare British Columbians into voting for him.”

Eby notes that the Green vote helped elect Conservatives ahead of New Democrats in 11 ridings during the last election, including the riding of North Island, where he was speaking at an unrelated campaign announcement in Campbell River, B.C. on Sunday.

He said that neither he nor his party have been perfect in government, and a lot of people are frustrated about having an election at this moment.

“You May still be frustrated, but I think we can all agree that this election is about more than election timing,” he said.

The election is about the future of the province, and not the small differences between New Democrats and Greens, who share a common vision in many areas, Eby said.

He said Conservatives offer “stark differences” around private health-care, cutting services, the tolerance of hate and division, and trade relations with the United States.

Both Greens and New Democrats have a shared vision that includes a strong public health-care system and protecting the environment, he said.

“So, I’m asking Green voters to think very carefully about the kind of province that we all want, because when we all work together as voters who share that vision, we win.”

Lowan denied the differences between New Democrats and Greens are small.

“Tell that to the families waiting on the $10-a-day child care he froze, the seniors waiting on the seven long-term care homes he delayed, and the renters still waiting for housing they can afford,” she said.

Lowan said voters aren’t asking for a perfect premier or government.

“They are asking for a government that keeps its word, makes life affordable, and makes sure care is there when they need it.”

Lowan said Saturday’s election of the Green Party’s Pete Fry as Vancouver’s new mayor showed that British Columbians are ready for Green leadership.

“British Columbians can send that same Green message across the province on election day,” she said.

Eby’s appeal to Green voters echoed a call he made two years ago when his party was elected in 2024 with a slim majority.

This petition to voters comes amid opinion polls that show his party trailing.

When asked if his request to Green voters was an acknowledgment that his party was lagging, Eby said the only poll that matters happens on election day.

The Conservatives said in a statement that Eby called the election because he saw an opportunity for himself.

“What he handed British Columbians is an opportunity for change,” it said. “Three weeks later, he is begging other parties’ voters to save him from his own record. That is what desperation looks like.”

Conservative interim leader Lorne Doerkson on Sunday announced plans to expand school meal programs in high-need communities, create a new, refundable tax credit worth up to $500 for every child for every year for sports, recreation, music and art camp and ban cellphones in schools.

“In a province as rich as British Columbia, tens of thousands of kids relying on food banks is unacceptable. Too many kids start the school day hungry,” he said during a campaign stop in Delta, B.C.

All school districts in B.C. have codes that restrict the use of personal devices in the classroom, but exact rules for different grades vary from district to district.

If elected, the party would also double the funding to replace playground equipment to $10 million per year, he said.

Doerkson also promised that his party would release a fully-costed platform on Sunday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 18, 2026.

stories.summary: At least seven people have been killed and dozens more are injured, while a fire remains held south of the town of Wainwright.
stories.author: Sean Previl, Jeff Semple
stories.content:
A preliminary investigation into the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright suggests a munition from a live training exercise sparked a fast-moving grass fire, causing Saturday’s explosion, according to multiple military sources.

Separate military sources told Global News that at least seven people died in the incident, and dozens more were injured at the base, located around 200 kilometres from Edmonton.

On Sunday, Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed that four service members perished and their next of kin have been notified, adding that dozens more were seriously injured.

“Yesterday afternoon, a violent fast-moving fire swept through Canadian Armed Forces Base in Wainwright, Alberta, and what followed was one of the worst tragedies for the forces on Canadian soil in peacetime,” Carney said.

Minister of National Defence David McGuinty said he is travelling to Edmonton and will be briefed on the latest developments regarding the incident.

Carney said flags will be flown at half-mast on all federal buildings across the country.

As the investigation continues, many details remain unknown, but here’s what is known so far about the calamity.

The Canadian Armed Forces confirmed Sunday that the fire ignited within a training area at approximately 4 p.m. MT on Saturday.

“The fire spread rapidly beyond the boundaries of the training area, while military and civilian emergency services responded quickly to control that fire and to support those affected by this tragic event,” the CAF said in a news release.

A source on scene told Global News troops were loading the injured to bring back to the base before going back into the field to collect more of their comrades.

Environment Canada had issued a warning of high winds for Alberta earlier in the day, with a windstorm hitting large areas of the province. Gusts reached up to 100 km/h, toppling trees, sending signs flying, and rolling garbage cans down streets.

It is unclear why military exercises with live munitions continued despite the high winds.

Residents who spoke with Global News said they heard the exercises until they went quiet, then heard sirens.

“There is that emotional piece, definitely; it’s hard our neighbour across the street is a serving member, our neighbours on both sides of us are former serving members,” said Mayor Bruce Pugh. “The CAF is like a family, very similar to this community.”

The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire south of town crossed the base fence earlier in the day and was being actively managed. At approximately midnight, the municipality said the fire was contained, but a fire watch would remain in place overnight.

CFB Wainwright is considered one of the Caf’s busiest bases and is used to train Canada’s military and prepare units for combat operations.

It’s considered, according to retired Maj.-Gen. David Fraser, “as real as it can be” in preparing soldiers for combat operations.

The base is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, and approximately 12 lodger units.

It is not yet known what was involved in Saturday’s military training, as previous exercises have involved artillery and armoured vehicles.

But Fraser told The Canadian Press training at the base involves more than just weapons training, with exercises covering everything in the Caf’s arsenal from firearms to aircraft.

Exercises are organized and methodical and Fraser says something went wrong at CFB Wainwright, adding those who undergo this training are well-versed in safety procedures. Safety staff also oversee every exercise.

According to the Government of Canada, more than 200 active gas wells and associated pipelines can be found in the CFB Wainwright area.

The area is also known for livestock grazing and recreational hunting, which has been allowed for more than four decades at the base.

The base is about 609 square-kilometres in size and located about 205 kilometres southeast of Edmonton and found within one kilometre of the town of Wainwright.

Acute Care Alberta advised Saturday evening that a Code Orange had been declared for multiple hospitals. A Code Orange is issued when a mass casualty incident or external disaster has occurred and many injured patients are expected to arrive.

Albertans have been advised to use emergency care resources wisely to make room for the tragedy’s victims.

Residents requiring immediate, emergency care for life-threatening illnesses or injuries were told to go to any of Edmonton’s other acute care facilities, if at all possible.

Ambulances from across Alberta were diverted to the base about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, taking them away from responding to 911 calls in other communities.

Stars air ambulance crews flew in from Edmonton and Saskatoon to provide assistance, Carney said.

Prior to Saturday’s explosion and fire, the Canadian Armed Forces have seen other deadly events.

The most recent occurred in July when a three-person rope team was performing a rescue exercise at the time of the incident. The three members fell into a crevasse in Jasper National Park, dropping about 20 metres. The three were responsive and stable and flown to hospital after being rescued.

One of the deadliest training exercises that happened on Canadian soil was in 1988 at CFB Chilliwack.

Students were practicing explosive cratering in the demolition phase of their military engineer officer training when a charge detonated prematurely during a session. According to the Canadian Military Engineers Association, 29 students and seven instructors were in attendance. Six students were killed and several others were injured.

A coroner’s inquest and board of inquiry concluded the a hotspot developed inside the camouflet tube, triggered by friction and heat generated when the tamping rod was used with excessive force. The hotspot likely ignited a blockage, causing a small detonation that then triggered the main charge. The incident was ruled as accidental.

There has also been a previous incident in the last decade at CFB Wainwright, when Sgt. Robert Dynerowicz died during a training exercise in 2017. He was commanding a light-armoured vehicle when the incident occurred. Three others were injured.

stories.title: What we know so far about the fire at CFB Wainwright
stories.summary: Prime Minister calls incident ‘one of the worst tragedies that our armed forces have experienced on Canadian soil in peacetime’
stories.author: Globe staff
stories.content:
A fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in eastern Alberta on Saturday killed four and wounded dozens.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said Sunday that in addition to four soldiers killed in the fire, 39 people were injured. Of those, she said, 19 people are in critical condition. All patients have been accounted for, and no others are awaiting transport, she said.

Early military communications viewed by The Globe say the deadly blaze began as a smoldering grass fire that was whipped into a “wall of flame” by high winds.

The flames then overtook Canadian Armed Forces members who were on a firing range, according to the reports, which were obtained by the Globe and Mail.

It remains unclear what first ignited the grass fire.

The Department of National Defence said the incident began after a fire ignited at about 4 p.m. local time Saturday in the training area of the military base.

A report issued Saturday night says the “fire index,” a measure of risk, was low. It suggests an “unexpected and sudden wind change” took place during the incident.

“During training a grass fire ignited, and strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction; the fire shifted toward the personnel on the range and overtook their admin area,” a report from Saturday says.

A second report issued Sunday morning, describes the initial fire as “smoldering” and said it “blew over 1 kilometre” before a “wall of flame” engulfed the “administration area of the live fire training range.”

Wainwright Fire Chief Aime Smyl said about 30 firefighters were still working to put out hot spots in the area on Sunday afternoon.

The Department of National Defence identified the four soldiers killed as Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, all of whom were based at Edmonton.

The four deceased all served with the 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry (Ppcli), Major-General Wade Rutland said Sunday.

Maj.-Gen. Rutland said the Ppcli soldiers were doing high-intensity preparatory combat training with live munitions, in advance of deployments to Latvia in April and May.

The incident is “one of the worst tragedies that our armed forces have experienced on Canadian soil in peacetime,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier on Sunday.

“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our Armed Forces whom we have lost. And I have asked the flags on all federal buildings to be flown at half-mast to honour them,” Mr. Carney said in an address from Parliament Hill in Ottawa.

Mr. Carney said those affected by the fire came from military bases across the country, including reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

Cathy Keane, a mayoral candidate in Oro-Medonte, Ont., said on social media Sunday that her eldest son is among the soldiers injured in the incident, and that the family was on their way to Alberta to be with him.

“Overnight, our family received the devastating news that our eldest son is among the military personnel critically injured in the incident in Wainwright, Alberta, ON Saturday,” Ms. Keane posted on Facebook.

The military based is located about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

The Alberta Energy Regulator said Sunday it had not received any reports of incidents involving energy infrastructure.

Multiple oil and gas producers operate on CFB Wainwright property.

The regulator posted on its website that it is communicating with operators in the area. Under law, energy companies must notify the AER immediately if an incident affects their assets or facilities.

Several natural gas wells are active on the grounds of the base, according to Alberta Geological Survey maps.

It’s also home to various natural gas pipelines, including a network owned by Sumerian Oil & Gas Inc., formerly Cleo Energy Corp., that runs through the grounds, along its northern and southern edge and southwest onto non-CFB land.

Sumerian issued a statement Sunday saying that all of its wells, pipelines and facilities – including roughly 300 well licences on the Wainwright training area – were placed under the care of the AER and Orphan Well Association on Oct. 5.

Acute Care Alberta, the agency that co-ordinates medical services at acute health centres in the province, said Sunday afternoon that all Code Orange activations have been ended.

The emergency alert is issued when an incident causes more casualties than emergency departments or urgent care resources can manage using routine procedures. It was activated Saturday to co-ordinate a response across health care teams and emergency services.

Mr. Carney noted air ambulance crews flew in from Edmonton and from Saskatoon and said paramedics, nurses, and doctors in Wainwright, Edmonton, Red Deer and Calgary are caring for the victims.

As of Sunday, patients had been transferred from Wainwright Health Centre to four facilities: the University of Alberta Hospital, Royal Alexandra Hospital, Foothills Medical Centre and Red Deer Regional Hospital Centre.

June Winger, president of the Union of National Defence Employees, which represents more than 20,000 civilian military members, said her organization will continue to update and support its members.

“Our thoughts are with everyone affected by the devastating fire at CFB Wainwright, especially the families, military personnel, civilian workers and community members impacted by this tragic incident,” she said. “I want to express my sincere gratitude to the firefighters, first responders and emergency personnel working tirelessly to protect lives and keep people safe.”

In a social media post, Premier Danielle Smith said Alberta is mourning alongside Canadian Armed Forces members and their loved ones.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said the province deployed resources to help Alberta first responders manage the incident.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford encouraged all Canadians to come together and support those impacted by the incident at CFB Wainwright.

With reports from Mercedes Stephenson, Steven Chase, Andrea Woo, Jeffrey Jones, Emma Graney, Jana G. Pruden, Matthew Scace, Jesse Winter, and Temur Durrani

stories.title: Ckha recognizes hospital staff after bus rollover
stories.summary: The Chatham-Kent Health Alliance has recognized hospital staff for their response after the school bus rollover near Highway 401 and Bloomfield Road on Oct. 11.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
The Chatham-Kent Health Alliance has recognized hospital staff for their response after the school bus rollover near Highway 401 and Bloomfield Road on Oct. 11. After the incident, Ckha had 26 patients come in. They were taken care of on top of the 110 additional patients the emergency department sees on a typical Sunday.

Many additional staff and physicians joined the response, helping us meet the needs of patients during an extraordinary situation. We are proud of everyone involved.” Hospital staff worked closely with emergency responders to ensure there was a coordinated response.

This response reflects the dedication of the people who serve our community every day.” Ckha thanks everyone involved.

stories.title: PM Carney says 4 dead, dozens injured in violent fire at Alberta military base
stories.summary: Wainwright - Prime Minister Mark Carney says four military members were killed and dozens more were seriously injured after a violent, fast-moving fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canada’s military says a grass fire that killed four soldiers and sent scores more to hospital with bad burns was known well beforehand but not considered a threat.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division, says the grass fire was a kilometre away and considered sufficiently under control that training exercises were allowed to continue Saturday afternoon at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in central Alberta.

However, he said conditions — including a violent, sudden windstorm — sent those flames racing over the Prairie landscape at lightning speed, landing right on top of the soldiers.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland with the Canadian Armed Forces says a grass fire that killed four service members was considered under control before severe winds hit the area, causing it to spread rapidly in seconds. Rutland says 39 others are injured, including 19 in critical condition. (Oct. 18, 2026)

“This was a very uncommon occurrence,” Rutland told a news conference Sunday.

“I spoke to my commander on the ground. He said within 30 seconds to a minute they saw no fire, and then there was a fire right on top of them.”

Rutland said there is a lot to consider. Did the fire move that quickly because of the wind? Or did it move unseen through foliage to surprise the soldiers? Or was it both?

“This is why we’re going to do a complete investigation as to the topography, field conditions, foliage, etc., because it all plays into what happened,” he said.

The fire killed four soldiers and injured 39 more, nineteen of whom are in critical condition.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith announced the casualty count and confirmed many have serious burns.

“The loss of life and injuries are heartbreaking,” Smith said.

The four deceased have been identified as: Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton; Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C.

The Canadian Armed Forces has identified the four soldiers who died in a fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta. Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division, says the service members were from British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta. (Oct. 18, 2026)

The wounded are being cared for in four hospitals in Edmonton, Calgary and Red Deer.

Rutland spoke at a news conference with Smith and Defence Minister David McGuinty.

McGuinty said those affected were soldiers and reservists from across the country.

“This loss reaches communities in every province,” he said.

Defence Minister David McGuinty says there have been deaths and injuries after a fire broke out Saturday at a military base in Alberta. McGuinty had few other details to share but he says the situation is unlike any other in recent memory. (Oct. 18, 2026)

Earlier Sunday in Ottawa, Prime Minister Mark Carney called it one of the “worst tragedies for the (Armed Forces) on Canadian soil in peacetime.”

Flags on all federal buildings were lowered to half-mast to pay tribute to the deceased.

CFB Wainwright is 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton. It is one of Canada’s busiest bases and is used mainly to train soldiers and prepare units for combat operations.

On Saturday, savage winds, gusting at times to 100 kilometres an hour had been racing through the province, toppling trees, knocking out power, slamming signs, and sending garbage cans and other debris skittering down alleys and roads.

Rutland said the affected unit was Charlie Company of the 3rd Battalion of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry. He said when the fire hit, the 84-member company was doing two exercises. Most were throwing hand grenades on a range while 10 soldiers were doing a simulated attack on an enemy when they found themselves suddenly caught in the path of the roaring fire.

After overwhelming the soldiers, the blaze then jumped the base fence and threatened nearby rural areas and the town of Wainwright.

Fire crews scrambled throughout Saturday night to contain it and, by 11 p.m., had it under control. No one had to be evacuated from the area.

Bruce Pugh, Wainwright’s mayor, said he regularly hears the booming sound of artillery and cannons being launched during training from the base, so he didn’t think much when his windows rattled Saturday afternoon.

“But what was different was that everything went silent after the rattle,” Pugh said in an interview Sunday outside his home, about five kilometres from the base.

“After that, we have friends who are physicians, nurses, (who) were hearing through personal channels that everybody was being called to help with a mass casualty event.”

Moments later, he recounted, came the sound of sirens and helicopters.

The response was rapid and massive — 22 ground ambulances, six planes, two helicopters.

Just before midnight, Armed Forces medical staff members dropped through the inky black sky, their parachutes illuminated by flare lights as they glided to the ground.

Alberta health officials invoked a Code Orange on Saturday night for hospitals in Edmonton and beyond. Code Orange is a call for hospitals to essentially clear the decks, find staff and free up beds as necessary to handle a mass casualty incident. That alert was lifted Sunday afternoon.

Smith said flags at provincial buildings in Alberta would also be flown at half-mast in the days ahead.

The base is in the Battle River—Crowfoot riding, represented by federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre.

Poilievre, speaking to reporters in Wainwright, said he has heard about incredible acts of bravery. Some soldiers, he said, ran toward danger to help and are now fighting for their lives in hospital.

“Please pray for Wainwright,” he said.

The King said in a statement Sunday that he and the Queen “send our special thoughts and prayers to the people of Alberta, and to the Canadian Armed forces and their families.”

“We extend our particular admiration and gratitude to the military and civilian emergency services, health-care workers and all those who have responded with such courage and dedication in the most challenging circumstances.”

The tragedy comes as Albertans are to deliver their final votes Monday on whether it’s time to look at leaving Canada. In Edmonton, the deadly fire was on the minds of pro-Canada supporters rallying at the legislature.

Rally organizer Gil McGowan, the head of the Alberta Federation of Labour, said it was heartwarming to see first responders from around the country jump to help.

“That is a reminder why we’re so much better staying in the Canadian federation,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 18, 2026

stories.title: London community gathers to remember Raman Devi at candlelight vigil
stories.summary: Candles illuminated Meadowgate Park on Saturday evening as community members gathered to remember Raman Devi, a mother of two young children who was killed inside her Summerside home last month.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Candles illuminated Meadowgate Park on Saturday evening as community members gathered to remember Raman Devi, a mother of two young children who was killed inside her Summerside home last month.

The vigil brought together family, friends, community leaders, and advocates to honour Devi’s life, support her loved ones, and call for an end to violence against women and girls.

Attendees observed a moment of silence and lit candles at dusk. Devi’s mother addressed the gathering, fighting back tears as she called for justice for her daughter.

Devi’s two young children were also in attendance.

Friends and community members spoke about the loss and the lasting impact of her death.

“Today, it’s hard to believe that a month has already passed since we lost you,” said Sandra Sanchez, Devi’s friend.

“Your presence, your smile — we wish we could talk to you again. And honestly, it still doesn’t feel real.”

Mandeep Singh, 41, of London was arrested at the scene and charged with second-degree murder . Police confirmed Singh and Devi were involved in an intimate relationship.

Jessie Rodger, executive director of Anova, said the circumstances of Devi’s death highlight the need for continued action to address violence against women.

“There is so much pain and sadness and how her life ended,” Rodger said.

“And it’s so important not to look away. The way she died reinforces how much more work we have to do.”

London West MPP Peggy Sattler also called for greater efforts to address intimate partner violence and gender-based violence.

Sattler said she has co-sponsored a private member’s bill, the Intimate Partner Violence as an Epidemic Act , which seeks to recognize intimate partner violence as an epidemic.

She said recognizing the scope of the problem is a critical first step toward addressing its impact across communities and socioeconomic backgrounds.

Jennifer Dunn, executive director of the London Abused Women’s Centre, urged those attending the vigil to turn their grief into action.

“We gather in grief, but we must also leave here with a commitment to look out for each other, to speak up, and to keep working toward a community where women and girls live free from violence,” Dunn said.

A fundraiser organized by members of the Sikh community has been established to help support Devi’s two children.

Organizers said the vigil was an opportunity to stand with Devi’s family and ensure her life is not defined solely by the circumstances of her death.

A list of resources and contact information for those experiencing intimate partner violence can be found on the LPS’ website .

stories.title: No sign of ‘terrorist activity’ in deadly fire at Alberta military base: Forces
stories.summary: The Armed Forces say there’s no indication a fire that erupted at an Alberta military base, resulting in deaths and injuries, was the result of terrorist activity. The fire ripped through a training area at CFB Wainwright — around 200 km southeast of Edmonton — on Saturday, spreading beyond the massive base southeast of Edmonton. […]
stories.author: Cole Fortner
stories.content:
By CityNews Staff and The Canadian Press

Posted October 18, 2026 11:46 am.

The Armed Forces say there’s no indication a fire that erupted at an Alberta military base, resulting in deaths and injuries, was the result of terrorist activity.

The fire ripped through a training area at CFB Wainwright — around 200 km southeast of Edmonton — on Saturday, spreading beyond the massive base southeast of Edmonton.

The military says it’s not confirming details or numbers of casualties until families have been notified.

Defence Minister David McGuinty says he’s on his way to Edmonton and will be briefed on the latest developments. Prime Minister Mark Carney is also expected to be speaking Sunday regarding the fatal fire at CFB Wainwright.

Late Saturday, the minister underscored the seriousness of the fire, saying he couldn’t “recall an incident like this in recent memory.”

The Forces say the full extent of the fire is still being determined.

“While the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity,” a spokesperson said in an email to The Canadian Press on Sunday.

“We will provide additional information as it becomes available.”

Fire crews worked to beat back flames that spread beyond the base and prevented the fire from reaching the town of Wainwright, where at least 10 ambulances were seen parked in and around the local health centre late Saturday.

Acute Care Alberta said significant medical resources were needed to respond and that a “code orange had been activated at several hospitals across the province.

It said the code is declared when health resources need to be co-ordinated for “an incident that results in multiple severe patients needing care at the same time.”

CFB Wainwright is one of Canada’s largest military training facilities and regularly hosts major training exercises involving members of the Canadian Armed Forces.

The fire also disrupted advance voting for Monday’s provincial referendum on whether Alberta should hold a binding separation vote.

Elections Alberta said two advance polling locations — in Lloydminster and Vermilion — were closed early Saturday and the ballots transported securely.

Oro-Medonte mayoral candidate Cathy Keane confirmed on a Facebook post that her son was critically injured in the blaze, saying, “Overnight, our family received the devastating news that our eldest son is among the military personnel critically injured in the incident in Wainwright, Alberta, ON Saturday. As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family. I will be travelling to Alberta and unable to continue door-knocking for the remainder of the mayoral campaign. Please share the pinned post with my information with your neighbours, friends and your community.”

She’d ended her statement saying, “Right now, I ask for your understanding as our family navigates an incredibly difficult and uncertain time. We are grateful for the kindness and support of our friends and community. Please hold your loved ones a little tighter tonight.”
