stories.title: The latest developments on the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta
stories.summary: Wainwright - Prime Minister Mark Carney says four military members were killed and dozens more were seriously injured after a violent, fast-moving fire at CFB Wainwright, a massive military training base about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Wainwright - Prime Minister Mark Carney says four military members were killed and dozens more were seriously injured after a violent, fast-moving fire at CFB Wainwright, a massive military training base about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Sunday that four service members were killed and dozens more seriously injured in a fire at a military base in Alberta, describing it as one of the worst peacetime tragedies for Canada’s military on domestic soil. (Oct. 18, 2026)

Here are the latest developments (all times Mountain):

Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, speaking to reporters in Wainwright, says he’s hearing about incredible acts of bravery as a devastating fire ripped through the nearby military base.

He says some soldiers ran toward the danger to help and are now paying the price, fighting for their lives in hospital.

He’s asking everyone to pray for Wainwright.

Poilievre represents the area as part of the Battle River—Crowfoot riding.

The military says soldiers killed and injured while training at CFB Wainwright were caught up in a sudden windstorm that overwhelmed them with fire moving at unbelievable speeds.

Maj.-Gen Wade Rutland says a grass fire had been burning for a while but was considered far enough away and contained so that training could continue.

He says when the storm kicked up, flames moved a kilometre in about 30 seconds and overwhelmed the soldiers.

Premier Danielle Smith says alongside the four who died, 39 are in various hospitals and 19 of those are in critical condition.

Rutland says officials are not sure how the fire started and it could be weeks before that’s determined.

Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division has identified the four soldiers killed in the fire at CFB Wainwright.

They are: Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton; Private Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask.; Private Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver, and Private Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C.

The Canadian Armed Forces has identified the four soldiers who died in a fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta. Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division, says the service members were from British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Alberta. (Oct. 18, 2026)

The head of the European Commission is sending condolences to Canada.

Ursula von der Leyen says on social media that she is saddened by the tragedy at CFB Wainwright.

She writes on the platform X: “My deepest condolences to the families of the service members who lost their lives.”

The commission is the executive branch of the European Union, which is a political and economic union of 27 member states.

Alberta health officials say they have ended the Code Orange alert that was invoked Saturday night for some hospitals in Edmonton and elsewhere.

Code Orange is a call for hospitals to essentially clear the decks, find staff and free up beds as necessary to handle a mass casualty incident.

The province says its response to Saturday’s fire involved 22 ground ambulances, six planes and two helicopters, and included help from Saskatchewan.

The patients in Wainwright have now been moved to four hospitals: two hospitals in Edmonton, one in Red Deer and one in Calgary.

Gil McGowan, organizer of a pro-Canada rally currently underway at the legislature in Edmonton, says the Wainwright tragedy “hangs like a real dark cloud” over the event.

McGowan, the head of the Alberta Federation of Labour, says the way first responders from around Canada selflessly stepped up to offer aid is a poignant reminder of why Canada is better united.

Albertans vote Monday on whether the province should stay in Canada or whether it’s time to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving Confederation.

Polls of Albertans before Premier Danielle Smith called the referendum and since then have indicated strong support to stay in Canada.

Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh, in an interview, says he knew something was wrong Saturday afternoon when the regular window-rattling boom of artillery that inaugurates the start of military training exercises at CFB Wainwright suddenly fell silent.

Immediately after, he says, there were sirens and the sound of helicopters racing in.

He says that just before midnight military medical personnel literally dropped from the sky to help, their red parachutes illuminated by flare lights.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has issued a statement calling the fire at CFB Wainwright “heartbreaking.”

She paid tribute to the health workers that managed the tragedy.

She says the province has convened its emergency management cabinet committee to co-ordinate the response.

The prime minister says he has asked the military to give the public a detailed account of what is known about the fire so far.

Mark Carney says that will be later today in Alberta, with Defence Minister David McGuinty, Eleanor Olszewski, the minister of emergency preparedness, and Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of the 1st Canadian Division.

He says they will be joined by provincial ministers and senior officials.

Prime Minister Mark Carney confirms four military members were killed and dozens more were injured in the fire.

Carney called the fire “violent” and fast-moving.

The Nato Military Committee is sending its deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims at CFB Wainwright.

It says in a statement that Wainwright is where so many Canadian soldiers and allies have trained for the hardest tasks of the profession.

It says those killed served “our common security” and that the committee will honour their memory.

The United States Ambassador to Canada says his “heart is heavy” for the Canadian Armed Forces community.

Pete Hoekstra says on social media that he’s praying for the families of those who died and for the full recovery of the service members injured.

Prime Minister Mark Carney says in a social media post that Canadian flags will be flown at half-mast at federal buildings across the country.

He says Canada stands with the service members at CFB Wainwright and their families.

Carney is expected to make a statement later today.

The Armed Forces say there’s no indication the fire that erupted at an Alberta military base, resulting in deaths and injuries, was the result of terrorist activity.

A spokesperson also says in an email that the incident at CFB Wainwright remains under investigation and that more information will be provided as it becomes available.

Defence Minister David McGuinty says in a social media post that he’s on his way to Edmonton.

He says he’s being briefed on the latest developments in the “terrible incident” at CFB Wainwright.

He says: “To the families and everyone in Wainwright: Canada stands with you.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney is expected to make a statement later today.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 18, 2026.

stories.title: At least seven killed, dozens more injured in CFB Wainwright explosion and fire: report
stories.summary: A reported explosion and fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta has resulted in multiple deaths and injuries.
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed that four members of the Canadian Armed Forces were killed and dozens more were seriously injured during a “violent, fast-moving fire” at CFB Wainwright in Alberta on Saturday.

In a press conference Sunday afternoon, Carney called it “one of the worst tragedies for the Forces on Canadian soil in peacetime.”

Around 4 p.m., a fire inside a training area quickly spread beyond its boundaries, requiring “military and civilian emergency services” to attack the fire and assist the affected, according to the latest update from National Defence on Sunday.

While officials have yet to confirm the “full extent of the impact,” General Jennie Carignan, Canada’s Chief of the Defence Staff, indicated that they have started identifying the deceased and notifying their next of kin.

“While casualty identification and notification processes are ongoing, I extend my deepest condolences to the loved ones of those who have lost their lives,” she said in Sunday’s update.

“This is a profoundly difficult moment for the entire Canadian Armed Forces.”

Global News earlier reported at least seven were killed, according to multiple Canadian Armed Forces sources.

The individuals told the outlet the explosion resulted from a gas line or gas well on the base being hit during a live-fire training exercise and that high winds fueled the resulting fire. Environment Canada, which had warned of high winds earlier in the day, later recorded gusts of 98 km/h at Edmonton International Airport Saturday afternoon.

“Military and civilian crews fought this fire through the night, in some of the worst conditions imaginable, risking their lives to protect their fellow Canadians,” Carney said.

As of early Sunday morning, the “wildfire south” of the town of Wainwright, located just northeast of the base, was being held and a fire watch remains in place, the municipal district said on social media.

Rookie soldier, 20, killed in fall from lookout tower during training exercises at CFB Wainwright

Canadian Armed Forces identifies soldier killed in training exercise as 29-year-old from B.C.

Carney said Minister of National Defence David McGuinty, Minister of Emergency Preparedness Eleanor Olszewski, and Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland of the Canadian Army, along with provincial officials, will provide Canadians with “a detailed account and formal briefing” on Sunday afternoon.

Several hospitals in the region, including Edmonton’s Royal Alexandra and the University of Alberta’s, were under code orange, which is activated only in mass casualty events, according to the Edmonton Journal. Acute Care Alberta (ACA) stood down the code later in the day.

Health care facilities in Wainwright itself, a town of less than 7,000, were “completely overwhelmed,” an ER doctor at the Royal Alexandra told CBC, noting the number of incoming patients “would overwhelm the city of Edmonton.”

“It is more patients than any of us want to count right now,” Dr. Warren Thirsk said. “It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster.”

At the Wainwright Health Centre, long-term patient Brandon Simmons told the Journal he watched as soldiers “arrived in a military medical bus.”

“And then they started to bring everyone out, assess the wounded,” he said. “No one was prepared for that.”

ACA, in a statement to National Post, said 30 units were dispatched to Wainwright — 22 ambulances, six airplanes and two helicopters — via EHS-Alberta and contracted service partners in Alberta and Saskatchewan.

“Active emergency response was sustained across the system for more than 10 hours, with patients transported to and receiving care at facilities across our entire province,” they wrote. Other hospitals where patients are being treated include Foothills Medical Centre and Red Deer Regional Hospital Centre.

“It is anticipated that care for patients impacted by this incident will be intensive and will add to existing high demand on acute care in Alberta,” ACA stated.

One of the deceased has been identified on Facebook by his mother as Shaun Farrell.

“​We want to thank everyone for your love, support, and prayers during this incredibly difficult time,” Patricia Farrell posted Sunday. “As our family navigates this profound loss, we kindly ask for privacy so that we May grieve together.”

One of the “critically injured” has been identified as the eldest son of Cathy Keane, who has suspended her campaign for mayor in Oro-Medont, Ont.

“As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family,” she shared on Facebook Sunday . “Right now, I ask for your understanding as our family navigates an incredibly difficult and uncertain time. We are grateful for the kindness and support of our friends and community.”

Charitable helicopter service Stars Ambulance also dispatched three aircraft to Wainwright Saturday night, according to its X account , and there are multiple reports of additional Canadian Armed Forces personnel parachuting into Wainwright.

Established on former Buffalo National Park land in 1940, CFB Wainwright — which once housed German prisoners of war following Wwii — is regarded as one of the country’s “busiest Army bases” and is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre (Cmtc) and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre (3 Cdtc). Roughly 700 military personnel and 300 civilians work on the more than 600-square-kilometre base.

Carney said many of the soldiers training in Wainwright are reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, often known as the Princess Pats, a regiment that fought in both World Wars, Korea, Afghanistan and peacekeeping missions the world over.

“That is the record, that is the standard, those are the values of the women and men who were training on the Alberta prairie yesterday afternoon when disaster struck.”

“Those we lost and who were injured were training to defend Canada. To serve Canada,” he added. “Now Canada serves them.”

The base also features “a bison herd of approximately 50 animals” that are pastured “in a protected part of the range and training area.” It’s not clear if the herd was affected.

“This is an active and delicate situation and soon to be an active and delicate investigation,” he said, promising more details for Canadians in due course, as they emerge.

“Right now our thoughts are with the families and all those who are helping to wrestle this very difficult situation to the ground.”

He said the RCMP was investigating.

Sunday morning, McGuinty said on X he was bound for Edmonton to be “briefed on the latest developments regarding the terrible incident.”

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, whose federal riding of Battle River-Crowfoot included Wainwright and the base, is also headed to the region, CBC reported Sunday. He’d already expressed his concern in an X post on Saturday, asking everyone to “Pray for Wainwright.”

“Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected,” Carney posted on social media Saturday, noting Ottawa was working with local authorities. “Premier Smith and I are in close contact as are our relevant ministers and officials.”

“All Canadians stand with the service members at CFB Wainwright, their families, and their community.”

Smith, in her own post to X , thanked “first responders and all those providing care and support to those affected.” She was on her way to Edmonton on Sunday and said flags on provincial government buildings will also be lowered to half-mast,

Other premiers expressing concern from afar as of Sunday morning included Ontario’s Doug Ford, Manitoba’s Wab Kinew, Nova Scotia’s Tim Houston, and Newfoundland and Labrador’s Tony Wakeham.

“As Canadians, let’s come together to support our brave men and women in uniform, who put their lives on the line to protect our freedoms and our country,” Ford wrote.

“I extend my support to the military members, families, and community affected by the fire at CFB Wainwright,” she wrote. “My thoughts are with the loved ones of those who lost their lives, those who were injured, and all those affected by this tragedy.”

“On behalf of the Union of National Defence Employees, we stand in solidarity with the entire Wainwright community and will continue to update and support our members during this difficult time.”

Condolences also came from outside Canada, with Nato military committee chair Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, who heralded the base’s importance as a training ground.

“Wainwright is where Canadian soldiers, and so many Allies with them, train for the hardest tasks of our profession. Those who fell there served our common security, and the Military Committee will honour their memory,” he shared to X.

Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine’s foreign minister, offered “heartfelt condolences” to family and loved ones of the deceased, wished a speedy recovery to the injured and said his country “stands in solidarity with Canada at this difficult time.”
paragraphs: Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed that four members of the Canadian Armed Forces were killed and dozens more were seriously injured during a “violent, fast-moving fire” at CFB Wainwright in Alberta on Saturday.
In a press conference Sunday afternoon, Carney called it “one of the worst tragedies for the Forces on Canadian soil in peacetime.”

Around 4 p.m., a fire inside a training area quickly spread beyond its boundaries, requiring “military and civilian emergency services” to attack the fire and assist the affected, according to the latest update from National Defence on Sunday.

While officials have yet to confirm the “full extent of the impact,” General Jennie Carignan, Canada’s Chief of the Defence Staff, indicated that they have started identifying the deceased and notifying their next of kin.
“While casualty identification and notification processes are ongoing, I extend my deepest condolences to the loved ones of those who have lost their lives,” she said in Sunday’s update.
“This is a profoundly difficult moment for the entire Canadian Armed Forces.”
Global News earlier reported at least seven were killed, according to multiple Canadian Armed Forces sources.

The individuals told the outlet the explosion resulted from a gas line or gas well on the base being hit during a live-fire training exercise and that high winds fueled the resulting fire. Environment Canada, which had warned of high winds earlier in the day, later recorded gusts of 98 km/h at Edmonton International Airport Saturday afternoon.
“Military and civilian crews fought this fire through the night, in some of the worst conditions imaginable, risking their lives to protect their fellow Canadians,” Carney said.

As of early Sunday morning, the “wildfire south” of the town of Wainwright, located just northeast of the base, was being held and a fire watch remains in place, the municipal district said on social media.
Rookie soldier, 20, killed in fall from lookout tower during training exercises at CFB Wainwright
Canadian Armed Forces identifies soldier killed in training exercise as 29-year-old from B.C.

Carney said Minister of National Defence David McGuinty, Minister of Emergency Preparedness Eleanor Olszewski, and Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland of the Canadian Army, along with provincial officials, will provide Canadians with “a detailed account and formal briefing” on Sunday afternoon.

Several hospitals in the region, including Edmonton’s Royal Alexandra and the University of Alberta’s, were under code orange, which is activated only in mass casualty events, according to the Edmonton Journal. Acute Care Alberta (ACA) stood down the code later in the day.

Health care facilities in Wainwright itself, a town of less than 7,000, were “completely overwhelmed,” an ER doctor at the Royal Alexandra told CBC, noting the number of incoming patients “would overwhelm the city of Edmonton.”
“It is more patients than any of us want to count right now,” Dr. Warren Thirsk said. “It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster.”
At the Wainwright Health Centre, long-term patient Brandon Simmons told the Journal he watched as soldiers “arrived in a military medical bus.”
“And then they started to bring everyone out, assess the wounded,” he said. “No one was prepared for that.”

ACA, in a statement to National Post, said 30 units were dispatched to Wainwright — 22 ambulances, six airplanes and two helicopters — via EHS-Alberta and contracted service partners in Alberta and Saskatchewan.

“Active emergency response was sustained across the system for more than 10 hours, with patients transported to and receiving care at facilities across our entire province,” they wrote. Other hospitals where patients are being treated include Foothills Medical Centre and Red Deer Regional Hospital Centre.
“It is anticipated that care for patients impacted by this incident will be intensive and will add to existing high demand on acute care in Alberta,” ACA stated.
One of the deceased has been identified on Facebook by his mother as Shaun Farrell.

“​We want to thank everyone for your love, support, and prayers during this incredibly difficult time,” Patricia Farrell posted Sunday. “As our family navigates this profound loss, we kindly ask for privacy so that we May grieve together.”
One of the “critically injured” has been identified as the eldest son of Cathy Keane, who has suspended her campaign for mayor in Oro-Medont, Ont.

“As a mother, right now I need to be with my son and family,” she shared on Facebook Sunday . “Right now, I ask for your understanding as our family navigates an incredibly difficult and uncertain time. We are grateful for the kindness and support of our friends and community.”

Charitable helicopter service Stars Ambulance also dispatched three aircraft to Wainwright Saturday night, according to its X account , and there are multiple reports of additional Canadian Armed Forces personnel parachuting into Wainwright.

Established on former Buffalo National Park land in 1940, CFB Wainwright — which once housed German prisoners of war following Wwii — is regarded as one of the country’s “busiest Army bases” and is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre (Cmtc) and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre (3 Cdtc). Roughly 700 military personnel and 300 civilians work on the more than 600-square-kilometre base.

Carney said many of the soldiers training in Wainwright are reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, often known as the Princess Pats, a regiment that fought in both World Wars, Korea, Afghanistan and peacekeeping missions the world over.
“That is the record, that is the standard, those are the values of the women and men who were training on the Alberta prairie yesterday afternoon when disaster struck.”
“Those we lost and who were injured were training to defend Canada. To serve Canada,” he added. “Now Canada serves them.”
The base also features “a bison herd of approximately 50 animals” that are pastured “in a protected part of the range and training area.” It’s not clear if the herd was affected.
“This is an active and delicate situation and soon to be an active and delicate investigation,” he said, promising more details for Canadians in due course, as they emerge.
“Right now our thoughts are with the families and all those who are helping to wrestle this very difficult situation to the ground.”
He said the RCMP was investigating.
Sunday morning, McGuinty said on X he was bound for Edmonton to be “briefed on the latest developments regarding the terrible incident.”

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, whose federal riding of Battle River-Crowfoot included Wainwright and the base, is also headed to the region, CBC reported Sunday. He’d already expressed his concern in an X post on Saturday, asking everyone to “Pray for Wainwright.”

“Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected,” Carney posted on social media Saturday, noting Ottawa was working with local authorities. “Premier Smith and I are in close contact as are our relevant ministers and officials.”
“All Canadians stand with the service members at CFB Wainwright, their families, and their community.”

Smith, in her own post to X , thanked “first responders and all those providing care and support to those affected.” She was on her way to Edmonton on Sunday and said flags on provincial government buildings will also be lowered to half-mast,
Other premiers expressing concern from afar as of Sunday morning included Ontario’s Doug Ford, Manitoba’s Wab Kinew, Nova Scotia’s Tim Houston, and Newfoundland and Labrador’s Tony Wakeham.
“As Canadians, let’s come together to support our brave men and women in uniform, who put their lives on the line to protect our freedoms and our country,” Ford wrote.

“I extend my support to the military members, families, and community affected by the fire at CFB Wainwright,” she wrote. “My thoughts are with the loved ones of those who lost their lives, those who were injured, and all those affected by this tragedy.”
“On behalf of the Union of National Defence Employees, we stand in solidarity with the entire Wainwright community and will continue to update and support our members during this difficult time.”
Condolences also came from outside Canada, with Nato military committee chair Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, who heralded the base’s importance as a training ground.

“Wainwright is where Canadian soldiers, and so many Allies with them, train for the hardest tasks of our profession. Those who fell there served our common security, and the Military Committee will honour their memory,” he shared to X.

Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine’s foreign minister, offered “heartfelt condolences” to family and loved ones of the deceased, wished a speedy recovery to the injured and said his country “stands in solidarity with Canada at this difficult time.”

stories.title: Defence Minister en route to Alberta after deadly fire at CFB Wainwright
stories.summary: David McGuinty confirmed multiple casualties and injuries at the military base related to the incident
stories.author: Steven Chase
stories.content:
The fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright that killed four and wounded dozens began as a smoldering grass fire that was whipped into a “wall of flame” by high winds, early internal military communications indicate.

The flames then overtook Canadian Armed Forces members who were on a firing range, according to the reports, which were obtained by the Globe and Mail.

It remains unclear what first ignited the grass fire.

The Department of National Defence said the incident began after a fire ignited at about 4 p.m. local time Saturday in the training area of the military base, which is located about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

The first report issued Saturday night says the “fire index,” a measure of risk, was low. It suggests an “unexpected and sudden wind change” took place during the incident.

“During training a grass fire ignited, and strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction; the fire shifted toward the personnel on the range and overtook their admin area,” a report from Saturday says.

A second report issued Sunday more describes the initial fire as “smoldering” and said it “blew over 1 kilometre” before a “wall of flame” engulfed the “administration area of the live fire training range.”

Two military sources confirmed the reports are authentic. The Globe and Mail is not naming the sources, who are not authorized to publicly disclose the documents.

The first report identified four people as “vital signs absent” and 31 wounded as “very serious (Priority A) or Serious (Priority B).” It also counted six to eight people with minor injuries.

The reports indicate that some of the dead and injured were army troops who were part of an exercise run by the 3rd Battalion of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

Environment Canada recorded 69 kilometre per hour wind gusts around 4 p.m., with a maximum gust for the day of 82 kilometres per hour. Forecasts issued at 5 a.m. and 11 a.m. warned of wind gusts up to 80 kilometres per hour.

The second internal military report also says there’s no evidence so far that ammunition or petroleum contributed to the incident.

“At this point there is no indication of any explosion involving ammunition or oil and gas infrastructure,” the Sunday report said.

“As part of the investigation, CAF engineers at Wainwright will be checking oil and gas infrastructure.”

The Alberta Energy Regulator issued a statement on Sunday that said it hadn’t received any report that oil and gas infrastructure was affected.

Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed the four deaths as he delivered a statement on Sunday. He described a “violent, fast-moving fire” that also seriously wounded dozens of personnel.

“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our Armed Forces whom we have lost. And I have asked the flags on all federal buildings to be flown at half-mast to honour them,” Mr. Carney said in an address from Parliament Hill in Ottawa.

He called the incident “one of the worst tragedies that our armed forces have experienced on Canadian soil in peacetime.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed four people were killed in a 'violent, fast-moving fire' at the military base.

The Prime Minister praised those who fought the fire and rescued victims.

“Military and civilian crews fought this fire throughout the night in some of the worst conditions imaginable, risking their lives to protect their fellow Canadians,” he said.

Mr. Carney said those affected by the fire came from military bases across the country, including reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

“Throughout Canada’s history, the Princess Pats have fought for freedom, democracy, human dignity. In the First World War, in the Second, in Korea, in Afghanistan, and during numerous peacekeeping missions over decades.”

The Prime Minister pledged that Canada would support the victims and their families.

“We will be there for their families for as long as they need. We will care for the injured through every step of their recovery, and we will stand by the women and men of our armed forces as they bear the weight of this loss,” he said.

“They will not carry it alone, because in Canada, we take care of one another.”

Around midnight, as response efforts were underway, two bright red flares dropped from the sky before seven Canadian Forces members parachuted onto the football field of the local high school across the street from the Wainwright hospital. They were soon met by a helicopter that touched down to unload medical equipment, including what appeared to be a ventilator that the troops wheeled into the hospital.

Nearby, paramedics loaded two patients on stretchers into waiting ambulances, which then sped off.

By Sunday morning, the scene at the Wainwright Health Centre was quiet. The ambulances that had continued moving patients late into the night were gone.

Access to CFB Wainwright was blocked. At the front gate of the base, civilian vehicles filed through a security checkpoint at sunrise.

Mr. Carney noted air ambulance crews flew in from Edmonton and from Saskatoon and said paramedics, nurses, and doctors in Wainwright, Edmonton, Red Deer and Calgary are caring for the victims.

“I would like to thank those Albertans and Canadians who are giving blood, who are feeding and housing the emergency crews, and who are providing solace and comfort to those in their darkest hour.”

The Department of National Defence said there’s no evidence so far that the Wainwright fire was caused by terrorism.

“While the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity,” spokeswoman Andrée-Anne Poulin said.

Mr. Carney said the Department of National Defence will provide an update in Wainwright later on Sunday.

Defence Minister David McGuinty was en route to the province to get briefed on what he described as the “terrible incident” at CFB Wainwright.

“To the families and everyone in Wainwright: Canada stands with you,” Mr. McGuinty said.

Late Saturday , Mr. McGuinty said the incident was unlike anything he could recall in recent memory.

paragraphs: The fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright that killed four and wounded dozens began as a smoldering grass fire that was whipped into a “wall of flame” by high winds, early internal military communications indicate.
The flames then overtook Canadian Armed Forces members who were on a firing range, according to the reports, which were obtained by the Globe and Mail.
It remains unclear what first ignited the grass fire.

The Department of National Defence said the incident began after a fire ignited at about 4 p.m. local time Saturday in the training area of the military base, which is located about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.
The first report issued Saturday night says the “fire index,” a measure of risk, was low. It suggests an “unexpected and sudden wind change” took place during the incident.

“During training a grass fire ignited, and strong winds caused the fire to spread rapidly and shift direction; the fire shifted toward the personnel on the range and overtook their admin area,” a report from Saturday says.

A second report issued Sunday more describes the initial fire as “smoldering” and said it “blew over 1 kilometre” before a “wall of flame” engulfed the “administration area of the live fire training range.”
Two military sources confirmed the reports are authentic. The Globe and Mail is not naming the sources, who are not authorized to publicly disclose the documents.
The first report identified four people as “vital signs absent” and 31 wounded as “very serious (Priority A) or Serious (Priority B).” It also counted six to eight people with minor injuries.
The reports indicate that some of the dead and injured were army troops who were part of an exercise run by the 3rd Battalion of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

Environment Canada recorded 69 kilometre per hour wind gusts around 4 p.m., with a maximum gust for the day of 82 kilometres per hour. Forecasts issued at 5 a.m. and 11 a.m. warned of wind gusts up to 80 kilometres per hour.
The second internal military report also says there’s no evidence so far that ammunition or petroleum contributed to the incident.
“At this point there is no indication of any explosion involving ammunition or oil and gas infrastructure,” the Sunday report said.
“As part of the investigation, CAF engineers at Wainwright will be checking oil and gas infrastructure.”
The Alberta Energy Regulator issued a statement on Sunday that said it hadn’t received any report that oil and gas infrastructure was affected.
Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed the four deaths as he delivered a statement on Sunday. He described a “violent, fast-moving fire” that also seriously wounded dozens of personnel.

“The nation is in mourning for those brave members of our Armed Forces whom we have lost. And I have asked the flags on all federal buildings to be flown at half-mast to honour them,” Mr. Carney said in an address from Parliament Hill in Ottawa.
He called the incident “one of the worst tragedies that our armed forces have experienced on Canadian soil in peacetime.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed four people were killed in a 'violent, fast-moving fire' at the military base.
The Prime Minister praised those who fought the fire and rescued victims.
“Military and civilian crews fought this fire throughout the night in some of the worst conditions imaginable, risking their lives to protect their fellow Canadians,” he said.
Mr. Carney said those affected by the fire came from military bases across the country, including reservists and soldiers from the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

“Throughout Canada’s history, the Princess Pats have fought for freedom, democracy, human dignity. In the First World War, in the Second, in Korea, in Afghanistan, and during numerous peacekeeping missions over decades.”
The Prime Minister pledged that Canada would support the victims and their families.

“We will be there for their families for as long as they need. We will care for the injured through every step of their recovery, and we will stand by the women and men of our armed forces as they bear the weight of this loss,” he said.
“They will not carry it alone, because in Canada, we take care of one another.”

Around midnight, as response efforts were underway, two bright red flares dropped from the sky before seven Canadian Forces members parachuted onto the football field of the local high school across the street from the Wainwright hospital. They were soon met by a helicopter that touched down to unload medical equipment, including what appeared to be a ventilator that the troops wheeled into the hospital.
Nearby, paramedics loaded two patients on stretchers into waiting ambulances, which then sped off.
By Sunday morning, the scene at the Wainwright Health Centre was quiet. The ambulances that had continued moving patients late into the night were gone.
Access to CFB Wainwright was blocked. At the front gate of the base, civilian vehicles filed through a security checkpoint at sunrise.
Mr. Carney noted air ambulance crews flew in from Edmonton and from Saskatoon and said paramedics, nurses, and doctors in Wainwright, Edmonton, Red Deer and Calgary are caring for the victims.
“I would like to thank those Albertans and Canadians who are giving blood, who are feeding and housing the emergency crews, and who are providing solace and comfort to those in their darkest hour.”
The Department of National Defence said there’s no evidence so far that the Wainwright fire was caused by terrorism.
“While the incident remains under investigation, at this time, there are no indications that it was the result of any terrorist activity,” spokeswoman Andrée-Anne Poulin said.
Mr. Carney said the Department of National Defence will provide an update in Wainwright later on Sunday.
Defence Minister David McGuinty was en route to the province to get briefed on what he described as the “terrible incident” at CFB Wainwright.
“To the families and everyone in Wainwright: Canada stands with you,” Mr. McGuinty said.

He said the Department of National Defence is working closely with the government of Alberta and local authorities, and he thanked first responders, Canadian Armed Forces members, and provincial officials for their efforts.
Late Saturday , Mr. McGuinty said the incident was unlike anything he could recall in recent memory.

The agency urged people in Edmonton to avoid going to the emergency department at the University of Alberta hospital so that patients coming from the military base could be prioritized.

Satellite imagery from Nasa’s wildfire surveillance system captured at least seven clusters of fire at the camp earlier Saturday night. A post on the Municipal District of Wainwright Facebook page said the wildfire had been held, but a watch would remain in place in case conditions changed.
June Winger, president of the Union of National Defence Employees, which represents more than 20,000 civilian military members, said her organization will continue to update and support its members.

“Our thoughts are with everyone affected by the devastating fire at CFB Wainwright, especially the families, military personnel, civilian workers and community members impacted by this tragic incident,” she said. “I want to express my sincere gratitude to the firefighters, first responders and emergency personnel working tirelessly to protect lives and keep people safe.”

stories.title: Canadians react to CFB Wainwright explosion and fire
stories.summary: Work is still underway to maintain control of the fire and offers of condolences continue to pour in with dozens injured and at least seven dead.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Condolences continue to pour in from across Canada and the world as emergency crews maintain the deadly fire that broke out at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright.

At least seven people have died with dozens more injured, according to multiple military sources.

“As Commander-in-Chief, and on behalf of all Canadians, I extend my support to the military members, families, and community affected by the fire at CFB Wainwright,” said Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour in a statement Sunday morning. “My thoughts are with the loved ones of those who lost their lives, those who were injured, and all those affected by this tragedy.”

The Canadian Armed Forces confirmed Sunday that the fire ignited within a training area at approximately 4 p.m. MT on Saturday.

It was the result of an explosion caused by a live-fire exercise hitting a gas line or gas well on the base, multiple Canadian Armed Forces sources told Global News.

“The fire spread rapidly beyond the boundaries of the training area, while military and civilian emergency services responded quickly to control that fire and to support those affected by this tragic event,” the CAF said in a news release.

Chief of the Defence Staff Jennie Carignan said the CAF and Department of National Defence are working with partners across the federal, provincial and municipal governments to “mobilize all necessary support.”

“Our soldiers, civilian personnel, and emergency responders are working closely with local authorities to respond to this situation,” she said in a statement. “On behalf of the Canadian Army, I extend my deepest condolences to the families, friends, and loved ones of those affected by this tragedy.”

Numerous leaders of all levels of government offered condolences overnight, including Prime Minister Mark Carney, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, and Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi.

But as the night wore on into the morning, more leaders like Arbour paid tribute.

“Canada is mourning a terrible tragedy at CFB Wainwright,” said Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas Sunday morning. “Our soldiers put their lives on the line in service to our country, and to lose them here at home is devastating.”

In Ontario, Premier Doug Ford and NDP Leader Marit Stiles both urged Canadians to come together.

“As Canadians, let’s come together to support our brave men and women in uniform, who put their lives on the line to protect our freedoms and our country,” Ford said on social media. “Ontario stands ready to help the recovery efforts however we can.”

“I cannot imagine the weight of this news for families with loved ones in the service. Canadians stand with you,” Stiles said.

Condolences were also offered from outside the country.

“Deeply saddened by the tragic incident and devastating fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta,” said Andril Sybiha, minister of foreign affairs for Ukraine. “My heartfelt condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.”

When the fire broke out, much of Alberta was under wind warnings with up to 100 km/h wind gusts fuelling the flames.

The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire south of town crossed the base fence earlier in the day and was being actively managed.

A fire watch for the community is in place, with the municipality urging residents to continue to avoid the incident area and keep roads clear.

— with files from Global News’ Karen Bartko, Amy Judd and Ashleigh Stewart

But as the night wore on into the morning, more leaders like Arbour paid tribute.

“Canada is mourning a terrible tragedy at CFB Wainwright,” said Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas Sunday morning. “Our soldiers put their lives on the line in service to our country, and to lose them here at home is devastating.”
In Ontario, Premier Doug Ford and NDP Leader Marit Stiles both urged Canadians to come together.

“As Canadians, let’s come together to support our brave men and women in uniform, who put their lives on the line to protect our freedoms and our country,” Ford said on social media. “Ontario stands ready to help the recovery efforts however we can.”
“I cannot imagine the weight of this news for families with loved ones in the service. Canadians stand with you,” Stiles said.
Condolences were also offered from outside the country.

“Deeply saddened by the tragic incident and devastating fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta,” said Andril Sybiha, minister of foreign affairs for Ukraine. “My heartfelt condolences to the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives.”
Fire remains held south of Wainwright
When the fire broke out, much of Alberta was under wind warnings with up to 100 km/h wind gusts fuelling the flames.
The Municipal District of Wainwright said the fire south of town crossed the base fence earlier in the day and was being actively managed.
A fire watch for the community is in place, with the municipality urging residents to continue to avoid the incident area and keep roads clear.
— with files from Global News’ Karen Bartko, Amy Judd and Ashleigh Stewart

stories.title: Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week
stories.summary: Canada
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Five things to watch for in the Canadian business world in the coming week:

Alberta referendum

Albertans vote on Monday on 10 referendum questions including whether or not to hold a binding referendum on the province leaving Canada. Elections Alberta officials say the separation question will be counted first with the result expected to be known sometime early the following morning.

Stellantis strike vote

Unifor, the union representing more than 9,000 workers at Stellantis, will release results Monday of a weekend strike vote by workers at the automaker. The union has said a strike mandate would give its bargaining committee leverage to reach a negotiated agreement, calling strike action a last resort. A major sticking point in the contract talks is the future of the Brampton, Ont., assembly plant, which Stellantis wants to sell to defence contractor Roshel.

Statistics Canada will release its September inflation reading on Monday when it publishes its consumer price index for the month. The report is expected to help give the Bank of Canada a look at how energy price pressures are influencing other parts of the economy. The annual inflation rate in August was three per cent, matching the pace set in July.

Outlook survey

The Bank of Canada will release its business outlook survey and its survey of consumer expectations on Monday. They come ahead of the central bank’s next interest rate decision and monetary policy report scheduled for Oct. 28.

Rogers results

Rogers Communications Inc. will report its third-quarter financial results on Friday. The company recently completed its purchase of the remaining 25 per cent stake in Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment it did not already hold, giving it complete ownership of the sports conglomerate that includes the Maple Leafs, Raptors, Toronto FC and Argonauts.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Alberta separatists rally at provincial legislature ahead of referendum
stories.summary: Leaders say movement for province to leave Canada is here to stay, regardless of vote outcome
stories.author: Matthew Scace
stories.content:
Dallas Pagenkopf stood at the front of the bus, looking over passengers dressed in deep-blue ball caps, hoodies and T-shirts.

More than a dozen provincial flags were neatly stacked below deck, next to Mr. Pagenkopf’s trolley cart stuffed with Alberta-themed car flags, caps and shirts. Dressed in denim and a leather vest, the 36-year-old took up a microphone and ran through the day’s itinerary.

“Oh, and last minute,” he said. “I’m selling some shirts and hats ... I’ve got a bunch of different things. If you haven’t seen it, come grab me.

“It’s gonna be a great day.”

With that, the bus left the Home Depot parking lot in Airdrie, Alta., beginning the pilgrimage to Edmonton, where faithful Alberta separatists gathered for a final rally ahead of Monday’s referendum.

The bus was one of 11 ferrying people to the provincial capital for the Saturday afternoon rally organized by Let Alberta Decide, a pro-independence group created by lawyer Keith Wilson and rancher Tanya Clemens.

Alberta Sheriffs estimated roughly 1,100 people gathered at the foot of the Alberta Legislature, capping more than a year of efforts by separatists to galvanize support for independence through a province-wide petition and at multiple town halls.

For the first time in the province’s history, Albertans will put secession to a vote on Monday – in this case, whether they wish to remain in Canada or have a second, binding separation referendum. More than a million residents have so far voted by mail or at advance polls.

Prime Minister Mark Carney campaigned in Calgary and Edmonton this week, packing convention centres in both cities as he urged people to vote to remain in Canada.

Several prominent separatists were on hand for Saturday’s rally, including Mr. Wilson, who spearheaded Let Alberta Decide’s campaign and raised $581,000 for the cause. Mitch Sylvestre and Jeffrey Rath, both with the Alberta Prosperity Project, attended the rally but weren’t part of the formal program.

Separatists are not expected to prevail in Monday’s vote. Public-opinion polls have shown that support for separation has remained largely unmoved over the campaign, and sits between 20 and 30 per cent.

Mr. Wilson said Saturday that regardless of the result, the separatist movement is here to stay.

“We’re going to get stronger. We’re going to get smarter. We’re going to get more clear,” he said.

He was joined by long-time separatist and columnist Corey Morgan, who similarly suggested that the movement has planted itself in Alberta, even if federalists prevail.

“It takes growing a movement to make something that lasts, and it’s here now,” Mr. Morgan said.

Aboard the bus to Edmonton, some supporters exhibited full-throated optimism going into Monday.

Debbie Mayhew sat in the back of the bus with her husband, Keith Brownlee. She said she’s seen polling online that shows 71-per-cent support for independence.

“I feel positive,” she said.

The retired couple moved to Calgary four years ago; they spend half the year in Alberta and the winter in California.

Ms. Mayhew wanted to get away from the Ontario humidity, but said politics pulled her and Mr. Brownlee to Alberta.

“Danielle Smith sounded like a promise,” she said.

Her feelings toward the Premier have changed. Ms. Mayhew, a United Conservative Party member, thinks Ms. Smith, who supports Alberta remaining in Canada, should not have picked a side. Despite her displeasure, she doesn’t think the Premier should lose her job.

Ms. Mayhew said she appreciates Mr. Wilson’s temperament. She thinks Mr. Sylvestre, chief executive of the Alberta Prosperity Project, is a straight-shooter and would trust him to lead an independent Alberta. Most people she talks to agree.

“You never heard that?” she asked over the din of chatter.

A few rows up, Paul Bauman kicked his legs up on the empty seat next to him. He wore a shiny blue sweater with an Alberta flag across the front. He bought it on Amazon.

Mr. Bauman will be at the UCP annual meeting in late November. He thinks Mr. Wilson should be premier.

“Oh yeah. I bought my ticket so I can put Danielle out.”

Others aren’t so sure about ousting Ms. Smith. Morad Rizkalla, a retired petroleum engineer who petitioned this winter for an independence referendum, argued that Ms. Smith never promised to campaign for separatists.

“Just be careful what you wish for because if you do split the vote ... it’s happened before. We split the party before, and you had NDP,” he said, referring to the NDP victory in the 2015 provincial election.

“Don’t be so quick to lop people’s head off here.”

stories.title: Community bike ride aims to raise awareness and push governments to improve cycling safety
stories.summary: Members of London’s cycling community took to the streets Saturday afternoon, calling for safer roads after a series of crashes involving cyclists in the region left riders with serious, life-threatening injuries last month.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
Members of London’s cycling community took to the streets Saturday afternoon, calling for safer roads after a series of crashes involving cyclists in the region left riders with serious, life-threatening injuries last month.

The community ride began at Gibbons Park before stopping at Victoria Park, bringing attention to the need for improved cycling safety and greater accountability from governments at all levels.

Luis Patricio, a London cycling volunteer, said recent incidents, highlight the urgent need for change.

“It’s really a matter of will and not a matter of knowledge or skills or resources,” Patricio said.

“It’s really just the willpower.”

Organizers hope the ride will keep the conversation going beyond Saturday’s event, encouraging residents to stay engaged and push for safer roads for everyone.

Patricio said governments must be held accountable for making streets safer, emphasizing the importance of protecting all road users.

Andrea Nair also took part in the ride, sharing her experience after her son was struck by a vehicle while riding his bicycle.

Nair said the driver failed to properly check for cyclists before moving forward. Her son was not injured, but the incident reinforced the importance of drivers being aware of their surroundings.

“I’m here to just remind drivers that they need to look for us, look for us, and see where we are before they proceed,” Nair said.

The ride comes as cycling safety remains a concern in London and the surrounding area, following several reported crashes last month involving cyclists who sustained serious, life-threatening injuries.

Organizers say improving safety requires a coordinated effort, with municipal, provincial, and federal governments working together on measures to better protect cyclists.

They hope Saturday’s ride will help build momentum for change and remind drivers that cyclists are among the many people sharing the road.

stories.title: Vancouver progressives take power as Green Pete Fry is elected mayor
stories.summary: Vancouver - Progressives have swept municipal elections in Vancouver, with Pete Fry chosen as the city's first Green mayor after a massive turnout.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - Hedy Fry is no stranger to election nights after more than three decades representing her riding in Vancouver as a Liberal member of Parliament.

But election night Saturday, when she watched her son Pete Fry become the city’s next Vancouver mayor, felt different, she said.

Without her name of the ballot, what she felt was pride.

“He’s paid a lot of attention to city politics ever since he was very young. And so, he knows what he wants and he knows how to build bridges,” she said in an interview Sunday.

“He knows how to work with disparate groups and he knows how to find common ground and that, I think, is going to be his strength. It’s going to a tough job, but he’s a hard-working guy.”

Pete Fry will become the city’s first Green mayor after a massive election turnout on Saturday saw progressives take nearly all the seats on city council, the park board and the school board.

Fry, who was first elected as a councillor in 2018, will be working with Greens and candidates from the Coalition of Progressive Electors, or Cope, each taking four seats out of 10, and OneCity Vancouver claiming a ninth seat for the left-of-centre camp.

The business-friendly ABC Party was decimated, with Ken Sim ousted from the mayor’s office and only one councillor elected.

It was a stark turnaround from 2022, when ABC won seven seats on council.

Hedy Fry said that while she was around to offer her son advice if he asked for it, she never gets involved in provincial or municipal politics, so that she can work with whichever group comes to power.

“I was very proud of my son,” she said.

He did this on his own steam without any help at all from me.”

She said the results from Saturday night make it clear that Vancouver voters wanted change and she told her son that its important he not betray the trust that has been placed in him.

“I think that’s what it’s about, trying to do your best to help and to make things better,” she said.

While no single party will have a majority on the new council, the progressive parties have already demonstrated an ability to work together, with Cope’s Stephanie Allen and OneCity’s William Azaroff ending their mayoral campaigns to give Fry a better chance.

Hedy Fry said her son has been building bridges with the people around him since a young age, after growing up in a household that encouraged forming opinions on issues.

“He’s always been the tallest boy in his class ever since he was in kindergarten, and they always called him the gentle giant because he always kind of tried to make peace and bridge gaps,” she said

“And I think he can do that. I think that it’s going to be a hard job for sure, but I think he can do that.

Preliminary results show Fry won handsomely with more than 98,000 votes, about 31,000 ahead of Sim, while the turnout of 209,000 was up 36 per cent compared with four years ago.

Green and Cope candidates won all seven commissioners’ seats on the Park Board, while Green, Cope, and OneCity candidates won all nine school trustee positions.

Cope’s Sean Orr, a socialist council incumbent who is suing Sim for defamation after the mayor falsely accused him of handing out illegal drugs, was the top vote-getter on council with more than 83,000 votes.

He celebrated by sharing a meme on social media showing him staring down Sim with laser eyes.

Richard Johnston, a professor emeritus in political science at the University of British Columbia, said the municipal elections across the province were largely a “bad year for incumbents” and that those who were re-elected, tended to lean more to the left.

“So, that also suggests that in addition to a kind of general anti-incumbent bias, there actually was an ideological tone to the swing,” he said.

He suggested this group of councillors in Vancouver May be more aligned than some of their predecessors and will be able to work together, calling them a “pretty pragmatic crowd.”

He said voters are focused on wanting results.

“I have to believe that many of these, if not most, but I would hope most, even all, have absorbed the ethos that honestly, we should focus on the urban issues, in particular the issues that we think we can deliver directly,” he said.

“As opposed to being nuclear weapons free or properly aligned on Palestine, or all the sort of things that progressives can easily get diverted to, or have in the past.”

He said the group is likely going to have to “stomach” things like the provincial government’s interest in involuntary care for people with drug addictions and mental health concerns, but could also make progress on issues like housing.

The inauguration for the winners is Nov. 2, more than a week after the upcoming provincial election on Oct. 24.

Johnston said the ability for Vancouver’s new progressive council to get things done could be influenced by who takes office in Victoria, suggesting a Conservative government provincially will not be sympathetic to priorities of a progressive municipal council.

“It would mean that to the extent that any reasonable agenda does require support from senior governments, they’re unlikely to see it from a Conservative government,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 18, 2026.

stories.title: Palestinian activist says election delay is about clinging to power, not Israeli 'obstacles'
stories.summary: Samer Sinijlawi says the Palestinian Authority postponed the elections in a bid to cling to power, not because of Israeli "obstacles."
stories.author: Ellie Hutchings
stories.content:
A Palestinian political activist says the Palestinian Authority postponed next month’s elections in a bid to cling to power, not because of Israeli “obstacles” as the authority’s officials claim.

“The main reason to postpone the election was that the current leadership would like to keep its power,” Samer Sinijlawi told National Post. “I’m confident that Israel did not care about these elections. They were busy in their own elections.”

He believes the postponement was “engineered” by the vice president, Hussein Al-Sheikh, who would inherit the PA presidency should the position become vacant.

“The situation in Gaza might not be perfect, and the situation in the West Bank is not perfect,” Sinijlawi said. “These are conditions that are almost permanent for Palestinians. So, if we keep using them (as a reason to postpone), we will never have elections.”

Sinijlawi is a Palestinian political activist who campaigns for Palestinian-Israeli coexistence. He is the head of the political movement New Path (Masar Jadid), which presents itself as a democratic, moderate alternative to the current Palestinian leadership. Sinijlawi publicly condemned Hamas following the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, which killed 1,200 people.

On Saturday, he wrote a letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney urging him to help preserve Palestinian elections scheduled for Nov. 28, after rumours circulated that they would be postponed. That same day, President Mahmoud Abbas announced the postponement of legislative elections as well as the presidential elections until September 2027, citing “obstacles ⁠posed by Israeli measures” as the reason for the postponement of “free, fair and inclusive elections.”

In a post on X, Israeli ​Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar called Abbas’ decree “yet ​another ridiculous lie designed to evade responsibility and accountability.”

The Nov. 28 elections would have been the first Palestinian elections since Hamas won a majority over Abbas’ party, Fatah, in 2006 across Gaza and the West Bank.

Sinijlawi said 90 per cent of eligible Palestinian voters had registered for the elections, roughly 62 per cent of whom are under the age of 39 and will have never had the opportunity to vote. He points out that a 39-year-old in Canada will have been able to vote in a general election at least six times.

“All the young talents, the smart, the wise young Palestinians, women and men who are not able to participate in the political system, are not able to be part of the decision-making, and are not affecting the leadership that is deciding all the details of their lives. These elections are going to change this,” he said.

“It is very disappointing news for millions of Palestinians who had prepared themselves for that day. We trusted the day, and we started working. We didn’t have elections for 21 years, and then we had a date. So Palestinians started mobilizing.”

Sinijlawi says the Canadian government has “an obligation” to intervene.

Carney announced his government’s commitment to recognize a Palestinian state in July 2025, which was partly based on the PA’s promise to hold general elections in 2026.

“There was a commitment that was given in writing to the international community, including to Canada,” Sinijlawi said. “If somebody does not respect this commitment, I think there should be consequences. And Canada needs to decide how to exert the right pressure in the right direction and get this done.”

After the PA announced the postponement of the elections, Global Affairs Canada released a joint statement with the Foreign Ministers of Australia, Canada, France and the U.K. on Tuesday, saying they “deeply regret” the decision.

“Credible elections are an important element of the commitment that President Abbas and the Palestinian Authority made to reform, including democratic renewal and accountable governance, and are in line with the July 2025 New York Declaration,” it read. “Strengthening Palestinian governance is essential to continue building the institutional foundations of a viable two-state solution, which is the only path to lasting peace and security for both Israel and Palestine.”

It added that the nations will “continue to support efforts to deliver on these elections.”

“The Canadian government offers no indication of what consequences the PA will face, while suggesting that Israel is somehow to blame for a decision made by the PA in cooperation with Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad, both listed by Canada as terrorist entities,” the advocacy group said in a statement on Tuesday.

“All of these challenges, and the current leadership for 21 years has not been able to find answers to them,” he said. “Maybe most of these issues could be related to Israel. stories.title: During waves of separation ideation, national poll probes Canadians' attachment to Canada, their province, and each other
stories.summary: Not surprisingly, Quebecers had the least sentiment of strong attachment to Canada, while respondents in Atlantic Canada were the opposite.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
Facing renewed separatist ideation and agitation in Quebec and Alberta, a new national public opinion poll says Canadians feel a strong attachment to their country — stronger than to their province — and share an abiding affinity for fellow Canadians, no matter where they live.

With Albertans voting Monday in a referendum asking whether the province should begin the process of holding a vote on separating from Canada and a separatist government elected in Quebec earlier this month, Canadian unity is again eating up airtime, timelines and headlines.

A national poll dissecting the feelings Canadians have for Canada, their province and each other casts a light on our national hearts.

“Despite the outcome of the Quebec election and some of the increasingly negative rhetoric about Canada in Alberta, what stands out in our findings is the relative stability and resilience of Canadian identity. Political discourse May suggest a country pulling apart, but Canadians’ attachment to their country and, importantly, to one another remains remarkably strong,” said Jack Jedwab, president of the Montreal-based Association for Canadian Studies (ACS).

The nationwide poll of Canadian adults was conducted last week by Ekos Research for the ACS and provided to Postmedia.

Perhaps not surprisingly, considering decades of separatist ideation, Quebecers expressed the lowest sentiment of strong attachment to Canada, while respondents in Atlantic Canada were on the opposite end of the scale, being the most boisterous in Canadian attachment, by a wide margin.

In Alberta, which is currently probing its own separation sentiment, a strong majority of respondents said they are very attached to Canada — although the percentage of Albertans saying they felt no attachment at all to Canada was higher even than in Quebec.

Nationally, the combined results from all respondents in the 10 provinces polled, found 60 per cent described themselves as very attached to Canada. Another 27 per cent said they were somewhat attached. Eight per cent nationally described feeling not very attached and four per cent said not at all attached.

At 45 per cent, Quebec was the only region that did not have a majority expressing strong attachment to Canada; 33 per cent said they felt somewhat attached, 14 per cent said not very attached and seven per cent said not at all attached.

Alberta had 61 per cent of respondents say they felt very attached to Canada; 23 per cent said somewhat attached, eight per cent not very attached, and another eight per cent say not attached at all, higher than those in Quebec in expressing that level of alienation.

In Atlantic Canada (the pollsters combined New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, and Newfoundland and Labrador) 79 per cent said they were strongly attached to Canada, and another 27 per cent said they felt somewhat attached. Only four per cent said not very attached and none said they felt no attachment at all.

The remaining provinces were roughly in the same territory on their expressions of attachment to Canada.

The proportion of respondents saying they felt very attached in the remaining provinces were: 62 per cent in B.C.; 63 per cent in Manitoba and Saskatchewan pooled together; and 65 per cent in Ontario. Those saying they felt somewhat attached were: 24 per cent in Manitoba and Saskatchewan; 28 per cent in Ontario; and 29 per cent in B.C.

Those expressing some alienation accounted for: 10 per cent in Manitoba and Saskatchewan; six per cent in B.C.; and five per cent in Ontario. Those expressing complete alienation were four per cent in Manitoba and Saskatchewan; three per cent in B.C.; and two per cent in Ontario.

The findings suggest that Quebecers continue to negotiate (provincial and Canadian) identities rather than simply choosing one over the other

Those in the Atlantic provinces not only have the strongest expression of attachment to Canada, but they also had the strongest attachment to their home province — 62 per cent said they felt very attached to their province.

Those who had the lowest proportion expressing strong attachment to their province were in Ontario, where only 27 per cent said they felt very attached, significantly lower than anywhere else.

The next lowest was Alberta, where 38 per cent said they felt very attached to their province, followed by Manitoba and Saskatchewan with 41 per cent, B.C. with 45 per cent, and Quebec with 47 per cent.

The national average was 39 per cent.

Despite disagreements and rivalries, the poll shows that Canadians feel a strong attachment to other Canadians.

Nationally, 63 per cent said they felt very strong attachment towards other Canadians and another 31 per cent said they felt somewhat attached. Only two per cent said they didn’t feel much attachment, and none said they felt no attachment at all.

The weakest in expressing affinity with other Canadians were Albertans.

Only 59 per cent of respondents in Alberta said they felt very much attachment to other Canadians, compared to 73 per cent in Atlantic Canada, 63 in Ontario, 62 in Quebec and B.C., and 60 in Manitoba and Saskatchewan.

Albertans were also most likely to say they felt not very much attachment to other Canadians, but it was still only five per cent, where it was either one or two per cent everywhere else.

“Quebec remains the exception in the extent to which provincial and Canadian identities compete, but that’s hardly new,” Jedwab said. “The findings suggest that Quebecers continue to negotiate these identities rather than simply choosing one over the other. Indeed, while only 45 per cent of Quebecers say they’re very attached to Canada, 62 per cent feel very strongly attached to other Canadians. That’s an important distinction that often gets lost in debates over sovereignty.”

Curiously, in the context of Alberta’s separation referendum, more respondents in Alberta said they felt no attachment at all to their province than said they felt no attachment to their country.

Alberta had the highest proportion of respondents feeling alienated from their province, at 11 per cent, followed by Manitoba and Saskatchewan at 10 per cent, six per cent in both Quebec and Ontario, three per cent in Atlantic provinces, and two per cent in B.C.

“There’s an important distinction between political alienation and national identification,” said Jedwab. “Whatever frustrations some Albertans May have with Ottawa, an important majority remain attached to Canada and to other Canadians. The concerns are more with governance and much less so with identity.”

Poll respondents were also asked which description best fits with how they see themselves: Canadian only, Canadian first but also provincial, equally Canadian and provincial, provincial first but also Canadian, or provincial only.

Nationally, the average of those saying Canadian only was 29 per cent. The regional breakdown showed those in Ontario to be the outliers, at 46 per cent, followed by 29 per cent in Alberta, 24 per cent in Manitoba and Saskatchewan, 22 per cent in B.C., 13 per cent in the Atlantic provinces, and 10 per cent in Quebec.

Those who said Canadian first but also provincial reached a national average of 34 per cent. That sentiment was shared equally strongest in the Atlantic provinces and B.C., with 44 per cent. Next came Manitoba and Saskatchewan at 35, followed by Ontario and Alberta both at 33, and Quebec landing at 28.

A national average of 17 per cent declared equal national and provincial affinity. Atlantic Canada and Manitoba and Saskatchewan were highest in the regional breakdown on that choice at 20 per cent, closely followed by Quebec at 19, B.C. at 17, Ontario at 15, and Alberta at 13.

Next, those choosing province first but also Canadian accounted for 14 per cent of respondents nationally. Quebecers were the big outliers at 31 per cent, followed by those in Atlantic Canada at 22, Albertans at 16, those in B.C. and Manitoba and Saskatchewan all at 11, and Ontarians by far the lowest at just two per cent.

Finally, those declaring only a provincial affiliation were a slim four per cent nationally. In Quebec it was nine per cent, Manitoba and Saskatchewan at eight, Alberta at six, B.C. at two, and Ontario and Atlantic Canada both at zero.

“One of the lessons of the survey is that many Canadians don’t want to be forced into choosing between their regional and Canadian identities. That’s particularly relevant in Quebec, where the relationship is more divided, but it also applies to Alberta, where most identify primarily as Canadian or as Canadian and Albertan.

“Despite the political divisions, the bonds between Canadians appear stronger than some of the rhetoric would have us believe.”

The survey questioned 1,232 Canadian adults from Oct. 9 to 15. Participants were randomly recruited by telephone and confirmed by live interviewers. This sample size has a margin of error plus or minus 2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

stories.title: More than 1,800 arrested in France during violent protests leaving devastation in their wakes
stories.summary: Emmanuel Macron's centrist government and far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen both blamed "ultra-left" groups for the violence.
stories.author: AFP
stories.content:
France was reeling on Sunday from widespread damage caused in violent protests the day before that saw 1,800 people arrested, a historic town hall torched and widespread looting.

The convulsion, which officials described as of extraordinary intensity, raised the stakes for President Emmanuel Macron, who is in his final months in power before elections to replace him in six months’ time. It followed weeks of student protests that had also turned violent at times.

Around “1,800 people have been arrested and now investigations are under way to identify the perpetrators of these acts so they can be brought to justice,” Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on X on Sunday.

In Paris, where police said a “record” 855 people had been arrested, streets were littered with the burnt-out remains of barricades built by protesters using bikes and bins and other materials. Several streets had smashed shop windows and the remains of torched cars.

The capital experienced “a level of violence that we have never, I believe, seen before,” said Paris deputy mayor Lamia El Aaraje.

Paris and many other cities, including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Strasbourg, had scores of shops pillaged by masked youths during the protests, which had been called against high inflation and the cost of living.

The city of Limoges lost its 19th-century town hall to a fire the local prefect, Maurice Barate, told LCI television had been deliberately set by “a wild horde.” The fire was only brought under control early Sunday.

Political recriminations flew over the scenes of destruction.

Macron’s centrist government and far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen both blamed “ultra-left” groups for the violence.

Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who had prominently backed the demonstrations, late Saturday urged demonstrators to stay away from any looting, describing it as “contrary to our methods.”

Paris’s Socialist deputy mayor, Lamia El Aaraje, accused Le Pen’s party of fuelling tensions around the protests to further her ambition of becoming president next year.

The far-right National Rally party was “acting like a pyromaniac firefighter,” El Aaraje said.

U.S. Vice President JD Vance also waded in, implying that the unrest stemmed from immigration.

“Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility,” Vance said on X.

500 arrested in Paris

In Paris, where startled tourists had been seen Saturday running with suitcases along streets filled with tear gas and protesters, the prosecutor’s office said more than 500 people were in custody.

It said arrests had been carried out through the night until early Sunday, with most taken into custody on suspicion of receiving stolen goods, association with intent to commit violence, and vandalism.

Officials in Lyon said 160 people were in custody there.

Around 500 police, firemen and paramedics were hurt in the protests, Interior Minister Nunez said, adding that the figure was provisional.

The violence took place on the sidelines of nationwide cost-of-living protests that the interior ministry said were attended by 550,000 people. The CGT union said 800,000 people participated.

Police used tear gas and water cannon against protesters who threw projectiles and aimed fireworks.

A 17-year-old boy had his right hand blown off by a crowd-control grenade in the southern city of Saint-Étienne.

Analyst Mujtaba Rahman of the Eurasia Group think tank said on X that Saturday’s “terrible scenes” were “not political protest in any true sense. Most of the real demonstrations against high oil prices and failing schools were peaceful”.

He added: “The violence came from a fringe of the ultra-left. The looting by opportunistic gangs from the poor suburbs. All good news for Marine Le Pen.”

During and after those demonstrations, gangs of youths roamed city streets, sporadically confronting police, while setting fires and attacking shuttered stores to break in and empty their shelves.

France’s Yellow Vest movement, which staged street protests eight years ago against Macron’s government over planned fuel-tax hikes, had called Saturday’s “yellow and youth” demonstrations.

The principal grievance was the cost of living, pushed up in part by the war in the Middle East that has helped send inflation soaring in Europe as elsewhere.

The principal grievance was the cost of living, pushed up in part by the war in the Middle East that has helped send inflation soaring in Europe as elsewhere.
