stories.title: 'I did everything for nothing': Pearson Airport gold heist ringleader says fortune lost
stories.summary: Star witness at the trial of a former Air Canada employee takes the stand and says kidnappers took the gold and cash.
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
The mastermind of the spectacular Toronto airport gold heist lost his share of the loot after fleeing to Pakistan, where he said he was kidnapped by police, blindfolded and tortured until he told them where he hid his gold and cash.

” Arsalan Chaudhary, 43, of Mississauga, Ont., testified Tuesday as a reluctant witness in court in Brampton, Ont.

Chaudhary said he was the man behind the gold heist, along with an inside man who worked with Air Canada, but after they split the stolen gold and cash, worth more than $22 million, he left Canada for Pakistan, where he was grabbed by men in police uniforms.

While he was in captivity and suffering torture and threatened with death, he was connected by FaceTime video calls to his kidnappers’ colleagues in Canada; he told them where to go to get his stash of gold hidden in a Toronto-area condo, and then to his family’s home to collect his cash.

“Before they could do anything further, I pretty much told them, ‘I’ll give you everything. You don’t need to do anything. You have me. My life is worth more than any money.’ They had their people go where the gold was, and they got the cash and the gold, everything.”

Once they had his loot, a hood was pulled over his head and driven from the small room where he had been held. When the car stopped, he said he was told to stay down and count to 30 before looking up or they would shoot him.

Chaudhary was asked by Crown prosecutor Jelena Vlacic how he felt at that point.

“I was just thankful to be alive,” he said, “and I wanted to get the F out of Pakistan Asap.

“All of this was not even worth it. I destroyed people’s lives. I did everything for nothing.”

Chaudhary is the star witness at the trial for an alleged co-accused in the gold heist, Parmpal Sidhu, a former Air Canada employee in the cargo warehouse where the crate of gold and cash was stolen in 2023 shortly after arriving on a flight from Zurich, Switzerland.

Although the trial is for Sidhu, who has pleaded not guilty to theft over $5,000 and conspiracy, Chaudhary said the Air Canada employee who was the key inside man at the cargo warehouse who he planned the heist with was Simran Preet Panesar, who is a wanted fugitive in the case, and believed to be living in India.

Chaudhary said that Panesar was in charge of getting the crate of gold and cash out of the cargo warehouse, and Chaudhary was in charge of handling it once it got out.

Chaudhary said he followed the truck that had collected the crate after Air Canada insiders redirected the cargo, as it headed north from the airport.

At a farm, which he said he couldn’t remember where, he, Panesar and the driver divided the loot with Chaudhary taking 30 per cent of the gold.

Chaudhary is in custody, serving his sentence at Maplehurst Correctional Complex, and was escorted into court by a police officer. He walked with casual confidence, almost a swagger.

His testimony was jagged, peppered frequently with him saying he didn’t recall key elements, such as most names and places, times and dates. He said he had post-traumatic stress disorder from his ordeal.

He said he was not testifying willingly, only after being served a subpoena by the Crown.

He pleaded guilty to theft over $5,000 in March and in April was sentenced to four years.

Chaudhary’s testimony continues today, and Sidhu’s trial continues for several days.

stories.title: Ontario father runs nearly 8,000 kilometres across Canada to raise awareness about mental health
stories.summary: By the time Myles Dininio reached the Pacific coast, he had raised more than $50,000 for Camh on his journey.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Silvia Pontecorvi, Omni News

Posted October 13, 2026 1:45 pm.

Last Updated October 13, 2026 1:52 pm.

For 148 days, Myles Dininio ran across Canada, covering nearly 8,000 kilometres from Newfoundland to British Columbia. But for the 40-year-old Ontario father of two, reaching the finish line wasn’t necessarily the accomplishment he had imagined.

“It never felt like a sense of accomplishment or a great achievement,” Dininio said. “I’ve been trying to process the end of it all, and understand what it is I am feeling.”

Dininio, from Zephyr, Ont., set out from Newfoundland on April 1 and reached Vancouver on Aug. 22, completing a cross-country journey aimed at raising awareness about mental health and funds for Toronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (Camh).

The challenge was deeply personal.

“Mental health has affected me my whole life,” he said. “From a very young age, I had little issues that I didn’t realize were known as mental health issues.”

Running thousands of kilometres across the country meant facing physical exhaustion, isolation and a daily mental battle.

“I quit this run probably 50 times in my head, ON the side of the road, but never actually followed it through,” Dininio recalled.

But what began as a test of endurance gradually became something much bigger.

Along the way, strangers joined him for stretches of the journey, offering encouragement and companionship. Others stopped to share their own experiences with mental health, sometimes opening up about deeply personal and painful struggles.

Dininio said listening to those stories was both moving and emotionally overwhelming. At first, he struggled with the weight of what people were sharing with him.

Those encounters eventually changed how he viewed the purpose of his run.

By the time Dininio reached the Pacific coast, his journey had raised more than $50,000 for Camh, one of Canada’s leading mental health research and treatment institutions.

But he says the impact of the conversations he had along the way became more meaningful than the money raised.

“I lost interest in the actual fundraising part, not lost interest, but the fundraising didn’t matter once I realized how many people I was actually reaching,” he said. “And that was worth more than any dollar amount.”

For Dininio, the experience reinforced the importance of talking openly about mental health and creating spaces where people feel comfortable sharing their struggles.

Now back home in Ontario, Dininio is adjusting to everyday life after nearly five months on the road.

While he continues to process the experience, he hopes the message behind his journey will resonate long after the running has stopped.

“One of the primary things when we deal with mental health issues is that we feel so alone,” he said. “And I think we all need to know we are not alone. There is always someone willing to listen.”

For Dininio, the nearly 8,000 kilometres were never just about reaching the other side of Canada. They were about reminding people that, even in their most difficult moments, they don’t have to face their struggles alone.

stories.title: 'Did you do your job?': Poilievre says Liberal government should have protected Stelco workers
stories.summary: N/A
stories.author: Jordan Gowling
stories.content:
Ottawa — Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is calling in to question whether the Liberal government did enough to secure job protections for steel workers at Stelco, after it approved its sale to American-based Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. in 2024.

“It was up to the Liberal government to negotiate job protections when it approved the takeover of Stelco a few years back,” said Poilievre, during a press conference in Windsor, Ont., ON Tuesday.

“So, the question really goes to the Liberals: Did you do your job and protect the steelworkers when the foreign takeover happened?” asked Poilievre.

Poilievre’s comments come after Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and Prime Minister Mark Carney have threatened legal action against Stelco’s Ohio-based parent company Cleveland Cliffs Inc., for laying off 500 workers at its plants in Hamilton and Lake Erie.

Stelco was acquired by Cleveland Cliffs in 2024, with the sale approved by Joly’s predecessor François-Philippe Champagne under the Investment Canada Act (ICA).

The approval was contingent on several binding commitments, including maintaining the same number of unionized employees and most non-unionized employees for a period of five years.

Stelco has cited the ongoing U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel, which remain at 50 per cent, as one of the main reasons for the cutbacks.

Earlier this month, Carney called the layoffs a “betrayal” to workers and said there was still federal money on the table for Stelco to retain its employees.

On Oct. 5, Joly sent a letter to Stelco president Paul Simon, in which she listed the remedies available to the government should the investor fail to comply under the ICA.

Those remedies include “an application to the superior court for orders that May include directing compliance, divestiture, or monetary penalties.”

On Sunday, in an interview with CBC News’ Rosemary Barton Live, Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves disputed the government’s claims.

“There is no provision in the contract that I have to keep employment at a certain level every single day of the five years,” he said. “If that was an imposition of the Canadian government, I would not have accepted.”

Goncalves has called the layoffs “temporary” until Canada and the U.S. have reached a trade agreement. Goncalves is a supporter of U.S. President Donald Trump’s Section 232 tariffs and said he’s prepared to fight the Canadian government in court.

Joly has received a response to her letter from Stelco. On Saturday, she said a legal team is reviewing it and “all options are on the table.”

On Tuesday, NDP Leader Avi Lewis called on the federal government to nationalize Stelco.

“It’s a positive sign that the federal government is preparing to take legal action, but a court process will take years to resolve,” said Lewis, in a statement.

“If we’re serious about saving these jobs and the Canadian steel industry, we need immediate action,” he added. “That action must include nationalizing the plant.”

Poilevre said Conservatives are calling on the federal government to pursue legal action, but more importantly get back to the negotiating table with the U.S., to secure a tariff-free trade deal.

stories.title: Roots shareholders approve deal for retailer to be taken private
stories.summary: New York-based Marquee Brands will acquire the company and pay shareholders $4.10 a share
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
Roots Corp. Root-T shareholders have voted in favour of the retailer going private through a transaction led by a New York brand management firm.

The apparel company says the shareholder vote passed but did not immediately disclose how much support the deal garnered.

The transaction is subject to other court and regulatory approvals but is expected to close in the fourth quarter of the year.

Under the deal with Marquee Brands announced in August, Roots shareholders will receive $4.10 per share.

Marquee will then use Club Monaco founder Joe Mimran’s company JM&A Design and Development Inc. to develop, manufacture and distribute Roots clothing for Canadian and U.S. stores.

Marquee Brands also manages the Martha Stewart, Laura Ashley and Roberto Cavalli labels and intends to expand Roots to other markets like Korea, India and Mexico.

stories.title: Canada's Wonderland closes Leviathan and Behemoth after roller coaster death in Georgia
stories.summary: One man was killed and four others injured on a ride at Six Flags Over Georgia, a theme park outside Atlanta run by the same company.
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Canada’s Wonderland has closed two of its roller coasters after one man was killed and four others injured on a similar ride at Six Flags Over Georgia, a theme park outside Atlanta.

Both parks are owned and operated by U.S.-based Six Flags, which has 34 properties in North America and two in Saudi Arabia. Canada’s Wonderland is its only Canadian location, after Montreal’s La Ronde was sold to EPR Properties of Missouri in May.

“I can confirm our coasters Leviathan and Behemoth were closed yesterday,” a Canada’s Wonderland spokesperson told National Post. “We do not have a timeline for reopening.”

The spokesperson added: “Out of an abundance of caution, we have temporarily closed similar attractions across our parks. The safety of our guests and team members is our highest priority.”

The park remains open Thursdays through Sundays (its regular fall hours) this month.

The death at Six Flags Over Georgia happened on Monday, according to local news reports. A man reportedly fell from Goliath , which the park refers to as a “hypercoaster,” meaning it has a height of least 61 metres. The ride, introduced in 2006, reaches speeds of 112 km/h.

The man, who has been identified by police as 42-year-old Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem of Atlanta, was reportedly thrown from his seat, fell and hit the ride multiple times. The park was evacuated after the incident.

CNN reported that what caused Kariem to fall off the roller coaster remains unclear, and that the cause of death has not been disclosed, nor have details of other injuries in the incident.

The accident left a number of riders in the next train of cars stuck on a steep incline when the ride was halted. News footage showed park workers rescuing those riders and leading them down the steep, open-air stairwell to the ground.

Six Flags temporarily closed nine roller coasters across six amusement parks on Monday, including the two at Canada’s Wonderland. Behemoth and Leviathan were both manufactured by Bolliger and Mabillard, the same company that made Goliath.

Canada’s Wonderland opened in 1981 in Vaughan, Ont., just north of Toronto. It was acquired by Paramount and became Paramount Canada’s Wonderland in 1993, but reverted to its original name after it was purchased by U.S.-based Cedar Fair Entertainment Co. in 2006. Cedar Fair and Six Flags merged in 2024.

The park boasts 18 roller coasters. The Behemoth opened in 2008 and features a climb to a height of 70 metres, followed by a 75-degree drop with speeds reaching 125 km/h, and a track length of over 1.6 km. The Leviathan , which opened four years later, has a climb 97.7 metres and an 80-degree drop, reaching speeds of 148 km/h.

stories.title: Canadians with children more likely to rely on charities, non-profits: survey
stories.summary: Two out of five Canadians said they relied on the service of a charity or a non-profit in the last 12 months, an Ipsos survey conducted for the RBC found on Tuesday.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Two out of five Canadians said they relied on the service of a charity or a non-profit in the last 12 months, an Ipsos survey conducted for the Royal Bank of Canada found on Tuesday.

However, the proportion of Canadians needing support is much higher among those who have children.

Canadians with children were far more likely (49 per cent) to seek support compared to those without kids (36 per cent), the RBC survey said.

Charities and non-profits working in the healthcare space found their services were most utilized (68 per cent) followed by food charities in second place (26 per cent) and education services (15 per cent) in third place.

Canadians also sought help from charities and non-profits working in sectors such as housing (12 per cent), social programming (12 per cent), employment (nine per cent), professional/skill development (six per cent) and cultural or recreational programming (six per cent).

Among those who used these services in the last 12 months, nearly four in five (79 per cent) said their use is “occasional” while more than one in five (21 per cent) said they “regularly” use help from charities or non-profit organizations.

The kind of service Canadians use depends on their age, with younger Canadians relying more on education and employment services while older Canadians rely mor heavily on healthcare supports.

Gen Z had the highest use of charities among all generations, with nearly half (44 per cent) having used these services in the last 12 months.

stories.title: Canadian ransomware negotiator arrested amid FBI hacker crackdown
stories.summary: A Canadian ransomware negotiator was arrested Thursday and faces unspecified extortion charges, according to court documents, prison records and a person familiar with the matter, as the FBI cracks down on a hacking group that stole information about its employees.
stories.author: Reuters Staff
stories.content:
Washington - A Canadian ransomware negotiator was arrested Thursday and faces unspecified extortion charges, according to court documents, prison records and a person familiar with the matter, as the FBI cracks down on a hacking group that stole information about its employees.

Edward Dubrovsky faces charges of conspiracy to “threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with intent to extort money” and “interference with commerce,” according to court documents filed with the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, which covers Philadelphia.

The records, which are partially sealed, provide conflicting spellings of his last name — “Dobrovsky” or “Dobrosky” — and do not identify his age, profession, or employer. A person briefed on the matter said the person was Canadian cybersecurity executive Edward Dubrovsky.

Federal prosecutors in Philadelphia did not return repeated messages seeking comment about the discrepancies. Attempts to reach Dubrovsky and his attorneys were unsuccessful. Repeated attempts to reach the company displayed on Dubrovsky’s LinkedIn profile, CyberSteward, were similarly unsuccessful.

CyberSteward advertises itself online as specializing in “threat actor engagement, cyber-extortions, complex negotiations, and settlement facilitation.” On LinkedIn, Dubrovsky presents himself as a specialist in the process of negotiating with cybercriminals over ransom payments.

Electronic wallet records leaked in 2010 and preserved by dark-web intelligence firm District 4 Labs identify Dubrovsky as a resident of Richmond Hill, north of Toronto, and put his current age at 54. Federal prison records show that a 54-year-old named Edward Dubrovsky is currently being detained at a federal detention centre in Philadelphia.

News of Dubrovsky’s arrest was earlier reported by Politico and independent journalist Brian Krebs .

The arrest comes as the Federal Bureau of Investigation is leading a global crackdown on the hacking group ShinyHunters, which rattled the bureau last month by stealing information on what it said was nearly every FBI employee.

When Reuters asked the FBI about Dubrovsky’s arrest, it referred the news agency to FBI Director Kash Patel’s statement on Friday revealing that the bureau had arrested a “suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group” and declined further comment.

🚨 Our agents in the field have arrested another suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group – the group believed to be responsible for the recent https://t.co/RG0D4I5KFS incident, which occurred on a platform managed by a third-party vendor. This is the latest arrest… — FBI Director Kash Patel (@FBIDirectorKash) October 9, 2026

Raphael Satter and AJ Vicens, Editing by Jamie Freed, Reuters

stories.title: Czech defence company CSG buys 9.5 per cent stake in MDA Space
stories.summary: has bought a 9.5 per cent stake in MDA Space Ltd., making it the Canadian company’s largest shareholder.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal — Czech defence company CSG has bought a 9.5 per cent stake in MDA Space Ltd ., making it the Canadian company’s largest shareholder.

CSG says it views MDA Space as a strategic investment and sees opportunities to explore potential co-operation between the two companies over time.

Latest updates on company news here

CSG chair Michal Strnad says MDA Space is a highly respected, well led, profitable and growing space company with exceptional technological capabilities.

He pointed to the possibility of co-investing with MDA in manufacturing or assembly facilities in Europe and partnering on strategic acquisitions.

MDA Space CEO Mike Greenley welcomed the investment and said CSG is a leading European industrial group with a proven track record in building high-quality defence businesses.

MDA Space shares were down 23 cents at $39.95 in early-afternoon trading on the Toronto Stock Exchange.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 13, 2026.

stories.title: A look at past referendums in Canada as Albertans reject future separation vote
stories.summary: Famously, a razor-thin majority rejected the idea of Quebec leaving Confederation and becoming its own country in 1995.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Albertans voted in a referendum Monday against separation. In early results, about 76 per cent of said they wanted the province to stay in Canada, while 24 per cent said they wanted the province to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

Here’s a look at some of the other referendums held across Canada:

The province asked residents whether it should adopt year-round daylight time — the time often used across Canada in the summer — to put an end to twice-yearly clock changes.

Out of more than 1 million votes, 50.2 per cent were against the idea, while 48.8 per cent were in favour of ditching clock changes.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Inside Canada's high-stakes pigeon racing world, a sport on life support

Premier Danielle Smith announced this year that starting Nov. 1, the province is adopting year-round daylight time.

She said it’s to gauge opinion and that most people will agree. She said if she’s wrong, the government could put the matter to a vote in 2027.

Voters weighed in on electoral reform alongside the provincial election.

It followed similar votes in 2016 and 2005, which both failed to eliminate the voting practice known as “first past the post.”

The referendum asked: “Should Prince Edward Island change its voting system to a mixed member proportional voting system?”

The threshold for a win in either direction would have been 17, but neither side was able to secure that number — 13 districts voted against, while 14 voted in favour.

After failed votes in 2009 and 2005, the province held a third referendum on electoral reform.

Out of all ballots received, 61.3 per cent voted to keep first past the post, while proportional representation got 38.7 per cent.

The referendum asked voters to chose between the existing first-past-the-post or the mixed-member proportional systems.

Voters overwhelmingly rejected mixed-member proportional representation, with Elections Ontario figures showing roughly 1.5 million people voted for change, while nearly 2.7 million voted against it.

Voters were asked whether the province should ban VLTs, following a 1999 campaign promise by former premier Bernard Lord.

“Should the province of New Brunswick continue to permit the legal and regulated operation of video gaming devices, commonly known as video lottery terminals?”

About 53 per cent were in favour of keeping VLTs, while 47 per cent were opposed.

New Brunswick was the first to allow VLTs after Ottawa, in 1985, allowed provinces and territories to operate the machines.

Newfoundlanders voted in on the churches’ role in the province’s education system.

The referendum asked: “Do you support a single school system where all children, regardless of their religious affiliation, attend the same schools where opportunities for religious education and observances are provided?”

More than 70 per cent of voters wanted to create a non-denominational public education system still allowing religious instruction and observance, ending the church-run school system.

In a similar vote two years earlier, voters narrowly approved the government’s plan to reform the church-run education system.

A razor-thin majority rejected the idea of the province leaving Confederation and becoming its own country.

In a dramatic campaign, the sovereigntist side came from behind to take a lead in the polls in the final weeks before the vote. In the end, 50.58 per cent voted no.

Another vote was held in 1980, and 60 per cent also said no to sovereignty.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 20, 2026.

stories.title: News publishers launch copyright suit against AI company Anthropic in Ontario
stories.summary: A coalition of news publishers that includes Canada’s largest newspapers is suing the artificial intelligence company Anthropic in an Ontario court.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija
stories.content:
A coalition of news publishers that includes Canada’s largest newspapers is suing the AI company Anthropic in an Ontario court.

Postmedia, Torstar, The Globe and Mail and The Canadian Press say Anthropic infringed on their copyright by using their content to develop its large language AI model Claude.

“Anthropic has capitalized on the commercial success of its AI models, building an expansive suite of services, and raised significant capital — all without obtaining a valid licence from any of the News Media Companies,” says the statement of claim.

“In doing so, Anthropic has been substantially and unjustly enriched to the detriment of the News Media Companies.”

The lawsuit, filed on Oct. 6, was first reported by the news site Cartt.CA. Anthropic has not responded to a request for comment. The allegations have not been proven in court.

The statement of claim says Anthropic breached the news media websites’ terms of service and circumvented technological protection measures they put in place to restrict copying of their content.

The claim says the news outlets “are responsible for generating a significant portion of Canada’s journalistic content — from daily print broadsheets to round-the-clock digital news coverage,” and collectively have millions of readers.

“To obtain content for ingestion into its models and services, Anthropic deliberately ‘scrapes’ (i.e. accesses and copies) enormous amounts of text data from the internet and from the Plaintiffs’ Websites,” the claim says.

The news outlets say Anthropic then uses that content, without authorization or consent, to develop its AI models. It says Anthropic also scrapes content on an ongoing basis in response to user prompts.

“Notwithstanding concerns raised by several content creators across various industries, including through numerous other lawsuits and public criticism, Anthropic has done nothing to curtail its unlawful behaviour,” the statement of claim says.

The same companies also launched, alongside CBC/Radio-Canada, a lawsuit against OpenAI in 2024. That case has yet to be settled.

paragraphs: A coalition of news publishers that includes Canada’s largest newspapers is suing the AI company Anthropic in an Ontario court.
Postmedia, Torstar, The Globe and Mail and The Canadian Press say Anthropic infringed on their copyright by using their content to develop its large language AI model Claude.

“Anthropic has capitalized on the commercial success of its AI models, building an expansive suite of services, and raised significant capital — all without obtaining a valid licence from any of the News Media Companies,” says the statement of claim.
“In doing so, Anthropic has been substantially and unjustly enriched to the detriment of the News Media Companies.”
The lawsuit, filed on Oct. 6, was first reported by the news site Cartt.CA. Anthropic has not responded to a request for comment. The allegations have not been proven in court.

“Notwithstanding concerns raised by several content creators across various industries, including through numerous other lawsuits and public criticism, Anthropic has done nothing to curtail its unlawful behaviour,” the statement of claim says.
The same companies also launched, alongside CBC/Radio-Canada, a lawsuit against OpenAI in 2024. That case has yet to be settled.

stories.title: Trial for man accused in Pearson gold heist hears more from key figure in case
stories.summary: A man who received a prison sentence for his role in the Toronto Pearson airport gold heist says on the day of the theft, he communicated with the man currently on trial.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
A man who received a prison sentence for his role in the Toronto Pearson airport gold heist has told a Brampton, Ont., court that on the day of the theft, he communicated with the man currently on trial in the case.

Arsalan Chaudhary returned to the witness stand today in the trial of Parmpal Sidhu, who has pleaded not guilty to charges of theft over $5,000 and conspiracy to commit an indictable offence in the 2023 heist.

Chaudhary was sentenced this spring to four years in prison after pleading guilty to theft over $5,000, and he was given 40 years to pay back $22 million in restitution.

His testimony in Sidhu’s trial was paused last week after he said that recalling his alleged abduction in Pakistan had left him traumatized.

Chaudhary testified today that he told Sidhu the truck and driver were ready on the day of the gold heist and that Sidhu replied, “OK.”

Chaudhary told court last week that he planned the heist with another man who is still wanted by authorities, and he ended up taking 30 per cent of boxes full of one-ounce gold bars.

He said he melted some of the gold before travelling to Pakistan, where he was kidnapped and abused until he gave up the loot.

Prosecutors allege that Sidhu, an Air Canada employee at the time, provided a doctored waybill that allowed another man to pick up more than $22 million in gold and currency from a Pearson airport cargo bay.

Peel regional police have said 6,600 gold bars weighing more than 400 kilograms were stolen from the airport on April 17, 2023, after the shipment arrived from Switzerland.

stories.title: U.S. won’t drop digital issues in trade talks: former negotiator
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canada’s former chief trade negotiator says that while digital issues will continue to be a source of trade tensions with the U.S., Canada can gain strength if it teams up with other allies that have similar interests.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - While digital issues will continue to be a source of trade tensions with the United States, Canada can gain strength if it teams up with other allies that have similar interests, Canada’s former chief trade negotiator said Monday.

Steve Verheul said the United States won’t simply drop issues like the Online News Act and digital sovereignty that it has identified as trade irritants.

“They’ve listed them as fairly fundamental concerns that they have and tend to pursue,” he said at the Canadian Chapter of the International Institute of Communications conference in Ottawa.

“The Online Streaming Act, the Online News Act, the sovereign cloud issue, control over data in Canada more broadly, that’s where the real battleground going forward with the U.S. is going to be on these kinds of issues.”

Verheul said the United States views policies targeting big tech companies as discriminatory. He said it’s difficult to design non-discriminatory policies because of how many of the largest digital companies are American.

Canada needs to work more closely with allies like the European Union to develop a more unified position on digital issues, he said.

Verheul said while Canada “needs to to maintain some level of independence on these issues,” it also must work with other countries that have similar interests.

“And we need to find some ways to move forward,” he added.

Eric Miller, president of the consulting group Rideau Potomac Strategy Group, spoke on a separate panel at the conference and gave the example of Netflix, which gets more than half of its revenue outside the U.S.

“If you begin to have policies which are unfavourable to large U.S. tech companies, it doesn’t take too many markets like Canada and the European Union co-ordinating to see how this would have very detrimental effects to them,” he said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has been working on establishing closer links with Europe, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed Canada could become the first associate member of the European Union.

Canada will host an Canada-EU Summit in Montreal at the end of October, where the two sides are expected to announce the next steps in the deepening partnership.

Canada cut off the latest round of trade negotiations with the United States in August citing several reasons, including American demands related to rules about Canadian content on streaming platforms, also known as discoverability. The CRTC is in the process of implementing those rules under the Online Streaming Act.

It’s not clear exactly which element of the Online Streaming Act is the source of the conflict. Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said in late August the United States had withdrawn its position on discoverability.

But U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has said the issue for the United States is streaming companies having to make financial contributions toward Canadian content — a proposal the Liberal government has backed away from.

Meredith Lilly, a professor at Carleton University’s Norman Paterson School of International Affairs, took part in the panel with Miller. She said Canada and the United States are likely to come to an agreement.

“I think that there is a landing zone that both sides will be able to agree on, and I anticipate that that will be keeping mandatory payments off … and Canada is going to be able to keep the discoverability piece of that,” she said.

The conference also heard that the cultural exemption Canada has under the current trade agreement allows the Americans to automatically retaliate if it is used.

Lilly said that means the United States could retaliate on things like cars or canola. “And so there is some potential that is going to pit parts of Canada against the cultural sector,” she said.

She said while the United States might have tolerated the cultural exemption when Canada was using it to subsidize arts and culture, that might not be the case if it extends to demanding financial contributions from American companies for Canadian content.

“If we start trying to use it to extract capital from large American firms to subsidize the creation of Canadian content and they can’t even use those subsidized funds, they are going to play hardball with us and it could be the end of the cultural exemption,” Lilly said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

stories.title: Swph is Offering Vaccination Clinics
stories.summary: Respiratory illnesses are starting to pop up, and Southwestern Public Health is reminding residents to get vaccinated.
stories.author: Kyle Freel
stories.content:
News Home

Monday, 19 October 2026 16:39

By Kyle Freel X @KFreelHeartFM

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

Respiratory illnesses are starting to pop up, and Southwestern Public Health is reminding residents to get vaccinated.

OXFORD COUNTY - Flu season is here, and Southwestern Public Health is encouraging people to get vaccinated.

SWPH will offer influenza and COVID-19 vaccination clinics this fall at its St. Thomas and Woodstock offices, as well as select community locations throughout the region. Starting today, adults 65 years and older, pregnant individuals, residents and staff of congregate living settings, health-care workers, along with other high-risk and priority populations can begin booking appointments. The general public will be able to book appointments on October 26th.

Flu vaccines are also available through participating pharmacies and health-care providers, while COVID-19 vaccines are available through pharmacies. Residents can book an appointment online by clicking here or by calling 1-800-922-0096.

The Health Unit also has these tips to help prevent the spread of respiratory illness: getting vaccinated against influenza, COVID-19 and RSV, staying home when sick, washing hands regularly, covering coughs and sneezes, and considering wearing a mask in healthcare settings or if at higher risk of severe illness.

Southwestern Public Health has also relaunched its respiratory virus dashboard, which provides up-to-date information in the coverage areas. You can find the dashboard by visiting the Southwestern Public Health website .

OPP Investigating Collision Involving Tillsonburg Resident A two-vehicle collision is under investigation and involves a person from Tillsonburg.

A Fallen Firefighter Honoured in Woodstock A memorial service was held in Woodstock to honour a fallen firefighter who served with the Woodstock Fire Department.

PJHL Recap - Oct 16th to Oct 18th The Braves and the Trojans celebrated to victories, while the Merchants celebrated a win and suffered a loss.

Navy Vets Recap - Oct 16th Woodstock beat London 3-1 on Friday.

Input Needed for RRHS Strategic Plan Rural Roads Health Services includes the hospitals in Tillsonburg and Ingersoll.

Sanitary Sewer Work Begins in Tillsonburg Old Vienna Road between Van Street and Vienna Road will be closed until mid-December.

Two Charged with Drug Trafficking in Woodstock Two people were arrested in the James Street area on October 14th.

Local MP and Guests Visit Oxford Schools Bullying and safe communities were the topics of discussion as Oxford's MP and special guests toured schools in Oxford County.

Oxford OPP Investigating Serious Collision Early this morning, the Oxford OPP and other first responders were called to a serious collision on the 401.

PJHL Preview - Oct 16th to Oct 18th Tavistock, Norwich and Thamesford all have home games in Junior C hockey action tonight.

Navy Vets Preview - Oct 16th The Woodstock Navy Vets will host the London Nationals at Southwood Arena tonight.

Norwich Curling Club Celebrates 70 Years with New Ice The club will be hosting an open house from 2:00 p.m. to 6:00 p.m. this Saturday.

Oxford Tourism Looking for Input Oxford Tourism has launched an online survey for residents, visitors, and tourism business operators.

Pedestrian Struck East of Shakespeare Police say the driver drove through a road closure barricade Thursday afternoon.

Unifor Local 636 Hosts Candidates Debate Residents in Woodstock had the opportunity to hear candidates answer questions as the municipal election draws closer.

Woodstock Police Briefs - Oct. 15th, 2026 A pair of theft investigations in the Friendly City results in charges.

Interview with the Warden - October 15th, 2026 He talked about snow removal, development charges, the Homelessness Support Centre, and more.

Student Stair Climb Back for Another Year The local high schools will go head to head to see who can raise the most money for United Way Oxford.

The Food Project Oxford Holds Open House It was a chance to learn and tour the facility that stores food items for many charities that serve the hungry in Oxford County.

stories.title: Stellantis workers vote overwhelmingly in favour of strike mandate
stories.summary: Unifor said Monday that 97.3 per cent of members who participated in a vote over the weekend are in favour of authorizing a strike if needed.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
Stellantis workers across Canada have delivered their union a strong strike mandate as talks have stalled between its bargaining committee and the company.

Unifor said Monday that 97.3 per cent of members who participated in a vote over the weekend are in favour of authorizing a strike if needed.

“Unifor members at Stellantis understand how difficult negotiations with the company have been and gave an overwhelming mandate to support their bargaining committee,” said Lana Payne, president of Unifor National, in a statement.

“Our members are united in their determination to reach a fair agreement with Stellantis that protects jobs for Canadian autoworkers,” she said.

Unifor, which represents more than 9,000 Stellantis workers, said over the weekend that a potential strike action remains a last resort and it hopes to still reach a deal.

But bargaining is at an impasse with the automaker after the company announced it planned to sell its Brampton assembly plan to Roshel, a defence contractor.

More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the plant when it stopped operations in 2023. Stellantis has argued that keeping the plant no longer made sense for its business, but that selling could support future workers.

While striking is a last resort, Unifor said “we will not back down and accept a deal that weakens Stellantis’ footprint within Canada’s auto industry due to broken commitments.”

Gas prices drove inflation up to 3.1% in September, says StatCan

stories.title: Beluga rescued from closed Ontario park dies in California
stories.summary: A California aquarium says a beluga rescued from Marineland in Ontario has died, adding to the number of deaths of animals relocated over the summer from the now-closed facility.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A California aquarium says a beluga rescued from Marineland in Ontario has died, adding to the number of deaths of animals relocated over the summer from the now-closed Canadian facility.

SeaWorld San Diego says in a Facebook post that Cyprus, a nine-year-old male beluga that arrived at the park on Aug. 22 stopped eating on Friday, and an ultrasound later determined the animal’s intestinal tract did not appear to be functioning normally.

It says Cyprus had been doing well since his arrival, eating consistently and interacting with his trainers and animal care team, along with two other rescued belugas.

But it notes belugas can mask discomfort or underlying concerns that are not immediately visible, and it says a full necropsy will be conducted.

Marineland in Niagara Falls, Ont., had said it was running out of money and could no longer care for the last captive whales and dolphins in Canada, and 30 of its belugas and four dolphins were transferred to other facilities in a mass relocation effort.

SeaWorld San Diego says the other rescued belugas in its care are in stable health and remain under close monitoring as they continue to adjust to their surroundings.

“As we have indicated, this process will take a considerable amount of time. Our commitment to the health, well-being and care of these belugas, like every animal we rescue, continues,” the facility said in its social media post on Sunday.

It said that after the necropsy is completed, the cause of Cyprus’s death will be shared with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

Less than two weeks ago, Shedd Aquarium in Chicago said Caspian, a 27-year-old female beluga that was relocated from Marineland, died despite efforts to save her.

Caspian had not been eating properly and blood samples showed abnormalities in her electrolyte levels, Shedd said.

Shedd said it performed necropsies on Peekachu and Rain, two other Marineland whales that died there, and concluded that they had chronic, pre-existing diseases.

A beluga named Jelly Bean and a dolphin named Echo also died at Oceanografic Valencia in Spain after the move.

stories.title: Canadians step up to give blood after fire at Alberta military base kills four
stories.summary: Some Canadians are rolling up their sleeves to give blood as the military town of Wainwright, Alta., mourns the four soldiers killed in a weekend training exercise gone fatally wrong.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
WAINWRIGHT - Residents of the town of Wainwright, Alta., are grieving after a deadly fire swept up by fierce winds overtook soldiers during a training exercise at the local military base Saturday, killing four and wounding dozens.

Sharon Pashko, 79, was among those who came out to the cenotaph on Monday to share her sorrow and offer words of support.

“It’s heartbreaking. My heart goes out to the families. There’s no words,” she said.

Pashko said she grew up in the military town and her uncle served at its commanding officer.

“The base has always been part of my home life and we always felt protected,” she said.

Pashko said she can see the local hospital from her home and it was “heartbreaking to see the ambulances going in.”

“Our community will go above and beyond,” she said. “I know we’ll do all that we can do to stand behind.”

A growing pile of brightly coloured flowers covers the base of the local cenotaph.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre laid a wreath there Monday. He said he has met with local groups “providing help to the wounded, families and everyone else out there that’s affected.”

Poilievre, whose federal riding of Battle River—Crowfoot includes the military base, said he was shocked by what happened.

“Fire is probably the most horrific way to die and when I learned that fire had struck one of our bases and potentially taken human life, I thought, ‘My God, it’s terrible.’ I said a prayer for them. I thought of their parents,” he said.

Defence Minister David McGuinty was also in town Monday to visit injured soldiers at the Wainwright hospital.

The minister’s office declined an interview request, saying it wanted to keep the focus on the injured military members and families who have lost loved ones.

McGuinty’s office issued a short statement on his behalf late Monday saying he visited leadership and Armed Forces members at CFB Wainwright on Monday. He was joined by Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski.

“In the face of profound loss, they have shown extraordinary strength, compassion and care for one another,” McGuinty said in his statement. “We will continue to stand with them and their families, and ensure they have the support they need.”

In Ottawa, the House of Commons held a moment of silence to honour the victims on Monday.

Poilievre told the House of Commons by video link that he personally met one of the deceased — Pte. Aidan Goulding, who was 23. The Conservative leader described him as “strong, handsome, polite” and a “real gentleman.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney told the House all MPs stand “united in grief” over a tragedy that touches every corner of the country.

Carney also told the House that 50 investigators are on the ground at the Wainwright base trying to determine what caused the deadly fire.

The prime minister said the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service is leading a full investigation into the tragedy, with support from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. He also told reporters he has absolute confidence in the military’s investigators.

“We will give them all the resources that they need,” Carney said. “There’s a few processes that we’ll go through here and we will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy as expeditiously and transparently as necessary.”

Defence officials said 84 members of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were in a training area at Wainwright, 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, when the disaster struck on Saturday.

Strong winds sent flames from a nearby grass fire racing across the Prairie landscape, stopping soldiers in their tracks and sending 39 of them to hospital — 19 in critical condition.

National Defence identified the deceased as Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Goulding of North Vancouver and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C.

Their deaths left a trail of grief across the country.

In Langley, B.C., Trevor Plater, Lykkemark’s former rugby coach in his senior year at Langley Secondary School, said the whole team and his schoolmates thought of Lykkemark as their best friend.

“He’s always looking out for everybody. He wasn’t necessarily somebody who talked a lot but he had a big impact when he did and he was always listening and paying attention,” Plater said.

Lykkemark, who was 19 when he died, was “a wonderful kid” who led by example and made everybody feel connected to the team, Plater added.

He was particularly close to former teammate Kane Lewis, who set up an online fundraiser for his friend’s family. Lewis said in a statement on the donation page — which has raised more than $20,000 — that he and Lykkemark joined the army at the same time and were in the same platoon for basic training.

“That’s where he became more than just a friend; he became a brother. He was always looking out for everyone and always kept himself in check,” Lewis said.

In Farrell’s hometown of Prince Albert, Sask., the city government lowered its flags to half-mast and set out a book of condolences at city hall.

“Our community is grieving alongside those who knew and loved Shaun,” the City of Prince Albert posted on social media.

“We recognize the profound sorrow this tragedy has brought to his family, friends and all those affected.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

— With files from Jack Farrell, Fakiha Baig and Aaron Sousa in Edmonton, from Nono Shen in Vancouver and Kyle Duggan in Ottawa

The prime minister said the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service is leading a full investigation into the tragedy, with support from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. He also told reporters he has absolute confidence in the military’s investigators.

“We will give them all the resources that they need,” Carney said. “There’s a few processes that we’ll go through here and we will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy as expeditiously and transparently as necessary.”
Defence officials said 84 members of the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were in a training area at Wainwright, 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, when the disaster struck on Saturday.
Strong winds sent flames from a nearby grass fire racing across the Prairie landscape, stopping soldiers in their tracks and sending 39 of them to hospital — 19 in critical condition.
National Defence identified the deceased as Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Goulding of North Vancouver and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C.
Their deaths left a trail of grief across the country.
In Langley, B.C., Trevor Plater, Lykkemark’s former rugby coach in his senior year at Langley Secondary School, said the whole team and his schoolmates thought of Lykkemark as their best friend.
“He’s always looking out for everybody. He wasn’t necessarily somebody who talked a lot but he had a big impact when he did and he was always listening and paying attention,” Plater said.
Lykkemark, who was 19 when he died, was “a wonderful kid” who led by example and made everybody feel connected to the team, Plater added.

He was particularly close to former teammate Kane Lewis, who set up an online fundraiser for his friend’s family. Lewis said in a statement on the donation page — which has raised more than $20,000 — that he and Lykkemark joined the army at the same time and were in the same platoon for basic training.
“That’s where he became more than just a friend; he became a brother. He was always looking out for everyone and always kept himself in check,” Lewis said.
In Farrell’s hometown of Prince Albert, Sask., the city government lowered its flags to half-mast and set out a book of condolences at city hall.
“Our community is grieving alongside those who knew and loved Shaun,” the City of Prince Albert posted on social media.
“We recognize the profound sorrow this tragedy has brought to his family, friends and all those affected.”

stories.title: Inquest into death of Regis Korchinski-Paquet hears from police
stories.summary: Toronto - A coroner's inquest into the death of a Toronto woman who fell from a 24th-floor balcony while police were in her home is hearing from one of the officers called to the incident.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - There was no reason to fear for Regis Korchinski-Paquet’s safety until she suddenly walked out onto her 24th-floor apartment’s balcony, a Toronto police officer told an inquest into the 29-year-old woman’s death Monday.

Const. Shane Beaudoin said he had allowed Korchinski-Paquet to go into her home because she needed to use the bathroom, and asked her to talk to a paramedic when she emerged because he thought it could help de-escalate what remained a heated family dispute.

Instead, he said, Korchinski-Paquet went out onto the balcony, knocking down the air conditioning unit on the way, then used her bodyweight to block the door.

“At this point, it’s the first time to me that the balcony has come into play. She’s made no references to it. She’s not made any sort of remarks that she’s suicidal or that she wants to hurt herself,” Beaudoin testified.

“There’s been no reason to fear for her physical safety because at this point there’s officers on scene, everybody’s separated ... So anyway, now she’s on the balcony and now I am very concerned.”

Moments later, Korchinski-Paquet let go of the door and headed to the balcony rail, swinging her left leg toward the neighbouring balcony, he said.

As she disappeared from view, the officer said he believed she had crossed over to the other balcony, so he requested that the emergency task force be called in.

“At that moment, I didn’t know that she had fallen. I thought she had gone over to the neighbour’s unit and was maybe hunkered down on that balcony.”

It was only after he’d left the apartment to go knock on the neighbour’s door that Beaudoin heard from another officer that Korchinski-Paquet had fallen, he said, at 5:43 p.m.

“That information came to basically everybody in the hallway at the same time,” including Korchinski-Paquet’s mother and brother, he said.

Five calls were made to 911 the afternoon of May 27, 2020, three of them by Korchinski-Paquet, the inquest heard last week.

Jurors have previously watched a compilation video combining the recordings of the calls and two police microphones with CCTV footage from the hallway outside her home and video from a police cruiser.

In her calls, Korchinski-Paquet expressed difficulty breathing and said she had thrown two bottles at her family in the hallway because she lost control after being attacked by her mother and brother. When asked if anyone had mental health issues, Korchinski-Paquet said she had epilepsy.

Her mother and brother also mentioned Korchinski-Paquet’s epilepsy on their calls, noting that she was often agitated after her seizures. Her brother, Reece Korchinski, said she assaulted him with knives after a dispute over the TV volume.

Six police officers and two paramedics responded to the calls, the inquest heard.

Then-Const. Adam Vandenbrink testified Monday that he was the first officer to arrive at the scene and was told to wait for backup. He didn’t know Beaudoin, who arrived shortly afterward, because the officer worked in another division, he said.

They went up together and could hear an argument as the elevator approached the 24th floor, he said. Neither he nor Beaudoin could recall discussing a strategy to deal with the situation, but Vandenbrink said all officers had received the same training on de-escalation.

Vandenbrink said he ended up talking to Korchinski-Paquet while Beaudoin went down the hall to speak to her mother and brother. He could smell wine and saw smashed glass in the hallway, he said.

“She wasn’t listening to my questions, she was yelling over top of me,” said Vandenbrink, who left the force roughly three years ago. He described Korchinski-Paquet as “agitated” and “aggressive.”

When another officer arrived, Vandenbrink said he asked his colleague to speak to her while he went to debrief with Beaudoin. It was during that conversation that he heard about Korchinski-Paquet’s seizures that day, as well as a general idea of what prompted the 911 calls, he said.

He had just stepped into the door frame of the apartment to make room for paramedics when Korchinski-Paquet ran out to the balcony, he said. The fallen air conditioner partially blocked the balcony door, preventing it from opening fully, and Korchinski-Paquet had to squeeze through the opening, he added.

Within seconds, she had stepped over the railing, and Vandenbrink said he could see her hands gripping it like someone hanging from a bar at the gym as she appeared to shimmy toward the balcony next door.

He believed Korchinski-Paquet was making her way to the other balcony, and another officer told them to leave the apartment to avoid agitating her further, he said.

Eventually, as officers knocked on the neighbour’s door, Vandenbrink and Const. Glenn Weddell went back into the apartment to try to see Korchinski-Paquet, he said. Weddell slowly inched toward the balcony, eventually poking his head out the door, but still couldn’t spot her, he said.

“I remember him just taking like half a step out onto the balcony, just enough to look over the edge and he says, ‘She fell,’” Vandenbrink said.

“And then it didn’t even register to me at that time ... I probably went right into a state of shock, didn’t really realize what was happening.”

Rushing to get outside, he shared the news with those in the hall and heard Korchinski-Paquet’s mother “start to wail,” he said.

By the time he got outside, paramedics had covered Korchinski-Paquet’s body with a blanket, he said.

Vandenbrink and Beaudoin both testified that they never set foot on the balcony, nor did they know at the time about postictal delirium, an altered mental state that can follow seizures.

Answering questions from the presiding coroner, Vandenbrink said he did not perceive Korchinski-Paquet as a person in crisis at the time, but may have classified her as such if he’d known seizures could lead to delirium.

An agreed narrative read at the inquest last week said Korchinski-Paquet had a history of seizures from epilepsy and often experienced confusion, “physically and verbally abusive behaviour,” and temporary amnesia afterward.

A neurologist who did not treat her but examined her records testified that Korchinski-Paquet on several occasions showed symptoms in keeping with postictal delirium or postictal psychosis.

Dr. Julien Hébert told the inquest that it would be “nearly impossible” to tell whether someone was acting aggressively due to delirium or psychosis after an epilepsy seizure or for some other reason without knowing their medical history.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.

stories.title: How community organizations are trying to fight voter apathy in this Toronto election
stories.summary: Toronto - Music blasted through speakers as people chatted enthusiastically outside a Toronto venue, moving between tents, a hotdog cart and an ice cream truck on a sunny October day.
stories.author: Sharif Hassan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Music blasted through speakers as people chatted enthusiastically outside a Toronto venue, moving between tents, a hotdog cart and an ice cream truck on a sunny October day.

What looked like an outdoor festival at Lawrence Heights Community Centre was a fair held to raise civic engagement and encourage the city’s residents to vote in the Oct. 26 municipal election.

The non-partisan event, organized by North York Harvest Food Bank, was attended by several groups including Voice the Vote, a joint initiative by Toronto Metropolitan University’s Democratic Engagement Exchange and United Way Greater Toronto.

Community members attended a fair held at Lawrence Heights Community Cetnre to raise awareness and boost turnout ahead of the upcoming municipal election. Organizers said around 20 event participants cast their ballots at a nearby advanced polling site on Oct. 9. (Oct 19, 2026)

Jonathan Dong stood behind a table, a mock ballot box and papers laid out in front him, talking to people and handing them Voice the Vote election handbooks.

“I think that participating in our democratic process, especially considering … how many people around the world aren’t able to cast a vote, is incredibly important,” Dong said in an interview.

“Showing up is how people know that you’re important, and if you don’t show up, you don’t get a say in what happens in the country, in your city, in your own backyard.”

In previous municipal elections, the city has seen what observers described as a worrying downward trend in voter participation.

In the 2023 mayoral byelection won by Olivia Chow, 37 per cent of eligible voters participated. Turnout was less than 30 per cent in the 2022 municipal election and about 41 per cent in 2018.

Across the province, overall voter turnout was nearly 33 per cent in the 2022 municipal elections and roughly 38 per cent in 2018, according to Association of Municipalities of Ontario data.

The turnout at Toronto’s advance polls in the upcoming election was robust, however, with more than 222,000 people casting their ballots early – the highest number in more than a decade.

Dong said he wants to do his part to battle voter apathy.

As a Chinese Canadian who lives in Richmond Hill north of Toronto, he said many voters in his community are particularly disconnected from the electoral process and as a result they don’t have enough representation in government.

“I think it’s very important to have the conversations within these communities to increase that representation and increase our voter turnout,” he said.

At the voter information event, two white posters glued on a wall were decorated with colourful sticky notes on which members of the community wrote why voting matters to them.

“Support for unhoused neighbours,” “a clean city,” and “mental health safety” were among the dozens of notes.

Meanwhile, two taxis were seen ferrying voters to advance polling sites and then bringing them back to the community centre.

Warren Epstein was among those who voted early. He stood by Rania Ahmed, the project lead at Democratic Engagement Exchange, and asked her to write a few messages for him on a poster that focused on affordability and more support for seniors like himself.

“You need people who are going to do things for the people and the senior citizens, and you want to make sure that the right people are voted in for the right activities,” Epstein said.

“And it is time for change.”

Ahmed said Voice the Vote’s 15-member team is trying to help people “feel more hopeful about their future” by leveraging their own communities.

“A lot of people actually don’t know … that the issue they care about is actually tied to their municipal government and not the provincial (or) federal,” she said.

Ahmed said the initiative also provides micro-grants for organizations and individuals who come up with project or event ideas for elections and civic engagement in Toronto, York and Peel regions.

The funding for the initiative comes from United Way. The charity’s senior public affairs officer, Abby Tait, said while the organization has taken part in similar efforts in previous elections, Voice the Vote is a more thought out project aimed at increasing turnout across the city, including among immigrant communities and younger people.

Tait said the idea was born in the summer of 2025, after back-to-back provincial and federal elections.

“So we kind of seized this long runway and said, ‘let’s build something really ambitious,’” she said.

“We developed this kind of community-led project that would really be focused on grounding the municipal election in the local issues that matter to people.”

She said Voice the Vote is using the United Way’s vast network of around 300 agencies to reach communities.

“You can’t have a healthy community if people feel like they have no agency in their community, that they’re not connected to it,” she said.

Roughly 200 people attended the event in Lawrence Heights earlier this month, and around 20 of them were taken to an advance polling site to cast their ballots, said Sarah Watson, the director of community engagement at North York Harvest Food Bank.

Watson said while the food bank can provide emergency support for people in need, it can’t change systemic issues such as lack of affordable housing, food insecurity or unsafe communities.

“We’re really trying to connect them with the electoral process so they can have some influence over who is in government and who is making changes on these issues,” she said.

“A lot of our community members feel like their voices aren’t heard … and when that happens again and again, it can be frustrating and it can cause people to disengage,” Watson added. “We really want to encourage people that it is worth participating, that their voices should be heard.”

Event participant Esther Johnson agreed, saying she will head to the polls on election day because she believes every vote counts.

For people who choose not to vote in this election, “it’s their loss,” she said. “If they’re not interested in… having the input, don’t complain.”

More than 50 candidates are vying to become the mayor of Canada’s largest city, but polls suggest incumbent Olivia Chow and councillor Brad Bradford are locked in a fierce competition one week before election day.

Lydia Miljan, a political-science professor at the University of Windsor, said there are reasons to believe more people will participate in Toronto’s electoral process this time around, given the tight race between the two leading mayoral candidates.

“It just depends on how closely people are following Toronto politics right now, and I think it’s getting in my feeds even down here,” she said. “So, it is heating up quite significantly.”

Miljan said voter turnout is generally lower in municipal elections because it can be overwhelming to take part in a process that elects the mayor, councillors and school board trustees all at once.

She said the lack of political parties giving people a “shortcut” on where local election candidates stand, and the movement of voters between wards in large cities can further suppress turnout.

But in order to have a healthy democracy, residents need to show up, she said.

“It is incumbent upon citizens, regardless of how long they’ve lived in that city, to really make an effort to cast their ballot.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 19, 2026.
